chapters.title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: My father's family name was Pirrip, and my first name was Philip. As a small child, the best I could manage with either name was Pip. So I called myself Pip, and that's what everyone called me.

I give Pirrip as my father's family name based on the evidence of his tombstone and my sister — Mrs. Joe Gargery, who married the blacksmith. I never saw my father or my mother, and never saw a picture of either of them. Their days came long before the age of photographs. So my earliest ideas about what they looked like came, unreasonably, from their tombstones. The shape of the letters on my father's gave me the odd notion that he was a square, stocky, dark man with curly black hair. From the style and wording of the inscription, "Also Georgiana Wife of the Above," I drew the childish conclusion that my mother was freckled and sickly. As for the five little stone markers, each about a foot and a half long, arranged in a neat row beside their grave and dedicated to the memory of five little brothers of mine — who gave up trying to make a living remarkably early in that universal struggle — I owe to them my firm belief that they had all been born lying on their backs with their hands in their pockets, and had never taken them out in this life.

Ours was the marsh country, down by the river, about twenty miles from the sea as the river wound. My first vivid impression of the world around me seems to have come on a memorable raw afternoon as evening approached. That was when I understood for certain that this bleak, nettle-covered place was the churchyard. That Philip Pirrip, late of this parish, and also Georgiana wife of the above, were dead and buried. That Alexander, Bartholomew, Abraham, Tobias, and Roger, infant children of the aforesaid, were also dead and buried. That the dark, flat wilderness beyond the churchyard, cut through with ditches and mounds and gates, with scattered cattle grazing on it, was the marshes. That the low gray line beyond was the river. That the distant, savage place from which the wind came rushing was the sea. And that the small, shivering bundle growing afraid of it all and beginning to cry was Pip.
"Hold your noise!" cried a terrible voice, as a man sprang up from among the graves beside the church porch. "Keep still, you little devil, or I'll cut your throat!"

A terrifying man, dressed all in coarse gray, with a great iron shackle on his leg. A man with no hat, with broken shoes, and with an old rag tied around his head. A man who had been soaked in water, covered in mud, cut by stones and flints, stung by nettles, and torn by thorns. He limped, shivered, glared, and growled. His teeth chattered in his head as he seized me by the chin.
"Oh! Don't cut my throat, sir," I pleaded in terror. "Please don't do it, sir."
"Tell us your name!" said the man. "Quick!"
"Pip, sir."
"Once more," said the man, staring at me. "Say it louder!"
"Pip. Pip, sir."
"Show us where you live," said the man. "Point out the place!"
I pointed to where our village lay, on the flat land among the alder trees, a mile or more from the church.

The man looked at me for a moment, then turned me upside down and emptied my pockets. There was nothing in them but a piece of bread. When the church came back to its normal position — for he was so sudden and strong that the whole world flipped before my eyes, and I saw the steeple under my feet — when the church righted itself, I say, I was sitting on a high tombstone, trembling, while he ate the bread ravenously.
"You young dog," said the man, licking his lips, "what fat cheeks you've got."
I believe they were fat, though at that time I was small for my age, and not strong.
"Damn me if I couldn't eat them," said the man, with a threatening shake of his head, "and I'm half a mind to do it!"
I desperately hoped he wouldn't, and held tighter to the tombstone he had put me on — partly to keep myself from falling off, partly to keep myself from crying.
"Now look here!" said the man. "Where's your mother?"
"There, sir!" said I.
He jumped, ran a few steps, then stopped and looked over his shoulder.
"There, sir!" I explained timidly. "Also Georgiana. That's my mother."
"Oh!" said he, coming back. "And is that your father next to your mother?"
"Yes, sir," said I. "Him too. Late of this parish."
"Ha!" he muttered, thinking it over. "Who do you live with — assuming you're allowed to live, which I haven't decided yet?"
"My sister, sir — Mrs. Joe Gargery — wife of Joe Gargery, the blacksmith, sir."
"Blacksmith, eh?" said he. And looked down at his leg.

After looking darkly at his leg and at me several times, he came closer to my tombstone. He took me by both arms and tilted me back as far as he could hold me, so that his eyes looked powerfully down into mine and mine looked helplessly up into his.
"Now look here," he said, "the question is whether you get to live. You know what a file is?"
"Yes, sir."
"And you know what food is?"
"Yes, sir."
After each question he tilted me over a little more, giving me a greater sense of helplessness and danger.
"You get me a file." He tilted me again. "And you get me food." He tilted me again. "You bring them both to me." He tilted me again. "Or I'll have your heart and liver out." He tilted me again.
I was terribly frightened and so dizzy that I clung to him with both hands and said, "If you would please let me stay upright, sir, maybe I wouldn't be sick, and maybe I could pay better attention."

He gave me one tremendous dip and roll, so that the church seemed to jump over its own weathercock. Then he held me by the arms in an upright position on top of the stone, and went on in these terrifying terms:

"You bring me, tomorrow morning early, that file and some food. You bring the lot to me, at that old Battery over there. You do it, and you never dare to say a word or make a sign about having seen me, or any person ever, and you'll be allowed to live. You fail, or you break my instructions in any way, no matter how small, and your heart and your liver will be torn out, roasted, and eaten. Now, I'm not alone, as you might think I am. There's a young man hiding with me, and compared to that young man, I am an angel. That young man hears the words I speak. That young man has his own special way of getting at a boy, and at his heart, and at his liver. It's useless for a boy to try to hide from that young man. A boy may lock his door, may be warm in bed, may tuck himself up, may pull the covers over his head, may think himself comfortable and safe, but that young man will softly creep his way to him and tear him open. I am keeping that young man from harming you at this very moment, with great difficulty. I find it very hard to hold that young man back from your insides. Now, what do you say?"
I said that I would get him the file, and I would get him whatever scraps of food I could, and I would come to him at the Battery early in the morning.
"Say 'Lord strike me dead if I don't!'" said the man.
I said so, and he put me down.
"Now," he went on, "you remember what you've promised, and you remember that young man, and you get home!"
"G-good night, sir," I stammered.
"Good night!" said he, glancing around at the cold, wet flatland. "I wish I were a frog. Or an eel!"

At the same time, he hugged his shuddering body in both arms — clasping himself as if to hold himself together — and limped toward the low church wall. As I watched him go, picking his way among the nettles and the brambles that covered the green mounds, he looked to my young eyes as if he were dodging the hands of dead people, stretching up cautiously from their graves to grab his ankle and pull him in.

When he reached the low church wall, he climbed over it like a man whose legs were numb and stiff, then turned around to look for me. When I saw him turning, I faced toward home and ran as fast as I could. But soon I looked over my shoulder and saw him heading toward the river again, still hugging himself with both arms, picking his way with sore feet among the great stones scattered across the marshes for stepping-places when the rains were heavy or the tide was in.

The marshes were just a long black horizontal line as I stopped to look after him. The river was another horizontal line, not as wide or as dark. The sky was a row of long, angry red streaks mixed with dense black ones. At the edge of the river I could just make out the only two dark shapes in the whole landscape that seemed to be standing upright. One was the beacon that guided the sailors — like a barrel without hoops on a pole — an ugly thing up close. The other was a gibbet, with chains hanging from it that had once held a pirate. The man was limping toward this last one, as if he were the pirate come back to life, climbing down and going back to hang himself up again. The thought gave me a terrible fright. As I watched the cattle raise their heads to stare after him, I wondered if they were thinking the same thing. I looked all around for the horrible young man but could see no sign of him. Still, I was frightened again, and ran home without stopping.

chapters.title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: My sister, Mrs. Joe Gargery, was more than twenty years older than me. She had built up quite a reputation with herself and the neighbors for having brought me up "by hand." Since I had to figure out what that expression meant on my own, and since I knew she had a hard and heavy hand that she regularly laid on her husband as well as on me, I assumed that Joe Gargery and I were both brought up by hand.

She was not a good-looking woman, my sister. I had a general impression that she must have made Joe Gargery marry her by hand, too. Joe was a fair man, with curls of pale hair on each side of his smooth face, and eyes of such an uncertain blue that they seemed to have somehow gotten mixed up with their own whites. He was a mild, good-natured, sweet-tempered, easygoing, foolish, dear fellow — a sort of Hercules in strength, and also in weakness.

My sister, Mrs. Joe, with her black hair and eyes, had such a constant redness of skin that I sometimes wondered whether she washed herself with a nutmeg grater instead of soap. She was tall and bony, and almost always wore a coarse apron, fastened behind with two loops, with a square, impenetrable bib in front that was stuck full of pins and needles. She considered it a great virtue in herself, and a strong reproach against Joe, that she wore this apron so much. Though I really see no reason why she should have worn it at all — or why, if she did wear it, she shouldn't have taken it off every day of her life.

Joe's forge was attached to our house, which was a wooden house, like many of the homes in our area at that time. When I ran home from the churchyard, the forge was shut up and Joe was sitting alone in the kitchen. Joe and I, being fellow sufferers who shared confidences, he told me something the moment I lifted the latch and peeked in at him sitting in the chimney corner.
"Mrs. Joe has been out a dozen times looking for you, Pip. And she's out now, making it a baker's dozen."
"Is she?"
"Yes, Pip," said Joe. "And what's worse, she's got Tickler with her."

At this grim news, I twisted the only button on my waistcoat round and round and stared at the fire in deep gloom. Tickler was a wax-tipped piece of cane, worn smooth from regular contact with my body.

"She sat down," said Joe, "and she got up, and she grabbed Tickler, and she rampaged out. That's what she did," said Joe, slowly clearing the fire between the lower bars with the poker and staring at it. "She rampaged out, Pip."
"Has she been gone long, Joe?" I always treated him as a larger species of child, and as no more than my equal.

"Well," said Joe, glancing up at the Dutch clock, "she's been on the rampage this last stretch for about five minutes, Pip. She's coming! Get behind the door, old chap, and put the towel between you."

I took his advice. My sister, Mrs. Joe, throwing the door wide open and finding something behind it, immediately guessed the cause and applied Tickler to investigate further. She finished by throwing me — I often served as a weapon in their marriage — at Joe, who, glad to get hold of me on any terms, passed me into the chimney corner and quietly fenced me in there with his great leg.

"Where have you been, you young monkey?" said Mrs. Joe, stamping her foot. "Tell me right now what you've been doing to wear me out with worry, or I'll have you out of that corner if you were fifty Pips and he was five hundred Gargerys."
"I've only been to the churchyard," said I, from my stool, crying and rubbing myself.
"Churchyard!" repeated my sister. "If it weren't for me, you'd have been to the churchyard long ago and stayed there. Who brought you up by hand?"
"You did," said I.
"And why did I do it, I'd like to know?" exclaimed my sister.
I whimpered, "I don't know."

"I don't either!" said my sister. "I'd never do it again! I know that. I can honestly say I've never had this apron off since you were born. It's bad enough being a blacksmith's wife — and him a Gargery — without being your mother."

My thoughts drifted from that question as I stared miserably at the fire. The fugitive out on the marshes with the iron on his leg, the mysterious young man, the file, the food, and the dreadful promise I was under to commit a theft from this very house — all of it rose before me in the glowing coals.

"Ha!" said Mrs. Joe, putting Tickler back in its place. "Churchyard, indeed! You may well say churchyard, you two." One of us, by the way, had not said it at all. "You'll drive me to the churchyard between you, one of these days, and oh, what a precious pair you'd be without me!"

As she set about laying the tea things, Joe peeked down at me over his leg, as if he were mentally adding us up and calculating what kind of pair we would actually make under those grim circumstances. After that, he sat feeling his right-side curls and whiskers, following Mrs. Joe around with his blue eyes, as he always did during stormy times.

My sister had a decisive way of cutting our bread and butter that never varied. First, with her left hand she jammed the loaf hard against her bib — where it sometimes picked up a pin, and sometimes a needle, which we later got into our mouths. Then she took some butter (not too much) on a knife and spread it on the loaf like a pharmacist making a plaster — using both sides of the knife with a slapping skill, trimming and shaping the butter around the crust. Then she gave the knife a final smart wipe on the edge of the plaster, and sawed a very thick round off the loaf. This she finally, before separating it from the loaf, chopped into two halves — one for Joe and one for me.

On this occasion, though I was hungry, I didn't dare eat my slice. I felt I had to keep something in reserve for my terrifying acquaintance and his even more terrifying companion, the young man. I knew Mrs. Joe's housekeeping was extremely strict, and that my thieving search might find nothing available in the pantry. So I decided to stuff my bread and butter down the leg of my trousers.

The willpower needed to actually do this was enormous. It felt like making up my mind to leap from the top of a tall building, or plunge into deep water. And it was made harder by innocent Joe. In our already-mentioned brotherhood as fellow sufferers, and in his good-natured companionship, it was our evening habit to compare how we bit through our slices by silently holding them up for each other's admiration. This spurred us on to new efforts. Tonight, Joe kept inviting me, by displaying his rapidly shrinking slice, to join our usual friendly competition. But each time he found me with my yellow mug of tea on one knee and my untouched bread and butter on the other. At last, I desperately decided that what I was planning had to be done, and had best be done in the least suspicious way possible. I took advantage of a moment when Joe had just looked at me, and got my bread and butter down my trouser leg.

Joe was clearly made uncomfortable by what he assumed was my loss of appetite. He took a thoughtful bite of his slice, which he didn't seem to enjoy. He turned it around in his mouth much longer than usual, pondering over it, and finally gulped it down like a pill. He was about to take another bite, and had just tilted his head to get a good grip on it, when his eye fell on me and he saw that my bread and butter was gone.
The wonder and alarm with which Joe froze mid-bite and stared at me were too obvious to escape my sister's notice.
"What's the matter now?" she said sharply, putting down her cup.
"I say, you know!" muttered Joe, shaking his head at me in serious disapproval. "Pip, old chap! You'll hurt yourself. It'll get stuck somewhere. You can't have chewed it, Pip."
"What's the matter now?" repeated my sister, more sharply than before.
"If you can cough any bit of it back up, Pip, I'd recommend you do it," said Joe, completely horrified. "Manners are manners, but your health is your health."

By this time my sister was quite desperate. She pounced on Joe and, grabbing him by both whiskers, knocked his head against the wall behind him for a while, as I sat in the corner looking on guiltily.
"Now, perhaps you'll tell me what's the matter," said my sister, out of breath, "you staring great stuck pig."
Joe looked at her helplessly, then took a helpless bite, and looked at me again.

"You know, Pip," said Joe solemnly, with his last bite in his cheek, speaking in a confidential voice as if we two were quite alone, "you and me are always friends, and I'd be the last to tell on you, any time. But such a —" he moved his chair and looked around the floor between us, then back at me — "such a tremendously fast bolt as that!"
"Been bolting his food, has he?" cried my sister.

"You know, old chap," said Joe, looking at me and not at Mrs. Joe, with his bite still in his cheek, "I bolted my food myself when I was your age — often — and as a boy I was among plenty of bolters. But I never saw your equal for bolting, Pip, and it's a wonder you haven't bolted yourself dead."
My sister made a dive at me and fished me up by the hair, saying nothing more than the awful words, "You come along and be dosed."

Some medical quack had brought back tar-water in those days as a miracle cure, and Mrs. Joe always kept a supply in the cupboard. She believed in its powers in direct proportion to its nastiness. Even at the best of times, so much of this stuff was given to me as a health tonic that I walked around smelling like a new fence. On this particular evening, the urgency of my case called for a full pint of the mixture, which was poured down my throat while Mrs. Joe held my head under her arm, like a boot held in a boot-jack. Joe got off with half a pint, but was made to swallow that — much to his distress, as he sat slowly chewing and thinking by the fire — "because he'd had a fright." Judging from my own experience, I'd say he certainly had a fright afterward, if he hadn't had one before.

Conscience is a terrible thing when it accuses man or boy. But when, in the case of a boy, that secret burden works together with another secret burden down the leg of his trousers, it is — as I can confirm — a great punishment. The guilty knowledge that I was going to rob Mrs. Joe (I never thought I was going to rob Joe, since I never thought of the household property as his) combined with the need to always keep one hand on my bread and butter as I sat, or when I was sent on errands around the kitchen, nearly drove me out of my mind. Then, as the marsh winds made the fire glow and flare, I thought I heard the voice outside of the man with the iron on his leg who had sworn me to secrecy, declaring that he couldn't and wouldn't starve until tomorrow but must be fed now. At other times I thought: What if the young man, who was being restrained from attacking me with such difficulty, should lose patience? What if he should mistake the time and decide he was entitled to my heart and liver tonight instead of tomorrow? If ever anybody's hair stood on end with terror, mine must have done so then. But perhaps nobody's ever did?

It was Christmas Eve, and I had to stir the pudding for the next day with a copper stick, from seven to eight by the Dutch clock. I tried it with the lump on my leg (which made me think again of the man with the lump on his), and found that the exercise was impossible — the bread and butter kept working its way down toward my ankle. Luckily, I managed to slip away and hide that part of my guilty conscience in my attic bedroom.
"Listen!" said I, when I had finished my stirring and was taking a final warm-up in the chimney corner before being sent to bed. "Was that cannon fire, Joe?"
"Ah!" said Joe. "There's another convict escaped."
"What does that mean, Joe?" said I.
Mrs. Joe, who always took it upon herself to explain everything, said snappishly, "Escaped. Escaped." Delivering the definition like a dose of tar-water.

While Mrs. Joe sat with her head bent over her needlework, I mouthed to Joe, "What's a convict?" Joe mouthed back such an elaborately careful answer that I could make out nothing but the single word "Pip."
"There was a convict escaped last night," said Joe, aloud, "after the sunset gun. And they fired a warning about him. And now it seems they're firing a warning about another one."
"Who's firing?" said I.
"Curse that boy," my sister cut in, frowning at me over her work. "What a questioner he is. Ask no questions, and you'll be told no lies."
It wasn't very polite to herself, I thought, to imply that she would tell me lies even if I did ask questions. But she was never polite unless there was company.

At this point Joe greatly increased my curiosity by taking great pains to open his mouth very wide and shape it into a word that looked to me like "Hulks." So I naturally pointed at Mrs. Joe and mouthed, "Her?" But Joe wouldn't hear of that at all. He opened his mouth very wide again and shook out the shape of a most emphatic word. But I couldn't make it out.
"Mrs. Joe," said I, as a last resort, "I should like to know — if you wouldn't mind — where the firing comes from?"
"Lord bless the boy!" exclaimed my sister, as if she didn't quite mean that but rather the opposite. "From the Hulks!"
"Oh!" said I, looking at Joe. "Hulks!"
Joe gave a reproachful cough, as much as to say, "Well, I told you so."
"And please, what are Hulks?" said I.

"That's the way with this boy!" exclaimed my sister, pointing at me with her needle and thread and shaking her head. "Answer him one question and he'll ask you a dozen right after. Hulks are prison ships, right across the marshes." We always used "meshes" for marshes in our part of the country.
"I wonder who gets put in prison ships, and why they're put there?" said I, in a general way, with quiet desperation.

That was too much for Mrs. Joe, who immediately stood up. "I'll tell you what, young fellow," she said. "I didn't bring you up by hand just to have you badger the life out of people. It would be a disgrace to me, not a credit, if I had. People are put in the Hulks because they murder, and because they rob, and forge, and do all sorts of bad things. And they always begin by asking questions. Now, you get along to bed!"

I was never allowed a candle to light my way to bed. As I went upstairs in the dark, with my head stinging — from Mrs. Joe's thimble tapping on it like a tambourine to accompany her last words — I felt terribly aware that the Hulks were conveniently close by for someone like me. I was clearly on my way there. I had begun by asking questions, and I was going to rob Mrs. Joe.

Since that time, which is far enough away now, I have often thought how few people know what secrecy there is in the young when they are terrified. No matter how unreasonable the terror, as long as it is terror. I was in mortal terror of the young man who wanted my heart and liver. I was in mortal terror of my questioner with the iron leg. I was in mortal terror of myself, from whom an awful promise had been extracted. I had no hope of rescue through my all-powerful sister, who pushed me away at every turn. I am afraid to think of what I might have done, in the secrecy of my terror, if I had been asked.

If I slept at all that night, it was only to dream of drifting down the river on a strong spring tide toward the Hulks. A ghostly pirate called out to me through a speaking trumpet as I passed the gibbet, telling me I'd better come ashore and be hanged right away instead of putting it off. I was afraid to sleep, even if I'd been inclined to, because I knew that at the first gray light of dawn I had to rob the pantry. There was no doing it at night, since there was no easy way to get a light. To get one, I would have had to strike flint and steel, making a noise like the pirate himself rattling his chains.

As soon as the great black curtain outside my little window was streaked with gray, I got up and went downstairs. Every board on the way, and every crack in every board, called after me: "Stop thief!" and "Get up, Mrs. Joe!" In the pantry, which was far more generously stocked than usual because of the season, I was badly frightened by a hare hanging up by its heels. I rather thought I caught it winking at me when my back was half turned. I had no time to check, no time to choose, no time for anything — I had no time to spare. I stole some bread, some rind of cheese, about half a jar of mincemeat (which I tied up in my handkerchief with my bread from the night before), some brandy from a stone bottle (which I poured into a glass bottle I had secretly been using to make Spanish-liquorice-water up in my room — topping up the stone bottle from a jug in the kitchen cupboard), a meat bone with very little on it, and a beautiful round pork pie. I nearly left without the pie, but I was tempted to climb up on a shelf to see what was carefully put away in a covered earthenware dish in a corner. I found it was the pie, and I took it, hoping it wasn't meant for use anytime soon and wouldn't be missed for a while.

There was a door in the kitchen that connected to the forge. I unlocked and unbolted it and got a file from among Joe's tools. Then I put the fastenings back as I had found them, opened the door I had come in through when I ran home the night before, shut it, and ran for the misty marshes.

chapters.title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: It was a frosty morning, and very damp. I had seen the moisture on the outside of my little window, as if some goblin had been crying there all night and using the glass as a handkerchief. Now I saw the dampness lying on the bare hedges and thin grass like a coarser kind of spiderweb, hanging from twig to twig and blade to blade. Every rail and gate was wet and clammy, and the marsh mist was so thick that the wooden signpost pointing people toward our village — a direction they never took, since they never came there — was invisible to me until I was right under it. Then, as I looked up at it while it dripped, it seemed to my guilty conscience like a phantom sentencing me to the Hulks.

The mist was even heavier when I got out on the marshes, so that instead of me running at things, everything seemed to rush at me. This was very unpleasant for a guilty mind. The gates and ditches and banks came bursting through the mist as if they cried out plainly, "A boy with somebody else's pork pie! Stop him!" The cattle appeared suddenly, staring with wide eyes and steaming from their nostrils, "Hey there, young thief!" One black ox with a white patch on its neck — which, to my awakened conscience, gave it something of a clerical look — fixed me so stubbornly with its eyes and turned its blunt head to follow me in such an accusing way that I blurted out, "I couldn't help it, sir! It wasn't for myself I took it!" At which he put down his head, blew a cloud of breath from his nose, and vanished with a kick of his back legs and a flourish of his tail.

All this time I was making my way toward the river. But no matter how fast I went, I couldn't warm my feet. The damp cold seemed fastened to them, just as the iron was fastened to the leg of the man I was running to meet. I knew my way to the Battery fairly well, having been down there on a Sunday with Joe. Joe had sat on an old cannon and told me that when I was apprenticed to him, properly bound, we would have such good times there! However, in the confusion of the mist, I ended up too far to the right and had to work my way back along the riverbank, over the loose stones above the mud and the stakes that marked the tide line. Hurrying along, I had just crossed a ditch I knew was very near the Battery and had just scrambled up the mound beyond it, when I saw the man sitting in front of me. His back was toward me, his arms were folded, and he was nodding forward, heavy with sleep.

I thought he would be more pleased if I came upon him with his breakfast unexpectedly, so I went forward softly and touched him on the shoulder. He instantly jumped up, and it was not the same man but another man!

And yet this man was dressed in coarse gray too, and had a great iron on his leg, and was lame, and hoarse, and cold, and was everything the other man was — except that he had a different face and wore a flat, broad-brimmed, low-crowned felt hat. All this I saw in a moment, for I had only a moment to see it. He swore at me, took a swing at me — it was a round, weak blow that missed and almost knocked himself down, making him stumble — and then he ran into the mist, stumbling twice as he went, and I lost him.
"It's the young man!" I thought, feeling my heart leap as I recognized him. I dare say I would have felt a pain in my liver too, if I had known where it was.

I was soon at the Battery after that, and there was the right man — hugging himself and limping back and forth, as if he had never stopped hugging and limping all night — waiting for me. He was terribly cold. I half expected to see him collapse and die of the cold right in front of me. His eyes looked so desperately hungry too, that when I handed him the file and he laid it down on the grass, it struck me he would have tried to eat it if he hadn't seen my bundle. He didn't turn me upside down this time to get at what I had, but left me right side up while I opened the bundle and emptied my pockets.
"What's in the bottle, boy?" said he.
"Brandy," said I.

He was already shoving mincemeat down his throat in the strangest way — more like a man frantically storing it away somewhere than a man eating it — but he stopped to take some of the liquor. He shivered so violently the whole time that it was all he could do to keep the neck of the bottle between his teeth without biting it off.
"I think you've got the fever," said I.
"I'm very much of your opinion, boy," said he.
"It's bad around here," I told him. "You've been lying out on the marshes, and they're terribly fever-ridden. Rheumatic too."
"I'll eat my breakfast before they kill me," said he. "I'd do that even if I was going to be strung up on that gallows over there right afterward. I'll beat the shivers that far, I'll bet you."

He was gobbling mincemeat, meat bone, bread, cheese, and pork pie all at once, staring distrustfully at the mist all around us and often stopping — even stopping his jaws — to listen. Some real or imagined sound, some clink on the river or breathing of an animal on the marsh, startled him, and he said suddenly:
"You're not a lying little imp? You brought no one with you?"
"No, sir! No!"
"And you didn't signal anyone to follow you?"
"No!"
"Well," said he, "I believe you. You'd be a fierce young hound indeed if at your age you could help hunt a wretched creature hunted as close to death as this poor wretched creature is!"
Something clicked in his throat as if he had clockwork inside him and was about to strike the hour. And he wiped his ragged rough sleeve across his eyes.
Pitying his misery, and watching as he gradually worked his way through the pie, I ventured to say, "I'm glad you enjoy it."
"Did you speak?"
"I said I was glad you enjoyed it."
"Thank you, my boy. I do."

I had often watched our large dog eating his food, and I now noticed a clear similarity between the dog's way of eating and the man's. The man took strong, sharp, sudden bites, just like the dog. He swallowed — or rather snapped up — every mouthful too soon and too fast. And he looked sideways here and there while he ate, as if he thought someone might come from any direction to take the pie away. He was altogether too unsettled to enjoy it properly, I thought, or to have anyone dining with him without snapping his jaws at the visitor. In all these ways he was very like the dog.

"I'm afraid you won't leave any of it for him," said I timidly, after a silence during which I had hesitated about the politeness of making the remark. "There's no more where that came from." It was the certainty of this fact that made me say it.
"Leave any for him? Who's him?" said my friend, stopping his crunching of pie crust.
"The young man. The one you spoke of. The one who was hiding with you."
"Oh yes!" he returned, with something like a gruff laugh. "Him? Yes, yes! He doesn't need any food."
"I thought he looked as if he did," said I.
The man stopped eating and studied me with the sharpest scrutiny and the greatest surprise.
"Looked? When?"
"Just now."
"Where?"
"Over there," said I, pointing. "Where I found him nodding asleep and thought it was you."
He held me by the collar and stared at me so hard that I began to think his first idea about cutting my throat had come back.

"Dressed like you, you know, only with a hat," I explained, trembling. "And — and" — I was very anxious to put this delicately — "and with the same reason for wanting to borrow a file. Didn't you hear the cannon last night?"
"Then there was firing!" he said to himself.
"I'm surprised you weren't sure of that," I replied, "since we heard it up at home, and that's farther away, and we were indoors besides."

"Why, see now!" said he. "When a man's alone on these flats, with a light head and an empty stomach, freezing and starving, he hears nothing all night but guns firing and voices calling. Hears? He sees the soldiers, with their red coats lit up by the torches they carry, closing in around him. Hears his number called, hears himself challenged, hears the rattle of the muskets, hears the orders: 'Make ready! Present! Cover him steady, men!' and is grabbed — and there's nothing! Why, if I saw one search party last night coming up in order — damn them, with their tramp, tramp — I saw a hundred. And as for firing! Why, I saw the mist shake with the cannon after it was broad daylight. But this man" — he had said all the rest as if he'd forgotten I was there — "did you notice anything about him?"
"He had a badly bruised face," said I, remembering what I hardly knew I knew.
"Not here?" exclaimed the man, striking his left cheek hard with the flat of his hand.
"Yes, there!"

"Where is he?" He crammed what little food was left into the front of his gray jacket. "Show me the way he went. I'll track him down like a bloodhound. Curse this iron on my sore leg! Give me that file, boy."

I pointed in the direction where the mist had swallowed the other man, and he looked up at it for an instant. But then he was down on the rank wet grass, filing at his iron like a madman, paying no attention to me or to his own leg. The leg had an old raw sore on it and was bloody, but he handled it as roughly as if it had no more feeling than the file. I was very afraid of him again now that he had worked himself into this fierce frenzy, and I was also very afraid of staying away from home any longer. I told him I had to go, but he took no notice, so I thought the best thing I could do was to slip away. The last I saw of him, his head was bent over his knee and he was working hard at his shackle, muttering angry curses at it and at his leg. The last I heard of him, I stopped in the mist to listen, and the file was still going.

chapters.title: Chapter 4
paragraphs: I fully expected to find a constable in the kitchen, waiting to arrest me. But not only was there no constable, no one had even discovered the robbery yet. Mrs. Joe was enormously busy getting the house ready for the day's celebrations, and Joe had been put on the kitchen doorstep to keep him out of the way of the dustpan — an object he inevitably wandered into, sooner or later, whenever my sister was vigorously sweeping the floors.
"And where the devil have you been?" was Mrs. Joe's Christmas greeting, when my conscience and I showed ourselves.
I said I had been down to hear the carols. "Ah! Well!" observed Mrs. Joe. "You might have done worse." No doubt about that, I thought.

"Perhaps if I weren't a blacksmith's wife, and — what's the same thing — a slave with her apron never off, I should have gone to hear the carols," said Mrs. Joe. "I'm rather fond of carols, myself, and that's the best reason for my never hearing any."

Joe, who had ventured into the kitchen after me as the dustpan retreated before us, drew the back of his hand across his nose with a peacekeeping air when Mrs. Joe shot him a look. When her eyes were turned away, he secretly crossed his two forefingers and showed them to me — our sign that Mrs. Joe was in a bad temper. This was so much her normal state that Joe and I would often go for weeks with our fingers crossed, like stone Crusaders with their legs.

We were to have a magnificent dinner: a leg of pickled pork with greens, and a pair of roast stuffed chickens. A beautiful mince pie had been made yesterday morning (which explained why the mincemeat hadn't been missed), and the pudding was already boiling. These elaborate preparations meant we got a hasty breakfast. "For I'm not," said Mrs. Joe, "going to have any formal stuffing and bursting and washing up now, with what I've got ahead of me, I promise you!"

So we had our slices handed out as if we were two thousand troops on a forced march instead of a man and a boy at home. We took apologetic gulps of milk and water from a jug on the dresser. Meanwhile, Mrs. Joe put up clean white curtains and tacked a new flowered strip across the wide chimney to replace the old one. She uncovered the little formal parlor across the passage, which was never uncovered at any other time but spent the rest of the year in a cool haze of silver paper. This even extended to the four little white ceramic poodles on the mantelshelf, each with a black nose and a basket of flowers in its mouth, each identical to the other. Mrs. Joe was a very clean housekeeper, but she had an extraordinary talent for making her cleanliness more uncomfortable and unwelcoming than dirt itself. Cleanliness is next to Godliness, and some people do the same with their religion.

My sister, having so much to do, was going to church by proxy — meaning Joe and I were going. In his work clothes, Joe was a sturdy, distinctive-looking blacksmith. In his Sunday clothes, he looked more like a well-dressed scarecrow than anything else. Nothing he wore fit him or seemed to belong to him, and everything chafed him. On this festive occasion, he emerged from his room when the cheerful bells were ringing, the picture of misery, in his full suit of Sunday penance. As for me, I think my sister had some general idea that I was a young offender whom a police officer had picked up at birth and delivered to her to be dealt with according to the law. I was always treated as if I had insisted on being born against the advice of reason, religion, morality, and my best friends. Even when I was taken to get new clothes, the tailor had orders to make them like a kind of reform school uniform, and on no account to let me have the free use of my limbs.

Joe and I going to church, therefore, must have been a moving sight for anyone with sympathy. Yet what I suffered on the outside was nothing compared to what I endured within. The terrors that seized me whenever Mrs. Joe went near the pantry or left the room were matched only by the remorse I felt over what my hands had done. Under the weight of my guilty secret, I wondered whether the Church would be powerful enough to shield me from the terrible young man's vengeance if I confessed everything. I came up with the idea that the moment during the service when the banns were read and the clergyman said, "You are now to declare it!" would be the right time for me to stand up and request a private meeting in the vestry. I'm far from sure I might not have astonished our small congregation by actually doing this, if it hadn't been Christmas Day and not a Sunday.

Mr. Wopsle, the parish clerk, was to dine with us, along with Mr. Hubble the wheelwright and Mrs. Hubble, and Uncle Pumblechook — Joe's uncle, though Mrs. Joe had claimed him as her own — who was a prosperous corn merchant in the nearest town and drove his own carriage. Dinner was at half past one. When Joe and I got home, we found the table laid, Mrs. Joe dressed, the dinner cooking, and the front door unlocked (it never was at any other time) for the company to enter by. Everything was most splendid. And still, not a word about the robbery.

The time came, bringing no relief to my feelings, and the company arrived. Mr. Wopsle, blessed with a Roman nose and a large shining bald forehead, had a deep voice he was uncommonly proud of. It was understood among his acquaintances that if you gave him free rein, he would put the clergyman to shame. He himself admitted that if the Church were "thrown open" — meaning opened to competition — he would not despair of making his mark. Since the Church was not thrown open, he was, as I've said, our parish clerk. But he punished the Amens tremendously. When he announced the psalm — always giving the whole verse — he looked all around the congregation first, as much as to say, "You have heard my colleague up there; now let me have your opinion of this."

I opened the door to the company — pretending it was our habit to use that door — and I opened it first to Mr. Wopsle, then to Mr. and Mrs. Hubble, and last of all to Uncle Pumblechook. Note: I was not allowed to call him uncle, under the severest penalties.

"Mrs. Joe," said Uncle Pumblechook — a large, heavy-breathing, middle-aged, slow man with a mouth like a fish, dull staring eyes, and sandy hair standing straight up on his head, so that he looked as if he had just nearly choked to death and had only just recovered — "I have brought you, as the compliments of the season — I have brought you, ma'am, a bottle of sherry wine — and I have brought you, ma'am, a bottle of port wine."

Every Christmas Day he presented himself as a great novelty with exactly the same words, carrying the two bottles like dumbbells. Every Christmas Day, Mrs. Joe replied, as she now replied, "Oh, Uncle Pumblechook! This is kind!" Every Christmas Day, he answered, as he now answered, "It's no more than you deserve. And now, are you all well, and how's Sixpence-worth of Halfpence?" — meaning me.

We ate dinner on these occasions in the kitchen, then moved to the parlor for the nuts, oranges, and apples — a transition much like Joe's change from his work clothes to his Sunday dress. My sister was unusually lively today, and was generally more gracious in Mrs. Hubble's company than in other company. I remember Mrs. Hubble as a little curly, sharp-edged person in sky-blue, who held a youthful position by convention because she had married Mr. Hubble — at some distant point — when she was much younger than he. I remember Mr. Hubble as a tough, high-shouldered, stooping old man who smelled of sawdust, with his legs set extraordinarily far apart. In my short days, I always saw miles of open country between them when I met him coming up the lane.

Among this good company I would have felt out of place, even if I hadn't robbed the pantry. Not because I was squeezed in at a sharp angle of the tablecloth, with the table in my chest and Pumblechook's elbow in my eye. Not because I wasn't allowed to speak (I didn't want to speak). Not because I was served the scaly tips of the drumsticks and those obscure corners of pork that the pig, when alive, had had the least reason to be proud of. No — I wouldn't have minded any of that, if they would only have left me alone. But they wouldn't leave me alone. They seemed to think the opportunity was lost if they didn't aim the conversation at me every now and then and jab the point in. I might as well have been an unfortunate little bull in a Spanish arena, I was so painfully prodded by these moral goads.

It began the moment we sat down to dinner. Mr. Wopsle said grace with theatrical flair — something like a religious mixture of the Ghost in Hamlet with Richard the Third, as it now seems to me — and ended with the very proper wish that we might be truly grateful. At which my sister fixed me with her eye and said, in a low, reproachful voice, "Do you hear that? Be grateful."
"Especially," said Mr. Pumblechook, "be grateful, boy, to those who brought you up by hand."

Mrs. Hubble shook her head and, studying me with a mournful certainty that I would come to no good, asked, "Why is it that the young are never grateful?" This moral mystery seemed too much for the company until Mr. Hubble solved it bluntly by saying, "Naturally vicious." Everyone murmured "True!" and looked at me in a particularly unpleasant and personal way.

Joe's authority and influence were even weaker, if possible, when there was company than when there wasn't. But he always helped and comforted me when he could, in his own way, and he always did so at dinner by giving me gravy, if there was any. There being plenty of gravy today, Joe spooned about half a pint onto my plate at this point.

A little later in the dinner, Mr. Wopsle reviewed the sermon with some severity and suggested — in his usual hypothetical case of the Church being "thrown open" — what kind of sermon he would have given. After sharing some highlights of that imaginary sermon, he remarked that the subject of the day's talk had been poorly chosen. This was all the less excusable, he added, when there were so many subjects "going around."

"True again," said Uncle Pumblechook. "You've hit it, sir! Plenty of subjects going around, for those who know how to catch them. That's what's needed. A man needn't go far to find a subject, if he's got his wits about him." Mr. Pumblechook added, after a short pause for thought, "Look at Pork alone. There's a subject! If you want a subject, look at Pork!"
"True, sir. Many a moral for the young," returned Mr. Wopsle — and I knew he was going to drag me into it before he said it — "might be drawn from that text."
("You listen to this," said my sister to me, in a severe aside.)
Joe gave me some more gravy.

"Swine," continued Mr. Wopsle in his deepest voice, pointing his fork at my blushing face as if he were saying my name, "swine were the companions of the Prodigal Son. The gluttony of swine is set before us as an example to the young." (I thought this was rich, coming from someone who had just been praising the pork for being so plump and juicy.) "What is disgusting in a pig is more disgusting in a boy."
"Or girl," suggested Mr. Hubble.
"Of course, or girl, Mr. Hubble," agreed Mr. Wopsle, rather irritably, "but there is no girl present."
"Besides," said Mr. Pumblechook, turning sharply on me, "think what you've got to be grateful for. If you'd been born a piglet — "
"He was, if ever a child was," said my sister emphatically.
Joe gave me some more gravy.
"Well, but I mean a four-legged piglet," said Mr. Pumblechook. "If you had been born one, would you be here now? Not you — "
"Unless in that form," said Mr. Wopsle, nodding toward the dish.

"But I don't mean in that form, sir," returned Mr. Pumblechook, who objected to being interrupted. "I mean, enjoying himself with his elders and betters, and improving himself with their conversation, and rolling in the lap of luxury. Would he have been doing that? No, he wouldn't. And what would have been your fate?" turning on me again. "You would have been sold for so many shillings at market price, and Dunstable the butcher would have come up to you as you lay in your straw. He would have tucked you under his left arm, and with his right hand he would have rolled up his sleeve to get a knife from his waistcoat pocket, and he would have cut your throat and had your life. No bringing up by hand then. Not a bit of it!"
Joe offered me more gravy, which I was afraid to take.
"He was a world of trouble to you, ma'am," said Mrs. Hubble, sympathizing with my sister.

"Trouble?" echoed my sister. "Trouble?" And then she launched into a terrifying catalog of all the illnesses I had been guilty of, all the sleepless nights I had caused, all the high places I had fallen from, all the low places I had fallen into, all the injuries I had done myself, and all the times she had wished me in my grave — and I had stubbornly refused to go there.

I think the Romans must have annoyed each other terribly with their noses. Perhaps that's what made them such a restless people. In any case, Mr. Wopsle's Roman nose annoyed me so much during the recital of my crimes that I would have liked to pull it until he howled. But everything I had endured up to this point was nothing compared to the awful feelings that seized me when my sister's speech ended and a silence fell, during which everyone looked at me (as I painfully felt) with outrage and disgust.
"Yet," said Mr. Pumblechook, gently leading the company back to the topic from which they had strayed, "Pork — when considered boiled — is rich too, isn't it?"
"Have a little brandy, uncle," said my sister.
Oh heavens, it had come at last! He would find it was weak, he would say it was weak, and I was done for! I held tight to the leg of the table under the cloth with both hands and waited for my fate.

My sister went for the stone bottle, came back with it, and poured his brandy. No one else was having any. The wretched man toyed with his glass — picked it up, held it to the light, put it down — prolonging my agony. All this time, Mrs. Joe and Joe were briskly clearing the table for the pie and pudding.

I couldn't take my eyes off him. Still gripping the table leg with both hands and feet, I watched the wretched man finger his glass playfully, pick it up, smile, throw his head back, and drink the brandy. Instantly afterward, the company was seized with unspeakable horror as he sprang to his feet, spun around several times in an appalling dance of coughing fits, and rushed out the door. He then became visible through the window, violently choking and spitting, making the most hideous faces, and apparently out of his mind.

I held on tight while Mrs. Joe and Joe ran to him. I didn't know how I had done it, but I had no doubt I had somehow murdered him. In my dreadful situation, it was a relief when he was brought back and, looking around at the company as if they had disagreed with him, sank into his chair with one significant gasp: "Tar!"
I had topped up the bottle from the tar-water jug. I knew he would be worse later. I shook the table like a spirit medium, through the force of my unseen grip on it.
"Tar!" cried my sister in amazement. "Why, how on earth could tar get in there?"

But Uncle Pumblechook, who ruled supreme in that kitchen, wouldn't hear the word, wouldn't hear of the subject, waved it all away with an imperious hand, and asked for hot gin and water. My sister, who had begun to look alarmingly thoughtful, had to busy herself getting the gin, the hot water, the sugar, and the lemon peel, and mixing them. For the time being, at least, I was saved. I still held onto the table leg, but now clutched it with the fervor of gratitude.

Gradually, I became calm enough to let go and have some pudding. Mr. Pumblechook had pudding. Everyone had pudding. The course ended, and Mr. Pumblechook had begun to beam under the warming influence of gin and water. I was starting to think I might get through the day, when my sister said to Joe, "Clean plates — cold."

I clutched the table leg again immediately and pressed it to my chest as if it were the companion of my youth and friend of my soul. I could see what was coming, and I knew this time I was truly finished.
"You must taste," said my sister, addressing the guests with her finest manner, "you must taste, to finish with, such a delightful and delicious present from Uncle Pumblechook!"
Must they! Let them not even hope to taste it!
"You must know," said my sister, rising, "it's a pie. A savory pork pie."

The company murmured their compliments. Uncle Pumblechook, feeling he had earned the gratitude of his fellow creatures, said — quite cheerfully, all things considered — "Well, Mrs. Joe, we'll do our best. Let's have a slice of this pie."

My sister went out to get it. I heard her footsteps heading for the pantry. I saw Mr. Pumblechook balance his knife. I saw appetite reawakening in the Roman nostrils of Mr. Wopsle. I heard Mr. Hubble remark that "a bit of savory pork pie would sit well on top of anything you could mention, and do no harm." And I heard Joe say, "You shall have some, Pip." I have never been entirely certain whether I let out a shrill yell of terror only in my mind, or loud enough for the whole company to hear. I felt I could bear no more and had to run. I let go of the table leg and ran for my life.

But I ran no further than the front door, because there I ran headfirst into a party of soldiers with their muskets. One of them held out a pair of handcuffs to me, saying, "Here you are, look sharp, come on!"

chapters.title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: The sight of a line of soldiers slamming the butts of their loaded muskets on our doorstep caused the dinner party to rise from the table in confusion. It also caused Mrs. Joe, re-entering the kitchen empty-handed, to stop short and stare, crying out in bewilderment, "Gracious goodness gracious me, what's gone — with the — pie!"

The sergeant and I were in the kitchen when Mrs. Joe stood staring. At that point, I partially recovered the use of my senses. It was the sergeant who had spoken to me, and he was now looking around at the company, with his handcuffs invitingly extended toward them in his right hand, and his left hand on my shoulder.

"Excuse me, ladies and gentlemen," said the sergeant, "but as I mentioned at the door to this smart young lad" — which he hadn't — "I am on a chase in the name of the King, and I need the blacksmith."
"And what might you want with him?" retorted my sister, quick to resent his being wanted at all.
"Ma'am," returned the gallant sergeant, "speaking for myself, I should answer: the honor and pleasure of his fine wife's acquaintance. Speaking for the King, I answer: a little job done."
This was received as rather clever from the sergeant, so much so that Mr. Pumblechook cried out, "Good again!"

"You see, blacksmith," said the sergeant, who had by this time identified Joe, "we've had an accident with these, and I find the lock on one of them has gone wrong and the coupling doesn't work properly. As they're needed for immediate service, will you have a look at them?"

Joe looked them over and announced that the job would require lighting his forge fire and would take closer to two hours than one. "Will it? Then set about it at once, blacksmith," said the brisk sergeant, "as it's on His Majesty's service. And if my men can lend a hand anywhere, they'll make themselves useful." With that, he called to his men, who came trooping into the kitchen one after another and stacked their weapons in a corner. Then they stood about, as soldiers do — hands loosely clasped in front of them, resting a knee or a shoulder, easing a belt or a pouch, or opening the door to spit stiffly over their high collars out into the yard.

I saw all these things without knowing I was seeing them, because I was in an agony of fear. But as I began to realize that the handcuffs were not for me, and that the military had pushed the matter of the pie into the background, I gathered together a little more of my scattered wits.
"Would you give me the time?" said the sergeant, addressing Mr. Pumblechook as a man whose intelligence justified the assumption that he was capable of telling time.
"It's just gone half past two."
"That's not so bad," said the sergeant, thinking it over. "Even if I have to wait here nearly two hours, that'll do. How far would you say the marshes are from here? Not more than a mile, I reckon?"
"Just a mile," said Mrs. Joe.
"That'll do. We begin to close in on them around dusk. A little before dusk, those are my orders. That'll do."
"Convicts, sergeant?" asked Mr. Wopsle, matter-of-factly.
"Yes!" returned the sergeant. "Two. They're known to still be out on the marshes, and they won't try to get clear before dark. Has anyone here seen anything of them?"
Everyone except me said no with confidence. Nobody thought of me.
"Well!" said the sergeant. "They'll find themselves trapped in a circle sooner than they expect. Now, blacksmith! If you're ready, His Majesty the King is."

Joe had taken off his coat, waistcoat, and cravat, put on his leather apron, and gone into the forge. One soldier opened its wooden windows, another lit the fire, another worked the bellows, and the rest stood around the blaze, which was soon roaring. Then Joe began to hammer and clang, hammer and clang, and we all watched.

The excitement of the coming pursuit not only captured everyone's attention but even made my sister generous. She drew a pitcher of beer from the cask for the soldiers, and invited the sergeant to have a glass of brandy. But Mr. Pumblechook said sharply, "Give him wine, ma'am. I'll bet there's no tar in that." So the sergeant thanked him and said that since he preferred his drink without tar, he would take wine, if it was equally convenient. When it was given to him, he drank to His Majesty's health with compliments of the season, downed it all in one mouthful, and smacked his lips.
"Good stuff, eh, sergeant?" said Mr. Pumblechook.
"I'll tell you something," returned the sergeant. "I suspect that stuff came from your cellar."
Mr. Pumblechook gave a fat sort of laugh and said, "Oh yes? Why?"
"Because," returned the sergeant, clapping him on the shoulder, "you're a man who knows quality when he sees it."
"You think so?" said Mr. Pumblechook, with his same laugh. "Have another glass!"

"With you. Cheers," returned the sergeant. "The top of mine to the bottom of yours — the bottom of yours to the top of mine — clink once, clink twice — the best tune on the musical glasses! Your health. May you live a thousand years, and never be a worse judge of the right stuff than you are at this moment!"

The sergeant tossed off his glass again and seemed quite ready for another. I noticed that Mr. Pumblechook, in his hospitality, appeared to forget that he had given the wine as a gift. He took the bottle from Mrs. Joe and got all the credit for passing it around with great joviality. Even I got some. And he was so generous with the wine that he even called for the other bottle and passed that around with equal liberality when the first was empty.

As I watched them all standing around the forge, enjoying themselves so much, I thought what wonderful sauce for their dinner my fugitive friend on the marshes was providing. They hadn't enjoyed themselves a quarter as much before the entertainment was heightened by the excitement he provided. And now, when they were all eagerly anticipating the capture of "the two villains," the bellows seemed to roar for the fugitives, the fire to flare for them, the smoke to hurry away in pursuit of them, Joe's hammer to ring for them. All the murky shadows on the wall shook at them in menace as the blaze rose and sank, and the red-hot sparks dropped and died. The pale afternoon outside almost seemed, to my pitying young imagination, to have turned pale on their account, poor wretches.

At last Joe's job was done, and the ringing and roaring stopped. As Joe put on his coat, he gathered the courage to suggest that some of us should go down with the soldiers to see what happened. Mr. Pumblechook and Mr. Hubble declined, on the grounds of wanting their pipes and the ladies' company. But Mr. Wopsle said he would go if Joe would. Joe said he was agreeable and would take me if Mrs. Joe approved. We never would have gotten permission, I'm sure, if not for Mrs. Joe's curiosity to know all the details and how it ended. As it was, she merely stipulated, "If you bring the boy back with his head blown to bits by a musket, don't look to me to put it together again."

The sergeant took a polite leave of the ladies and parted from Mr. Pumblechook like a comrade — though I doubt he was quite as fully appreciative of that gentleman's qualities in dry conditions as when something wet was available. His men picked up their muskets and fell in. Mr. Wopsle, Joe, and I received strict orders to stay in the rear and speak no word after we reached the marshes. When we were all out in the raw air and steadily moving toward our business, I whispered treasonously to Joe, "I hope we won't find them, Joe." And Joe whispered to me, "I'd give a shilling if they'd escaped, Pip."

No stragglers from the village joined us, for the weather was cold and threatening, the path dreary, the footing bad, darkness was coming on, and people had good fires indoors and were enjoying the holiday. A few faces hurried to glowing windows and watched us pass, but none came out. We passed the signpost and went straight on to the churchyard. There we were stopped for a few minutes by a signal from the sergeant's hand, while two or three of his men searched among the graves and examined the porch. They came back without finding anything, and then we struck out across the open marshes, through the gate beside the churchyard. A bitter sleet drove against us on the east wind, and Joe took me on his back.

Now that we were out on the dismal wilderness where they had no idea I had been within the last eight or nine hours, and where I had seen both men hiding, I considered for the first time, with great dread, what would happen if we came upon them. Would my particular convict assume that I had brought the soldiers? He had asked me if I was a lying imp, and had said I would be a fierce young hound if I joined the hunt against him. Would he believe I was both imp and hound in treacherous earnest, and had betrayed him?

It was no use asking myself this now. There I was on Joe's back, and there was Joe beneath me, charging at the ditches like a hunter and urging Mr. Wopsle not to fall on his Roman nose and to keep up with us. The soldiers were in front, spread out in a wide line with gaps between each man. We were following the route I had started on that morning, and from which I had gone wrong in the mist. Either the mist hadn't come back yet, or the wind had blown it away. Under the low red glare of sunset, the beacon, the gibbet, the mound of the Battery, and the far shore of the river were all clearly visible, though everything was a watery gray color.

With my heart thumping like a blacksmith's hammer against Joe's broad shoulder, I looked all around for any sign of the convicts. I could see none. I could hear none. Mr. Wopsle had alarmed me more than once with his puffing and heavy breathing, but I knew those sounds by now and could tell them apart from the sounds of the pursuit. I got a terrible fright when I thought I heard the file still going, but it was only a sheep bell. The sheep stopped eating and looked timidly at us. The cattle, their heads turned from the wind and sleet, stared angrily as if they blamed us for both nuisances. But aside from these things and the dying shudder of daylight in every blade of grass, there was no break in the bleak stillness of the marshes.

The soldiers were moving toward the old Battery, and we were following a little way behind, when all of a sudden we all stopped. On the wind and rain, a long shout had reached us. It came again. It was some distance to the east, but it was long and loud. In fact, there seemed to be two or more shouts raised together, judging by the confusion in the sound.

The sergeant and the nearest men were discussing this under their breath when Joe and I caught up. After another moment's listening, Joe (who was a good judge) agreed with them, and Mr. Wopsle (who was a bad judge) agreed too. The sergeant, a decisive man, ordered that the shout should not be answered but that they should change course and head toward it at double speed. So we angled to the right, toward the east, and Joe pounded along so fast that I had to hold on tight to keep my seat.

It was a real run now, and what Joe called, in the only two words he spoke the whole time, "a real one." Down banks and up banks, over gates, splashing into ditches, and crashing through coarse rushes — no man cared where he went. As we got closer to the shouting, it became clearer that more than one voice was making it. Sometimes it seemed to stop altogether, and then the soldiers stopped. When it broke out again, the soldiers ran toward it faster than ever, and we followed. Before long, we were close enough to hear one voice crying "Murder!" and another: "Convicts! Runaways! Guard! This way for the runaway convicts!" Then both voices would seem to be smothered in a struggle, and then they would break out again. When it came to this, the soldiers ran like deer, and so did Joe.
The sergeant ran in first when we had tracked down the noise, and two of his men close behind him. Their guns were cocked and aimed when we all ran in.
"Here are both men!" panted the sergeant, struggling at the bottom of a ditch. "Surrender, you two! Confound you for a pair of wild beasts! Pull apart!"

Water was splashing, mud was flying, oaths were being sworn, and blows were being struck. More men went down into the ditch to help the sergeant and dragged out, separately, my convict and the other one. Both were bleeding, panting, cursing, and struggling. But of course I recognized them both instantly.
"Listen!" said my convict, wiping blood from his face with his ragged sleeves and shaking torn hair from his fingers. "I caught him! I'm giving him up to you! Remember that!"
"It's not much to boast about," said the sergeant. "It won't do you much good, my man, being in the same situation yourself. Handcuffs!"
"I don't expect it to do me any good. I don't want it to do me more good than it does right now," said my convict, with a greedy laugh. "I caught him. He knows it. That's enough for me."

The other convict was deathly pale to look at, and in addition to the old bruise on the left side of his face, seemed to be bruised and torn all over. He couldn't even catch his breath enough to speak until they were both handcuffed separately, but leaned on a soldier to keep from falling.
"Take notice, guard — he tried to murder me," were his first words.

"Tried to murder him?" said my convict scornfully. "Try and fail? I caught him and turned him in — that's what I did. I not only stopped him from getting off the marshes, I dragged him here — dragged him this far on his way back. He's a gentleman, if you please, this villain. Now the Hulks have their gentleman back, thanks to me. Murder him? It would hardly be worth my while to murder him, when I could do worse and drag him back!"
The other one still gasped, "He tried — he tried to — murder me. Bear — bear witness."

"Look here!" said my convict to the sergeant. "I got clear of the prison ship single-handed. I made a break for it and I did it. I could have gotten clear of these freezing flats too — look at my leg; you won't find much iron on it — if I hadn't discovered that he was here. Let him go free? Let him benefit from what I found? Let him use me as a tool again? Once more? No, no, no. If I had died at the bottom of that ditch" — and he swung his manacled hands toward it — "I would have held onto him so tight that you'd have been sure to find him in my grip."
The other fugitive, who was obviously terrified of his companion, repeated, "He tried to murder me. I would have been a dead man if you hadn't come."
"He lies!" said my convict with fierce energy. "He's a born liar, and he'll die a liar. Look at his face — isn't it written there? Let him look me in the eye. I dare him to do it."

The other, attempting a scornful smile that couldn't quite control the nervous twitching of his mouth, looked at the soldiers and looked around at the marshes and at the sky, but certainly did not look at the speaker.
"Do you see him?" continued my convict. "Do you see what a villain he is? Do you see those shifty, wandering eyes? That's how he looked when we were tried together. He never looked at me."

The other, constantly working his dry lips and casting his eyes restlessly about, did at last turn them for a moment on the speaker with the words, "You're not much to look at," and a half-taunting glance at the bound hands. At that, my convict became so furiously enraged that he would have lunged at him if the soldiers hadn't intervened. "Didn't I tell you," said the other convict then, "that he would murder me if he could?" And anyone could see that he was shaking with fear, and that strange white flakes were breaking out on his lips, like thin snow.
"Enough of this talk," said the sergeant. "Light those torches."

As one of the soldiers, who carried a basket instead of a gun, knelt down to open it, my convict looked around for the first time and saw me. I had climbed down from Joe's back at the edge of the ditch when we arrived, and hadn't moved since. I looked at him eagerly when he looked at me, and slightly moved my hands and shook my head. I had been waiting for him to see me so I could try to assure him I was innocent. I'm not at all sure he understood my meaning, because he gave me a look I couldn't read, and the whole moment passed in an instant. But if he had looked at me for an hour or a day, I could not have remembered his face afterward as having been more intent.

The soldier with the basket soon got a light and lit three or four torches, keeping one and handing out the others. It had been almost dark before, but now it seemed completely dark, and soon after, very dark. Before we left that spot, four soldiers standing in a ring fired twice into the air. Soon we saw other torches lit in the distance behind us, and others on the marshes across the river. "All right," said the sergeant. "March."

We hadn't gone far when three cannons were fired ahead of us with a sound that seemed to burst something inside my ear. "You're expected on board," said the sergeant to my convict. "They know you're coming. Don't fall behind, my man. Close up here."

The two were kept apart, each walking surrounded by a separate guard. I was holding Joe's hand now, and Joe carried one of the torches. Mr. Wopsle had wanted to turn back, but Joe was determined to see it through, so we went on with the group. There was a reasonably good path now, mostly along the edge of the river, with a detour here and there where a ditch crossed, with a little windmill on it and a muddy sluice gate. When I looked back, I could see the other lights coming along behind us. The torches we carried dropped great blotches of fire on the path, and I could see those too, lying smoking and flickering. Beyond that, I could see nothing but black darkness. Our torches warmed the air around us with their smoky blaze, and the two prisoners seemed to rather like that as they limped along among the muskets. We couldn't go fast because of their lameness, and they were so exhausted that two or three times we had to stop while they rested.

After about an hour of this, we came to a rough wooden hut and a landing place. There was a guard in the hut, and they challenged us, and the sergeant answered. Then we went into the hut, where there was a smell of tobacco and whitewash, a bright fire, a lamp, a rack of muskets, a drum, and a low wooden bunk like an oversized shelf, big enough to hold about a dozen soldiers at once. Three or four soldiers lying on it in their heavy coats were not very interested in us. They just raised their heads for a sleepy stare and then lay down again. The sergeant made some kind of report and an entry in a book, and then the convict I call the other convict was led off with his guard to go aboard first.

My convict never looked at me, except that once. While we stood in the hut, he stood before the fire, gazing thoughtfully at it, or propping his feet up on the hearth one at a time, looking at them thoughtfully as if he pitied them for what they'd been through. Suddenly, he turned to the sergeant and said:
"I want to say something about this escape. It may stop some people being suspected because of me."

"You can say what you like," returned the sergeant, standing coolly with his arms folded and looking at him, "but you don't need to say it here. You'll have plenty of opportunity to talk about it and hear about it before this is over, you know."
"I know, but this is a different point, a separate matter. A man can't starve — at least I can't. I took some food from the village over there, where the church stands almost out on the marshes."
"You mean stole," said the sergeant.
"And I'll tell you where from. From the blacksmith's."
"Hello!" said the sergeant, staring at Joe.
"Hello, Pip!" said Joe, staring at me.
"It was some scraps of food — that's what it was — and a drop of liquor, and a pie."
"Have you happened to miss such an article as a pie, blacksmith?" asked the sergeant, confidentially.
"My wife did, at the very moment you came in. Didn't you know, Pip?"
"So," said my convict, turning his eyes on Joe in a gloomy way, without the least glance at me, "you're the blacksmith, are you? Then I'm sorry to say, I ate your pie."

"God knows you're welcome to it — as far as it was ever mine," returned Joe, with a careful nod toward Mrs. Joe. "We don't know what you've done, but we wouldn't have you starve to death for it, poor miserable creature. Would we, Pip?"

The something that I had noticed before clicked in the man's throat again, and he turned his back. The boat had returned, and his guard was ready, so we followed him to the landing place made of rough stakes and stones, and watched him get into the boat, which was rowed by a crew of convicts like himself. No one seemed surprised to see him, or interested in seeing him, or glad to see him, or sorry to see him. No one spoke a word, except that somebody in the boat growled, as if to dogs, "Give way, you!" which was the signal for the dip of the oars. By the light of the torches, we saw the black Hulk lying a little way out from the muddy shore, like a wicked Noah's Ark. Barred and chained and moored by massive rusty chains, the prison ship seemed to my young eyes to be shackled like the prisoners. We watched the boat pull alongside, and we watched him climb up and disappear. Then the ends of the torches were flung hissing into the water and went out, as if it were all over with him.

chapters.title: Chapter 6
paragraphs: My guilty state of mind about the theft I had so unexpectedly gotten away with did not push me toward an honest confession. But I hope there was some trace of good at the bottom of it.

I don't recall feeling any guilt toward Mrs. Joe, once the fear of being found out was lifted from me. But I loved Joe — perhaps for no better reason, in those early days, than because the dear man let me love him — and when it came to him, my conscience was not so easily settled. It weighed heavily on my mind (especially when I first saw him looking around for his file) that I ought to tell Joe the whole truth. Yet I didn't, because I was afraid that if I did, he would think worse of me than I was. The fear of losing Joe's trust, and of sitting forever after in the chimney corner at night staring at my lost companion and friend, kept me silent. I told myself that if Joe knew, I could never again see him sitting by the fire stroking his fair whiskers without thinking he was brooding over it. That if Joe knew, I could never see him glance at yesterday's meat or pudding when it appeared on today's table without thinking he suspected I had been in the pantry. That if Joe knew, and at any later time in our life together remarked that his beer was flat or cloudy, the conviction that he suspected tar in it would bring a rush of blood to my face. In short, I was too cowardly to do what I knew was right, just as I had been too cowardly to avoid doing what I knew was wrong. I had had no experience of the world at that time, and I was imitating none of its many people who act the same way. Entirely self-taught, I discovered this course of action on my own.

Since I was sleepy before we were far from the prison ship, Joe took me on his back again and carried me home. He must have had a tiring journey of it, for Mr. Wopsle, being exhausted, was in such a terrible temper that if the Church had been thrown open, he would probably have excommunicated the whole expedition, starting with Joe and me. In his non-clerical capacity, he kept sitting down in the wet to such an insane extent that when his coat was taken off to be dried at the kitchen fire, the evidence on his trousers would have convicted him if it had been a hanging offense.

By that time I was stumbling around the kitchen floor like a little drunkard, having been newly set on my feet after being fast asleep, and having woken in the heat and light and noise of conversation. As I came to my senses (with the help of a hard thump between the shoulders and my sister's encouraging cry of "Yah! Was there ever such a boy as this!"), I found Joe telling everyone about the convict's confession. All the visitors were suggesting different ways the convict had gotten into the pantry. Mr. Pumblechook concluded, after carefully surveying the premises, that he had first climbed onto the roof of the forge, then onto the roof of the house, and then let himself down the kitchen chimney by a rope made of bedding cut into strips. And since Mr. Pumblechook was very certain of himself and drove his own carriage — over everybody — it was agreed that it must be so. Mr. Wopsle did wildly cry out "No!" with the feeble spite of a tired man, but since he had no theory and no coat on, he was unanimously ignored — not to mention that he was steaming heavily from behind as he stood with his back to the kitchen fire to dry out, which didn't exactly inspire confidence.

This was all I heard that night before my sister grabbed me — an offense to the company's eyes in my sleepy state — and helped me up to bed with such a strong hand that I seemed to have fifty boots on, banging them all against the edges of the stairs. My guilty state of mind, as I have described it, began before I was up the next morning and lasted long after the subject had died out and ceased to be mentioned except on rare occasions.

chapters.title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: At the time when I stood in the churchyard reading the family tombstones, I had just enough learning to spell them out. My understanding of even their simple meaning was not very accurate. I read "wife of the Above" as a compliment to my father's promotion to heaven. And if any of my dead relatives had been described as "Below," I would certainly have formed the worst opinion of that family member. My understanding of the religious duties my Catechism bound me to was equally off.
