I have a vivid memory of believing that my promise to "walk in the same all the days of my life" meant I was obligated to always go through the village in one particular direction, and never to vary it by turning down by the wheelwright's or up by the mill.

When I was old enough, I was to be apprenticed to Joe. Until I could reach that dignity, I was not to be what Mrs. Joe called "Pompeyed" — or, as I understood it, pampered. So I was not only the odd-job boy around the forge, but whenever a neighbor needed an extra boy to scare birds, pick up stones, or do any such work, I was given the job. However, to protect our superior position, a money box was kept on the kitchen mantelshelf, and it was publicly known that all my earnings went into it. I had an impression that the money was eventually going to help pay off the National Debt, but I knew I had no hope of any personal share in the treasure.

Mr. Wopsle's great-aunt ran an evening school in the village. That is to say, she was a ridiculous old woman of limited means and unlimited frailty, who fell asleep from six to seven every evening in the company of young people who paid twopence a week each for the improving opportunity of watching her do it. She rented a small cottage, and Mr. Wopsle had the upstairs room, where we students could hear him reading aloud in a most dignified and terrifying manner, occasionally bumping on the ceiling. There was a pretense that Mr. Wopsle "examined" the students once a quarter. What he actually did was roll up his sleeves, slick up his hair, and deliver Mark Antony's funeral speech over the body of Caesar. This was always followed by Collins's Ode on the Passions, in which I particularly admired Mr. Wopsle as Revenge throwing his blood-stained sword down like thunder and taking up the war trumpet with a withering look. I did not yet know, as I would in later life when I encountered the actual Passions, how unfavorably both Collins and Wopsle compared.

Mr. Wopsle's great-aunt, besides running this Educational Institution, kept a little general shop in the same room. She had no idea what stock she had or what the price of anything was, but there was a little greasy notebook kept in a drawer that served as a price list, and by this guide Biddy handled all the shop's business. Biddy was Mr. Wopsle's great-aunt's granddaughter. I confess myself unable to work out what relation she was to Mr. Wopsle. She was an orphan like me and, like me, had been brought up by hand. She was most noticeable, I thought, for her extremities: her hair always needed brushing, her hands always needed washing, and her shoes always needed mending and pulling up at the heel. This description applies only to weekdays. On Sundays, she went to church all dressed up.

Partly on my own, and more with Biddy's help than Mr. Wopsle's great-aunt's, I struggled through the alphabet as if it were a thorn bush, getting considerably scratched by every letter. After that I fell among those thieves, the nine figures, who seemed every evening to find new ways to disguise themselves and escape recognition. But at last I began, in a dim and groping way, to read, write, and do arithmetic, on the very smallest scale.

One night I was sitting in the chimney corner with my slate, working hard on a letter to Joe. I think it must have been a full year after our hunt on the marshes, for it was a long time after, and it was winter and a hard frost. With an alphabet on the hearth at my feet for reference, I managed in an hour or two to print and smear this message:
"MI DEER JO i OPE U R KRWITE WELL i OPE i SHAL SON B HABELL 4 2 TEEDGE U JO AN THEN WE SHORL B SO GLODD AN WEN i M PRENGTD 2 U JO WOT LARX AN BLEVE ME INF XN PIP."

There was no actual need for me to communicate with Joe by letter, since he was sitting right beside me and we were alone. But I delivered this written message (slate and all) with my own hand, and Joe received it as a miracle of learning.
"I say, Pip, old chap!" cried Joe, opening his blue eyes wide. "What a scholar you are! Aren't you?"
"I should like to be," said I, glancing at the slate as he held it, with a suspicion that the writing was rather uneven.
"Why, here's a J," said Joe, "and an O, as good as anything! Here's a J and an O, Pip, and a J-O, Joe."

I had never heard Joe read aloud any more than this single syllable. I had noticed at church last Sunday, when I accidentally held our prayer book upside down, that it seemed to suit him just as well as if it had been right way up. Wanting to use this chance to find out whether, in teaching Joe, I would have to start from the very beginning, I said, "Ah! But read the rest, Joe."
"The rest, eh, Pip?" said Joe, looking at it with a slow, searching eye. "One, two, three. Why, here's three J's, and three O's, and three J-O, Joes in it, Pip!"
I leaned over Joe and, with the help of my finger, read him the whole letter.
"Astonishing!" said Joe when I had finished. "You ARE a scholar."
"How do you spell Gargery, Joe?" I asked him, with modest superiority.
"I don't spell it at all," said Joe.
"But supposing you did?"
"It can't be supposed," said Joe. "Though I'm uncommonly fond of reading, too."
"Are you, Joe?"

"Uncommonly. Give me," said Joe, "a good book, or a good newspaper, and sit me down by a good fire, and I ask no more. Lord!" he continued, after rubbing his knees a little. "When you do come to a J and an O, and you say, 'Here, at last, is a J-O, Joe,' how interesting reading is!"
From this I gathered that Joe's education, like the steam engine, was still in its infancy. Pursuing the subject, I asked:
"Didn't you ever go to school, Joe, when you were as little as me?"
"No, Pip."
"Why didn't you ever go to school, Joe, when you were as little as me?"

"Well, Pip," said Joe, taking up the poker and settling into his usual habit when he was thinking, of slowly raking the fire between the lower bars, "I'll tell you. My father, Pip, he was a drinker, and when he was drunk, he beat my mother something terrible. It was about the only hammering he did, in fact, except on me. And he hammered at me with a fury only matched by the fury with which he didn't hammer at his anvil. You're listening and understanding, Pip?"
"Yes, Joe."

"So, my mother and I ran away from my father several times. Then my mother would go out to work, and she'd say, 'Joe,' she'd say, 'now, please God, you'll get some schooling, child.' And she'd send me to school. But my father was so good in his heart that he couldn't bear to be without us. So he'd come with a great crowd and make such a scene at the doors of the houses where we were staying that they had to give us up. And then he took us home and beat us. Which, you see, Pip," said Joe, pausing in his thoughtful raking of the fire and looking at me, "was a setback to my learning."
"Certainly, poor Joe!"

"Though mind you, Pip," said Joe, with a thoughtful tap or two of the poker on the top bar, "giving everyone their due and keeping things fair between man and man, my father was good in his heart, don't you see?"
I didn't see, but I didn't say so.
"Well!" Joe went on. "Somebody has to keep the pot boiling, Pip, or the pot won't boil, don't you know?"
I saw that, and said so.

"So my father didn't object to me going to work. I went to work at my present trade, which was his too, if he'd followed it, and I worked pretty hard, I assure you, Pip. In time I was able to support him, and I kept him until he died of a fit. And it was my intention to have put on his tombstone that, 'Whatever his failings were, Remember, reader, he was good in his heart.'"
Joe recited this couplet with such obvious pride and careful precision that I asked him if he had made it himself.

"I made it," said Joe. "My own self. I made it in a moment. It was like striking out a horseshoe complete in a single blow. I was never so surprised in all my life — could hardly believe my own head — to tell you the truth, hardly believed it was my own head. As I was saying, Pip, it was my intention to have it carved on his stone. But poetry costs money, cut it however you will, big or small, and it wasn't done. Not to mention the funeral bearers — all the money that could be spared was needed for my mother. She was in poor health, and completely broken. She didn't last long after that, poor soul, and her share of peace came round at last."
Joe's blue eyes turned a little watery. He rubbed first one of them, then the other, in a most awkward and uncomfortable way, with the round knob on top of the poker.

"It was lonely then," said Joe, "living here alone, and I got to know your sister. Now, Pip" — Joe looked at me firmly, as if he knew I was not going to agree — "your sister is a fine figure of a woman."
I couldn't help looking at the fire, in an obvious state of doubt.

"Whatever family opinions, or whatever the world's opinions on that subject may be, Pip, your sister is" — Joe tapped the top bar with the poker after every word — "a — fine — figure — of — a — woman!"
I could think of nothing better to say than, "I'm glad you think so, Joe."
"So am I," returned Joe, catching me up. "I am glad I think so, Pip. A little redness, or a little matter of bone here or there, what does it matter to me?"
I wisely observed that if it didn't matter to him, who did it matter to?

"Certainly!" agreed Joe. "That's it. You're right, old chap! When I got to know your sister, everyone was talking about how she was bringing you up by hand. Very kind of her too, all the neighbors said, and I said the same. As for you," Joe went on, with a look of seeing something very unpleasant indeed, "if you could have known how small and weak and pitiful you were, dear me, you'd have formed the lowest opinion of yourself!"
Not exactly enjoying this, I said, "Never mind me, Joe."

"But I did mind you, Pip," he returned with tender simplicity. "When I asked your sister to keep company, and to be called in church whenever she was willing and ready to come to the forge, I said to her, 'And bring the poor little child. God bless the poor little child,' I said to your sister, 'there's room for him at the forge!'"
I burst out crying and begging his pardon, and hugged Joe around the neck. He dropped the poker to hug me and to say, "Always the best of friends, aren't we, Pip? Don't cry, old chap!"
When this little interruption was over, Joe continued:

"Well, you see, Pip, and here we are! That's about how it stands. Now, when you take me in hand for my learning, Pip — and I tell you beforehand I am terribly slow, most terribly slow — Mrs. Joe mustn't see too much of what we're up to. It must be done, as I might say, on the sly. And why on the sly? I'll tell you why, Pip."
He had picked up the poker again. Without it, I doubt he could have continued his explanation.
"Your sister is given to government."
"Given to government, Joe?" I was startled, for I had some vague idea — and I'm afraid I must add, hope — that Joe had handed her over to the Lords of the Admiralty or the Treasury.
"Given to government," said Joe. "By which I mean the government of you and me."
"Oh!"
"And she's not keen on having scholars around the place," Joe continued, "and especially wouldn't be keen on me becoming a scholar, for fear I might rise up. Like a sort of rebel, don't you see?"
I was about to ask a question and had gotten as far as "Why — " when Joe stopped me.

"Wait a moment. I know what you're going to say, Pip — wait! I don't deny that your sister plays the tyrant over us now and again. I don't deny that she knocks us down and comes down on us hard. At such times as when your sister is on the rampage, Pip" — Joe dropped his voice to a whisper and glanced at the door — "honesty forces me to admit that she is a Terror."
Joe pronounced this word as if it began with at least twelve capital letters.
"Why don't I stand up to her? That was your question when I interrupted you, Pip?"
"Yes, Joe."

"Well," said Joe, passing the poker to his left hand so he could stroke his whiskers — and I never had any hope of him whenever he took up that peaceful habit — "your sister is a master mind. A master mind."

"What's that?" I asked, hoping to catch him off guard. But Joe was readier with his definition than I expected, and completely silenced me by arguing in a circle and answering with a fixed look: "Her."

"And I'm not a master mind," Joe continued, once he had unfixed his gaze and gone back to his whiskers. "And last of all, Pip — and this I want to say very seriously to you, old chap — I saw so much in my poor mother of a woman working and slaving and breaking her honest heart and never getting any peace in her life, that I'm terrified of going wrong by not treating a woman right. I'd far rather go wrong the other way and put up with a little hardship myself. I wish it was only me who got the worst of it, Pip. I wish there was no Tickler for you, old chap. I wish I could take it all on myself. But this is the plain truth of it, Pip, and I hope you'll forgive my shortcomings."

Young as I was, I believe I gained a new admiration for Joe that night. We were equals afterward, as we had been before. But afterward, at quiet times when I sat looking at Joe and thinking about him, I had a new feeling — an awareness that I was looking up to Joe in my heart.

"However," said Joe, rising to add more fuel to the fire, "here's the Dutch clock working itself up to strike eight, and she's not home yet! I hope Uncle Pumblechook's horse hasn't put a foot on a piece of ice and gone down."

Mrs. Joe made occasional trips with Uncle Pumblechook on market days, to help him buy household supplies and goods that required a woman's judgment. Uncle Pumblechook, being a bachelor who placed no trust in his servant, relied on her for this. This was market day, and Mrs. Joe was out on one of these trips.

Joe built up the fire and swept the hearth, and then we went to the door to listen for the carriage. It was a dry, cold night, the wind blew sharply, and the frost was white and hard. A man would die tonight from lying out on the marshes, I thought. And then I looked at the stars and considered how awful it would be for a man to turn his face up to them as he froze to death, and see no help or pity in all their glittering multitude.
"Here comes the horse," said Joe, "ringing like a peal of bells!"

The sound of her iron shoes on the hard road was quite musical as she came along at a much brisker trot than usual. We got a chair out, ready for Mrs. Joe to step down, stirred up the fire so they might see a bright window, and took a final look around the kitchen to make sure nothing was out of place. When we had finished these preparations, they drove up, wrapped to the eyes. Mrs. Joe was soon on the ground, and Uncle Pumblechook was soon down too, covering the horse with a cloth. We were soon all in the kitchen, bringing so much cold air in with us that it seemed to drive all the heat out of the fire.
"Now," said Mrs. Joe, unwrapping herself with haste and excitement, throwing her bonnet back on her shoulders where it hung by the strings, "if this boy isn't grateful tonight, he never will be!"
I looked as grateful as any boy possibly could who had absolutely no idea why he was supposed to look that way.
"It's only to be hoped," said my sister, "that he won't be pampered. But I have my fears."
"She's not in that line, ma'am," said Mr. Pumblechook. "She knows better."

She? I looked at Joe, mouthing "She?" Joe looked at me, mouthing "She?" My sister, catching him in the act, he drew the back of his hand across his nose with his usual peacekeeping air on such occasions, and looked at her.
"Well?" said my sister, in her snappish way. "What are you staring at? Is the house on fire?"
"Which some person," Joe politely hinted, "mentioned — she."
"And she is a she, I suppose?" said my sister. "Unless you call Miss Havisham a he. And I doubt even you'd go that far."
"Miss Havisham, up town?" said Joe.
"Is there any Miss Havisham down town?" returned my sister.

"She wants this boy to go and play there. And of course he's going. And he had better play there," said my sister, shaking her head at me as if encouraging me to be extremely lighthearted and playful, "or I'll thrash him."

I had heard of Miss Havisham up town — everybody for miles around had heard of Miss Havisham up town — as an enormously rich and stern lady who lived in a large and gloomy house barricaded against robbers, and who led a life of complete seclusion.
"Well, I never!" said Joe, astonished. "I wonder how she came to know Pip!"
"Idiot!" cried my sister. "Who said she knew him?"
"Which some person," Joe politely hinted again, "mentioned that she wanted him to go and play there."

"And couldn't she ask Uncle Pumblechook if he knew of a boy to go and play there? Isn't it just barely possible that Uncle Pumblechook is a tenant of hers, and that he might sometimes — we won't say quarterly or half-yearly, since that would be asking too much of you — but sometimes — go there to pay his rent? And couldn't she then ask Uncle Pumblechook if he knew of a boy to go and play there? And couldn't Uncle Pumblechook, being always considerate and thoughtful for us — though you may not think it, Joseph," in a tone of the deepest reproach, as if he were the most heartless of nephews, "then mention this boy, standing here showing off" — which I solemnly declare I was not doing — "that I have forever been a willing slave to?"
"Good again!" cried Uncle Pumblechook. "Well put! Neatly pointed! Good indeed! Now, Joseph, you know the situation."

"No, Joseph," said my sister, still in a reproachful tone, while Joe apologetically drew the back of his hand back and forth across his nose, "you do not yet — though you may not think it — know the situation. You may think you do, but you do not, Joseph. For you do not know that Uncle Pumblechook, being aware that for all we know, this boy's fortune may be made by his going to Miss Havisham's, has offered to take him into town tonight in his own carriage, keep him overnight, and take him with his own hands to Miss Havisham's tomorrow morning. And good heavens!" cried my sister, tearing off her bonnet in sudden desperation, "here I stand talking to complete fools, with Uncle Pumblechook waiting, the horse catching cold at the door, and the boy covered in grime and dirt from the top of his head to the sole of his foot!"

With that, she pounced on me like an eagle on a lamb, and my face was shoved into wooden bowls in sinks, and my head was stuck under taps of water barrels, and I was soaped, kneaded, toweled, thumped, scratched, and scraped, until I was quite beside myself. (I may note here that I believe myself to be better acquainted than any living person with the ridged effect of a wedding ring passed unsympathetically over the human face.)

When my washing was done, I was put into clean clothes of the stiffest kind, like a young penitent into sackcloth, and was strapped into my tightest and most fearsome suit. I was then handed over to Mr. Pumblechook, who formally received me as if he were the sheriff, and delivered the speech he had clearly been dying to make all along: "Boy, be forever grateful to all friends, but especially to those who brought you up by hand!"
"Goodbye, Joe!"
"God bless you, Pip, old chap!"

I had never been parted from him before, and what with my feelings and the soap suds, I could at first see no stars from the carriage. But they twinkled out one by one, without throwing any light on the questions of why on earth I was going to play at Miss Havisham's, and what on earth I was expected to play at.

chapters.title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: Mr. Pumblechook's shop on the High Street of the market town had a peppery, floury character, as befitted a corn merchant and seedsman. It seemed to me that he must be a very happy man indeed, to have so many little drawers in his shop. I wondered, when I peeked into one or two on the lower rows and saw the tied-up brown paper packets inside, whether the flower seeds and bulbs ever longed for a fine day to break out of those little jails and bloom.

It was early the morning after my arrival that I had this thought. The night before, I had been sent straight to bed in an attic with a sloping roof, so low in the corner where the bed was that the tiles were within a foot of my eyebrows. That same early morning, I discovered a strange connection between seeds and corduroy. Mr. Pumblechook wore corduroy, and so did his shop assistant. Somehow there was a general look and smell about the corduroy that was very seed-like, and a general look and smell about the seeds that was very corduroy-like, so that I could hardly tell which was which. I also noticed that Mr. Pumblechook seemed to conduct his business by looking across the street at the saddler, who seemed to run his business by watching the coachmaker, who seemed to get on in life by putting his hands in his pockets and staring at the baker, who folded his arms and stared at the grocer, who stood at his door and yawned at the chemist. The watchmaker, always bent over a little desk with a magnifying glass at his eye, always inspected by a group of country folk peering at him through his shop window, seemed to be the only person on the High Street whose trade actually occupied his attention.

Mr. Pumblechook and I had breakfast at eight in the parlor behind the shop, while the shop assistant had his mug of tea and chunk of bread and butter on a sack of peas in the front. I found Mr. Pumblechook wretched company. Besides sharing my sister's idea that my diet should be punishing and penitential — besides giving me as much dry bread as possible with as little butter, and putting so much warm water in my milk that it would have been more honest to leave the milk out entirely — his conversation consisted of nothing but arithmetic. When I politely bid him good morning, he said pompously, "Seven times nine, boy?" And how was I supposed to answer, ambushed like that, in a strange place, on an empty stomach? I was hungry, but before I had swallowed a bite, he began a running sum that lasted through the whole breakfast. "Seven?" "And four?" "And eight?" "And six?" "And two?" "And ten?" And so on. After each number was dealt with, it was all I could do to get a bite or a sip before the next one came, while he sat comfortably, guessing nothing, eating bacon and hot rolls in what I can only describe as a gorging manner.

For these reasons, I was very glad when ten o'clock came and we set off for Miss Havisham's, though I was not at all easy about how I would perform under that lady's roof. Within a quarter of an hour we reached Miss Havisham's house. It was old brick, gloomy, and had a great many iron bars on it. Some windows had been bricked up. Of those that remained, all the lower ones were barred with rusty iron. There was a courtyard in front, and that was barred too. We had to wait after ringing the bell until someone came to open it. While we waited at the gate, I peeked in (even then Mr. Pumblechook said, "And fourteen?" but I pretended not to hear him) and saw that beside the house there was a large brewery. No brewing was going on in it, and none seemed to have gone on for a very long time.

A window was raised, and a clear voice demanded, "What name?" To which my escort replied, "Pumblechook." The voice returned, "Quite right," and the window was shut again, and a young lady came across the courtyard with keys in her hand.
"This," said Mr. Pumblechook, "is Pip."
"This is Pip, is it?" returned the young lady, who was very pretty and seemed very proud. "Come in, Pip."
Mr. Pumblechook was coming in too, when she stopped him with the gate.
"Oh!" she said. "Did you wish to see Miss Havisham?"
"If Miss Havisham wished to see me," returned Mr. Pumblechook, flustered.
"Ah!" said the girl. "But you see, she doesn't."

She said it so decisively, and in such an unarguable way, that Mr. Pumblechook, though ruffled in his dignity, could not protest. But he eyed me severely — as if I had done something to him! — and departed with the words reproachfully delivered: "Boy! Let your behavior here be a credit to those who brought you up by hand!" I was not entirely free from the fear that he would come back to call through the gate, "And sixteen?" But he didn't.

My young guide locked the gate, and we went across the courtyard. It was paved and clean, but grass was growing in every crack. The brewery buildings had a little lane connecting them to it, and the wooden gates of that lane stood open, and the whole brewery beyond stood open, all the way to the high surrounding wall. Everything was empty and abandoned. The cold wind seemed to blow colder there than outside the gate, and it made a shrill noise howling in and out of the open sides of the brewery, like the sound of wind in the rigging of a ship at sea.
She saw me looking at it, and she said, "You could drink every drop of strong beer that's brewed there now without any harm, boy."
"I should think I could, miss," said I, shyly.
"Better not try to brew beer there now, or it would turn out sour, boy. Don't you think so?"
"It looks like it, miss."

"Not that anybody intends to try," she added, "for that's all done with, and the place will stand idle until it falls down. As for strong beer, there's enough of it in the cellars already to drown the Manor House."
"Is that the name of this house, miss?"
"One of its names, boy."
"It has more than one, then, miss?"
"One more. Its other name was Satis, which is Greek, or Latin, or Hebrew, or all three — or all one to me — for 'enough.'"
"Enough House," said I. "That's a curious name, miss."

"Yes," she replied. "But it meant more than it said. It meant, when it was given, that whoever had this house could want nothing else. They must have been easily satisfied in those days, I should think. But don't dawdle, boy."

Though she called me "boy" so often, and with a casualness that was far from flattering, she was about my own age. She seemed much older than me, of course, being a girl and beautiful and self-assured. She was as scornful of me as if she had been twenty-one and a queen.

We went into the house through a side door — the great front entrance had two chains across it outside — and the first thing I noticed was that the hallways were all dark, and that she had left a candle burning there. She picked it up, and we went through more hallways and up a staircase, and still it was all dark, and only the candle lit our way.
At last we came to the door of a room, and she said, "Go in."
I answered, more from shyness than politeness, "After you, miss."
To this she returned: "Don't be ridiculous, boy. I am not going in." And she scornfully walked away, and — what was worse — took the candle with her.

This was very uncomfortable, and I was half afraid. However, the only thing to do was knock at the door, so I knocked, and was told from inside to enter. I entered and found myself in a fairly large room, brightly lit with wax candles. Not a glimpse of daylight could be seen in it. It was a dressing room, as I guessed from the furniture, though much of it was of forms and uses I had never seen before. But the most prominent thing in it was a draped table with a gilded mirror, and I recognized at once that it was a fine lady's dressing table.

Whether I would have identified it so quickly if there had been no fine lady sitting at it, I cannot say. In an armchair, with an elbow resting on the table and her head leaning on that hand, sat the strangest lady I have ever seen, or ever will see.

She was dressed in rich materials — satins, lace, and silks — all white. Her shoes were white. She had a long white veil hanging from her hair, and she had bridal flowers in her hair, but her hair was white. Some bright jewels sparkled on her neck and hands, and more jewels lay sparkling on the table. Dresses, less splendid than the one she wore, and half-packed trunks were scattered about. She had not quite finished dressing, for she had only one shoe on — the other was on the table near her hand — her veil was only half arranged, her watch and chain were not put on, and some lace for her bodice lay with those trinkets, and with her handkerchief, gloves, some flowers, and a prayer book, all jumbled together around the mirror.

It was not in the first few moments that I saw all these things, though I saw more of them in those first moments than you might expect. But I saw that everything within my view that should have been white had been white long ago, and had lost its shine and become faded and yellow. I saw that the bride inside the bridal dress had withered like the dress and like the flowers, and had no brightness left except the brightness of her sunken eyes. I saw that the dress had been put on the rounded figure of a young woman, and that the figure it now hung loose on had shrunk to skin and bone. Once, I had been taken to see some ghastly waxwork at the fair, representing some impossible figure lying in state. Once, I had been taken to one of our old marsh churches to see a skeleton in the ashes of a rich dress that had been dug out of a vault under the church floor. Now, waxwork and skeleton seemed to have dark eyes that moved and looked at me. I would have cried out, if I could.
"Who is it?" said the lady at the table.
"Pip, ma'am."
"Pip?"
"Mr. Pumblechook's boy, ma'am. Come — to play."
"Come nearer. Let me look at you. Come close."

It was when I stood before her, avoiding her eyes, that I noticed the surrounding objects in detail. I saw that her watch had stopped at twenty minutes to nine, and that a clock in the room had also stopped at twenty minutes to nine.
"Look at me," said Miss Havisham. "You are not afraid of a woman who has never seen the sun since you were born?"
I regret to say that I was not afraid of telling the enormous lie contained in the answer "No."
"Do you know what I touch here?" she said, laying her hands, one upon the other, on her left side.
"Yes, ma'am." (It reminded me of the young man.)
"What do I touch?"
"Your heart."
"Broken!"

She uttered the word with an eager look, strong emphasis, and a strange smile that had a kind of pride in it. Afterward she kept her hands there for a little while, then slowly took them away as if they were heavy.
"I am tired," said Miss Havisham. "I want entertainment, and I have done with men and women. Play."
I think even my most argumentative reader would agree that she could hardly have asked an unfortunate boy to do anything in the wide world more difficult to do under the circumstances.

"I sometimes have strange fancies," she went on, "and I have a strange fancy that I want to see some play. There, there!" — with an impatient movement of the fingers of her right hand — "play, play, play!"

For a moment, with the fear of my sister's punishment before my eyes, I had a desperate idea of running around the room pretending to be Mr. Pumblechook's carriage. But I felt so unequal to the performance that I gave it up and stood looking at Miss Havisham in what I suppose she took for a stubborn manner, since she said, when we had studied each other for a good while:
"Are you sullen and obstinate?"

"No, ma'am. I am very sorry for you, and very sorry I can't play just now. If you complain of me, I shall get into trouble with my sister, so I would do it if I could. But it's so new here, and so strange, and so fine — and melancholy — " I stopped, afraid I might say too much, or had already said it, and we studied each other again.
Before she spoke again, she turned her eyes from me and looked at the dress she wore, and at the dressing table, and finally at herself in the mirror.
"So new to him," she murmured, "so old to me. So strange to him, so familiar to me. So melancholy to both of us! Call Estella."
Since she was still looking at her reflection, I thought she was still talking to herself, and kept quiet.
"Call Estella," she repeated, flashing a look at me. "You can do that. Call Estella. At the door."

To stand in the dark in a mysterious hallway of an unknown house, shouting "Estella" to a scornful young lady who was neither visible nor answering, and feeling it a terrible liberty to roar out her name, was almost as bad as playing to order. But she answered at last, and her light came along the dark passage like a star.

Miss Havisham beckoned her to come close and took up a jewel from the table and tried its effect against her fair young chest and against her pretty brown hair. "Your own, one day, my dear, and you will use it well. Let me see you play cards with this boy."
"With this boy? Why, he is a common laboring boy!"
I thought I overheard Miss Havisham answer — only it seemed so unlikely — "Well? You can break his heart."
"What do you play, boy?" asked Estella of me, with the greatest contempt.
"Nothing but Beggar My Neighbor, miss."
"Beggar him," said Miss Havisham to Estella. So we sat down to cards.

It was then I began to understand that everything in the room had stopped, like the watch and the clock, a long time ago. I noticed that Miss Havisham put the jewel down on exactly the spot she had picked it up from. As Estella dealt the cards, I glanced at the dressing table again and saw that the shoe on it, once white, now yellow, had never been worn. I looked down at the foot missing its shoe, and saw that the silk stocking on it, once white, now yellow, had been walked to rags. Without this freezing of everything, this standing still of all the pale decayed objects, not even the withered bridal dress on the shrunken form could have looked so much like grave clothes, or the long veil so much like a shroud.

So she sat, corpse-like, as we played cards. The frills and trimmings on her bridal dress looked like crumbling paper. I knew nothing then about the discoveries sometimes made of bodies buried in ancient times, which crumble to dust the moment they are clearly seen. But I have often thought since that she must have looked as if the natural light of day would have struck her to dust.
"He calls the knaves Jacks, this boy!" said Estella with contempt, before our first game was over. "And what coarse hands he has! And what thick boots!"
I had never thought of being ashamed of my hands before, but I began to see them as a very poor pair. Her contempt for me was so strong that it became infectious, and I caught it.
She won the game, and I dealt. I misdealt, as was only natural when I knew she was watching for me to make a mistake, and she denounced me as a stupid, clumsy laboring boy.
"You say nothing of her," remarked Miss Havisham to me, as she watched. "She says many hard things of you, but you say nothing of her. What do you think of her?"
"I don't like to say," I stammered.
"Tell me in my ear," said Miss Havisham, bending down.
"I think she is very proud," I replied, in a whisper.
"Anything else?"
"I think she is very pretty."
"Anything else?"
"I think she is very insulting." (She was looking at me then with a look of supreme disgust.)
"Anything else?"
"I think I should like to go home."
"And never see her again, though she is so pretty?"
"I am not sure that I wouldn't like to see her again, but I should like to go home now."
"You shall go soon," said Miss Havisham, aloud. "Play the game out."

Except for that one strange smile at the beginning, I would have felt almost certain that Miss Havisham's face could not smile. It had settled into a watchful, brooding expression — most likely when everything around her had frozen in time — and it looked as if nothing could ever lift it again. Her chest had sunk so that she stooped. Her voice had dropped so that she spoke in a low tone, with a dead stillness about her. Altogether, she had the look of someone who had collapsed, body and soul, inside and out, under the weight of a crushing blow.
I played the game to the end with Estella, and she beat me. She threw the cards down on the table when she had won them all, as if she despised them for having been won from me.
"When shall I have you here again?" said Miss Havisham. "Let me think."
I was beginning to remind her that today was Wednesday, when she stopped me with her same impatient gesture.
"There, there! I know nothing of days of the week. I know nothing of weeks of the year. Come again after six days. You hear?"
"Yes, ma'am."
"Estella, take him down. Let him have something to eat, and let him wander around and look about while he eats. Go, Pip."

I followed the candle down, as I had followed it up, and she set it in the place where we had found it. Until she opened the side door, I had assumed, without thinking about it, that it must be nighttime. The rush of daylight completely confused me, and made me feel as if I had been in the candlelight of that strange room for many hours.
"You are to wait here, you boy," said Estella. And she disappeared and closed the door.

I took the chance of being alone in the courtyard to look at my coarse hands and my common boots. My opinion of them was not favorable. They had never troubled me before, but they troubled me now, as vulgar things attached to me. I resolved to ask Joe why he had ever taught me to call those picture cards Jacks, when they ought to be called knaves. I wished Joe had been brought up more properly, and then I would have been too.

She came back with some bread and meat and a little mug of beer. She put the mug down on the stones of the yard and gave me the bread and meat without looking at me, as rudely as if I were a dog in disgrace. I was so humiliated, hurt, rejected, offended, angry, sorry — I cannot find the right name for the stinging pain — God knows what its name was — that tears sprang to my eyes. The moment they appeared, the girl looked at me with a quick delight in having caused them. This gave me the power to hold them back and look at her. So she gave a contemptuous toss of her head — but with a sense, I thought, of having been too sure that I was wounded — and left me.

But when she was gone, I looked around for a place to hide my face, and got behind one of the gates in the brewery lane, and leaned my sleeve against the wall and pressed my forehead to it and cried. As I cried, I kicked the wall and gave my hair a hard twist. So bitter were my feelings, and so sharp was the nameless pain, that it needed some physical outlet.

My sister's upbringing had made me sensitive. In the small world where children live, whoever brings them up, there is nothing so keenly felt as injustice. It may be only small injustice that the child faces, but the child is small, and its world is small, and its rocking horse stands as many hands high, in proportion, as a full-grown racehorse. Within myself, I had endured, from babyhood, a constant battle with injustice. I had known, from the time I could speak, that my sister, in her unpredictable and violent authority, was unjust to me. I had held a deep conviction that her bringing me up "by hand" gave her no right to bring me up by beatings. Through all my punishments, humiliations, forced fasts, and sleepless nights, I had clung to this belief. And from dwelling on it so much, alone and unprotected, I had become morally timid and very sensitive.

I got rid of my hurt feelings for the time by kicking them into the brewery wall and twisting them out of my hair. Then I smoothed my face with my sleeve and came out from behind the gate. The bread and meat were welcome, and the beer was warm and tingling, and I was soon in good enough spirits to look around.

It was certainly a deserted place, down to the pigeon house in the brewery yard, which had been blown crooked on its pole by some high wind and would have made any pigeons think they were at sea — if there had been any pigeons. But there were no pigeons in the dovecote, no horses in the stable, no pigs in the sty, no malt in the storehouse, no smell of grain and beer in the vats. All the purposes and smells of the brewery might have evaporated with its last wisp of smoke. In a side yard, there was a wilderness of empty casks, which had a faint sour memory of better days lingering about them. But it was too sour to count as a sample of the beer that was gone — and in this respect, I remember those abandoned casks as being like most others.

Behind the far end of the brewery was an overgrown garden with an old wall. It was not so high that I couldn't scramble up and hold on long enough to look over it. I saw that the overgrown garden was the garden of the house, tangled with weeds, but with a track worn on the green and yellow paths, as if someone sometimes walked there. And Estella was walking away from me even then. But she seemed to be everywhere. When I gave in to the temptation of the casks and began walking on them, I saw her walking on them at the end of the yard. She had her back to me and held her pretty brown hair spread out in both hands, and never looked around, and passed out of my view. And in the brewery itself — by which I mean the large, paved, lofty space where they used to make the beer, and where the brewing equipment still stood. When I first went in, feeling oppressed by its gloom, and stood near the door looking around, I saw her pass among the dead fires, climb some light iron stairs, and go out through a gallery high overhead, as if she were going out into the sky.

It was in this place, and at this moment, that a strange thing happened to my imagination. I thought it strange then, and I thought it stranger long afterward. I turned my eyes — a little dazzled from looking up at the frosty light — toward a great wooden beam in a low corner of the building near me on my right, and I saw a figure hanging there by the neck. A figure all in yellowish white, with only one shoe on its feet. It hung so that I could see the faded trimmings of the dress were like crumbling paper, and that the face was Miss Havisham's, with a movement passing over the whole face as if she were trying to call to me. In the terror of seeing the figure, and in the terror of being certain it had not been there a moment before, I first ran from it, and then ran toward it. And my terror was greatest of all when I found no figure there.

Nothing less than the frosty light of the cheerful sky, the sight of people passing beyond the bars of the courtyard gate, and the reviving influence of the rest of the bread and meat and beer would have brought me around. Even with those aids, I might not have recovered as soon as I did, except that I saw Estella approaching with the keys to let me out. She would have some fair reason for looking down on me, I thought, if she saw me frightened. And she would have no fair reason.

She gave me a triumphant glance as she passed me, as if she was glad that my hands were so coarse and my boots were so thick. She opened the gate and stood holding it. I was passing out without looking at her, when she touched me with a taunting hand.
"Why don't you cry?"
"Because I don't want to."
"You do," said she. "You have been crying till you are half blind, and you are near crying again now."

She laughed contemptuously, pushed me out, and locked the gate behind me. I went straight to Mr. Pumblechook's and was immensely relieved to find him not at home. Leaving word with the shop assistant about what day I was wanted at Miss Havisham's again, I set off on the four-mile walk to our forge, pondering as I went on everything I had seen, and deeply aware that I was a common laboring boy, that my hands were coarse, that my boots were thick, that I had fallen into the despicable habit of calling knaves Jacks, that I was much more ignorant than I had thought last night, and generally that I was in a low and sorry state.

chapters.title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: When I got home, my sister was very curious to know all about Miss Havisham's and asked a stream of questions. I soon found myself getting roughly bumped from behind on the back of the neck and the small of my back, and having my face shoved against the kitchen wall, because I did not answer those questions at sufficient length.

If a fear of not being understood is hidden in the hearts of other young people to anything like the extent it was hidden in mine — which I think is likely, since I have no particular reason to think I was unusually odd — it is the key to many silences. I felt certain that if I described Miss Havisham's as my eyes had seen it, I would not be understood. Not only that, but I felt certain that Miss Havisham herself would not be understood. And although she was completely incomprehensible to me, I had a feeling that there would be something coarse and disloyal about dragging her as she really was (to say nothing of Miss Estella) before Mrs. Joe's scrutiny. So I said as little as I could, and had my face shoved against the kitchen wall.

The worst of it was that that bullying old Pumblechook, consumed by curiosity about everything I had seen and heard, came rattling over in his carriage at teatime to have the details revealed to him. And the mere sight of the man, with his fishy eyes and gaping mouth, his sandy hair standing inquisitively on end, and his waistcoat heaving with windy arithmetic, made me stubbornly silent.
"Well, boy," Uncle Pumblechook began, as soon as he was seated in the chair of honor by the fire. "How did you get on up town?"
I answered, "Pretty well, sir," and my sister shook her fist at me.
"Pretty well?" Mr. Pumblechook repeated. "Pretty well is no answer. Tell us what you mean by pretty well, boy?"

Whitewash on the forehead perhaps hardens the brain into a state of stubbornness. In any case, with whitewash from the wall on my forehead, my stubbornness was absolute. I thought for some time and then answered, as if I had discovered a new idea, "I mean pretty well."

My sister was about to fly at me with an exclamation of impatience — I had no chance of defense, since Joe was busy in the forge — when Mr. Pumblechook stepped in with, "No! Don't lose your temper. Leave this boy to me, ma'am. Leave this boy to me." Mr. Pumblechook then turned me toward him, as if he were going to cut my hair, and said:
"First, to get our thoughts in order: forty-three pence?"

I calculated the consequences of replying "Four hundred pounds," and finding them against me, got as close to the answer as I could — which was somewhere about eightpence off. Mr. Pumblechook then drilled me through my pence table from "twelve pence make one shilling" up to "forty pence make three and fourpence," and then triumphantly demanded, as if he had finished me off, "Now! How much is forty-three pence?" To which I replied, after a long pause for thought, "I don't know." And I was so irritated that I almost doubt I did know.
Mr. Pumblechook worked his head like a screw to get it out of me, and said, "Is forty-three pence seven and sixpence three farthings, for instance?"
"Yes!" said I. And although my sister instantly boxed my ears, it was highly satisfying to see that the answer ruined his little quiz and brought him to a dead stop.
"Boy! What is Miss Havisham like?" Mr. Pumblechook began again when he had recovered, folding his arms tight on his chest and applying the pressure.
"Very tall and dark," I told him.
"Is she, uncle?" asked my sister.
Mr. Pumblechook winked agreement. From which I immediately concluded that he had never actually seen Miss Havisham, for she was nothing of the kind.
"Good!" said Mr. Pumblechook smugly. "This is the way to handle him! We're making progress, I think, ma'am?"
"I'm sure, uncle," returned Mrs. Joe, "I wish you had him all the time. You know so well how to deal with him."
"Now, boy! What was she doing when you went in today?" asked Mr. Pumblechook.
"She was sitting," I answered, "in a black velvet coach."
Mr. Pumblechook and Mrs. Joe stared at each other — as well they might — and both repeated, "In a black velvet coach?"

"Yes," said I. "And Miss Estella — that's her niece, I think — handed her cake and wine at the coach window, on a gold plate. And we all had cake and wine on gold plates. And I got up behind the coach to eat mine, because she told me to."
"Was anybody else there?" asked Mr. Pumblechook.
"Four dogs," said I.
"Large or small?"
"Immense," said I. "And they fought for veal cutlets out of a silver basket."
Mr. Pumblechook and Mrs. Joe stared at each other again, in utter amazement. I was completely out of control — a reckless witness under torture — and would have told them anything.
"Where was this coach, for heaven's sake?" asked my sister.

"In Miss Havisham's room." They stared again. "But there weren't any horses pulling it." I added this saving detail at the last moment, rejecting the four richly decorated horses I had wildly considered inventing.
"Can this be possible, uncle?" asked Mrs. Joe. "What can the boy mean?"
"I'll tell you, ma'am," said Mr. Pumblechook. "My opinion is, it's a sedan chair. She's eccentric, you know — very eccentric — quite eccentric enough to spend her days in a sedan chair."
"Did you ever see her in it, uncle?" asked Mrs. Joe.
"How could I," he returned, forced to admit it, "when I've never seen her in my life? Never laid eyes on her!"
"Goodness, uncle! And yet you have spoken to her?"

"Why, don't you know," said Mr. Pumblechook irritably, "that when I have been there, I have been taken up to the outside of her door, and the door has stood open a crack, and she has spoken to me that way? Don't tell me you don't know that, ma'am. Anyway, the boy went there to play. What did you play at, boy?"
"We played with flags," I said. (I beg to note that I think of myself with amazement when I recall the lies I told on this occasion.)
"Flags!" echoed my sister.

"Yes," said I. "Estella waved a blue flag, and I waved a red one, and Miss Havisham waved one sprinkled all over with little gold stars, out of the coach window. And then we all waved our swords and cheered."
"Swords!" repeated my sister. "Where did you get swords from?"
"Out of a cupboard," said I. "And I saw pistols in it — and jam — and pills. And there was no daylight in the room, but it was all lit up with candles."

"That's true, ma'am," said Mr. Pumblechook, with a solemn nod. "That's how it is, for that much I've seen myself." And then they both stared at me, and I, with a bold show of innocence on my face, stared at them and pleated the right leg of my trousers with my right hand.

If they had asked me any more questions, I would undoubtedly have given myself away. I was already on the point of mentioning a balloon in the yard, and would have said it except that my invention was torn between the balloon and a bear in the brewery. But they were so busy discussing the marvels I had already presented that I escaped. The subject still occupied them when Joe came in from his work to have a cup of tea. My sister related my invented experiences to him, more for the relief of her own mind than for his enjoyment.

Now, when I saw Joe open his blue eyes wide and roll them all around the kitchen in helpless amazement, I was overtaken by guilt — but only about him, not in the least about the other two. Toward Joe, and Joe only, I thought of myself as a young monster, while they sat debating what benefits would come to me from Miss Havisham's acquaintance and favor. They had no doubt that Miss Havisham would "do something" for me. Their doubts were about what form that something would take. My sister held out for "property." Mr. Pumblechook favored a handsome payment to apprentice me to some respectable trade — say, the corn and seed trade, for instance. Joe fell into the deepest disgrace with both of them for his bright suggestion that I might only be given one of the dogs that fought for the veal cutlets. "If a fool's head can't come up with better ideas than that," said my sister, "and you have work to do, you had better go and do it." So he went.

After Mr. Pumblechook had driven off, and while my sister was washing up, I crept into the forge to Joe and stayed with him until he had finished for the night. Then I said, "Before the fire goes out, Joe, I should like to tell you something."
"Should you, Pip?" said Joe, drawing his stool near the forge. "Then tell us. What is it, Pip?"
"Joe," said I, taking hold of his rolled-up shirt sleeve and twisting it between my finger and thumb, "you remember all that about Miss Havisham's?"
"Remember?" said Joe. "I should think so! Amazing!"
"It's a terrible thing, Joe. It isn't true."
"What are you telling me, Pip?" cried Joe, falling back in the greatest amazement. "You don't mean to say it's — "
"Yes I do. It's lies, Joe."

"But not all of it? You don't really mean, Pip, that there was no black velvet co — ?" For I stood shaking my head. "But at least there were dogs, Pip? Come, Pip," said Joe, pleadingly, "even if there weren't any veal cutlets, at least there were dogs?"
"No, Joe."
"A dog?" said Joe. "A puppy? Come on?"
"No, Joe. There was nothing at all of the kind."
As I fixed my eyes hopelessly on Joe, Joe stared at me in dismay. "Pip, old chap! This won't do, old fellow! I say! Where do you expect to end up?"
"It's terrible, Joe, isn't it?"
"Terrible?" cried Joe. "Awful! What got into you?"

"I don't know what got into me, Joe," I replied, letting go of his shirt sleeve and sitting down in the ashes at his feet, hanging my head. "But I wish you hadn't taught me to call knaves at cards Jacks. And I wish my boots weren't so thick and my hands weren't so coarse."

And then I told Joe that I felt very miserable, and that I hadn't been able to explain myself to Mrs. Joe and Pumblechook, who were so rude to me. And that there had been a beautiful young lady at Miss Havisham's who was dreadfully proud, and that she had said I was common, and that I knew I was common, and that I wished I were not common. And that the lies had come of it somehow, though I didn't know how.
This was a question of deep philosophy, at least as difficult for Joe to deal with as for me. But Joe took the matter entirely out of the realm of philosophy, and in doing so, solved it.

"There's one thing you can be sure of, Pip," said Joe, after some thought. "Lies are lies. However they come, they shouldn't come, and they come from the father of lies, and lead to the same place. Don't tell any more of them, Pip. That isn't the way to stop being common, old chap. And as for being common, I don't see it clearly at all. You are uncommon in some things. You're uncommonly small. And you're an uncommonly good scholar."
"No, I am ignorant and backward, Joe."
"Why, look at what a letter you wrote last night! Written in print, even! I've seen letters — ah! and from gentlefolk! — that I'll swear weren't written in print," said Joe.
"I have learned next to nothing, Joe. You think too much of me. That's all it is."

"Well, Pip," said Joe, "be it so or not, you have to be a common scholar before you can be an uncommon one, I should hope! The king on his throne, with his crown on his head, can't sit and write his acts of Parliament in print without having begun, when he was a young prince, with the alphabet. Ah!" added Joe, with a shake of his head full of meaning, "and begun at A, too, and worked his way to Z. And I know what that's like, though I can't say I've quite done it myself."
There was some hope in this piece of wisdom, and it rather encouraged me.

"Whether common people in common jobs," Joe went on thoughtfully, "might not be better off keeping company with other common people, instead of going out to play with uncommon ones — which reminds me to hope that there was a flag, maybe?"
"No, Joe."

"I'm sorry there wasn't a flag, Pip. Whether that might be or might not be, it's not something we can look into now without putting your sister on the rampage, and that's not something to be done on purpose. Look here, Pip, at what a true friend says to you. And this is what your true friend says: If you can't become uncommon by going straight, you'll never get there by going crooked. So don't tell any more lies, Pip, and live well and die happy."
"You're not angry with me, Joe?"

"No, old chap. But bearing in mind that those were — what I mean to say — of a shocking and outrageous sort, referring to the ones involving veal cutlets and dog fighting — a sincere well-wisher would advise, Pip, that you think about them when you go upstairs to bed. That's all, old chap, and don't ever do it again."

When I got up to my little room and said my prayers, I did not forget Joe's advice. Yet my young mind was in such a disturbed and ungrateful state that I thought long after I lay down about how common Estella would consider Joe, a mere blacksmith. How thick his boots were, and how coarse his hands. I thought about how Joe and my sister were sitting in the kitchen, and how I had come up to bed from the kitchen, and how Miss Havisham and Estella never sat in a kitchen but were far above the level of such common activities. I fell asleep recalling what I "used to do" when I was at Miss Havisham's — as though I had been there weeks or months instead of hours, and as though it were an old subject of memory instead of one that had come up only that day.

That was a memorable day for me, for it made great changes in me. But it is the same with any life. Imagine one particular day struck out of it, and think how different its course would have been. Pause, you who read this, and think for a moment of the long chain of iron or gold, of thorns or flowers, that would never have bound you, if not for the forming of the first link on one memorable day.

chapters.title: Chapter 10
paragraphs: The brilliant idea occurred to me a morning or two later when I woke that the best step I could take toward making myself uncommon was to get everything Biddy knew out of her. Following this shining plan, I mentioned to Biddy when I went to Mr. Wopsle's great-aunt's that evening that I had a particular reason for wanting to get on in life, and that I would be very grateful if she would share all her knowledge with me. Biddy, who was the most obliging of girls, immediately said she would, and actually began to carry out her promise within five minutes.

The educational system established by Mr. Wopsle's great-aunt may be summarized as follows. The students ate apples and shoved straws down one another's backs, until Mr. Wopsle's great-aunt gathered her strength and made a wild lunge at them with a birch rod. After receiving this charge with every sign of mockery, the students formed a line and passed a ragged book from hand to hand with a great buzzing. The book had an alphabet in it, some numbers and tables, and a little spelling — that is to say, it once had. As soon as this book began to circulate, Mr. Wopsle's great-aunt fell into a coma, caused either by sleep or a bout of rheumatism. The students then held a competition on the subject of boots, to determine who could stomp the hardest on whose toes. This exercise lasted until Biddy charged at them and handed out three battered Bibles (shaped as if they had been clumsily cut off the end of something), more illegibly printed than any reading material I have since encountered, spotted all over with rust stains, and with various specimens of the insect world crushed between their pages. This part of the curriculum was usually enlivened by several fights between Biddy and rebellious students. When the fights were over, Biddy called out a page number, and then we all read aloud what we could — or couldn't — in a frightful chorus, Biddy leading with a high, shrill, monotonous voice, and none of us having the least idea of, or respect for, what we were reading about. When this horrible racket had lasted a certain time, it mechanically woke Mr. Wopsle's great-aunt, who lurched at some random boy and pulled his ears. This was understood to end the lesson for the evening, and we emerged into the air with shrieks of intellectual triumph. It is fair to say that no student was forbidden from amusing himself with a slate or even with ink (when there was any), but it was not easy to pursue that branch of study in winter. The little shop in which classes were held — which was also Mr. Wopsle's great-aunt's sitting room and bedroom — was lit only by one dim candle with no snuffers.

It seemed to me that becoming uncommon would take time under these circumstances. Nevertheless, I resolved to try. That very evening Biddy began on our special agreement, sharing some information from her little price catalog under the heading of moist sugar, and lending me, to copy at home, a large old English D which she had copied from a newspaper heading and which I assumed, until she told me what it was, to be the design for a buckle.

Of course there was a pub in the village, and of course Joe liked to smoke his pipe there sometimes. I had received strict orders from my sister to collect him at the Three Jolly Bargemen that evening on my way from school, and bring him home or face the consequences. So to the Three Jolly Bargemen I went.

There was a bar at the Jolly Bargemen, with some alarmingly long chalk tallies on the wall beside the door, which seemed to me to never get paid off. They had been there ever since I could remember and had grown more than I had. But there was plenty of chalk in our area, and perhaps the people never missed a chance to put it to use.

It being Saturday night, I found the landlord looking rather grimly at these records. But since my business was with Joe and not with him, I merely wished him good evening and passed into the common room at the end of the hallway, where there was a bright, large kitchen fire. Joe was smoking his pipe in company with Mr. Wopsle and a stranger. Joe greeted me as usual with "Hello, Pip, old chap!" and the moment he said it, the stranger turned his head and looked at me.

He was a secretive-looking man I had never seen before. His head was tilted to one side, and one of his eyes was half closed, as if he were taking aim at something with an invisible gun. He had a pipe in his mouth. He took it out, slowly blew all his smoke away while watching me the whole time, and nodded. So I nodded, and then he nodded again, and made room on the bench beside him for me to sit down.

But since I was used to sitting beside Joe whenever I came to that place, I said, "No, thank you, sir," and dropped into the space Joe made for me on the opposite bench. The strange man, after glancing at Joe and seeing that his attention was elsewhere, nodded to me again when I had sat down, and then rubbed his leg — in a very odd way, I thought.
"You were saying," said the strange man, turning to Joe, "that you're a blacksmith."
"Yes. I said it, you know," said Joe.
"What'll you drink, Mr. — ? You didn't mention your name, by the way."
Joe mentioned it now, and the strange man used it. "What'll you drink, Mr. Gargery? My treat? To top things off?"
"Well," said Joe, "to tell you the truth, I'm not much in the habit of drinking at anybody's expense but my own."
"Habit? No," returned the stranger, "but just this once, and on a Saturday night too. Come! Name your drink, Mr. Gargery."
"I wouldn't wish to be difficult company," said Joe. "Rum."
"Rum," repeated the stranger. "And will the other gentleman name his choice?"
"Rum," said Mr. Wopsle.
"Three rums!" cried the stranger, calling to the landlord. "Glasses all round!"
"This other gentleman," observed Joe, by way of introducing Mr. Wopsle, "is a gentleman you'd like to hear speak up. Our parish clerk."
"Ah!" said the stranger, quickly, cocking his eye at me. "The lonely church, right out on the marshes, with graves around it!"
"That's the one," said Joe.

The stranger, with a comfortable sort of grunt over his pipe, put his legs up on the bench he had to himself. He wore a broad-brimmed traveler's hat, and under it a handkerchief tied over his head like a cap, so that no hair showed. As he looked at the fire, I thought I saw a cunning expression, followed by a half-laugh, cross his face.
"I'm not familiar with this country, gentlemen, but it seems lonely country toward the river."
"Most marshes are," said Joe.
"No doubt, no doubt. Do you find any gypsies, now, or tramps, or vagrants of any sort out there?"
"No," said Joe. "Nothing but a runaway convict now and then. And we don't find them easily. Eh, Mr. Wopsle?"
Mr. Wopsle, with a grand recollection of past discomfort, agreed — but not warmly.
"Seems you've been out after such?" asked the stranger.
"Once," returned Joe. "Not that we wanted to catch them, you understand. We went out as onlookers — me and Mr. Wopsle and Pip. Didn't we, Pip?"
"Yes, Joe."

The stranger looked at me again — still with that cocked eye, as if he were expressly taking aim at me with his invisible gun — and said, "He's a healthy-looking young bag of bones, that. What is it you call him?"
"Pip," said Joe.
"Christened Pip?"
"No, not christened Pip."
"Surname Pip?"
"No," said Joe. "It's a kind of family name he gave himself as a baby, and he's been called by it since."
"Your son?"

"Well," said Joe thoughtfully — not, of course, that there was any real need to think about it, but because it was the way at the Jolly Bargemen to appear to consider deeply everything that was discussed over pipes — "well — no. No, he isn't."
"Nephew?" said the strange man.
"Well," said Joe, with the same show of deep thought, "he's not — no, to be honest, he's not — my nephew."
"What the blazes is he?" asked the stranger. Which seemed to me an unnecessarily forceful question.

Mr. Wopsle stepped in at that point. As one who knew all about family relationships, having professional reason to remember which female relatives a man could not marry, he explained the connection between me and Joe. Getting into the swing of things, Mr. Wopsle finished with a most ferociously snarling passage from Richard the Third, and seemed to think he had fully explained himself when he added, "As the poet says."

And here I should note that whenever Mr. Wopsle referred to me, he considered it necessary to ruffle my hair and poke it into my eyes. I cannot understand why everybody of his standing who visited our house always put me through the same irritating treatment. Yet I cannot recall a single time in my early youth when I was mentioned in our family circle without some large-handed person taking similar liberties with my eyes.

All this while, the strange man looked at nobody but me, and looked at me as if he were determined to take his shot at me at last and bring me down. But he said nothing after his "blazes" remark, until the glasses of rum and water were brought. Then he made his move, and it was the most extraordinary move.

It was not a spoken remark, but a performance in silent gesture, and it was clearly aimed at me. He stirred his rum and water pointedly at me, and he tasted his rum and water pointedly at me. And he stirred it and he tasted it — not with the spoon that was brought to him, but with a file.

He did this so that nobody but I saw the file. When he had finished, he wiped the file and put it in his breast pocket. I knew it to be Joe's file, and I knew that he knew my convict, the moment I saw it. I sat gazing at him, spellbound. But he now settled back on his bench, paid me very little attention, and talked mainly about turnips.

There was a pleasant sense of cleaning up and pausing quietly before going on with life in our village on Saturday nights, which encouraged Joe to dare to stay out half an hour longer on Saturdays than on other nights. The half hour and the rum and water running out together, Joe got up to go and took me by the hand.
"Wait half a moment, Mr. Gargery," said the strange man. "I think I've got a bright new shilling somewhere in my pocket, and if I have, the boy shall have it."
He fished it out from a handful of small change, folded it in some crumpled paper, and gave it to me. "Yours!" said he. "Mind! Your own."

I thanked him, staring at him far beyond the bounds of good manners, and holding tight to Joe. He said good night to Joe, and good night to Mr. Wopsle (who left with us), and gave me only a look with his aiming eye — no, not a look, for he closed it. But wonders may be done with an eye by hiding it.

On the way home, if I had been in the mood for talking, the conversation would have been entirely one-sided. Mr. Wopsle left us at the door of the Jolly Bargemen, and Joe walked the whole way home with his mouth wide open, to rinse the rum out with as much air as possible. But I was stunned by this resurfacing of my old crime and old acquaintance, and could think of nothing else.

My sister was not in a particularly bad temper when we presented ourselves in the kitchen. Joe was encouraged by this unusual circumstance to tell her about the bright shilling. "A fake one, I'll bet," said Mrs. Joe triumphantly, "or he wouldn't have given it to the boy! Let's see it."
I took it out of the paper, and it proved to be a good one. "But what's this?" said Mrs. Joe, throwing down the shilling and snatching up the paper. "Two one-pound notes?"

Nothing less than two fat, sweaty one-pound notes that seemed to have been on the friendliest terms with every cattle market in the county. Joe grabbed his hat and ran with them to the Jolly Bargemen to return them to their owner. While he was gone, I sat on my usual stool and stared blankly at my sister, feeling fairly certain that the man would not be there.

Soon Joe came back, saying that the man was gone, but that he had left word at the Three Jolly Bargemen about the notes. Then my sister sealed them up in a piece of paper, put them under some dried rose petals in a decorative teapot on top of a cabinet in the parlor. There they remained, a nightmare to me, many and many a night and day.

I slept badly when I got to bed, thinking about the strange man taking aim at me with his invisible gun, and about what a guilty, coarse, common thing it was to be in a secret conspiracy with convicts — a part of my lowly career that I had previously forgotten. I was haunted by the file, too. I was possessed by a dread that when I least expected it, the file would reappear. I lulled myself to sleep by thinking about Miss Havisham's, next Wednesday. And in my sleep I saw the file coming at me out of a door, without seeing who held it, and I screamed myself awake.

chapters.title: Chapter 11
paragraphs: At the appointed time I returned to Miss Havisham's, and my hesitant ring at the gate brought out Estella. She locked it after letting me in, as she had before, and again led me into the dark passage where her candle stood. She took no notice of me until she had the candle in her hand, when she looked over her shoulder and said haughtily, "You are to come this way today," and led me to a completely different part of the house.

The passage was a long one and seemed to run through the whole square basement of the Manor House. We crossed only one side of the square, however, and at the end of it she stopped, put her candle down, and opened a door. Here, daylight reappeared, and I found myself in a small paved courtyard. The opposite side was formed by a separate house that looked as if it had once belonged to the manager or head clerk of the now-dead brewery. There was a clock on the outer wall of this house. Like the clock in Miss Havisham's room, and like Miss Havisham's watch, it had stopped at twenty minutes to nine.

We went in at the door, which stood open, and into a gloomy room with a low ceiling, on the ground floor at the back. There were several people in the room, and Estella said to me as she joined them, "You are to go and stand there, boy, till you are wanted." "There" being the window, I crossed to it and stood "there," in a very uncomfortable state of mind, looking out.

It opened onto the ground and looked into a miserable corner of the neglected garden, at a mess of rotting cabbage stalks and one box tree that had been clipped round long ago, like a pudding, and had a new growth on top of a different color, as if that part of the pudding had stuck to the pot and burned. This was my humble thought as I studied the box tree. There had been some light snow overnight, and it lay nowhere else that I knew of, but it had not quite melted from the cold shadow of this patch of garden. The wind caught it up in little swirls and threw it at the window, as if punishing me for coming there.

I guessed that my arrival had stopped conversation in the room, and that the others were looking at me. I could see nothing of the room except the fire's reflection in the window glass, but I stiffened in every joint with the awareness that I was being closely inspected.

There were three ladies in the room and one gentleman. Before I had been standing at the window five minutes, they had somehow conveyed to me that they were all flatterers and frauds, but that each of them pretended not to know that the others were flatterers and frauds. Because admitting that you knew it would have made you one yourself.

They all had a listless, dreary air of waiting for somebody's pleasure, and the most talkative of the ladies had to speak quite stiffly to hold back a yawn. This lady, whose name was Camilla, reminded me very much of my sister, except that she was older and — as I discovered when I caught sight of her — had blunter features. Indeed, when I knew her better, I began to think it was a mercy she had any features at all, so blank and flat was the dead wall of her face.
"Poor dear soul!" said this lady, with a bluntness quite like my sister's. "Nobody's enemy but his own!"
"It would be much more commendable to be somebody else's enemy," said the gentleman. "Far more natural."
"Cousin Raymond," observed another lady, "we are supposed to love our neighbor."
"Sarah Pocket," returned Cousin Raymond, "if a man is not his own neighbor, who is?"

Miss Pocket laughed, and Camilla laughed and said, stifling a yawn, "The idea!" But I thought they seemed to think it rather a good idea too. The other lady, who had not spoken yet, said gravely and emphatically, "Very true!"

"Poor soul!" Camilla went on (I knew they had all been looking at me in the meantime). "He is so very strange! Would anyone believe that when Tom's wife died, he actually could not be persuaded to see the importance of the children having the deepest mourning trimmings on their clothes? 'Good Lord!' says he, 'Camilla, what can it matter as long as the poor bereaved little things are in black?' So like Matthew! The idea!"
"Good points in him, good points in him," said Cousin Raymond. "Heaven forbid I should deny good points in him. But he never had, and he never will have, any sense of what is proper."

"You know I was obliged," said Camilla, "I was obliged to be firm. I said, 'It WILL NOT DO, for the credit of the family.' I told him that without deep trimmings, the family was disgraced. I cried about it from breakfast till dinner. I damaged my digestion. And at last he stormed out in his violent way and said, with an oath, 'Then do as you like.' Thank goodness it will always be a comfort to me to know that I instantly went out in pouring rain and bought the things."
"He paid for them, did he not?" asked Estella.
"It's not the question, my dear child, who paid for them," returned Camilla. "I bought them. And I shall often think of that with peace, when I wake up in the night."

The ringing of a distant bell, combined with the echo of some cry or call along the passage I had come through, interrupted the conversation and caused Estella to say to me, "Now, boy!" As I turned around, they all looked at me with the utmost contempt, and as I went out, I heard Sarah Pocket say, "Well, I am sure! What next!" and Camilla add, with indignation, "Was there ever such a thing! The idea!"
As we were going with our candle along the dark passage, Estella stopped suddenly and, turning around, said in her taunting way, with her face quite close to mine:
"Well?"
"Well, miss?" I answered, nearly falling over her and catching myself.
She stood looking at me, and of course I stood looking at her.
"Am I pretty?"
"Yes. I think you are very pretty."
"Am I insulting?"
"Not so much as you were last time," said I.
"Not so much?"
"No."
She flared up when she asked the last question, and she slapped my face with all the force she had when I answered it.
"Now?" said she. "You little coarse monster, what do you think of me now?"
"I shall not tell you."
"Because you are going to tell upstairs. Is that it?"
"No," said I, "that's not it."
"Why don't you cry again, you little wretch?"

"Because I'll never cry for you again," said I. Which was, I suppose, as false a declaration as was ever made. For I was inwardly crying for her then, and I know what I know of the pain she cost me afterward.
We went on our way upstairs after this episode, and as we were going up, we met a gentleman groping his way down.
"Whom have we here?" asked the gentleman, stopping and looking at me.
"A boy," said Estella.

He was a burly man with an exceedingly dark complexion, an exceedingly large head, and a correspondingly large hand. He took my chin in his large hand and turned my face up to look at me by the light of the candle. He was prematurely bald on top of his head and had bushy black eyebrows that wouldn't lie flat but stood up bristling. His eyes were set very deep in his head and were disagreeably sharp and suspicious. He had a large watch chain, and strong black stubble where his beard and whiskers would have been if he had let them grow. He was nothing to me, and I could not have foreseen then that he would ever be anything to me, but it happened that I had this chance to observe him well.
"Boy from the neighborhood? Hey?" said he.
"Yes, sir," said I.
"How do you come here?"
"Miss Havisham sent for me, sir," I explained.
"Well! Behave yourself. I have plenty of experience with boys, and you're a bad lot. Now mind!" said he, biting the side of his great forefinger as he frowned at me, "you behave yourself!"

With those words he released me — which I was glad of, for his hand smelled of scented soap — and went on his way downstairs. I wondered whether he could be a doctor. But no, I thought, he couldn't be a doctor, or he would have a quieter and more persuasive manner. There was not much time to think about it, for we were soon in Miss Havisham's room, where she and everything else were just as I had left them. Estella left me standing near the door, and I stood there until Miss Havisham noticed me from the dressing table.
"So!" she said, without being startled or surprised. "The days have worn away, have they?"
"Yes, ma'am. Today is — "
"There, there, there!" with the impatient movement of her fingers. "I don't want to know. Are you ready to play?"
I was forced to answer, with some confusion, "I don't think I am, ma'am."
"Not at cards again?" she demanded, with a searching look.
"Yes, ma'am. I could do that, if I was wanted."
"Since this house strikes you as old and grim, boy," said Miss Havisham impatiently, "and you are unwilling to play, are you willing to work?"
I could answer this question with a better heart than the other, and I said I was quite willing.
"Then go into that opposite room," said she, pointing at the door behind me with her withered hand, "and wait there till I come."

I crossed the staircase landing and entered the room she pointed out. Like the other, daylight was completely shut out of this room, and it had a stale, airless smell that was oppressive. A fire had recently been lit in the damp, old-fashioned grate, and it was more inclined to go out than burn up. The reluctant smoke hanging in the room seemed colder than the clearer air outside — like our own marsh mist.
