Some dusty candelabras on the high mantelpiece faintly lit the room — or it would be more accurate to say, faintly disturbed its darkness. It was a spacious room, and must once have been handsome, but everything visible in it was covered with dust and mold, and crumbling to pieces. The most prominent thing was a long table with a cloth spread on it, as if a feast had been in preparation when the house and the clocks all stopped together. Some kind of centerpiece sat in the middle of this cloth, so heavily covered with cobwebs that its shape was impossible to make out. As I looked along the yellow expanse from which it seemed to grow like a black fungus, I saw speckled spiders with blotchy bodies running toward it and away from it, as if some matter of the greatest public importance had just occurred in the spider community.

I heard mice too, rustling behind the panels, as if the same event were important to them. But the black beetles took no notice of the commotion, and crept about the hearth in a heavy, elderly way, as if they were nearsighted and hard of hearing, and not on speaking terms with each other.

These crawling things had fascinated my attention, and I was watching them from a distance, when Miss Havisham laid a hand on my shoulder. In her other hand she had a crutch-topped walking stick, on which she leaned. She looked like the witch of the place.
"This," said she, pointing to the long table with her stick, "is where I will be laid when I am dead. They shall come and look at me here."
With a vague fear that she might get up on the table right then and there and die at once — the living version of the ghastly waxwork at the fair — I shrank from her touch.
"What do you think that is?" she asked me, pointing again with her stick. "That, where those cobwebs are?"
"I can't guess what it is, ma'am."
"It's a great cake. A bride's cake. Mine!"
She looked wildly around the room, then said, leaning on me while her hand twitched on my shoulder, "Come, come, come! Walk me, walk me!"

I understood from this that the work I had to do was to walk Miss Havisham round and round the room. So I started at once, and she leaned on my shoulder, and we went at a pace that might have been an imitation — inspired by my first impulse under that roof — of Mr. Pumblechook's carriage horse.

She was not physically strong, and after a little time said, "Slower!" Still, we went at an impatient, irregular speed, and as we went, she twitched the hand on my shoulder and worked her mouth. I was led to believe we were going fast because her thoughts were going fast. After a while she said, "Call Estella!" so I went out on the landing and shouted that name as I had done before. When her light appeared, I returned to Miss Havisham, and we started round and round the room again.

If Estella had come just to watch, I would have felt quite unhappy enough. But she brought with her the three ladies and the gentleman I had seen downstairs, and I didn't know what to do. Out of politeness, I would have stopped, but Miss Havisham twitched my shoulder, and we pressed on — with my shamefaced awareness that they would think the whole thing was my doing.
"Dear Miss Havisham," said Miss Sarah Pocket. "How well you look!"
"I do not," returned Miss Havisham. "I am yellow skin and bone."
Camilla brightened when Miss Pocket was rebuffed like that, and she murmured, gazing pityingly at Miss Havisham, "Poor dear soul! Certainly not to be expected to look well, poor thing. The idea!"

"And how are you?" said Miss Havisham to Camilla. Since we were close to Camilla then, I would have stopped as a matter of course, but Miss Havisham wouldn't stop. We swept on, and I felt that I was deeply annoying to Camilla.
"Thank you, Miss Havisham," she returned. "I am as well as can be expected."
"Why, what's the matter with you?" asked Miss Havisham, with great sharpness.
"Nothing worth mentioning," replied Camilla. "I don't wish to make a display of my feelings, but I have habitually thought of you more at night than is good for me."
"Then don't think of me," retorted Miss Havisham.

"Very easily said!" remarked Camilla, politely suppressing a sob, while her upper lip twitched and her tears overflowed. "Raymond is a witness to what ginger and smelling salts I have to take in the night. Raymond is a witness to what nervous jerking I get in my legs. Choking and nervous jerking, however, are nothing new to me when I think anxiously about those I love. If I could be less affectionate and sensitive, I would have better digestion and iron nerves. I certainly wish it could be so. But as for not thinking of you in the night — the idea!" Here, a burst of tears.

The Raymond referred to, I understood, was the gentleman present, and I understood him to be Mr. Camilla. He came to the rescue at this point and said in a soothing, complimentary voice, "Camilla, my dear, it is well known that your family feelings are gradually undermining you to the extent of making one of your legs shorter than the other."
"I am not aware," observed the solemn lady whose voice I had heard only once, "that to think of any person is to make a great claim upon that person, my dear."

Miss Sarah Pocket, whom I now saw to be a little dry, brown, wrinkled old woman with a small face that might have been made of walnut shells and a large mouth like a cat's without the whiskers, supported this position by saying, "No, indeed, my dear. Hmm!"
"Thinking is easy enough," said the solemn lady.
"What is easier, you know?" agreed Miss Sarah Pocket.

"Oh, yes, yes!" cried Camilla, whose fermenting feelings seemed to rise from her legs to her chest. "It's all very true! It's a weakness to be so affectionate, but I can't help it. No doubt my health would be much better otherwise, but still I wouldn't change my nature if I could. It causes much suffering, but it's a comfort to know I have it, when I wake up in the night." Here another burst of feeling.
Miss Havisham and I had never stopped all this time, but kept going round and round the room — now brushing against the visitors' clothes, now giving them the full length of the dismal chamber.

"There's Matthew!" said Camilla. "Never mixing with any family ties, never coming here to see how Miss Havisham is! I have collapsed on the sofa with my corset strings cut, and lain there insensible for hours, with my head over the side and my hair all down and my feet I don't know where — "
("Much higher than your head, my love," said Mr. Camilla.)
"I have gone off into that state for hours and hours on account of Matthew's strange and inexplicable conduct, and nobody has thanked me."
"Really, I should think not!" put in the solemn lady.
"You see, my dear," added Miss Sarah Pocket (a pleasantly vicious person), "the question to ask yourself is, who did you expect to thank you, my love?"

"Without expecting any thanks, or anything of the sort," resumed Camilla, "I have remained in that state for hours and hours. Raymond is a witness to the extent of my choking, and how completely useless ginger has been. I have been heard at the piano tuner's across the street, where the poor mistaken children even thought it was pigeons cooing in the distance — and now to be told — " Here Camilla put her hand to her throat and began to produce quite chemical reactions there.
When this same Matthew was mentioned, Miss Havisham stopped me and herself, and stood looking at the speaker. This change had a powerful effect in bringing Camilla's chemistry to a sudden end.

"Matthew will come and see me at last," said Miss Havisham sternly, "when I am laid on that table. That will be his place — there," striking the table with her stick, "at my head! And yours will be there! And your husband's there! And Sarah Pocket's there! And Georgiana's there! Now you all know where to stand when you come to feast upon me. And now go!"
At the mention of each name, she had struck the table with her stick in a new place. She now said, "Walk me, walk me!" and we went on again.

"I suppose there's nothing to be done," exclaimed Camilla, "but obey and leave. It's something to have seen the object of one's love and duty for even so short a time. I shall think of it with a melancholy satisfaction when I wake up in the night. I wish Matthew could have that comfort, but he rejects it. I am determined not to make a display of my feelings, but it's very hard to be told you want to feast on your relatives — as if you were a giant — and to be told to go. The very idea!"

Mr. Camilla intervening, as Mrs. Camilla laid her hand on her heaving chest, that lady assumed a brave manner which I guessed was meant to express her intention of collapsing and choking the moment she was out of sight. Blowing a kiss to Miss Havisham, she was escorted out. Sarah Pocket and Georgiana competed over who should leave last. But Sarah was too shrewd to be outdone and circled around Georgiana with such artful slipperiness that Georgiana was forced to go first. Sarah Pocket then made her separate exit with, "Bless you, Miss Havisham dear!" and a smile of forgiving pity on her walnut-shell face for the weaknesses of the rest.

While Estella was away lighting them downstairs, Miss Havisham still walked with her hand on my shoulder, but more and more slowly. At last she stopped before the fire, and said, after muttering and staring at it for some seconds:
"This is my birthday, Pip."
I was about to wish her many happy returns, when she raised her stick.
"I don't allow it to be spoken of. I don't allow those who were here just now, or anyone, to speak of it. They come here on the day, but they dare not refer to it."
Of course I made no further effort to refer to it.

"On this day of the year, long before you were born, this heap of decay" — stabbing with her stick at the pile of cobwebs on the table, but not touching it — "was brought here. It and I have worn away together. The mice have gnawed at it, and sharper teeth than mice's teeth have gnawed at me."

She held the head of her stick against her heart as she stood looking at the table — she in her once-white dress, all yellow and withered; the once-white cloth all yellow and withered; everything around ready to crumble at a touch.

"When the ruin is complete," said she, with a ghastly look, "and when they lay me dead in my bride's dress on the bride's table — which shall be done, and which will be the final curse upon him — so much the better if it is done on this day!"

She stood looking at the table as if she were looking at her own figure lying there. I stayed quiet. Estella returned, and she too stayed quiet. It seemed to me that we continued like this for a long time. In the heavy air of the room, and the heavy darkness that brooded in its far corners, I even had the alarming thought that Estella and I might soon begin to decay ourselves.

At length, not coming out of her trance gradually but all at once, Miss Havisham said, "Let me see you two play cards. Why have you not begun?" With that, we returned to her room and sat down as before. I was beaten, as before. And again, as before, Miss Havisham watched us the whole time, directed my attention to Estella's beauty, and made me notice it all the more by trying her jewels on Estella's chest and hair.

Estella, for her part, treated me as before, except that she did not lower herself to speak. When we had played half a dozen games, a day was set for my return, and I was taken down to the yard to be fed in the same dog-like manner. There, too, I was again left to wander about as I pleased.

Whether a gate in the garden wall that I had scrambled up to peek over last time was, on that occasion, open or shut does not much matter. Enough to say that I saw no gate then, and I saw one now. Since it stood open, and since I knew Estella had let the visitors out — for she had returned with the keys in her hand — I strolled into the garden and wandered all over it. It was quite a wilderness, and there were old melon frames and cucumber frames in it, which in their decay seemed to have sprouted a crop of old hat pieces and boots, with the occasional weedy growth resembling a battered saucepan.

When I had exhausted the garden and a greenhouse with nothing in it but a collapsed grapevine and some bottles, I found myself in the gloomy corner I had looked out at from the window. Never doubting for a moment that the house was now empty, I looked in at another window and found myself, to my great surprise, exchanging a stare with a pale young gentleman with red eyelids and light hair.
This pale young gentleman quickly disappeared and reappeared beside me. He had been at his books when I found myself staring at him, and I now saw that he was ink-stained.
"Hello!" said he. "Young fellow!"
"Hello" being a general greeting best answered with itself, I said, "Hello!" — politely leaving out "young fellow."
"Who let you in?" said he.
"Miss Estella."
"Who gave you permission to wander about?"
"Miss Estella."
"Come and fight," said the pale young gentleman.

What could I do but follow him? I have often asked myself that question since. But what else could I do? His manner was so decisive, and I was so astonished, that I followed where he led, as if I were under a spell.

"Wait a minute, though," he said, spinning around before we had gone many steps. "I ought to give you a reason for fighting too. There it is!" In the most annoying manner, he instantly slapped his hands together, daintily kicked one leg up behind him, pulled my hair, slapped his hands again, ducked his head, and butted it into my stomach.

This bull-like move, besides being undeniably a liberty, was particularly unpleasant right after bread and meat. So I hit him, and was about to hit him again, when he said, "Aha! Would you?" and began dancing backward and forward in a way I had never seen before.

"Laws of the game!" said he. Here he hopped from his left leg to his right. "Regular rules!" Here he hopped from his right to his left. "Come to the ground and go through the proper form!" Here he dodged back and forth, doing all sorts of things while I looked at him helplessly.

I was secretly afraid of him when I saw how skilled he looked. But I felt, morally and physically, that his light head of hair had no business in the pit of my stomach, and that I had a right to consider it rude. So I followed him without a word to a secluded corner of the garden, formed by the meeting of two walls and hidden by some rubbish. When he asked if I was satisfied with the ground, and I said yes, he begged my leave to step away for a moment. He quickly returned with a bottle of water and a sponge dipped in vinegar. "Available for both," he said, placing them against the wall. And then he proceeded to pull off not just his jacket and waistcoat but his shirt too, in a manner that was lighthearted, businesslike, and bloodthirsty all at once.

Although he didn't look very healthy — he had spots on his face and a rash around his mouth — these dreadful preparations completely alarmed me. I judged him to be about my own age, but he was much taller, and he had a way of spinning himself around that was very impressive. Otherwise, he was a young gentleman in a gray suit (when not stripped for battle), with his elbows, knees, wrists, and heels considerably more developed than the rest of him.

My heart sank when I saw him squaring up to me with every sign of scientific precision, studying my body as if carefully choosing which bone to aim for. I have never been so surprised in my life as when I threw my first punch and saw him lying on his back, looking up at me with a bloody nose and his face extremely foreshortened.

But he was on his feet in an instant, and after sponging himself with a great show of skill, began squaring up again. The second greatest surprise of my life was seeing him on his back again, looking up at me out of a black eye.

His spirit inspired me with great respect. He seemed to have no strength, and he never once hit me hard, and he was always knocked down. But he would be up again in a moment, sponging himself or drinking from the water bottle with the greatest satisfaction in following proper form. Then he came at me with such an air and display that I believed he really was going to finish me off at last. He got badly bruised, for I am sorry to say that the more I hit him, the harder I hit him. But he came up again and again and again, until at last he got a bad fall with the back of his head against the wall. Even after that crisis, he got up and turned around and around confusedly a few times, not knowing where I was. But finally he went to his knees at his sponge and threw it up, panting out, "That means you have won."

He seemed so brave and innocent that although I had not started the fight, I felt only a gloomy satisfaction in my victory. Indeed, I go so far as to think that I regarded myself, while getting dressed, as a kind of savage young wolf or other wild beast. However, I got dressed, grimly wiping my bloody face now and then, and I said, "Can I help you?" and he said, "No thanks," and I said, "Good afternoon," and he said, "Same to you."

When I got to the courtyard, I found Estella waiting with the keys. But she neither asked me where I had been nor why I had kept her waiting. There was a bright flush on her face, as though something had happened to delight her. Instead of going straight to the gate, she stepped back into the passage and beckoned me.
"Come here! You may kiss me, if you like."

I kissed her cheek as she turned it to me. I think I would have gone through a great deal to kiss her cheek. But I felt that the kiss was given to the coarse common boy the way a piece of money might have been, and that it was worth nothing.

What with the birthday visitors, and the cards, and the fight, my stay had lasted so long that when I neared home, the light on the sandbar off the point on the marshes was gleaming against a black night sky, and Joe's furnace was throwing a path of fire across the road.

chapters.title: Chapter 12
paragraphs: My mind grew very uneasy on the subject of the pale young gentleman. The more I thought about the fight, and recalled him on his back in various stages of swollen and reddened face, the more certain it seemed that something would be done to me. I felt that the pale young gentleman's blood was on my hands, and that the law would avenge it. Without any definite idea of the penalties I had earned, it was clear to me that village boys could not go prowling around the country, raiding the houses of gentlefolk and beating up the studious youth of England, without leaving themselves open to severe punishment. For some days, I even stayed close to home and looked out the kitchen door with the greatest caution before going on an errand, in case the officers from the county jail should pounce on me. The pale young gentleman's nose had stained my trousers, and I tried to wash out that evidence of my guilt in the dead of night. I had cut my knuckles against his teeth, and I twisted my imagination into a thousand knots devising unbelievable ways of explaining that damning detail when I should be dragged before the judges.

When the day came round for my return to the scene of my violent crime, my terrors reached their peak. Whether officers of justice, specially sent down from London, would be lying in ambush behind the gate. Whether Miss Havisham, preferring to take personal vengeance for an outrage done to her house, might rise in those grave clothes of hers, draw a pistol, and shoot me dead. Whether hired boys — a numerous band of mercenaries — might be waiting to attack me in the brewery and beat me until I was no more. It was high praise of my confidence in the pale young gentleman's character that I never imagined him part of these attacks. They always came into my mind as the actions of his unwise relatives, driven on by the state of his face and an outraged sympathy with the family features.

However, go to Miss Havisham's I must, and go I did. And behold! Nothing came of the fight. It was not mentioned in any way, and no pale young gentleman was to be found on the premises. I found the same gate open and explored the garden, and even looked in at the windows of the separate house. But my view was suddenly blocked by closed shutters inside, and all was lifeless. Only in the corner where the fight had taken place could I find any evidence of the young gentleman's existence. There were traces of his blood in that spot, and I covered them with garden soil to hide them from the eye of man.

On the broad landing between Miss Havisham's own room and that other room where the long table was laid out, I saw a garden chair — a light chair on wheels that you pushed from behind. It had been placed there since my last visit, and I entered that same day on a regular routine of pushing Miss Havisham in this chair (when she was tired of walking with her hand on my shoulder) round her own room, across the landing, and round the other room. Over and over and over again we would make these circuits, and sometimes they would last as long as three hours straight. I naturally fall into a general mention of these trips as many, because it was immediately settled that I should return every other day at noon for these purposes, and because I am now going to summarize a period of at least eight or ten months.

As we grew more used to each other, Miss Havisham talked more to me, and asked me questions like what had I learned and what was I going to be? I told her I was going to be apprenticed to Joe, I believed. I went on at length about knowing nothing and wanting to know everything, hoping she might offer some help toward that goal. But she didn't. On the contrary, she seemed to prefer me being ignorant. Nor did she ever give me any money — or anything except my daily dinner — or ever mention that I should be paid for my services.

Estella was always around, and always let me in and out, but never told me I might kiss her again. Sometimes she would coldly put up with me. Sometimes she would lower herself to notice me. Sometimes she would be quite friendly. Sometimes she would tell me fiercely that she hated me. Miss Havisham would often ask me in a whisper, or when we were alone, "Does she grow prettier and prettier, Pip?" And when I said yes (for indeed she did), she would seem to enjoy it greedily. Also, when we played cards, Miss Havisham would look on with a greedy delight in Estella's moods, whatever they were. And sometimes, when her moods were so many and so contradictory that I was puzzled what to say or do, Miss Havisham would embrace her with excessive fondness, murmuring something in her ear that sounded like, "Break their hearts, my pride and hope, break their hearts and have no mercy!"

There was a song Joe used to hum fragments of at the forge, with a refrain of Old Clem. This was not a very formal way of honoring a patron saint, but I believe Old Clem held that role for smiths. It was a song that imitated the rhythm of beating iron, and was really just an excuse to work in Old Clem's respected name. It went: hammer boys round — Old Clem! With a thump and a sound — Old Clem! Beat it out, beat it out — Old Clem! With a clink for the stout — Old Clem! Blow the fire, blow the fire — Old Clem! Roaring dryer, soaring higher — Old Clem! One day, soon after the chair appeared, Miss Havisham suddenly said to me, with the impatient movement of her fingers, "There, there, there! Sing!" I was surprised into humming this little song as I pushed her across the floor. It happened to catch her fancy so much that she took it up in a low, brooding voice, as if she were singing in her sleep. After that, it became our custom to sing it as we moved about, and Estella would often join in. Though the whole tune was so quiet, even when there were three of us, that it made less noise in the grim old house than the lightest breath of wind.

What could I become with these surroundings? How could my character fail to be shaped by them? Is it any wonder that my thoughts were dazed, as my eyes were, when I came out into the natural light from those misty yellow rooms?

Perhaps I might have told Joe about the pale young gentleman, if I had not previously been led into those enormous inventions I had confessed to. Under the circumstances, I felt that Joe could hardly fail to see in the pale young gentleman an appropriate passenger for the black velvet coach. So I said nothing about him. Besides, that reluctance to have Miss Havisham and Estella discussed, which had come over me from the beginning, grew much stronger as time went on. I placed complete trust in no one but Biddy. But I told poor Biddy everything. Why it came naturally to me to do so, and why Biddy had a deep concern in everything I told her, I did not know then, though I think I know now.

Meanwhile, meetings went on in the kitchen at home that were almost unbearably irritating to my frustrated spirit. That donkey Pumblechook often came over at night to discuss my prospects with my sister. And I really do believe — to this day, with less guilt than I ought to feel — that if these hands could have removed a pin from his carriage wheel, they would have done it. The wretched man had such a stubbornly narrow mind that he could not discuss my prospects without having me in front of him — as if to operate on — and he would drag me up from my stool (usually by the collar) where I sat quietly in a corner. Putting me before the fire as if I were about to be cooked, he would begin by saying, "Now, ma'am, here is this boy! Here is this boy that you brought up by hand. Hold up your head, boy, and be forever grateful to those who did it. Now, ma'am, with respect to this boy!" And then he would ruffle my hair the wrong way — which from my earliest memory, as I've already mentioned, I have deeply resented anyone doing — and would hold me before him by the sleeve, a spectacle of stupidity matched only by himself.

Then he and my sister would launch into such foolish speculation about Miss Havisham, about what she would do with me and for me, that I used to want — quite painfully — to burst into angry tears, fly at Pumblechook, and pummel him all over. In these conversations, my sister spoke to me as if she were painfully pulling out one of my teeth with every reference. Meanwhile, Pumblechook, self-appointed as my patron, would sit watching me with a critical eye, like an architect of my fortunes who considered himself stuck on a very unrewarding job.

In these discussions, Joe took no part. But he was often talked at while they were going on, because Mrs. Joe noticed he was not in favor of me being taken from the forge. I was now fully old enough to be apprenticed to Joe. When Joe sat with the poker on his knees, thoughtfully raking the ashes between the lower bars, my sister would interpret that innocent action as opposition on his part so thoroughly that she would pounce on him, take the poker from his hands, shake him, and put it away. There was a most irritating end to every one of these debates. Quite suddenly, with nothing leading up to it, my sister would stop herself mid-yawn, and catching sight of me, would swoop down with, "Come! That's enough of you! You get along to bed. You've given enough trouble for one night, I hope!" As if I had begged them, as a favor, to make my life miserable.

We went on this way for a long time, and it seemed likely we would continue this way for a long time more, when one day Miss Havisham stopped short as she and I were walking, she leaning on my shoulder, and said with some displeasure:
"You are growing tall, Pip!"
I thought it best to suggest, through a thoughtful look, that this might be caused by circumstances beyond my control.

She said no more at the time, but she soon stopped and looked at me again, and again after that, and looked frowning and moody. On the next day I came, when our usual exercise was over and I had brought her back to her dressing table, she stopped me with the impatient movement of her fingers:
"Tell me the name again of that blacksmith of yours."
"Joe Gargery, ma'am."
"Meaning the master you were to be apprenticed to?"
"Yes, Miss Havisham."
"You had better be apprenticed at once. Would Gargery come here with you, and bring your papers, do you think?"
I indicated that I had no doubt he would consider it an honor to be asked.
"Then let him come."
"At any particular time, Miss Havisham?"
"There, there! I know nothing about times. Let him come soon, and come along with you."

When I got home that night and delivered this message for Joe, my sister "went on the rampage" to a more alarming degree than ever before. She asked me and Joe whether we thought she was a doormat under our feet, and how we dared to treat her this way, and what company we graciously thought she was fit for. When she had exhausted a torrent of such questions, she threw a candlestick at Joe, burst into loud sobbing, got out the dustpan — which was always a very bad sign — put on her coarse apron, and began cleaning to a terrible extent. Not satisfied with a dry cleaning, she got a pail and scrubbing brush, and cleaned us out of house and home, so that we stood shivering in the back yard. It was ten o'clock at night before we dared to creep back in, and then she asked Joe why he hadn't married a slave outright. Joe offered no answer, poor fellow, but stood feeling his whiskers and looking dejectedly at me, as if he thought it really might have been a better choice.

chapters.title: Chapter 13
paragraphs: It was a trial to my feelings, on the day after next, to see Joe dressing himself in his Sunday clothes to come with me to Miss Havisham's. However, since he thought his best suit necessary for the occasion, it was not for me to tell him he looked far better in his work clothes. Especially because I knew he made himself so terribly uncomfortable entirely on my account, and that it was for me he pulled his shirt collar so high behind that it made the hair on the top of his head stand up like a tuft of feathers.

At breakfast, my sister declared her intention of coming to town with us and being left at Uncle Pumblechook's, to be collected "when we had done with our fine ladies" — a way of putting it from which Joe seemed to expect the worst. The forge was shut up for the day, and Joe chalked on the door (as he always did on the very rare occasions when he wasn't at work) the single word HOUT, accompanied by a sketch of an arrow supposed to be flying in the direction he had gone.

We walked to town, my sister leading the way in a very large bonnet and carrying a basket like the Great Seal of England in plaited straw, a pair of overshoes, a spare shawl, and an umbrella, though it was a fine bright day. I'm not quite sure whether these articles were carried as a penance or a show of wealth. But I rather think they were displayed as property — much as Cleopatra or any other royal lady on the warpath might display her riches in a parade.

When we reached Pumblechook's, my sister swept in and left us. Since it was almost noon, Joe and I went straight on to Miss Havisham's house. Estella opened the gate as usual, and the moment she appeared, Joe took his hat off and stood weighing it by the brim in both his hands, as if he had some urgent reason for being precise to a fraction of an ounce.

Estella took no notice of either of us, but led the way that I knew so well. I followed close behind her, and Joe came last. When I looked back at Joe in the long passage, he was still weighing his hat with the greatest care and was coming after us in long strides on the tips of his toes.
Estella told me we were both to go in, so I took Joe by the coat cuff and led him into Miss Havisham's presence. She was seated at her dressing table and turned to look at us immediately.
"Oh!" said she to Joe. "You are the husband of the sister of this boy?"

I could hardly have imagined dear old Joe looking so unlike himself or so much like some extraordinary bird — standing there speechless, with his tuft of feathers ruffled and his mouth open as if he wanted a worm.
"You are the husband," repeated Miss Havisham, "of the sister of this boy?"
It was very irritating. But throughout the entire interview, Joe persisted in addressing me instead of Miss Havisham.

"Which I mean to say, Pip," Joe now observed, in a manner that was at once forceful, confidential, and very polite, "as I up and married your sister, and I was at the time what you might call — if you were so inclined — a single man."
"Well!" said Miss Havisham. "And you have raised the boy with the intention of taking him as your apprentice. Is that so, Mr. Gargery?"

"You know, Pip," replied Joe, "as you and me were always friends, and it was looked forward to between us, as being bound to lead to good times. Not that, Pip, if you had ever had objections to the business — such as it being open to soot and grime, or anything like that — not that they wouldn't have been listened to, don't you see?"
"Has the boy," said Miss Havisham, "ever made any objection? Does he like the trade?"

"Which it is well known to yourself, Pip," returned Joe, strengthening his former mixture of argument, confidence, and politeness, "that it was the wish of your own heart." (I saw the idea suddenly strike him that he would adapt his tombstone couplet to the occasion, before he went on to say) "And there wasn't no objection on your part, and Pip it was the great wish of your heart!"

It was completely useless for me to try to make him understand that he should be speaking to Miss Havisham. The more faces and gestures I made at him to do so, the more confidential, argumentative, and polite he became — to me.
"Have you brought his apprenticeship papers with you?" asked Miss Havisham.

"Well, Pip, you know," replied Joe, as if that were a little unreasonable, "you yourself saw me put them in my hat, and therefore you know they are here." With which he took them out and gave them, not to Miss Havisham, but to me. I am afraid I was ashamed of the dear good fellow — I know I was ashamed of him — when I saw that Estella stood at the back of Miss Havisham's chair and that her eyes danced with mischief. I took the papers from his hand and gave them to Miss Havisham.
"You expected," said Miss Havisham, as she looked them over, "no payment with the boy?"
"Joe!" I protested, for he made no reply at all. "Why don't you answer — "

"Pip," returned Joe, cutting me short as if he were hurt, "which I mean to say that wasn't a question needing an answer between you and me, and you know the answer full well is No. You know it to be No, Pip, and why should I say it?"
Miss Havisham glanced at him as if she understood what he really was better than I had thought possible, given what he was there, and took up a little bag from the table beside her.
"Pip has earned a payment here," she said, "and here it is. There are twenty-five guineas in this bag. Give it to your master, Pip."
As if completely overwhelmed by her strange figure and the strange room, Joe, even at this point, persisted in addressing me.

"This is very generous on your part, Pip," said Joe, "and it is received with gratitude, though never expected, near or far or anywhere. And now, old chap," said Joe — giving me first a burning and then a freezing sensation, for I feared that familiar phrase was being aimed at Miss Havisham — "and now, old chap, may we do our duty! May you and me do our duty, both of us, by one another, and by those whose generous gift has — been conveyed — to be — for the satisfaction of mind — of those who never — " here Joe showed that he felt he had fallen into terrible difficulties, until he triumphantly rescued himself with the words, "and from myself, far be it!" These words had such a round and convincing sound to him that he said them twice.
"Goodbye, Pip!" said Miss Havisham. "Let them out, Estella."
"Am I to come again, Miss Havisham?" I asked.
"No. Gargery is your master now. Gargery! One word!"

Calling him back as I went out the door, I heard her say to Joe in a clear, emphatic voice, "The boy has been a good boy here, and that is his reward. Of course, as an honest man, you will expect no other and no more."

How Joe got out of the room, I have never been able to determine. But I know that when he did, he was steadily heading upstairs instead of down, and was deaf to all my calls until I went after him and grabbed hold of him. In another minute we were outside the gate, and it was locked, and Estella was gone. When we stood in the daylight alone again, Joe backed up against a wall and said to me, "Astonishing!" And there he stayed so long, saying "Astonishing" at intervals, so often, that I began to think his senses were never coming back. At length he extended his remark into, "Pip, I do assure you, this is as-TON-ishing!" and so, by degrees, became able to talk and walk away.

I have reason to think that Joe's mind was actually sharpened by what he had been through, and that on our way to Pumblechook's he invented a cunning plan. My reason is found in what took place in Mr. Pumblechook's parlor, where, when we arrived, my sister sat in conference with that detested seedsman.
"Well?" cried my sister, addressing us both at once. "And what's happened to you? I'm surprised you'd lower yourselves to come back to such poor company as this, I'm sure!"
"Miss Havisham," said Joe, with a fixed look at me like an effort of memory, "made it very particular that we should give her — was it compliments or respects, Pip?"
"Compliments," I said.
"Which that was my own belief," answered Joe. "Her compliments to Mrs. J. Gargery — "
"Much good they'll do me!" observed my sister, but rather pleased too.
"And wishing," pursued Joe, with another fixed look at me like another effort of memory, "that the state of Miss Havisham's health was such as would have — allowed, was it, Pip?"
"Of her having the pleasure," I added.
"Of ladies' company," said Joe. And drew a long breath.

"Well!" cried my sister, with a softened glance at Mr. Pumblechook. "She might have had the politeness to send that message in the first place, but better late than never. And what did she give young Rascal here?"
"She gave him," said Joe, "nothing."
Mrs. Joe was about to explode, but Joe went on.

"What she gave," said Joe, "she gave to his friends. 'And by his friends,' was her explanation, 'I mean into the hands of his sister, Mrs. J. Gargery.' Those were her words: 'Mrs. J. Gargery.' She may not have known," added Joe, with an appearance of thought, "whether it was Joe or George."
My sister looked at Pumblechook, who smoothed the elbows of his wooden armchair and nodded at her and at the fire, as if he had known all about it beforehand.
"And how much have you got?" asked my sister, laughing. Actually laughing!
"What would present company say to ten pounds?" demanded Joe.
"They'd say," returned my sister curtly, "pretty well. Not too much, but pretty well."
"It's more than that, then," said Joe.
That fearful fraud Pumblechook immediately nodded and said, as he rubbed the arms of his chair, "It's more than that, ma'am."
"Why, you don't mean to say — " began my sister.
"Yes I do, ma'am," said Pumblechook. "But wait a moment. Go on, Joseph. Good for you! Go on!"
"What would present company say," proceeded Joe, "to twenty pounds?"
"Handsome would be the word," returned my sister.
"Well, then," said Joe, "it's more than twenty pounds."
That abject hypocrite Pumblechook nodded again and said with a patronizing laugh, "It's more than that, ma'am. Good again! Keep it going, Joseph!"
"Then to end the suspense," said Joe, happily handing the bag to my sister, "it's twenty-five pounds."

"It's twenty-five pounds, ma'am," echoed that most shameless of swindlers, Pumblechook, rising to shake hands with her. "And it's no more than your merits — as I said when my opinion was asked — and I wish you joy of the money!"

If the villain had stopped here, his crime would have been bad enough. But he deepened his guilt by proceeding to take charge of me with a right of ownership that left all his former offenses far behind.

"Now you see, Joseph and wife," said Pumblechook, grabbing me by the arm above the elbow, "I am one of those who always sees things through to the finish. This boy must be bound, right away. That's my way. Bound right away."
"Goodness knows, Uncle Pumblechook," said my sister, clutching the money, "we're deeply grateful to you."

"Never mind me, ma'am," returned that diabolical corn merchant. "A pleasure's a pleasure the world over. But this boy, you know — we must have him bound. I said I'd see to it — to tell you the truth."

The magistrates were sitting in the Town Hall nearby, and we went over immediately to have me formally bound as apprentice to Joe. I say we went over, but I was pushed over by Pumblechook, exactly as if I had just picked a pocket or set fire to a haystack. Indeed, the general impression in court was that I had been caught red-handed. As Pumblechook shoved me before him through the crowd, I heard some people say, "What's he done?" and others, "He's a young one, too, but looks bad, doesn't he?" One mild and kindly-looking person even gave me a pamphlet decorated with a picture of a wicked young man loaded with chains, and titled TO BE READ IN MY CELL.

The Town Hall was a strange place, I thought, with higher pews than a church, and with people leaning over them to watch, and with mighty magistrates (one with a powdered head) leaning back in chairs with folded arms, or taking snuff, or falling asleep, or writing, or reading newspapers, and with some shining black portraits on the walls that my untrained eye saw as a mix of toffee and bandages. Here, in a corner, my apprenticeship papers were duly signed and witnessed, and I was "bound." Mr. Pumblechook held onto me the whole time, as if we had stopped by on our way to the gallows to get these little formalities out of the way.

When we came out again and got rid of the boys who had been excited by the hope of seeing me publicly tortured — and who were very disappointed to find that my friends were merely gathering around me — we went back to Pumblechook's. There my sister became so thrilled by the twenty-five guineas that nothing would do but we must have a dinner out of that windfall at the Blue Boar, and that Pumblechook must go over in his carriage and bring the Hubbles and Mr. Wopsle.

It was agreed and done, and I passed a most miserable day. For it somehow seemed obvious to everyone that I was a blemish on the celebration. And to make it worse, they all asked me from time to time — in short, whenever they had nothing else to do — why I wasn't enjoying myself. And what could I possibly do then but say I was enjoying myself — when I wasn't?

However, they were the adults and they had their way, and they made the most of it. That swindling Pumblechook, elevated to the role of generous mastermind behind the whole occasion, actually sat at the head of the table. And when he addressed them on the subject of my being bound, and had gleefully congratulated them on my being liable to imprisonment if I played cards, drank strong liquor, kept late hours or bad company, or indulged in other sins that the wording of my apprenticeship papers seemed to consider inevitable, he placed me standing on a chair beside him to illustrate his remarks.

My only other memories of the great celebration are: that they wouldn't let me fall asleep, but whenever they saw me nodding off, woke me up and told me to enjoy myself. That, rather late in the evening, Mr. Wopsle performed Collins's Ode and threw his blood-stained sword down like thunder, with such effect that a waiter came in and said, "The businessmen downstairs send their compliments and say this isn't a circus." That they were all in excellent spirits on the road home and sang "O Lady Fair!" Mr. Wopsle taking the bass and declaring with a tremendously strong voice (in reply to the nosy character who leads that song by wanting to know everyone's private business) that he was the man with his white locks flowing, and that he was on the whole the weakest pilgrim going.
Finally, I remember that when I got to my little bedroom, I was truly miserable, and had a strong conviction that I would never like Joe's trade. I had liked it once, but once was not now.

chapters.title: Chapter 14
paragraphs: It is a most miserable thing to feel ashamed of home. There may be dark ingratitude in it, and the punishment may be fair and well deserved. But that it is a miserable thing, I can testify.

Home had never been a very pleasant place to me, because of my sister's temper. But Joe had made it sacred, and I had believed in it. I had believed in the formal parlor as the most elegant room. I had believed in the front door as a mysterious gateway to the Temple of the State, whose solemn opening came with a sacrifice of roast chickens. I had believed in the kitchen as a plain but respectable room. I had believed in the forge as the glowing road to manhood and independence. Within a single year, all this had changed. Now it was all coarse and common, and I would not have had Miss Havisham and Estella see it for anything.

How much of my ungrateful state of mind was my own fault, how much Miss Havisham's, how much my sister's, is now of no importance to me or anyone. The change was made in me. The thing was done. Well or badly done, forgivably or unforgivably, it was done.

Once, it had seemed to me that when I should at last roll up my sleeves and go into the forge as Joe's apprentice, I would be special and happy. Now that the reality was in my hands, I only felt that I was dusty with coal dust, and that I carried a weight on my daily thoughts compared to which the anvil was a feather. There have been times in my later life — as I suppose in most lives — when I have felt for a time as if a thick curtain had fallen on all its interest and romance, shutting me out from anything but dull endurance. Never has that curtain dropped so heavy and blank as when my path in life lay stretched out straight before me through the newly begun road of apprenticeship to Joe.

I remember that later in my apprenticeship, I used to stand in the churchyard on Sunday evenings when night was falling, comparing my own outlook with the windy marsh view, and finding a likeness between them by thinking how flat and low both were, and how across both came an unknown way and a dark mist and then the sea. I was just as dejected on the first working day of my apprenticeship as in that later time. But I am glad to know that I never breathed a murmur to Joe while my apprenticeship lasted. It is about the only thing I am glad to know about myself in that connection.

For, though it includes what I am about to add, all the credit for what I am about to add belongs to Joe. It was not because I was faithful, but because Joe was faithful, that I never ran away to become a soldier or a sailor. It was not because I had a strong sense of the value of hard work, but because Joe had a strong sense of it, that I worked with reasonable effort against my inclination. It is not possible to know how far the influence of any good-hearted, honest, dutiful man spreads into the world. But it is very possible to know how it has touched yourself as it passes by. And I know perfectly well that whatever good mixed itself with my apprenticeship came from plain, contented Joe, and not from restlessly ambitious, discontented me.

What I wanted, who can say? How can I say, when I never knew? What I dreaded was that in some unlucky hour, when I was at my grimiest and most common, I should look up and see Estella looking in at one of the wooden windows of the forge. I was haunted by the fear that she would, sooner or later, find me out with a black face and hands, doing the coarsest part of my work, and would triumph over me and despise me. Often after dark, when I was pumping the bellows for Joe and we were singing Old Clem, the thought of how we used to sing it at Miss Havisham's would seem to show me Estella's face in the fire — with her pretty hair blowing in the wind and her eyes scorning me. Often at such a time I would look toward those panels of black night in the wall where the wooden windows were, and would imagine that I saw her just drawing her face away, and would believe that she had come at last.
After that, when we went in to supper, the place and the meal would look more humble than ever, and I would feel more ashamed of home than ever, in my own ungrateful heart.

chapters.title: Chapter 15
paragraphs: As I was getting too big for Mr. Wopsle's great-aunt's room, my education under that ridiculous woman came to an end. Not, however, before Biddy had taught me everything she knew, from the little price catalog to a comic song she had once bought for a halfpenny. Although the only coherent part of this piece of literature was the opening lines,
When I went to London town, sirs, Too rul loo rul Too rul loo rul Wasn't I done very brown, sirs? Too rul loo rul Too rul loo rul

— still, in my desire to be wiser, I learned this composition by heart with the utmost seriousness. Nor do I recall questioning its merit, except that I thought (as I still do) the amount of "Too rul" was somewhat excessive for the poetry. In my hunger for knowledge, I proposed to Mr. Wopsle that he share some intellectual crumbs with me, and he kindly agreed. As it turned out, however, he only wanted me as a dramatic prop — to be contradicted and embraced and wept over and bullied and grabbed and stabbed and knocked about in all sorts of ways. I soon gave up that course of instruction, though not before Mr. Wopsle in his poetic fury had thoroughly battered me.

Whatever I learned, I tried to pass on to Joe. This statement sounds so noble that I cannot in good conscience let it pass without explanation. I wanted to make Joe less ignorant and common so that he might be more worthy of my company and less open to Estella's criticism.

The old Battery out on the marshes was our classroom, and a broken slate and a short piece of chalk were our teaching tools — to which Joe always added a pipe of tobacco. I never knew Joe to remember anything from one Sunday to the next, or to learn, under my instruction, any piece of information whatever. Yet he would smoke his pipe at the Battery with a far wiser air than anywhere else — even a scholarly air — as if he considered himself to be making immense progress. Dear fellow, I hope he did.

It was pleasant and quiet out there, with the sails on the river passing beyond the earthwork, and sometimes, when the tide was low, looking as if they belonged to sunken ships still sailing along the bottom. Whenever I watched the vessels heading out to sea with their white sails spread, I somehow thought of Miss Havisham and Estella. And whenever the light fell slanting, far off, on a cloud or a sail or a green hillside or the water line, it was the same — Miss Havisham and Estella and the strange house and the strange life seemed to have something to do with everything that was beautiful.

One Sunday, when Joe had so thoroughly enjoyed his pipe and so contentedly called himself "most awfully dull" that I had given up on him for the day, I lay on the earthwork for some time with my chin on my hand, seeing traces of Miss Havisham and Estella all over the landscape, in the sky and in the water. At last I decided to mention a thought about them that had been on my mind.
"Joe," said I, "don't you think I ought to pay Miss Havisham a visit?"
"Well, Pip," returned Joe, slowly considering. "What for?"
"What for, Joe? What is any visit made for?"

"There are some visits, perhaps," said Joe, "that will always be open to that question, Pip. But when it comes to visiting Miss Havisham — she might think you wanted something, expected something from her."
"Don't you think I could say that I didn't, Joe?"
"You could, old chap," said Joe. "And she might believe it. Then again, she might not."
Joe felt, as I did, that he had made a good point there, and he puffed hard on his pipe to keep himself from weakening it by saying it again.

"You see, Pip," Joe went on, as soon as he was past that danger, "Miss Havisham did the generous thing by you. When Miss Havisham did the generous thing by you, she called me back to say to me that that was all."
"Yes, Joe. I heard her."
"ALL," Joe repeated, very emphatically.
"Yes, Joe. I tell you, I heard her."
"What I mean to say, Pip, is that her meaning might have been — call it a day! — as you were! — me to the north, and you to the south! — stay apart!"
I had thought of that too, and it was far from comforting to find that he had thought of it, for it seemed to make it more likely.
"But, Joe."
"Yes, old chap."
"Here I am, getting on in the first year of my apprenticeship, and since the day I was bound, I have never thanked Miss Havisham, or asked after her, or shown that I remember her."

"That's true, Pip. And unless you were to make her a set of horseshoes, all four — and what I mean to say is that even a set of horseshoes might not be the best present, given a total absence of hooves — "
"I don't mean that kind of remembrance, Joe. I don't mean a present."

But Joe had gotten the idea of a present in his head and couldn't let it go. "Or even," said he, "if you were helped to knock her up a new chain for the front door — or say a couple hundred heavy-duty screws for general use — or some light fancy article, such as a toasting fork when she had her muffins — or a gridiron when she had a fish or the like — "
"I don't mean any present at all, Joe," I interrupted.

"Well," said Joe, still going on as though I had insisted, "if I were you, Pip, I wouldn't. No, I would not. For what's a door chain when she's already got one up? And heavy-duty screws are open to misunderstanding. And if it was a toasting fork, you'd go for brass and do yourself no credit. And the finest craftsman can't show off his skill in a gridiron — for a gridiron is a gridiron," said Joe, earnestly pressing this upon me as if trying to wake me from a delusion, "and you may aim at whatever you like, but a gridiron it will come out, whether you want it to or not, and you can't help yourself — "
"My dear Joe," I cried in desperation, grabbing his coat, "don't go on like that. I never thought of giving Miss Havisham any present."
"No, Pip," Joe agreed, as if he had been arguing for that all along, "and what I say to you is, you are right, Pip."
"Yes, Joe. But what I wanted to say was, since we're rather slow right now, if you would give me a half-holiday tomorrow, I think I'd go up town and pay a call on Miss Est — Havisham."
"Whose name," said Joe gravely, "is not Estavisham, Pip, unless she's been renamed."
"I know, Joe, I know. It was a slip. What do you think of it, Joe?"

In short, Joe thought that if I thought well of it, he thought well of it. But he was particular about one condition: if I were not received warmly, or if I were not encouraged to come again as a visit with no ulterior motive, simply one of gratitude for a favor received, then this experimental trip should have no follow-up. I promised to accept these conditions.

Now, Joe employed a journeyman at weekly wages whose name was Orlick. He claimed that his first name was Dolge — an obvious impossibility — but he was a man of such stubborn nature that I believe he was under no delusion about this, but willfully imposed that name on the village as an insult to its intelligence. He was a broad-shouldered, loose-limbed, dark fellow of great strength, never in a hurry, and always slouching. He never even seemed to come to work on purpose, but would slouch in as if by accident. When he went to the Jolly Bargemen to eat his dinner, or went away at night, he would slouch out like Cain or the Wandering Jew, as if he had no idea where he was going and no intention of ever coming back. He lodged with a sluice keeper out on the marshes. On workdays he would come slouching from his hermitage, with his hands in his pockets and his dinner loosely tied in a bundle around his neck, dangling on his back. On Sundays he mostly lay all day on the sluice gates, or leaned against haystacks and barns. He always slouched, with his eyes on the ground. When spoken to or otherwise required to raise them, he looked up in a half-resentful, half-puzzled way, as though his only thought ever was that it was rather odd and unfair that he should never be thinking.

This morose journeyman had no liking for me. When I was very small and timid, he let me understand that the Devil lived in a black corner of the forge, and that he knew the fiend very well. Also that it was necessary to build up the fire, once every seven years, with a live boy, and that I might consider myself fuel. When I became Joe's apprentice, Orlick was perhaps confirmed in some suspicion that I would replace him. In any case, he liked me even less. Not that he ever said or did anything openly hostile. I only noticed that he always beat his sparks in my direction, and that whenever I sang Old Clem, he came in out of time.

Dolge Orlick was at work the next day when I reminded Joe of my half-holiday. He said nothing at first, as he and Joe had just gotten a piece of hot iron between them and I was at the bellows. But after a while he said, leaning on his hammer:

"Now, master! Surely you're not going to favor only one of us. If young Pip gets a half-holiday, do the same for old Orlick." I suppose he was about twenty-five, but he usually spoke of himself as an ancient person.
"Why, what will you do with a half-holiday if you get it?" said Joe.
"What will I do with it? What will he do with it? I'll do as much with it as him," said Orlick.
"As for Pip, he's going up town," said Joe.
"Well then, as for old Orlick, he's going up town," retorted that worthy. "Two can go up town. It's not only one who can go up town."
"Don't lose your temper," said Joe.
"I will if I like," growled Orlick. "Some people and their going up town! Now, master! Come on. No playing favorites in this shop. Be a man!"

The master refusing to discuss the subject until the journeyman was in a better temper, Orlick plunged at the furnace, drew out a red-hot bar, charged at me with it as if he were going to run it through my body, whisked it around my head, laid it on the anvil, and hammered it out — as if it were me, I thought, and the sparks were my spurting blood — and finally said, when he had hammered himself hot and the iron cold, and he again leaned on his hammer:
"Now, master!"
"Are you all right now?" demanded Joe.
"Yes. I'm all right," said gruff old Orlick.
"Then, since you generally stick to your work as well as most men," said Joe, "let it be a half-holiday for everyone."
My sister had been standing silently in the yard, within earshot — she was the most shameless spy and eavesdropper — and she instantly looked in at one of the windows.
"Just like you, you fool!" said she to Joe. "Giving holidays to great idle brutes like that. You are a rich man, upon my life, to waste wages that way. I wish I were his master!"
"You'd be everybody's master if you dared," retorted Orlick, with an ugly grin.
("Leave her alone," said Joe.)

"I'd be a match for all fools and all rogues," returned my sister, working herself into a mighty rage. "And I couldn't be a match for the fools without being a match for your master, who's the dunder-headed king of the fools. And I couldn't be a match for the rogues without being a match for you, who are the blackest-looking and the worst rogue between here and France. Now!"
"You're a foul shrew, Mother Gargery," growled the journeyman. "If that makes a judge of rogues, you ought to be a good one."
("Leave her alone, will you?" said Joe.)

"What did you say?" cried my sister, beginning to scream. "What did you say? What did that fellow Orlick say to me, Pip? What did he call me, with my husband standing by? Oh! Oh! Oh!" Each of these exclamations was a shriek. And I must note about my sister, what is equally true of all the violent women I have ever seen, that passion was no excuse for her. It is undeniable that instead of falling into a passion, she consciously and deliberately took extraordinary pains to force herself into one, and became blindly furious by regular stages. "What was the name he gave me before the man who swore to defend me? Oh! Hold me! Oh!"
"Ah!" growled the journeyman, between his teeth. "I'd hold you, if you were my wife. I'd hold you under the pump, and choke it out of you."
("I tell you, leave her alone," said Joe.)

"Oh! To hear him!" cried my sister, with a clap of her hands and a scream together — which was her next stage. "To hear the names he's calling me! That Orlick! In my own house! Me, a married woman! With my husband standing by! Oh! Oh!" Here my sister, after a fit of clapping and screaming, beat her hands on her chest and on her knees, threw off her cap, and pulled her hair down — which were the final stages on her road to frenzy. Being by this time a perfect Fury and a complete success, she made a dash at the door, which I had fortunately locked.

What could the wretched Joe do now, after his ignored parenthetical warnings, but stand up to his journeyman and ask what he meant by interfering between himself and Mrs. Joe? And further, whether he was man enough to fight? Old Orlick felt the situation called for nothing less, and put up his fists at once. So, without even pulling off their singed and burned aprons, they went at each other like two giants. But if any man in that neighborhood could stand toe to toe with Joe, I never saw him. Orlick, as easily as the pale young gentleman, was very soon among the coal dust, and in no hurry to come out of it. Then Joe unlocked the door and picked up my sister, who had fainted at the window (but had seen the fight first, I think), and who was carried into the house and laid down. She was urged to revive, but would do nothing but struggle and clench her hands in Joe's hair. Then came that particular calm and silence that follows all uproars. And then, with the vague feeling I have always connected with such a lull — namely that it was Sunday and somebody was dead — I went upstairs to dress.

When I came down again, I found Joe and Orlick sweeping up, with no other signs of disturbance than a slit in one of Orlick's nostrils, which was neither attractive nor decorative. A pot of beer had appeared from the Jolly Bargemen, and they were sharing it by turns in a peaceable manner. The calm had a soothing and philosophical effect on Joe, who followed me out to the road to say, as a parting observation that might do me good, "On the rampage, Pip, and off the rampage, Pip — such is life!"

With what absurd emotions (for we find feelings that are very serious in a man quite comical in a boy) I found myself going to Miss Havisham's again matters little here. Nor how I passed and repassed the gate many times before I could make up my mind to ring. Nor how I debated whether I should go away without ringing. Nor how I certainly would have gone, if my time had been my own, to come back later.
Miss Sarah Pocket came to the gate. No Estella.
"What, you here again?" said Miss Pocket. "What do you want?"

When I said I had only come to see how Miss Havisham was, Sarah evidently debated whether to send me away. But unwilling to take responsibility for that, she let me in, and soon brought the sharp message that I was to "come up."
Everything was unchanged, and Miss Havisham was alone.
"Well?" said she, fixing her eyes on me. "I hope you want nothing? You'll get nothing."
"No indeed, Miss Havisham. I only wanted you to know that I am doing very well in my apprenticeship, and am always very grateful to you."
"There, there!" with the old restless fingers. "Come now and then. Come on your birthday. Ah!" she cried suddenly, spinning herself and her chair toward me. "You are looking around for Estella? Hey?"
I had been looking around — for Estella, in fact — and I stammered that I hoped she was well.
"Abroad," said Miss Havisham. "Being educated as a lady. Far out of reach. Prettier than ever. Admired by all who see her. Do you feel that you have lost her?"

There was such malicious pleasure in the way she said those last words, and she broke into such a disagreeable laugh, that I was at a loss for what to say. She spared me the trouble by dismissing me. When the gate was closed behind me by Sarah of the walnut-shell face, I felt more than ever dissatisfied with my home and with my trade and with everything. And that was all I gained from that visit.

As I was wandering along the High Street, looking gloomily into the shop windows and thinking what I would buy if I were a gentleman, who should come out of the bookshop but Mr. Wopsle. He had in his hand the affecting tragedy of George Barnwell, which he had just bought for sixpence, intending to inflict every word of it on Pumblechook, with whom he was going to have tea. The moment he saw me, he seemed to consider it a special act of Providence that an apprentice had been placed in his path to be read at. He grabbed me and insisted I come with him to Pumblechook's parlor. Since I knew it would be miserable at home, and since the nights were dark and the way was dreary, and almost any company was better than none, I didn't resist much. So we turned into Pumblechook's just as the street and the shops were lighting up.

Since I never attended any other performance of George Barnwell, I don't know how long it usually takes. But I know very well that it took until half past nine that night, and that when Mr. Wopsle got to Newgate Prison, I thought he would never reach the scaffold, he became so much slower than at any earlier point in his disgraceful career. I thought it a bit much that he should complain of being cut down in his prime after all, since he had been going to seed, page after page, from the very start. This, however, was merely a matter of length and boredom. What stung me was the identification of the whole affair with my innocent self. When Barnwell began to go wrong, I declare that I felt positively apologetic, Pumblechook's indignant stare blamed me so strongly. Wopsle too took pains to show me in the worst light. At once brutal and weepy, I was made to murder my uncle with no excuses whatever. The villain Millwood beat me in every argument. It became pure madness for my master's daughter to care a fig for me. And all I can say about my gasping, procrastinating conduct on the fatal morning is that it was worthy of the general feebleness of my character. Even after I was happily hanged and Wopsle had closed the book, Pumblechook sat staring at me and shaking his head, saying, "Take warning, boy, take warning!" — as if it were well known that I was planning to murder a near relation, provided I could persuade one to be my benefactor.

It was a very dark night when it was all over, and when I set out with Mr. Wopsle for the walk home. Beyond town, we found a heavy mist, and it fell wet and thick. The turnpike lamp was a blur, seemingly out of its usual place, and its rays looked like solid matter in the fog. We were remarking on this, and saying how the mist rose with a change of wind from a certain part of the marshes, when we came upon a man slouching in the shelter of the turnpike house.
"Hello!" we said, stopping. "Orlick, is that you?"
"Yes," he answered, slouching out. "I was standing by for a minute, on the chance of company."
"You're late," I remarked.
Orlick not unreasonably answered, "Well? And you're late."
"We have been," said Mr. Wopsle, elated by his recent performance, "we have been enjoying, Mr. Orlick, an intellectual evening."
Old Orlick growled, as if he had nothing to say to that, and we all went on together. I asked him whether he had been spending his half-holiday up and down town.
"Yes," said he. "All of it. I came in behind you. I didn't see you, but I must have been pretty close behind you. By the way, the guns are going again."
"At the Hulks?" said I.
"Yes! Some of the birds have flown from the cages. The guns have been going since dark, roughly. You'll hear one in a minute."

Sure enough, we had not walked many yards further when the familiar boom came toward us, muffled by the mist, and rolled heavily away along the low ground by the river, as if it were pursuing and threatening the fugitives.
"A good night for escaping," said Orlick. "We'd have a hard time bringing down a jailbird on the wing tonight."

The subject was a loaded one for me, and I thought about it in silence. Mr. Wopsle, as the ill-treated uncle of the evening's tragedy, fell to meditating aloud in his garden at Camberwell. Orlick, with his hands in his pockets, slouched heavily at my side. It was very dark, very wet, very muddy, and so we splashed along. Now and then the sound of the signal cannon broke upon us again and rolled sullenly along the river. I kept myself to myself and my thoughts. Mr. Wopsle died gracefully at Camberwell, and with great spirit on Bosworth Field, and in the greatest agony at Glastonbury. Orlick sometimes growled, "Beat it out, beat it out — Old Clem! With a clink for the stout — Old Clem!" I thought he had been drinking, but he was not drunk.

So we came to the village. The road by which we approached it took us past the Three Jolly Bargemen, which we were surprised to find — it being eleven o'clock — in a state of commotion, with the door wide open and hastily lit lamps scattered about. Mr. Wopsle went in to ask what was wrong, guessing that a convict had been caught, but came running out in a great hurry.
"There's something wrong," said he, without stopping, "up at your place, Pip. Run!"
"What is it?" I asked, keeping up with him. So did Orlick, at my side.
"I can't quite make it out. The house seems to have been violently broken into when Joe Gargery was out. Possibly by convicts. Somebody has been attacked and hurt."

We were running too fast to say more, and we didn't stop until we reached our kitchen. It was full of people — the whole village was there, or in the yard — and there was a surgeon, and there was Joe, and there was a group of women, all on the floor in the middle of the kitchen. The bystanders drew back when they saw me, and so I became aware of my sister — lying unconscious and motionless on the bare boards where she had been knocked down by a tremendous blow to the back of the head, dealt by some unknown hand while her face was turned toward the fire — destined never to be on the rampage again, while she was the wife of Joe.

chapters.title: Chapter 16
paragraphs: With my head full of George Barnwell, I was at first inclined to believe that I must have had some part in the attack on my sister. At the very least, as her close relative — widely known to be in her debt — I seemed a more logical suspect than anyone else. But in the clearer light of next morning, when I began to reconsider and heard the matter discussed on all sides, I took a more reasonable view.

Joe had been at the Three Jolly Bargemen, smoking his pipe, from a quarter past eight to a quarter to ten. While he was there, my sister had been seen standing at the kitchen door, exchanging good nights with a farm laborer heading home. The man couldn't be precise about the time — he got hopelessly confused when he tried — except that it must have been before nine. When Joe came home at five minutes to ten, he found her struck down on the floor, and immediately called for help. The fire hadn't burned unusually low, and the candle wick wasn't especially long. The candle, however, had been blown out.

Nothing had been taken from any part of the house. Apart from the blown-out candle — which stood on a table between the door and my sister, behind her as she faced the fire — there was no disturbance in the kitchen except what she herself had caused in falling and bleeding. But there was one remarkable piece of evidence. She had been struck with something blunt and heavy on the head and spine. After the blows were dealt, something heavy had been thrown down on her with great force as she lay face-down. And on the ground beside her, when Joe picked her up, was a convict's leg-iron that had been filed apart.

Joe examined this iron with a blacksmith's eye and declared it had been filed through some time ago. When the hue and cry went off to the Hulks and people came to examine the iron, Joe's opinion was confirmed. They wouldn't say when it had left the prison ships it had clearly once belonged to. But they claimed to know for certain that this particular manacle had not been worn by either of the two convicts who escaped the night before. Furthermore, one of those two had already been recaptured and still had his iron on.

Knowing what I knew, I formed my own theory. I believed it was my convict's iron — the one I had seen and heard him filing on the marshes. But I didn't believe he had put it to this latest use. I believed one of two other people had gotten hold of it and turned it to this cruel purpose. Either Orlick, or the strange man who had shown me the file.

As for Orlick: he had gone to town exactly as he told us when we picked him up at the turnpike. He'd been seen around town all evening, in various groups at several public houses, and he'd come back with me and Mr. Wopsle. There was nothing against him except the quarrel — and my sister had quarreled with him, and with everyone else around her, ten thousand times. As for the strange man: if he'd come back for his two bank-notes, there could have been no dispute about them, because my sister was fully prepared to return them. Besides, there had been no argument. The attacker had come in so silently and suddenly that she was struck down before she could even turn around.

It was horrible to think that I had provided the weapon, however unintentionally. But I could hardly think otherwise. I suffered unspeakable torment as I considered and reconsidered whether I should finally break the spell of my childhood and tell Joe the whole story. For months afterward, I settled the question every day with a firm no, then reopened and re-argued it the next morning. The debate always came down to this: the secret was so old now, had so grown into me and become part of who I was, that I couldn't tear it away. Beyond my fear that the confession would drive Joe from me — now more likely than ever, given all the mischief it had led to — I had an additional fear that he wouldn't believe me at all. He'd file it away alongside the fabulous dogs and veal cutlets as another monstrous invention. Of course, I temporized with myself — for wasn't I wavering between right and wrong, as one always does? — and resolved to make a full confession if some new opportunity arose to help identify the attacker.

The constables and the Bow Street men from London — for this happened in the days of the now-extinct red-waistcoated police — were around the house for a week or two. They did pretty much what I have heard and read of similar authorities doing in other such cases. They arrested several obviously wrong people. They ran their heads very hard against wrong ideas and persisted in trying to fit the facts to their theories, instead of drawing theories from the facts. They also stood around the door of the Jolly Bargemen with knowing, reserved expressions that filled the whole neighborhood with admiration. And they had a mysterious way of taking their drinks that was almost as good as catching the culprit. But not quite — because they never did.

Long after these officers of the law had departed, my sister lay very ill in bed. Her sight was disturbed, so she saw objects multiplied and grabbed at phantom teacups and wineglasses instead of the real ones. Her hearing was badly impaired, her memory too, and her speech was unintelligible. When at last she recovered enough to come downstairs, we still had to keep my slate beside her so she could write what she couldn't say. Since she was — quite apart from her terrible handwriting — a worse than average speller, and since Joe was a worse than average reader, extraordinary confusions arose between them. I was always called in to sort them out. Administering mutton instead of medicine, substituting Tea for Joe, and reading baker as bacon were among the mildest of my own mistakes.

Her temper, however, was greatly improved, and she was patient. A trembling uncertainty in all her movements soon became her normal state. Afterward, every two or three months, she would put her hands to her head and then remain for about a week in some dark mental fog. We were at a loss to find a suitable attendant for her, until a convenient circumstance solved the problem. Mr. Wopsle's great-aunt conquered a longstanding habit of being alive, and Biddy became part of our household.

It may have been about a month after my sister's reappearance in the kitchen when Biddy came to us with a small speckled box containing everything she owned in the world, and became a blessing to the household. Above all, she was a blessing to Joe. The dear fellow was terribly distressed by the constant sight of his ruined wife. He'd grown accustomed, while tending to her in the evenings, to turn to me now and then and say, with his blue eyes moist: "She were such a fine figure of a woman once, Pip!" Biddy instantly took the cleverest charge of her, as though she'd studied her from infancy. Joe became able to appreciate the greater quiet of his life, and to get down to the Jolly Bargemen now and then for a change that did him good. It was typical of the police that they had all, to varying degrees, suspected poor Joe — though he never knew it — and had unanimously agreed he was one of the deepest spirits they had ever encountered.
Biddy's first triumph in her new role was solving a puzzle that had completely defeated me. I had tried hard at it but gotten nowhere. It was this:

Again and again, my sister had traced a character on the slate that looked like a strange T, then called our attention to it with the greatest urgency as something she particularly wanted. I had tried every T-word I could think of, from tar to toast to tub. At last it struck me that the mark looked like a hammer. When I shouted that word in my sister's ear, she began hammering on the table and gave a qualified nod. So I brought in all our hammers, one after another, but none was right. Then I thought of a crutch — similar shape — and borrowed one from the village, presenting it to my sister with considerable confidence. But she shook her head so violently that we feared, in her weak and shattered condition, she might dislocate her neck.

When my sister found that Biddy was quick to understand her, the mysterious symbol reappeared on the slate. Biddy looked at it thoughtfully, heard my explanation, looked thoughtfully at my sister, looked thoughtfully at Joe — who was always represented on the slate by his initial letter — and ran into the forge. Joe and I followed.
"Why, of course!" cried Biddy, her face triumphant. "Don't you see? It's him!"

Orlick, without a doubt! She had lost his name and could only signify him by his hammer. We told him we wanted him to come to the kitchen, and he slowly laid down his hammer, wiped his brow with his arm, gave it another wipe with his apron, and came slouching out with that curious, loose, vagabond bend in his knees that was so distinctly his.

I confess I expected to see my sister denounce him, and I was disappointed by the actual result. She showed the greatest anxiety to be on good terms with him.
