She was clearly delighted that he had been produced at last, and gestured that he should be given something to drink. She watched his face as if desperate to confirm that he was taking kindly to his reception. She showed every possible desire to win him over. There was a humble, appeasing quality to everything she did — the kind I've seen in a child's manner toward a harsh master. After that day, it was rare for a day to pass without her drawing the hammer on her slate, and without Orlick slouching in to stand stubbornly before her, as baffled as I was about what to make of it.

chapters.title: Chapter 17
paragraphs: I now fell into a regular routine of apprentice life, varied beyond the limits of the village and the marshes by nothing more remarkable than the arrival of my birthday and another visit to Miss Havisham. I found Miss Sarah Pocket still on duty at the gate. I found Miss Havisham exactly as I had left her, and she spoke of Estella in the very same way, if not the very same words. The visit lasted only a few minutes, and she gave me a guinea as I was leaving and told me to come again on my next birthday. I should mention that this became a yearly custom. I tried to refuse the guinea the first time, but that only made her ask me very angrily if I expected more. After that, I took it.

The dull old house was so unchanging — the yellow light in the darkened room, the faded ghost in the chair by the dressing-table mirror — that I felt as if the stopped clocks had stopped Time itself in that mysterious place. While I and everything else outside it grew older, it stood still. Daylight never entered the house, not in my thoughts and memories of it, any more than in actual fact. It bewildered me, and under its influence I continued in my heart to hate my trade and be ashamed of home.

Gradually, though, I became aware of a change in Biddy. Her shoes no longer slipped at the heel. Her hair grew bright and neat. Her hands were always clean. She was not beautiful — she was ordinary, and could never be like Estella — but she was pleasant and wholesome and good-natured. She had been with us no more than a year (I remember she was newly out of mourning when it struck me) before I noticed one evening that she had curiously thoughtful and attentive eyes. Eyes that were very pretty and very good.

It came from my lifting my own eyes from a task I was working at — copying passages from a book, to improve myself two ways at once — and seeing Biddy watching what I was doing. I put down my pen, and Biddy paused in her needlework without putting it down.
"Biddy," said I, "how do you manage it? Either I'm very stupid, or you're very clever."
"What is it that I manage? I don't know," returned Biddy, smiling.
She managed our whole domestic life, and wonderfully too. But I didn't mean that, though it made what I did mean all the more surprising.

"How do you manage, Biddy," said I, "to learn everything I learn, and always keep up with me?" I was beginning to be rather proud of my knowledge, since I spent my birthday guineas on it and set aside most of my pocket money for the same purpose. Though I have no doubt now that the little I knew was extremely overpriced.
"I might as well ask you," said Biddy, "how you manage."
"No, because when I come in from the forge at night, anyone can see me working away at it. But you never work at it, Biddy."
"I suppose I must catch it like a cough," said Biddy quietly, and went on with her sewing.

Pursuing this idea as I leaned back in my wooden chair and watched Biddy sewing with her head tilted to one side, I began to think her rather an extraordinary girl. I now recalled that she was equally knowledgeable about our trade terms, the names of our different kinds of work, and our various tools. In short, whatever I knew, Biddy knew. In theory, she was already as good a blacksmith as I was, or better.
"You are one of those people, Biddy," said I, "who make the most of every chance. You never had a chance before you came here, and look how you've improved!"
Biddy looked at me for a moment and went on with her sewing. "I was your first teacher, though, wasn't I?" she said as she sewed.
"Biddy!" I exclaimed in amazement. "Why, you are crying!"
"No I'm not," said Biddy, looking up and laughing. "What put that in your head?"

What could have put it there but the gleam of a tear as it dropped onto her work? I sat silent, recalling what a drudge she had been until Mr. Wopsle's great-aunt successfully overcame that unfortunate habit of being alive — so highly desirable a habit to be rid of, according to some people. I recalled the hopeless circumstances that had surrounded her in the miserable little shop and the miserable little noisy evening school, with that miserable old bundle of incompetence always to be dragged along and propped up. I reflected that even in those difficult times, whatever was now developing in Biddy must have already been there in some latent form. In my first restlessness and discontent, I had turned to her for help as a matter of course. Biddy sat quietly sewing, shedding no more tears. And while I looked at her and thought about it all, it occurred to me that perhaps I had not been grateful enough to Biddy. I might have been too reserved, and should have shared more of my confidence with her.
"Yes, Biddy," I said, when I had finished turning it over, "you were my first teacher, and at a time when we never imagined we'd be together like this, in this kitchen."
"Ah, poor thing!" replied Biddy. It was like her self-forgetfulness to redirect the remark to my sister, getting up to fuss over her and make her more comfortable. "That's sadly true!"
"Well!" said I, "we must talk together more, as we used to. And I must confide in you more, as I used to. Let's have a quiet walk on the marshes next Sunday, Biddy, and a long chat."

My sister was never left alone now, but Joe more than readily agreed to look after her that Sunday afternoon. Biddy and I went out together. It was summertime, and the weather was lovely. When we had passed the village and the church and the churchyard, and were out on the marshes where we could see the sails of ships, I began to blend Miss Havisham and Estella with the view in my usual way. When we came to the riverside and sat down on the bank, with the water rippling at our feet and making everything quieter than it would have been without that sound, I decided it was a good time and place to let Biddy into my inner confidence.
"Biddy," said I, after swearing her to secrecy, "I want to be a gentleman."
"Oh, I wouldn't, if I were you!" she replied. "I don't think it would answer."
"Biddy," said I, with some severity, "I have particular reasons for wanting to be a gentleman."
"You know best, Pip. But don't you think you're happier as you are?"
"Biddy," I exclaimed impatiently, "I am not at all happy as I am. I'm disgusted with my trade and with my life. I've never taken to either, since I was bound. Don't be absurd."
"Was I absurd?" said Biddy, quietly raising her eyebrows. "I'm sorry for that. I didn't mean to be. I only want you to do well and be comfortable."

"Well then, understand once and for all that I never shall or can be comfortable — or anything but miserable — there, Biddy! — unless I can lead a very different sort of life from the one I lead now."
"That's a pity!" said Biddy, shaking her head with a sorrowful air.

Now, I too had so often thought it a pity that, in the strange kind of quarrel I was always having with myself, I was half inclined to weep with frustration when Biddy gave voice to her feeling — and mine. I told her she was right, and I knew it was deeply regrettable, but still it couldn't be helped.

"If I could have settled down," I said to Biddy, plucking at the short grass within reach, much as I had once pulled my feelings out of my hair and kicked them into the brewery wall — "if I could have settled down and been half as fond of the forge as I was when I was little, I know it would have been much better for me. You and I and Joe would have wanted nothing then. Joe and I might have gone into partnership when I was out of my time. I might even have grown up to keep company with you, and we might have sat on this very bank on a fine Sunday, quite different people. I should have been good enough for you, shouldn't I, Biddy?"
Biddy sighed as she looked at the ships sailing on, and answered, "Yes. I'm not overly particular." It didn't sound exactly flattering, but I knew she meant well.

"Instead of that," said I, plucking up more grass and chewing a blade or two, "see how I'm going on. Dissatisfied and uncomfortable, and — what would it matter to me, being coarse and common, if nobody had told me so!"
Biddy turned her face suddenly toward mine and looked at me far more attentively than she had looked at the sailing ships.
"That was neither a very true nor a very polite thing to say," she remarked, turning her eyes back to the ships. "Who said it?"

I was flustered, for I had broken away without quite seeing where I was headed. But it couldn't be taken back now, so I answered: "The beautiful young lady at Miss Havisham's. She's more beautiful than anybody ever was, and I admire her dreadfully, and I want to be a gentleman on her account." Having made this lunatic confession, I began throwing my torn-up grass into the river, as if half thinking of following it.
"Do you want to be a gentleman to spite her, or to win her over?" Biddy asked me quietly, after a pause.
"I don't know," I answered moodily.

"Because if it's to spite her," Biddy went on, "I should think — but you know best — that might be better and more independently done by simply not caring about her words. And if it's to win her over, I should think — but you know best — she was not worth winning."

Exactly what I myself had thought, many times. Exactly what was perfectly obvious to me at that moment. But how could I, a poor bewildered village boy, avoid that wonderful inconsistency into which the best and wisest of men fall every day?
"It may be perfectly true," said I to Biddy, "but I admire her dreadfully."

At that point I turned over onto my face, grabbed a good handful of hair on each side of my head, and wrenched it hard. All the while knowing the madness of my heart to be so very mad and misplaced that I was quite aware it would have served my face right if I'd lifted it by the hair and knocked it against the pebbles as punishment for belonging to such an idiot.

Biddy was the wisest of girls, and she tried to reason with me no further. She put her hand — a comfortable hand, though roughened by work — on my hands, one after the other, and gently took them out of my hair. Then she softly patted my shoulder in a soothing way, while I cried a little with my face on my sleeve — exactly as I had done in the brewery yard — feeling vaguely convinced that I was very much ill-used by somebody, or by everybody. I couldn't say which.

"I'm glad of one thing," said Biddy, "and that is that you've felt you could give me your confidence, Pip. And I'm glad of another, which is that of course you know you may depend on my keeping it and always deserving it. If your first teacher — dear! such a poor one, and so much in need of being taught herself! — had been your teacher now, she thinks she knows what lesson she would set. But it would be a hard one to learn, and you've gone beyond her, and it's no use now." With a quiet sigh for me, Biddy rose from the bank and said, with a fresh and pleasant change of voice, "Shall we walk a little farther, or go home?"
"Biddy," I cried, jumping up and putting my arm around her neck and giving her a kiss, "I shall always tell you everything."
"Till you're a gentleman," said Biddy.
"You know I never shall be, so that's always. Not that I have any occasion to tell you anything, for you know everything I know — as I told you at home the other night."
"Ah!" said Biddy, almost in a whisper, looking away at the ships. And then she repeated, with that same pleasant change of voice: "Shall we walk a little farther, or go home?"

I said to Biddy we would walk a little farther, and we did. The summer afternoon softened into summer evening, and it was very beautiful. I began to consider whether I was not more naturally and wholesomely situated, after all, right here — rather than playing beggar-my-neighbor by candlelight in the room with the stopped clocks, despised by Estella. I thought it would be very good for me if I could get her out of my head, along with all those other memories and fantasies, and go to work determined to enjoy what I had, stick to it, and make the best of it. I asked myself whether I didn't surely know that if Estella were beside me at that moment instead of Biddy, she would make me miserable. I was forced to admit that I did know it for a certainty. "Pip," I said to myself, "what a fool you are!"

We talked a good deal as we walked, and everything Biddy said seemed right. Biddy was never insulting, or changeable, or Biddy today and somebody else tomorrow. She would have felt only pain, not pleasure, from causing me pain. She would far rather have wounded herself than me. How could it be, then, that I didn't like her much better than the other?
"Biddy," said I, as we walked homeward, "I wish you could set me right."
"I wish I could!" said Biddy.
"If I could only get myself to fall in love with you — you don't mind my speaking so openly to such an old acquaintance?"
"Oh dear, not at all!" said Biddy. "Don't mind me."
"If I could only manage it, that would be the thing for me."
"But you never will, you see," said Biddy.

It didn't seem quite so unlikely to me that evening as it would have a few hours earlier. So I said I wasn't quite sure of that. But Biddy said she was, and she said it firmly. In my heart I believed she was right. And yet I took it rather badly that she should be so certain on the point.

When we came near the churchyard, we had to cross an embankment and get over a stile near a sluice gate. There, from the gate or the rushes or the ooze — which was quite in his stagnant style — up started Old Orlick.
"Halloa!" he growled. "Where are you two going?"
"Where should we be going but home?"
"Well then," said he, "I'm jiggered if I don't see you home!"

This threat of being jiggered was a favorite imaginary scenario of his. He attached no definite meaning to the word that I'm aware of, but used it — like his own invented Christian name — to menace people and suggest something savagely harmful. When I was younger, I had a general belief that if he had jiggered me personally, he would have done it with a sharp and twisted hook.

Biddy was very much against his coming with us, and whispered to me, "Don't let him come. I don't like him." Since I didn't like him either, I took the liberty of saying we thanked him, but we didn't need seeing home. He received this information with a howl of laughter and dropped back, but came slouching after us at a little distance.
Curious to know whether Biddy suspected him of having had a hand in the murderous attack my sister had never been able to give any account of, I asked her why she didn't like him.
"Oh!" she replied, glancing over her shoulder as he slouched after us. "Because I — I'm afraid he likes me."
"Did he ever tell you he liked you?" I asked indignantly.
"No," said Biddy, glancing over her shoulder again. "He never told me so. But he dances at me whenever he can catch my eye."

However novel and peculiar this evidence of affection, I did not doubt the accuracy of her interpretation. I was very heated indeed about Old Orlick's daring to admire her — as heated as if it were an outrage against me personally.
"But it makes no difference to you, you know," said Biddy calmly.
"No, Biddy, it makes no difference to me. Only I don't like it. I don't approve of it."
"Nor do I," said Biddy. "Though that makes no difference to you."
"Exactly," said I. "But I must tell you, I should have no opinion of you, Biddy, if he danced at you with your consent."

I kept an eye on Orlick after that night, and whenever circumstances favored his dancing at Biddy, I got in front of him to block the display. He had planted himself firmly in Joe's establishment, thanks to my sister's sudden fondness for him, or I would have tried to get him dismissed. He understood perfectly and returned my good intentions, as I had reason to know later.

And now, because my mind was not confused enough already, I complicated its confusion fifty thousand times over by having moods and phases when I was certain that Biddy was immeasurably better than Estella. That the plain, honest working life I was born to had nothing to be ashamed of, but offered me all the self-respect and happiness I needed. At those times, I would decide once and for all that my disaffection for dear old Joe and the forge was gone. That I was growing up properly, heading for a partnership with Joe and a life with Biddy. Then all at once some devastating memory of the Havisham days would hit me like a bomb and scatter my resolve in all directions. And scattered wits take a long time gathering up. Often, before I had collected them, they would be blown apart again by a single stray thought: that perhaps, after all, Miss Havisham was going to make my fortune when my time was up.
If my time had actually run out, it would have left me still at the height of my bewilderment, I'm sure. It never did run out, however, but was brought to an early end, as I will now relate.

chapters.title: Chapter 18
paragraphs: It was the fourth year of my apprenticeship to Joe, and it was a Saturday night. A group sat gathered around the fire at the Three Jolly Bargemen, listening as Mr. Wopsle read the newspaper aloud. I was one of them.

A hugely popular murder had been committed, and Mr. Wopsle was drenched in blood to the eyebrows. He savored every horrible adjective in the description and threw himself into the role of every witness at the inquest. He faintly moaned "I am done for" as the victim, and he barbarously bellowed "I'll serve you out" as the murderer. He gave the medical testimony in pointed imitation of our local doctor. He piped and shook as the aged turnpike-keeper who had heard blows, trembling so extremely as to raise doubts about that witness's mental competence. The coroner, in Mr. Wopsle's hands, became Timon of Athens; the beadle, Coriolanus. He enjoyed himself thoroughly. We all enjoyed ourselves and were delightfully comfortable. In this cozy state of mind we arrived at the verdict: Willful Murder.

Then, and not before, I became aware of a strange gentleman leaning over the back of the settle opposite me, watching. There was an expression of contempt on his face, and he bit the side of a thick forefinger as he studied the group.
"Well!" said the stranger to Mr. Wopsle, when the reading was done. "You have settled it all to your own satisfaction, I have no doubt?"
Everyone jumped and looked up, as if he were the murderer himself. He looked at everyone coldly and sarcastically.
"Guilty, of course?" said he. "Out with it. Come!"
"Sir," returned Mr. Wopsle, "without having the honor of your acquaintance, I do say Guilty." At this, we all took courage enough to join in a murmur of agreement.

"I know you do," said the stranger. "I knew you would. I told you so. But now I'll ask you a question. Do you know, or do you not know, that the law of England supposes every man to be innocent until he is proved — proved — to be guilty?"
"Sir," Mr. Wopsle began to reply, "as an Englishman myself, I—"
"Come!" said the stranger, biting his forefinger at him. "Don't evade the question. Either you know it, or you don't know it. Which is it?"
He stood with his head on one side and himself tilted the same way, in a bullying, interrogative manner. He jabbed his forefinger at Mr. Wopsle — as if to single him out — before biting it again.
"Now!" said he. "Do you know it, or don't you?"
"Certainly I know it," replied Mr. Wopsle.

"Certainly you know it. Then why didn't you say so at first? Now, I'll ask you another question" — taking possession of Mr. Wopsle as if he had a right to him — "do you know that none of these witnesses have yet been cross-examined?"
Mr. Wopsle was beginning, "I can only say—" when the stranger stopped him.

"What? You won't answer the question, yes or no? Now, I'll try you again." He jabbed his finger at him once more. "Pay attention. Are you aware, or are you not aware, that none of these witnesses have yet been cross-examined? Come, I only want one word from you. Yes, or no?"
Mr. Wopsle hesitated, and we all began to form rather a poor opinion of him.
"Come!" said the stranger. "I'll help you. You don't deserve help, but I'll help you. Look at that paper you hold in your hand. What is it?"
"What is it?" repeated Mr. Wopsle, eyeing it, much at a loss.
"Is it," pursued the stranger in his most sarcastic and suspicious manner, "the printed paper you have just been reading from?"
"Undoubtedly."
"Undoubtedly. Now, turn to that paper and tell me whether it distinctly states that the prisoner expressly said his legal advisers instructed him to reserve his defense entirely."
"I read that just now," Mr. Wopsle pleaded.

"Never mind what you read just now, sir. I don't ask you what you read just now. You may read the Lord's Prayer backwards if you like — and perhaps have done so before today. Turn to the paper. No, no, no, my friend — not to the top of the column. You know better than that. To the bottom, to the bottom." (We all began to think Mr. Wopsle full of tricks.) "Well? Have you found it?"
"Here it is," said Mr. Wopsle.

"Now, follow that passage with your eye and tell me whether it distinctly states that the prisoner expressly said he was instructed by his legal advisers wholly to reserve his defense. Come! Do you make that of it?"
Mr. Wopsle answered, "Those are not the exact words."
"Not the exact words!" repeated the gentleman bitterly. "Is that the exact substance?"
"Yes," said Mr. Wopsle.

"Yes," repeated the stranger, looking around at the rest of us with his right hand extended toward the witness Wopsle. "And now I ask you: what do you say to the conscience of the man who, with that passage before his eyes, can lay his head on his pillow after pronouncing a fellow creature guilty, unheard?"
We all began to suspect that Mr. Wopsle was not the man we had thought him, and that he was starting to be found out.

"And that same man, remember," pursued the gentleman, jabbing his finger heavily at Mr. Wopsle, "that same man might be called as a juror on this very trial. And having committed himself so deeply, he might return to the bosom of his family and lay his head on his pillow, after solemnly swearing that he would well and truly try the case between Our Sovereign Lord the King and the prisoner at the bar, and would give a true verdict according to the evidence, so help him God!"
We were all deeply persuaded that the unfortunate Wopsle had gone too far and had better stop in his reckless career while there was still time.

The strange gentleman, with an authority not to be disputed and a manner suggesting he knew some secret about every one of us that would ruin us if he chose to reveal it, left the back of the settle and came into the space between the two settles, in front of the fire. There he remained standing, his left hand in his pocket, biting the forefinger of his right.

"From information I have received," said he, looking around at us as we all quailed before him, "I have reason to believe there is a blacksmith among you, by the name of Joseph — or Joe — Gargery. Which is the man?"
"Here is the man," said Joe.
The strange gentleman beckoned him out of his place, and Joe went.
"You have an apprentice," pursued the stranger, "commonly known as Pip? Is he here?"
"I am here!" I cried.

The stranger did not recognize me, but I recognized him as the gentleman I had met on the stairs during my second visit to Miss Havisham. I had known him the moment I saw him looking over the settle. Now, standing face to face with him, his hand on my shoulder, I checked off again in detail: his large head, his dark complexion, his deep-set eyes, his bushy black eyebrows, his heavy watch chain, his strong black dots of beard and whisker, and even the smell of scented soap on his big hand.

"I wish to have a private conference with you two," said he, when he had studied me at his leisure. "It will take a little time. Perhaps we had better go to your place of residence. I prefer not to reveal my business here. You may share as much or as little of it as you please with your friends afterward. I have nothing to do with that."

In a wondering silence, the three of us walked out of the Jolly Bargemen. In a wondering silence, we walked home. Along the way, the strange gentleman occasionally looked at me and occasionally bit the side of his finger. As we neared the house, Joe — vaguely sensing the occasion called for ceremony — went ahead to open the front door. Our conference was held in the best parlor, feebly lit by a single candle.

It began with the strange gentleman sitting down at the table, drawing the candle toward him, and looking over some entries in his pocketbook. He then put the book away and set the candle slightly to one side, peering around it into the darkness at Joe and me to determine which was which.

"My name," he said, "is Jaggers, and I am a lawyer in London. I am fairly well known. I have unusual business to transact with you, and I'll begin by explaining that it is not of my own making. If my advice had been asked, I should not be here. It was not asked, and here I am. What I have to do as the confidential agent of another, I do. No less, no more."
Finding he could not see us well from where he sat, he got up, threw one leg over the back of a chair, and leaned on it — one foot on the seat, one foot on the ground.

"Now, Joseph Gargery. I am the bearer of an offer to relieve you of this young fellow, your apprentice. You would not object to canceling his indentures, at his request and for his benefit? You would want nothing for doing so?"
"Lord forbid that I should want anything for not standing in Pip's way," said Joe, staring.
"Lord forbidding is pious, but beside the point," returned Mr. Jaggers. "The question is: would you want anything? Do you want anything?"
"The answer is," returned Joe sternly, "No."
I thought Mr. Jaggers glanced at Joe as if he considered him a fool for his selflessness. But I was too overwhelmed by breathless curiosity and surprise to be sure.
"Very well," said Mr. Jaggers. "Remember the admission you have made, and don't try to go back on it later."
"Who's going to try?" retorted Joe.
"I don't say anyone is. Do you keep a dog?"
"Yes, I do keep a dog."

"Bear in mind, then, that Brag is a good dog, but Holdfast is a better. Bear that in mind, will you?" repeated Mr. Jaggers, shutting his eyes and nodding at Joe as if forgiving him something. "Now, I return to this young fellow. And the communication I have to make is this: he has great expectations."
Joe and I gasped and looked at one another.

"I am instructed to communicate to him" — said Mr. Jaggers, jabbing his finger sideways at me — "that he will come into a handsome property. Further, that it is the desire of the present possessor of that property that he be immediately removed from his present sphere of life and from this place, and be brought up as a gentleman — in a word, as a young fellow of great expectations."
My dream had come true. My wildest fantasy was surpassed by sober reality. Miss Havisham was going to make my fortune on a grand scale.

"Now, Mr. Pip," pursued the lawyer, "I address the rest of what I have to say to you. You are to understand, first, that it is the request of the person from whom I take my instructions that you always bear the name of Pip. You will have no objection, I imagine, to your great expectations being encumbered with that easy condition. But if you have any objection, this is the time to mention it."
My heart was beating so fast, and there was such a ringing in my ears, that I could barely stammer I had no objection.

"I should think not! Now you are to understand, secondly, Mr. Pip, that the name of the person who is your liberal benefactor remains a profound secret, until that person chooses to reveal it. I am empowered to mention that it is the person's intention to reveal it firsthand, by word of mouth, to you directly. When or where that intention may be carried out, I cannot say. No one can say. It may be years from now. Now, you are to understand clearly that you are most strictly forbidden from making any inquiry on this subject. Or any allusion or reference, however distant, to any individual whatsoever as the individual, in all your communications with me. If you have a suspicion in your own breast, keep it there. It is not the least bit relevant what the reasons for this prohibition are. They may be the strongest and gravest reasons, or they may be mere whim. This is not for you to ask about. The condition is laid down. Your acceptance of it, and your observance of it as binding, is the only remaining condition that I am charged with by the person from whom I take my instructions, and for whom I am not otherwise responsible. That person is the person from whom you derive your expectations, and the secret is held solely by that person and by me. Again, not a very difficult condition to attach to such a rise in fortune. But if you have any objection to it, this is the time to mention it. Speak out."
Once more, I stammered with difficulty that I had no objection.

"I should think not! Now, Mr. Pip, I have done with stipulations." Though he called me Mr. Pip and was beginning to warm to me somewhat, he still could not shake a certain air of bullying suspicion. Even now he occasionally shut his eyes and jabbed his finger at me as he spoke, as much as to say he knew all sorts of things to my discredit, if he only chose to mention them. "We come next to the mere details of arrangement. You must know that, although I have used the term 'expectations' more than once, you are not endowed with expectations only. There is already lodged in my hands a sum of money more than sufficient for your proper education and maintenance. You will please consider me your guardian. Oh!" — for I was about to thank him — "I tell you at once, I am paid for my services, or I would not render them. It is considered that you must be better educated, in keeping with your changed position, and that you will appreciate the importance and necessity of immediately taking up that advantage."
I said I had always longed for it.

"Never mind what you have always longed for, Mr. Pip," he retorted. "Keep to the record. If you long for it now, that's enough. Am I to understand you are ready to be placed at once under a proper tutor? Is that it?"
I stammered yes, that was it.
"Good. Now, your preferences are to be consulted. I don't think that wise, mind, but it's my trust. Have you ever heard of any tutor you would prefer over another?"
I had never heard of any tutor except Biddy and Mr. Wopsle's great-aunt, so I replied in the negative.

"There is a certain tutor of whom I have some knowledge, who I think might suit the purpose," said Mr. Jaggers. "I don't recommend him, mind you — I never recommend anybody. The gentleman I speak of is one Mr. Matthew Pocket."

Ah! I caught at the name instantly. Miss Havisham's relation. The Matthew whom Mr. and Mrs. Camilla had spoken of. The Matthew whose place was to be at Miss Havisham's head when she lay dead in her bride's dress on the bride's table.
"You know the name?" said Mr. Jaggers, looking shrewdly at me, then shutting his eyes as he waited for my answer.
My answer was that I had heard the name.
"Oh!" said he. "You have heard of the name. But the question is, what do you say to it?"
I said, or tried to say, that I was much obliged to him for his recommendation—
"No, my young friend!" he interrupted, shaking his great head very slowly. "Recollect yourself!"
Not recollecting myself, I began again: that I was much obliged to him for his recommendation—

"No, my young friend," he interrupted, shaking his head and frowning and smiling at the same time. "No, no, no. It's very well done, but it won't do. You are too young to pin that on me. Recommendation is not the word, Mr. Pip. Try another."
Correcting myself, I said that I was much obliged to him for his mention of Mr. Matthew Pocket—
"That's more like it!" cried Mr. Jaggers. And (I added) I would gladly try that gentleman.
"Good. You had better try him in his own house. The way shall be prepared for you, and you can see his son first, who is in London. When will you come to London?"
I said — glancing at Joe, who stood looking on, motionless — that I supposed I could come right away.
"First," said Mr. Jaggers, "you should have some new clothes to come in, and they should not be working clothes. Say this day week. You'll want some money. Shall I leave you twenty guineas?"

He produced a long purse with the greatest coolness, counted out the coins on the table, and pushed them over to me. This was the first time he had taken his leg off the chair. He sat straddling it after pushing the money across, swinging his purse and eyeing Joe.
"Well, Joseph Gargery? You look dumbfounded."
"I am!" said Joe, very firmly.
"It was understood that you wanted nothing for yourself, remember?"
"It were understood," said Joe. "And it are understood. And it ever will be similar according."
"But what," said Mr. Jaggers, swinging his purse, "what if it was in my instructions to make you a present, as compensation?"
"As compensation for what?" Joe demanded.
"For the loss of his services."

Joe laid his hand on my shoulder with a woman's touch. I have often thought of him since as like the steam hammer that can crush a man or pat an eggshell — that combination of strength and gentleness. "Pip is that hearty welcome," said Joe, "to go free with his services, to honor and fortune, as no words can tell him. But if you think as money can make compensation to me for the loss of the little child — what come to the forge — and ever the best of friends!—"

Oh, dear good Joe, whom I was so ready to leave and so ungrateful to — I see you again, with your muscular blacksmith's arm before your eyes, and your broad chest heaving, and your voice dying away. Oh, dear good faithful tender Joe, I feel the loving tremble of your hand on my arm, as solemnly this day as if it had been the rustle of an angel's wing!

But I encouraged Joe at the time. I was lost in the maze of my future fortunes, and could not retrace the paths we had walked together. I begged Joe to be comforted, for (as he said) we had always been the best of friends, and (as I said) we always would be. Joe wiped his eyes with his free wrist, as if intent on gouging himself, but said not another word.
Mr. Jaggers had watched all this like a man regarding Joe as the village idiot, and me as his keeper. When it was over, he said, weighing the purse he had stopped swinging:

"Now, Joseph Gargery, I warn you this is your last chance. No half measures with me. If you mean to accept a present that I have been charged to make you, speak out and you shall have it. If on the contrary you mean to say—" Here, to his great amazement, Joe suddenly began circling him with every sign of readiness for a fight.

"Which I mean to say," cried Joe, "that if you come into my place bull-baiting and badgering me, come out! Which I mean to say, if you're a man, come on! Which I mean to say, what I say, I mean to say and stand or fall by!"

I drew Joe away, and he immediately calmed down. He merely stated to me, in a polite and obliging manner — and as a courteous notice to anyone it might concern — that he were not going to be bull-baited and badgered in his own place. Mr. Jaggers had risen when Joe got fired up, and had backed near the door. Without showing any inclination to come back in, he delivered his parting remarks from there. They were these:

"Well, Mr. Pip, I think the sooner you leave here — as you are to be a gentleman — the better. Let it stand for this day week, and you shall receive my printed address in the meantime. You can take a coach at the stagecoach office in London and come straight to me. Understand that I express no opinion, one way or another, on the trust I undertake. I am paid for undertaking it, and I do so. Now, understand that, finally. Understand that!"
He was jabbing his finger at both of us, and I think would have gone on, but for seeming to think Joe dangerous, and going off.
Something came into my head that made me run after him as he headed down to the Jolly Bargemen, where he had left a hired carriage.
"I beg your pardon, Mr. Jaggers."
"Hello!" said he, turning around. "What's the matter?"
"I want to be quite right, Mr. Jaggers, and to follow your directions. So I thought I had better ask. Would there be any objection to my saying goodbye to anyone I know around here, before I go?"
"No," said he, looking as if he hardly understood me.
"I don't mean just in the village, but up in town as well."
"No," said he. "No objection."

I thanked him and ran home. There I found that Joe had already locked the front door, abandoned the best parlor, and was seated by the kitchen fire with a hand on each knee, gazing intently at the burning coals. I too sat down before the fire and gazed at the coals. Nothing was said for a long time.

My sister was in her cushioned chair in her corner. Biddy sat with her needlework before the fire. Joe sat next to Biddy, and I sat next to Joe, in the corner opposite my sister. The more I looked into the glowing coals, the less able I was to look at Joe. The longer the silence lasted, the less able I felt to speak.
At last I managed, "Joe, have you told Biddy?"
"No, Pip," returned Joe, still looking at the fire and holding his knees tight, as if he had private information that they intended to make off somewhere. "Which I left it to yourself, Pip."
"I would rather you told, Joe."
"Pip's a gentleman of fortune, then," said Joe, "and God bless him in it!"

Biddy dropped her work and looked at me. Joe held his knees and looked at me. I looked at both of them. After a pause, they both congratulated me heartily. But there was a certain touch of sadness in their congratulations that I rather resented.

I took it upon myself to impress on Biddy — and through Biddy, Joe — the solemn obligation I considered my friends to be under: to know nothing and say nothing about the source of my fortune. It would all come out in good time, I said, and in the meantime nothing was to be said except that I had come into great expectations from a mysterious patron. Biddy nodded thoughtfully at the fire as she picked up her work again, and said she would be very careful. Joe, still gripping his knees, said, "Ay, ay, I'll be ekervally particular, Pip." Then they congratulated me again, and went on to express so much astonishment at the idea of my being a gentleman that I didn't half like it.

Biddy then went to great lengths to convey some idea of what had happened to my sister. To the best of my belief, these efforts completely failed. She laughed and nodded her head many times, and even repeated after Biddy the words "Pip" and "Property." But I doubt they held any more meaning for her than an election slogan, and I cannot suggest a darker picture of her state of mind.

I never could have believed it without experiencing it, but as Joe and Biddy became cheerful and relaxed again, I grew quite gloomy. Dissatisfied with my fortune, of course I could not be. But it is possible that I may have been, without quite knowing it, dissatisfied with myself.

In any case, I sat with my elbow on my knee and my face in my hand, staring into the fire, as those two talked about my going away and what they should do without me, and all that. Whenever I caught one of them looking at me — though never unkindly, and they looked often, especially Biddy — I felt offended, as if they were expressing some distrust of me. Though Heaven knows they never did, by word or sign.

At those times I would get up and look out the door. Our kitchen door opened straight onto the night and stood open on summer evenings to air the room. The very stars to which I raised my eyes, I am afraid I thought poor and humble ones, for shining on the rustic surroundings among which I had lived my life.
"Saturday night," said I, when we sat at our supper of bread and cheese and beer. "Five more days, and then the day before the day! They'll pass quickly."
"Yes, Pip," said Joe, whose voice sounded hollow in his beer mug. "They'll pass quickly."
"Quickly, quickly," said Biddy.

"I've been thinking, Joe, that when I go to town on Monday to order my new clothes, I'll tell the tailor I'll come and put them on there, or have them sent to Mr. Pumblechook's. It would be very disagreeable to be stared at by everyone here."

"Mr. and Mrs. Hubble might like to see you in your new genteel figure too, Pip," said Joe, industriously cutting his bread with cheese on it in the palm of his left hand, and glancing at my untouched supper as if remembering the time when we used to compare slices. "So might Wopsle. And the Jolly Bargemen might take it as a compliment."
"That's just what I don't want, Joe. They would make such a business of it — such a coarse and common business — that I couldn't bear myself."
"Ah, that indeed, Pip!" said Joe. "If you couldn't bear yourself—"
Biddy asked me here, as she sat holding my sister's plate, "Have you thought about when you'll show yourself to Mr. Gargery, and your sister, and me? You will show yourself to us, won't you?"
"Biddy," I returned with some resentment, "you are so exceedingly quick that it's hard to keep up with you."
("She always were quick," observed Joe.)
"If you had waited another moment, Biddy, you would have heard me say that I shall bring my clothes here in a bundle one evening — most likely the evening before I go away."

Biddy said no more. Graciously forgiving her, I soon exchanged an affectionate good night with her and Joe, and went up to bed. When I got into my little room, I sat down and took a long look at it — a mean little room that I should soon be parted from and raised above, forever. It was furnished with fresh young memories too, and even at that moment I fell into much the same confused division of mind between it and the better rooms I was going to, as I so often had between the forge and Miss Havisham's, and Biddy and Estella.

The sun had been shining brightly all day on my attic roof, and the room was warm. As I opened the window and stood looking out, I saw Joe come slowly through the dark door below and take a turn or two in the air. Then I saw Biddy come and bring him a pipe and light it for him. He never smoked so late, and it seemed to suggest that he wanted comforting, for some reason.

Presently he stood at the door directly beneath me, smoking his pipe, and Biddy stood there too, talking to him quietly. I knew they talked of me, for I heard my name mentioned in a tender tone by both of them, more than once. I would not have listened for more, even if I could have heard more. So I drew away from the window and sat down in my one chair by the bed, feeling it very sad and strange that this first night of my bright fortunes should be the loneliest I had ever known.

Looking toward the open window, I saw light wisps of smoke from Joe's pipe floating there, and I fancied it was like a blessing from Joe — not forced on me or displayed before me, but pervading the air we shared together. I put out my light and crept into bed. It was an uneasy bed now, and I never slept the old sound sleep in it anymore.

chapters.title: Chapter 19
paragraphs: Morning made a considerable difference in my general outlook on life, and brightened it so much that it scarcely seemed the same. What weighed heaviest on my mind was the thought that six days still lay between me and departure. I couldn't shake the fear that something might happen to London in the meantime, and that when I got there, it would be either greatly deteriorated or gone entirely.

Joe and Biddy were sympathetic and pleasant when I spoke of our approaching separation, but they only mentioned it when I did. After breakfast, Joe brought out my indentures from the cabinet in the best parlor, and we put them in the fire. I felt that I was free. With the full novelty of my emancipation upon me, I went to church with Joe, and thought perhaps the clergyman wouldn't have read that passage about the rich man and the kingdom of Heaven if he had known the whole story.

After our early dinner, I strolled out alone, intending to take one final look at the marshes and be done with them. As I passed the church, I felt — as I had felt during the morning service — a sublime compassion for the poor creatures who were destined to go there, Sunday after Sunday, all their lives, and to lie at last in obscurity among the low green mounds. I promised myself that I would do something for them one day, and formed an outline plan to bestow a dinner of roast beef and plum pudding, a pint of ale, and a gallon of condescension upon everybody in the village.

If I had often thought before, with something close to shame, of my connection with the fugitive I had once seen limping among those graves, what were my thoughts this Sunday, when the place recalled that wretch — ragged and shivering, with his convict's iron and badge! My comfort was that it had all happened a long time ago. He had doubtless been transported far away. He was dead to me, and might well be actually dead besides.

No more low, wet grounds. No more ditches and sluice gates. No more of these grazing cattle — though they seemed, in their dull way, to wear a more respectful air now, and to turn around so they might stare as long as possible at the possessor of such great expectations. Farewell, monotonous companions of my childhood! From now on, I was bound for London and greatness — not for blacksmith's work in general, and not for you! I made my triumphant way to the old Battery, and lying down there to consider the question of whether Miss Havisham intended me for Estella, fell asleep.
When I woke, I was much surprised to find Joe sitting beside me, smoking his pipe. He greeted me with a cheerful smile as I opened my eyes, and said:
"As being the last time, Pip, I thought I'd follow."
"And Joe, I am very glad you did."
"Thankee, Pip."
"You may be sure, dear Joe," I went on, after we had shaken hands, "that I shall never forget you."

"No, no, Pip!" said Joe comfortably. "I'm sure of that. Ay, ay, old chap! Bless you, it were only necessary to get it well round in a man's mind, to be certain on it. But it took a bit of time to get it well round, the change come so uncommon sudden — didn't it?"

Somehow, I was not entirely pleased by Joe's being so securely confident of me. I should have liked him to show some emotion, or to say, "It does you credit, Pip," or something of that sort. So I made no remark on his first point, and merely said, regarding his second, that the news had indeed come suddenly, but that I had always wanted to be a gentleman, and had often speculated on what I would do if I were one.
"Have you though?" said Joe. "Astonishing!"
"It's a pity now, Joe," said I, "that you didn't get on a little more when we had our lessons here, isn't it?"

"Well, I don't know," returned Joe. "I'm so awful dull. I'm only master of my own trade. It were always a pity as I was so awful dull — but it's no more of a pity now than it was this day twelvemonth — don't you see?"

What I had meant was that when I came into my property and was able to do something for Joe, it would have been much more pleasant if he had been better qualified for a rise in station. He was so perfectly innocent of my meaning, however, that I decided I would mention it to Biddy instead.

So when we had walked home and had tea, I took Biddy into our little garden by the side of the lane. After casually mentioning, to lift her spirits, that I should never forget her, I said I had a favor to ask.
"And it is, Biddy," said I, "that you will not miss any opportunity to help Joe along a little."
"How, helping him along?" asked Biddy, with a steady sort of look.
"Well! Joe is a dear good fellow — in fact, I think he is the dearest fellow that ever lived — but he is rather backward in some things. For instance, Biddy, in his learning and his manners."
Although I was looking at Biddy as I spoke, and although she opened her eyes very wide when I had spoken, she did not look at me.
"Oh, his manners! Won't his manners do, then?" asked Biddy, plucking a blackcurrant leaf.
"My dear Biddy, they do very well here—"
"Oh! They do very well here?" interrupted Biddy, looking closely at the leaf in her hand.
"Hear me out — but if I were to move Joe into a higher sphere, as I shall hope to do when I fully come into my property, they would hardly do him justice."
"And don't you think he knows that?" asked Biddy.
It was such a provoking question — for the idea had never in the most distant way occurred to me — that I said snappishly:
"Biddy, what do you mean?"

Biddy, having rubbed the leaf to pieces between her hands — and the smell of a blackcurrant bush has ever since reminded me of that evening in the little garden by the lane — said, "Have you never considered that he may be proud?"
"Proud?" I repeated, with scornful emphasis.
"Oh, there are many kinds of pride," said Biddy, looking directly at me and shaking her head. "Pride is not all of one kind—"
"Well? Why are you stopping?" said I.

"Not all of one kind," Biddy resumed. "He may be too proud to let anyone take him out of a place that he is fit to fill, and fills well and with respect. To tell you the truth, I think he is — though it sounds bold of me to say so, since you must know him far better than I do."
"Now, Biddy," said I, "I am very sorry to see this in you. I did not expect it. You are envious, Biddy, and grudging. You are dissatisfied about my rise in fortune, and you can't help showing it."
"If you have the heart to think so," returned Biddy, "say so. Say so over and over again, if you have the heart to think so."

"If you have the heart to be so, you mean, Biddy," said I, in a virtuous and superior tone. "Don't put it off on me. I am very sorry to see it, and it's a — it's a bad side of human nature. I did intend to ask you to use whatever little opportunities you might have, after I was gone, to improve dear Joe. But after this, I ask you nothing. I am extremely sorry to see this in you, Biddy," I repeated. "It's a — it's a bad side of human nature."

"Whether you scold me or approve of me," returned poor Biddy, "you may equally depend on my trying to do all in my power, here, at all times. And whatever opinion you take away of me will make no difference to how I remember you. Yet a gentleman should not be unjust either," said Biddy, turning her head away.

I again warmly repeated that it was a bad side of human nature (in which sentiment, setting aside its application, I have since seen reason to think I was right), and I walked down the little path away from Biddy. Biddy went into the house, and I went out through the garden gate and took a dejected stroll until supper time — again feeling it very sad and strange that this, the second night of my bright fortunes, should be as lonely and unsatisfying as the first.

But morning once more brightened my view, and I extended my forgiveness to Biddy, and we dropped the subject. Putting on the best clothes I had, I went into town as early as I could hope to find the shops open, and presented myself before Mr. Trabb, the tailor. He was having his breakfast in the parlor behind his shop, and did not think it worth his while to come out to me, but called me in to him.
"Well!" said Mr. Trabb, in a hearty, hail-fellow-well-met sort of way. "How are you, and what can I do for you?"

Mr. Trabb had sliced his hot roll into three feather beds, and was slipping butter between the blankets and tucking it in. He was a prosperous old bachelor, and his open window looked into a prosperous little garden and orchard. There was a prosperous iron safe set into the wall beside his fireplace, and I had no doubt that heaps of his prosperity were stored inside it in bags.
"Mr. Trabb," said I, "it's an unpleasant thing to mention, because it looks like boasting. But I have come into a handsome property."
A change came over Mr. Trabb. He forgot the butter in bed, got up from the bedside, and wiped his fingers on the tablecloth, exclaiming, "Lord bless my soul!"

"I am going up to my guardian in London," said I, casually drawing some guineas out of my pocket and looking at them, "and I want a fashionable suit of clothes to go in. I wish to pay for them" — I added, otherwise I thought he might only pretend to make them — "with ready money."

"My dear sir," said Mr. Trabb, respectfully bending his body, opening his arms, and taking the liberty of touching me on the outside of each elbow, "don't hurt me by mentioning that. May I venture to congratulate you? Would you do me the favor of stepping into the shop?"

Mr. Trabb's boy was the most audacious boy in all that countryside. When I had entered, he was sweeping the shop, and he had enlivened his labor by sweeping over me. He was still sweeping when I came into the shop with Mr. Trabb, and he knocked the broom against every possible corner and obstacle to express — as I understood it — equality with any blacksmith, alive or dead.

"Stop that noise," said Mr. Trabb with the greatest sternness, "or I'll knock your head off! Do me the favor of being seated, sir. Now, this" — said Mr. Trabb, taking down a roll of cloth and flowing it out over the counter, preparatory to getting his hand under it to show the sheen — "is a very fine article. I can recommend it for your purpose, sir, because it really is extra superior. But you shall see some others. Give me Number Four, you!" (This to the boy, with a dreadfully severe stare, foreseeing the danger of that scoundrel brushing me with it, or taking some other liberty.)

Mr. Trabb never took his stern eye off the boy until he had deposited Number Four on the counter and was at a safe distance again. Then he commanded him to bring Number Five and Number Eight. "And let me have none of your tricks here," said Mr. Trabb, "or you shall repent it, you young scoundrel, the longest day you have to live."

Mr. Trabb then bent over Number Four and, in a sort of respectful confidence, recommended it to me as a light article for summer wear. An article much in fashion among the nobility and gentry. An article that it would always be an honor to him to reflect that a distinguished fellow townsman — if he might claim me as a fellow townsman — had worn. "Are you bringing Numbers Five and Eight, you vagabond," said Mr. Trabb to the boy, "or shall I kick you out of the shop and bring them myself?"

I selected the materials for a suit, with the help of Mr. Trabb's judgment, and went back into the parlor to be measured. For although Mr. Trabb already had my measurements and had previously been quite content with them, he said apologetically that it "wouldn't do under existing circumstances, sir — wouldn't do at all." So Mr. Trabb measured and calculated me in the parlor as if I were an estate and he the finest species of surveyor, and gave himself such a world of trouble that I felt no suit of clothes could possibly repay him for his efforts. When he had at last finished and arranged to send the articles to Mr. Pumblechook's on Thursday evening, he said, with his hand on the parlor door: "I know, sir, that London gentlemen cannot be expected to patronize local work as a rule. But if you would give me a turn now and then, in the way of a townsman, I should greatly appreciate it. Good morning, sir, much obliged. — Door!"

The last word was flung at the boy, who had not the least idea what it meant. But I saw him wilt as his master ushered me out with his hands. And my first real experience of the stupendous power of money was this: it had morally flattened Trabb's boy.

After this memorable event, I went to the hatter's, and the bootmaker's, and the hosier's, and felt rather like Mother Hubbard's dog, whose outfit required the services of so many trades. I also went to the coach office and booked my seat for seven o'clock Saturday morning. It was not necessary to explain everywhere that I had come into a handsome property, but whenever I said anything to that effect, the tradesman in question immediately stopped gazing out the window at the High Street and focused his attention entirely on me. When I had ordered everything I wanted, I headed toward Pumblechook's. As I approached that gentleman's place of business, I saw him standing at his door.

He was waiting for me with great impatience. He had been out early with the chaise cart and had called at the forge and heard the news. He had prepared a meal for me in the Barnwell parlor, and he too ordered his shopman to "get out of the way" as my sacred person passed.
"My dear friend," said Mr. Pumblechook, taking me by both hands when he and I and the food were alone, "I give you joy of your good fortune. Well deserved, well deserved!"
This was coming to the point, and I thought it a sensible way of putting things.
"To think," said Mr. Pumblechook, after snorting admiringly at me for some moments, "that I should have been the humble instrument of leading up to this — it is a proud reward."
I begged Mr. Pumblechook to remember that nothing was to be said or hinted on that point.
"My dear young friend," said Mr. Pumblechook, "if you will allow me to call you so—"

I murmured "Certainly," and Mr. Pumblechook took me by both hands again and communicated a movement to his waistcoat that had an emotional appearance, though it was rather low down. "My dear young friend, rely upon my doing my little all in your absence, by keeping the fact before the mind of Joseph. — Joseph!" said Mr. Pumblechook, in the manner of a compassionate plea. "Joseph!! Joseph!!!" Then he shook his head and tapped it, expressing his sense of Joe's deficiency.

"But my dear young friend," said Mr. Pumblechook, "you must be hungry. You must be exhausted. Be seated. Here is a chicken sent round from the Boar. Here is a tongue sent round from the Boar. Here are one or two little things sent round from the Boar, that I hope you may not despise. But do I" — said Mr. Pumblechook, getting up again the moment after he had sat down — "see before me him as I ever sported with in his times of happy infancy? And may I — may I—?"
This "May I" meant: might he shake hands? I consented, and he was fervent, and then sat down again.

"Here is wine," said Mr. Pumblechook. "Let us drink: Thanks to Fortune, and may she ever pick out her favorites with equal judgment! And yet I cannot" — said Mr. Pumblechook, getting up again — "see before me One — and likewise drink to One — without again expressing — May I — may I—?"

I said he might, and he shook hands with me again, emptied his glass, and turned it upside down. I did the same. And if I had turned myself upside down before drinking, the wine could not have gone more directly to my head.

Mr. Pumblechook helped me to the liver wing and to the best slice of tongue — none of those out-of-the-way dead-end cuts of pork now — and took, comparatively speaking, no care of himself at all. "Ah! Poultry, poultry! You little thought," said Mr. Pumblechook, addressing the fowl in the dish, "when you was a young fledgling, what was in store for you. You little thought you was to be refreshment beneath this humble roof for one as — Call it a weakness if you will," said Mr. Pumblechook, rising again, "but may I? May I—?"
It began to be unnecessary to repeat the formality of saying he might, so he just did it. How he managed it so often without stabbing himself with my knife, I don't know.

"And your sister," he resumed, after a little steady eating, "which had the honor of bringing you up by hand! It's a sad picture, to reflect that she's no longer equal to fully understanding the honor. May—"
I saw he was about to come at me again, and I stopped him.
"We'll drink her health," said I.

"Ah!" cried Mr. Pumblechook, leaning back in his chair, completely limp with admiration. "That's the way you know 'em, sir!" (I don't know who sir was, but it certainly wasn't me, and there was no third person present.) "That's the way you know the noble-minded, sir! Ever forgiving and ever gracious. It might" — said the servile Pumblechook, putting down his untouched glass in a hurry and getting up again — "to a common person, have the appearance of repeating — but may I—?"
When he had done it, he resumed his seat and drank to my sister. "Let us never be blind," said Mr. Pumblechook, "to her faults of temper. But it is to be hoped she meant well."
Around this time, I began to notice he was getting flushed in the face. As for myself, I felt all face — steeped in wine and stinging.

I mentioned to Mr. Pumblechook that I wanted my new clothes sent to his house, and he was ecstatic at being so honored. I mentioned my reason for wanting to avoid attention in the village, and he praised it to the skies. There was nobody but himself, he hinted, worthy of my confidence, and — in short, might he? Then he asked me tenderly whether I remembered our boyish games with sums, and how we had gone together to have me bound apprentice, and, in effect, how he had always been my favorite companion and chosen friend. If I had drunk ten times as many glasses of wine as I had, I should still have known that he had never stood in that relation to me, and should in my heart of hearts have rejected the idea. Yet for all that, I remember feeling convinced that I had been much mistaken about him, and that he was a sensible, practical, good-hearted, first-rate fellow.

By degrees, he came to place such great confidence in me as to ask my advice about his own affairs. He mentioned that there was an opportunity for a grand merger and monopoly of the corn and seed trade on those premises, if expanded — such as had never occurred before in that or any other neighborhood. All that was wanting for the realization of a vast fortune, he considered, was More Capital. Those were the two little words: more capital. Now it seemed to him, Pumblechook, that if that capital were invested in the business through a sleeping partner, sir — which sleeping partner would have nothing to do but walk in, by self or deputy, whenever he pleased, and examine the books — and walk in twice a year and take his profits away in his pocket, to the tune of fifty percent — it seemed to him that this might be an opening for a young gentleman of spirit combined with property, which would be worthy of his attention. But what did I think? He had great confidence in my opinion. What did I think? I gave it as my opinion. "Wait a bit!" The united grandeur and clarity of this view so struck him that he no longer asked if he might shake hands with me, but said he really must — and did.

We drank all the wine, and Mr. Pumblechook pledged himself over and over again to keep Joseph up to the mark (I don't know what mark), and to render me efficient and constant service (I don't know what service). He also revealed to me for the first time in my life — and certainly after keeping his secret remarkably well — that he had always said of me: "That boy is no common boy, and mark me, his fortune will be no common fortune." He said with a tearful smile that it was a singular thing to think of now, and I said so too. Finally, I went out into the air with a hazy impression that there was something unusual in the behavior of the sunshine, and found that I had sleepily reached the turnpike without noticing the road at all.
There I was roused by Mr. Pumblechook calling after me. He was a long way down the sunny street, making frantic gestures for me to stop. I stopped, and he came up breathless.

"No, my dear friend," said he, when he had recovered enough wind to speak. "Not if I can help it. This occasion shall not entirely pass without that affability on your part. — May I, as an old friend and well-wisher? May I?"

We shook hands for the hundredth time at least, and he ordered a young cart driver out of my way with the greatest indignation. Then he blessed me and stood waving his hand until I had passed the bend in the road. After that, I turned into a field and had a long nap under a hedge before continuing my way home.

I had little luggage to take to London, for not much of my small wardrobe was suited to my new station. But I began packing that same afternoon, and wildly packed up things I knew I would need the next morning, pretending there was not a moment to lose.

So Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday passed. On Friday morning I went to Mr. Pumblechook's to put on my new clothes and pay my visit to Miss Havisham. Mr. Pumblechook's own room was given up to me for dressing, decorated with clean towels especially for the occasion. My clothes were rather a disappointment, of course. Probably every new and eagerly expected garment ever put on since clothes were invented falls a little short of the wearer's hopes. But after I had worn my new suit for half an hour, and had gone through an immensity of posing before Mr. Pumblechook's very limited mirror in the futile effort to see my legs, it seemed to fit me better. Since it was market morning in a neighboring town ten miles off, Mr. Pumblechook was not at home. I had not told him exactly when I meant to leave, and was unlikely to shake hands with him again before departing. This was all as it should be, and I went out in my new array — terribly ashamed of having to pass the shopman, and suspecting after all that I was at a personal disadvantage, something like Joe's in his Sunday suit.

I went by a roundabout route to Miss Havisham's, using all the back ways, and rang the bell with difficulty on account of the stiff, long fingers of my gloves. Sarah Pocket came to the gate and positively reeled back when she saw me so changed. Her walnut-shell face turned from brown to green and yellow.
"You?" said she. "You? Good gracious! What do you want?"
"I am going to London, Miss Pocket," said I, "and want to say goodbye to Miss Havisham."
I was not expected, for she left me locked in the yard while she went to ask if I was to be admitted. After a very short delay, she returned and took me up, staring at me the whole way.

Miss Havisham was taking exercise in the room with the long spread table, leaning on her crutch stick. The room was lit as it always was, and at the sound of our entrance, she stopped and turned. She was just then beside the rotted bride-cake.
"Don't go, Sarah," she said. "Well, Pip?"
"I start for London tomorrow, Miss Havisham," I said, being exceedingly careful with my words, "and I thought you would kindly not mind my taking leave of you."
"This is a fine figure, Pip," said she, making her crutch stick play around me as if she, the fairy godmother who had transformed me, were bestowing the finishing touch.
"I have come into such good fortune since I last saw you, Miss Havisham," I murmured. "And I am so grateful for it, Miss Havisham!"
"Yes, yes!" said she, looking with delight at the discomfited and envious Sarah. "I have seen Mr. Jaggers. I have heard about it, Pip. So you go tomorrow?"
"Yes, Miss Havisham."
"And you are adopted by a rich person?"
"Yes, Miss Havisham."
"Not named?"
"No, Miss Havisham."
"And Mr. Jaggers is made your guardian?"
"Yes, Miss Havisham."

She fairly gloated over these questions and answers, so keen was her enjoyment of Sarah Pocket's jealous dismay. "Well!" she went on. "You have a promising career before you. Be good — deserve it — and follow Mr. Jaggers's instructions." She looked at me, and looked at Sarah, and Sarah's watchful face was wrung into a cruel smile. "Goodbye, Pip! You will always keep the name of Pip, you know."
"Yes, Miss Havisham."
"Goodbye, Pip!"

She stretched out her hand, and I went down on my knee and put it to my lips. I had not planned how I should take leave of her; it came naturally at that moment. She looked at Sarah Pocket with triumph in her strange eyes. And so I left my fairy godmother, with both hands on her crutch stick, standing in the midst of the dimly lit room beside the rotten bride-cake hidden in cobwebs.

Sarah Pocket conducted me down as if I were a ghost who must be seen out. She could not get over my appearance and was utterly confounded. I said, "Goodbye, Miss Pocket," but she merely stared, and did not seem collected enough to realize I had spoken. Clear of the house, I made my way back to Pumblechook's as fast as I could, took off my new clothes, made them into a bundle, and went home in my old ones — carrying the bundle, to tell the truth, much more at ease, though it was an extra burden.

And now those six days that were supposed to crawl had raced by and were gone, and tomorrow looked me in the face more steadily than I could look at it. As the six evenings had dwindled — to five, to four, to three, to two — I had become more and more appreciative of Joe and Biddy's company. On this last evening I dressed up in my new clothes for their delight, and sat in my splendor until bedtime. We had a hot supper for the occasion, graced by the inevitable roast fowl, and some flip to finish with. We were all very low, and none the higher for pretending to be cheerful.

I was to leave our village at five in the morning, carrying my little portmanteau, and I had told Joe that I wished to walk away alone. I am afraid — deeply afraid — that this wish came from my sense of the contrast there would be between me and Joe if we went to the coach together. I had told myself there was no taint of this in the arrangement. But when I went up to my little room on this last night, I felt compelled to admit that it might be so, and I had an impulse to go down again and beg Joe to walk with me in the morning. I did not.

All night, coaches filled my broken sleep — going to wrong places instead of London, and having in the traces now dogs, now cats, now pigs, now men — never horses. Fantastic failed journeys occupied me until dawn broke and the birds were singing. Then I got up and partly dressed, and sat at the window to take a last look out. And in taking it, fell asleep.

Biddy was up so early to make my breakfast that, although I didn't sleep at the window more than an hour, I smelled the smoke of the kitchen fire when I jolted awake with the terrible idea that it must be late afternoon. But long after that, and long after I had heard the clinking of teacups and was quite ready, I couldn't find the courage to go downstairs. I stayed up there, repeatedly unlocking and unstrapping my small portmanteau and locking and strapping it up again, until Biddy called up that I was late.

It was a hurried breakfast with no taste to it. I rose from the meal, saying with a sort of forced briskness, as if it had only just occurred to me: "Well! I suppose I must be off!" Then I kissed my sister, who was laughing and nodding and shaking in her usual chair. I kissed Biddy. I threw my arms around Joe's neck. Then I took up my little portmanteau and walked out. The last I saw of them was when I heard a scuffle behind me and, looking back, saw Joe throwing an old shoe after me and Biddy throwing another. I stopped to wave my hat, and dear old Joe waved his strong right arm above his head, crying hoarsely, "Hooroar!" And Biddy put her apron to her face.

I walked away at a good pace, thinking it was easier to go than I had expected, and reflecting that it would never have done to have an old shoe thrown after the coach in sight of the whole High Street. I whistled and made nothing of going. But the village was very peaceful and quiet, and the light mists were solemnly rising as if to show me the world. And I had been so innocent and small there, and all beyond was so unknown and vast, that in a moment, with a strong heave and sob, I broke into tears. It was by the finger-post at the end of the village. I laid my hand upon it and said, "Goodbye, oh my dear, dear friend!"

Heaven knows we need never be ashamed of our tears, for they are rain upon the blinding dust of earth, overlying our hard hearts. I was better after I had cried than before — more sorry, more aware of my own ingratitude, more gentle. If I had cried before, I should have had Joe with me then.

So humbled was I by those tears, and by their breaking out again during the quiet walk, that when I was on the coach and it was clear of the town, I considered with an aching heart whether I should get down when we changed horses and walk back, and have another evening at home and a better parting. We changed, and I had not made up my mind, and still told myself for comfort that it would be perfectly possible to get down and walk back when we changed again. And while I was busy with these thoughts, I would fancy I saw an exact likeness of Joe in some man coming along the road toward us, and my heart would beat high — as if he could possibly be there!
We changed again, and yet again, and it was now too late and too far to go back. So I went on. And the mists had all solemnly risen now, and the world lay spread before me.
THIS IS THE END OF THE FIRST STAGE OF PIP'S EXPECTATIONS.

chapters.title: Chapter 20
paragraphs: The journey from our town to the capital took about five hours. It was a little past midday when the four-horse stagecoach I was riding got tangled in the snarl of traffic around the Cross Keys, Wood Street, Cheapside, London.

We Britons had at that time firmly settled that it was treason to doubt we had and were the best of everything. Otherwise, while I was overwhelmed by the immensity of London, I think I might have had some faint suspicion that it was rather ugly, crooked, narrow, and dirty.

Mr. Jaggers had duly sent me his address: Little Britain. He had written after it on his card, "just out of Smithfield, and close by the coach office." Nevertheless, a cab driver, who seemed to have as many capes on his greasy greatcoat as he had years on him, packed me into his coach and hemmed me in with a folding, jingling barrier of steps, as if he were going to take me fifty miles. His climbing up to his box — which I remember was decorated with an old, weather-stained, pea-green covering, moth-eaten to rags — was quite a job of work. It was a wonderful carriage, with six great coronets on the outside, and ragged things behind for I don't know how many footmen to hold onto, and a spiked frame below them to prevent amateurs from trying.

I had barely had time to appreciate the coach — and to think how like a straw yard it was, and yet how like a rag shop, and to wonder why the horses' nose bags were kept inside — when I noticed the driver beginning to climb down, as if we were about to stop. And stop we did, in a gloomy street, at certain offices with an open door, on which was painted MR. JAGGERS.
"How much?" I asked the driver.
The driver answered, "A shilling — unless you wish to make it more."
I naturally said I had no wish to make it more.
"Then it must be a shilling," observed the driver. "I don't want to get into trouble. I know him!" He darkly closed one eye at Mr. Jaggers's name, and shook his head.

When he had got his shilling, and had in due course completed the climb to his box, and had gotten away — which appeared to relieve his mind — I went into the front office with my little portmanteau in my hand and asked: was Mr. Jaggers at home?
"He is not," returned the clerk. "He is in court at present. Am I addressing Mr. Pip?"
I confirmed that he was addressing Mr. Pip.

"Mr. Jaggers left word: would you wait in his room? He couldn't say how long he might be, having a case on. But it stands to reason, his time being valuable, that he won't be longer than he can help."

With those words, the clerk opened a door and ushered me into an inner chamber at the back. There we found a gentleman with one eye, in a velveteen suit and knee breeches, who wiped his nose with his sleeve on being interrupted in reading the newspaper.
"Go and wait outside, Mike," said the clerk.
I began to say that I hoped I was not interrupting, when the clerk shoved this gentleman out with as little ceremony as I had ever seen, tossed his fur cap out after him, and left me alone.

Mr. Jaggers's room was lit only by a skylight, and was a most dismal place. The skylight was set at an eccentric pitch like a broken head, and the distorted neighboring houses looked as if they had twisted themselves to peer down at me through it. There were not as many papers about as I had expected, and there were some odd objects that I had not expected — such as an old rusty pistol, a sword in a scabbard, several strange-looking boxes and packages, and two dreadful face casts on a shelf, peculiarly swollen and twitchy about the nose. Mr. Jaggers's own high-backed chair was of deadly black horsehair, with rows of brass nails around it, like a coffin. I could picture how he leaned back in it, biting his forefinger at his clients. The room was small, and the clients seemed to have had a habit of backing up against the wall. The wall, especially opposite Mr. Jaggers's chair, was greasy with shoulders. I recalled, too, that the one-eyed gentleman had shuffled back against the wall when I was the innocent cause of his being turned out.

I sat down in the client's chair placed opposite Mr. Jaggers's and became fascinated by the dismal atmosphere. I noticed that the clerk had the same air of knowing something to everybody else's disadvantage as his master did. I wondered how many other clerks there were upstairs, and whether they all claimed the same damaging mastery over their fellow creatures. I wondered what the history was of all the odd clutter around the room, and how it came to be there. I wondered whether the two swollen faces were of Mr. Jaggers's family, and if he was so unfortunate as to have had such ill-looking relatives, why he stuck them on that dusty shelf for the soot and flies to settle on, instead of giving them a place at home. Of course, I had no experience of a London summer day, and my spirits may have been oppressed by the hot, exhausted air and the dust and grit that lay thick on everything. But I sat wondering and waiting in Mr. Jaggers's stuffy room until I really could not bear the two casts on the shelf above his chair, and got up and went out.

When I told the clerk I would take a walk while I waited, he advised me to go around the corner into Smithfield. So I came into Smithfield, and the shameful place, all smeared with filth and fat and blood and foam, seemed to stick to me. I scrubbed it off with all possible speed by turning into a street where I saw the great black dome of St. Paul's bulging at me from behind a grim stone building that a bystander said was Newgate Prison. Following the prison wall, I found the roadway covered with straw to muffle the noise of passing vehicles. From this, and from the quantity of people standing about smelling strongly of spirits and beer, I gathered that the trials were on.

While I looked about me there, an exceedingly dirty and partially drunk officer of the court asked if I would like to step in and hear a trial or so.
