He informed me that he could give me a front seat for half a crown, with a full view of the Lord Chief Justice in his wig and robes — mentioning that awesome figure like a waxwork, and presently offering him at the reduced price of eighteenpence. When I declined on the grounds of an appointment, he was kind enough to take me into a yard and show me where the gallows was kept, and also where people were publicly whipped. Then he showed me the Debtors' Door, out of which the condemned came to be hanged — heightening the interest of that dreadful entrance by telling me that "four of 'em" would come out at that door the day after tomorrow at eight in the morning, to be killed in a row. This was horrible, and gave me a sickening idea of London. All the more so because the Lord Chief Justice's self-appointed guide wore — from hat to boots and back up to his handkerchief — mildewed clothes that had clearly not belonged to him originally, and which I got it into my head he had bought cheap from the executioner. Under these circumstances, I thought myself well rid of him for a shilling.

I dropped into the office to ask if Mr. Jaggers had come in yet, found he had not, and strolled out again. This time I made a tour of Little Britain and turned into Bartholomew Close. Now I became aware that other people were waiting for Mr. Jaggers, as well as I. There were two furtive-looking men lounging in Bartholomew Close, thoughtfully fitting their feet into the pavement cracks as they talked. One of them said to the other as they first passed me that "Jaggers would do it if it was to be done." There was a group of three men and two women standing at a corner. One of the women was crying into her dirty shawl, and the other comforted her by saying, as she pulled her own shawl over her shoulders, "Jaggers is for him, 'Melia, and what more could you have?" There was a red-eyed little man who came into the Close while I was lingering there, in company with a second little man whom he sent on an errand. While the messenger was gone, I watched this man — who was of a highly excitable temperament — performing a jig of anxiety under a lamppost, accompanying himself in a kind of frenzy with the words: "O Jaggerth, Jaggerth, Jaggerth! All otherth ith Cag-Maggerth, give me Jaggerth!" These testimonials to my guardian's popularity made a deep impression on me, and I admired and wondered more than ever.

At length, as I was looking out through the iron gate of Bartholomew Close into Little Britain, I saw Mr. Jaggers coming across the road toward me. All the others waiting saw him at the same time, and there was quite a rush at him. Mr. Jaggers, putting a hand on my shoulder and walking me along at his side without saying anything to me, addressed himself to his followers.
First, he took the two furtive men.

"Now, I have nothing to say to you," said Mr. Jaggers, jabbing his finger at them. "I want to know no more than I know. As to the result, it's a toss-up. I told you from the first it was a toss-up. Have you paid Wemmick?"
"We made the money up this morning, sir," said one of the men submissively, while the other studied Mr. Jaggers's face.
"I don't ask you when you made it up, or where, or whether you made it up at all. Has Wemmick got it?"
"Yes, sir," said both men together.
"Very well; then you may go. Now, I won't have it!" said Mr. Jaggers, waving his hand to push them behind him. "If you say a word to me, I'll throw up the case."
"We thought, Mr. Jaggers—" one of the men began, pulling off his hat.

"That's what I told you not to do," said Mr. Jaggers. "You thought! I think for you; that's enough for you. If I want you, I know where to find you; I don't want you to find me. Now I won't have it. I won't hear a word."
The two men looked at each other as Mr. Jaggers waved them behind again, and humbly fell back and were heard no more.
"And now you!" said Mr. Jaggers, suddenly stopping and turning on the two women with the shawls, from whom the three men had meekly separated. "Oh! Amelia, is it?"
"Yes, Mr. Jaggers."
"And do you remember," retorted Mr. Jaggers, "that but for me you wouldn't be here and couldn't be here?"
"Oh yes, sir!" exclaimed both women together. "Lord bless you, sir, we know that well!"
"Then why," said Mr. Jaggers, "do you come here?"
"My Bill, sir!" the crying woman pleaded.

"Now, I tell you what!" said Mr. Jaggers. "Once for all. If you don't know that your Bill's in good hands, I know it. And if you come here bothering about your Bill, I'll make an example of both your Bill and you, and let him slip through my fingers. Have you paid Wemmick?"
"Oh yes, sir! Every farthing."
"Very well. Then you have done all you have to do. Say another word — one single word — and Wemmick shall give you your money back."
This terrible threat caused the two women to back off immediately. No one remained now but the excitable man, who had already raised the hem of Mr. Jaggers's coat to his lips several times.
"I don't know this man!" said Mr. Jaggers, in the same devastating manner. "What does this fellow want?"
"My dear Mithter Jaggerth. Own brother to Habraham Latharuth?"
"Who's he?" said Mr. Jaggers. "Let go of my coat."
The petitioner, kissing the hem of the garment once more before releasing it, replied: "Habraham Latharuth, on thuthpithion of plate."
"You're too late," said Mr. Jaggers. "I am over the way."
"Holy father, Mithter Jaggerth!" cried my excitable acquaintance, turning white. "Don't thay you're again Habraham Latharuth!"
"I am," said Mr. Jaggers, "and there's an end of it. Get out of the way."

"Mithter Jaggerth! Half a moment! My own cuthen'th gone to Mithter Wemmick at thith prethent minute, to hoffer him hany termth. Mithter Jaggerth! Half a quarter of a moment! If you'd have the condethenthun to be bought off from the t'other thide — at hany thuperior prithe! — money no object! — Mithter Jaggerth — Mithter—!"

My guardian shook off his supplicant with supreme indifference and left him dancing on the pavement as if it were red hot. Without further interruption, we reached the front office, where we found the clerk and the man in velveteen with the fur cap.
"Here's Mike," said the clerk, getting down from his stool and approaching Mr. Jaggers confidentially.

"Oh!" said Mr. Jaggers, turning to the man, who was tugging a lock of hair in the middle of his forehead like the Bull in Cock Robin pulling at the bell rope. "Your man comes on this afternoon. Well?"
"Well, Master Jaggers," returned Mike, in the voice of a man suffering from a permanent cold, "after a deal of trouble, I've found one, sir, as might do."
"What is he prepared to swear?"
"Well, Master Jaggers," said Mike, wiping his nose on his fur cap this time, "in a general way, anything."

Mr. Jaggers suddenly became furious. "Now, I warned you before," said he, jabbing his forefinger at the terrified client, "that if you ever presumed to talk that way here, I'd make an example of you. You infernal scoundrel, how dare you tell me that?"
The client looked scared, but bewildered too, as if he had no idea what he'd done wrong.
"Spooney!" said the clerk in a low voice, giving him a nudge with his elbow. "Soft head! Need you say it to his face?"
"Now, I ask you, you blundering fool," said my guardian very sternly, "once more and for the last time: what is the man you have brought here prepared to swear?"

Mike looked hard at my guardian, as if trying to learn a lesson from his face, and slowly replied: "Either to character, or to having been in his company and never left him all the night in question."
"Now, be careful. In what station of life is this man?"
Mike looked at his cap, and at the floor, and at the ceiling, and at the clerk, and even at me, before beginning to reply nervously: "We've dressed him up like—" when my guardian thundered:
"What? You will, will you?"
("Spooney!" added the clerk again, with another nudge.)
After some helpless casting about, Mike brightened and began again:
"He is dressed like a respectable pieman. A sort of pastry cook."
"Is he here?" asked my guardian.
"I left him," said Mike, "sitting on some doorsteps round the corner."
"Take him past that window and let me see him."

The window in question was the office window. All three of us went to it, behind the wire blind, and presently saw the client walk by in a casual manner with a murderous-looking tall individual in a short suit of white linen and a paper cap. This guileless confectioner was by no means sober, and had a black eye in the green stage of recovery, which had been painted over.
"Tell him to take his witness away immediately," said my guardian to the clerk in extreme disgust, "and ask him what he means by bringing such a fellow as that."

My guardian then took me into his own room, and while he lunched standing — from a sandwich box and a pocket flask of sherry (he seemed to bully his very sandwich as he ate it) — he informed me of the arrangements he had made for me. I was to go to Barnard's Inn, to young Mr. Pocket's rooms, where a bed had been sent in for me. I was to remain with young Mr. Pocket until Monday. On Monday I was to go with him to his father's house on a visit, so I could try how I liked it. Also, I was told what my allowance was to be — it was a very generous one — and was handed from one of my guardian's drawers the cards of certain tradesmen with whom I was to deal for all kinds of clothes, and whatever else I could reasonably want. "You will find your credit good, Mr. Pip," said my guardian, whose flask of sherry smelled like a whole cask as he hastily refreshed himself, "but I shall by this means be able to check your bills and pull you up if I find you living beyond your means. Of course you'll go wrong somehow, but that's no fault of mine."

After I had pondered a little over this encouraging sentiment, I asked Mr. Jaggers if I could send for a coach. He said it was not worth the trouble — I was so near my destination. Wemmick should walk round with me, if I liked.

I then discovered that Wemmick was the clerk in the next room. Another clerk was summoned from upstairs to take his place while he was out, and I accompanied him into the street, after shaking hands with my guardian. We found a fresh set of people lingering outside, but Wemmick made a way among them by saying coolly yet firmly, "I tell you it's no use; he won't have a word to say to any of you." We soon got clear of them, and went on side by side.

chapters.title: Chapter 21
paragraphs: Studying Mr. Wemmick as we walked along, to see what he looked like in daylight, I found him to be a dry man, rather short, with a square wooden face whose expression seemed to have been imperfectly chipped out with a dull chisel. There were some marks in it that might have been dimples if the material had been softer and the tool finer, but which, as it was, were only dents. The chisel had made three or four attempts at embellishment around his nose but had given up without trying to smooth them. I judged him to be a bachelor from the frayed condition of his linen, and he appeared to have suffered a good many bereavements. He wore at least four mourning rings, plus a brooch depicting a lady and a weeping willow beside a tomb with an urn on it. I noticed, too, that several rings and seals hung from his watch chain, as if he were quite laden with mementos of departed friends. He had glittering eyes — small, keen, and black — and thin, wide, mottled lips. He had had them, to the best of my belief, for forty to fifty years.
"So you were never in London before?" said Mr. Wemmick to me.
"No," said I.
"I was new here once," said Mr. Wemmick. "Strange to think of now!"
"You are well acquainted with it now?"
"Why, yes," said Mr. Wemmick. "I know how things work here."
"Is it a very wicked place?" I asked, more for the sake of saying something than for information.
"You may get cheated, robbed, and murdered in London. But there are plenty of people anywhere who'll do that for you."
"If there is bad blood between you and them," said I, trying to soften it a little.
"Oh, I don't know about bad blood," returned Mr. Wemmick. "There's not much bad blood about it. They'll do it if there's anything to be got by it."
"That makes it worse."
"You think so?" returned Mr. Wemmick. "Much the same, I should say."

He wore his hat on the back of his head and looked straight before him, walking in a self-contained way as if there were nothing in the streets worth his attention. His mouth was such a post-office of a mouth that he had a mechanical appearance of smiling. We had reached the top of Holborn Hill before I realized it was merely a mechanical appearance, and that he was not smiling at all.
"Do you know where Mr. Matthew Pocket lives?" I asked Mr. Wemmick.
"Yes," said he, nodding in the direction. "At Hammersmith, west of London."
"Is that far?"
"Well! Say five miles."
"Do you know him?"
"Why, you're a regular cross-examiner!" said Mr. Wemmick, looking at me with approval. "Yes, I know him. I know him!"

There was an air of tolerance or depreciation in the way he said these words that rather depressed me. I was still looking sideways at his block of a face, searching for any encouraging note to the text, when he said here we were at Barnard's Inn. My depression was not helped by this announcement, for I had supposed Barnard's Inn to be a hotel kept by Mr. Barnard, to which the Blue Boar in our town was a mere public house. Instead, I now found that Barnard was a disembodied spirit, or a fiction, and his inn the dingiest collection of shabby buildings ever squeezed together in a rank corner as a club for tomcats.

We entered this haven through a wicket gate and were disgorged through a short passage into a melancholy little square that looked to me like a flat burial ground. I thought it had the most dismal trees, the most dismal sparrows, the most dismal cats, and the most dismal houses — about half a dozen — that I had ever seen. The windows of the chambers into which those houses were divided were in every stage of dilapidated blind and curtain, crippled flowerpot, cracked glass, dusty decay, and miserable makeshift. While TO LET, TO LET, TO LET glared at me from empty rooms, as if no new wretches ever came there, and the vengeful spirit of Barnard were being slowly appeased by the gradual suicide of the present occupants and their unholy burial under the gravel. A grimy mourning of soot and smoke clothed this forlorn creation of Barnard's, and it had strewn ashes on its head, and was undergoing penance and humiliation as a mere dustbin. That was the visual impression. Meanwhile, dry rot and wet rot and all the silent rots that rot in neglected roof and cellar — rot of rat and mouse and bug and nearby coaching stables — faintly reached my nose and moaned: "Try Barnard's Mixture."
So disappointing was this first realization of my great expectations that I looked at Mr. Wemmick in dismay. "Ah!" said he, misreading me. "The seclusion reminds you of the country. Me too."

He led me into a corner and up a flight of stairs — which appeared to me to be slowly collapsing into sawdust, so that one of these days the upper lodgers would look out their doors and find themselves with no way down — to a set of chambers on the top floor. MR. POCKET, JUN., was painted on the door, and there was a label on the letter box: "Return shortly."
"He hardly expected you'd come so soon," Mr. Wemmick explained. "You don't need me anymore?"
"No, thank you," said I.
"As I keep the cash," Mr. Wemmick observed, "we shall most likely meet fairly often. Good day."
"Good day."
I put out my hand, and Mr. Wemmick at first looked at it as if he thought I wanted something. Then he looked at me and said, correcting himself:
"To be sure! Yes. You're in the habit of shaking hands?"
I was rather confused, thinking it must be out of London fashion, but said yes.
"I have got so out of it!" said Mr. Wemmick. "Except at last. Very glad, I'm sure, to make your acquaintance. Good day!"

When we had shaken hands and he was gone, I opened the staircase window and was nearly beheaded, for the ropes had rotted away and it came down like a guillotine. Luckily it was so quick that I hadn't put my head out. After this escape, I was content to take a foggy view of the inn through the window's encrusted dirt, and to stand dolefully looking out, telling myself that London was decidedly overrated.

Mr. Pocket Junior's idea of "shortly" was not mine, for I had nearly driven myself mad looking out for half an hour, and had written my name with my finger several times in the grime of every pane, before I heard footsteps on the stairs. Gradually there rose before me the hat, head, necktie, waistcoat, trousers, and boots of a young man of about my own standing. He had a paper bag under each arm and a basket of strawberries in one hand, and was out of breath.
"Mr. Pip?" said he.
"Mr. Pocket?" said I.

"Dear me!" he exclaimed. "I am extremely sorry! But I knew there was a coach from your part of the country at midday, and I thought you would come by that one. The fact is, I've been out on your account — not that that's any excuse — for I thought, coming from the country, you might like a little fruit after dinner, and I went to Covent Garden Market to get it fresh."
For a reason that I had, I felt as if my eyes would pop out of my head. I acknowledged his kindness incoherently, and began to think this was a dream.
"Dear me!" said Mr. Pocket Junior. "This door sticks so!"

As he was rapidly making jam of his fruit by wrestling with the door while the paper bags were under his arms, I begged him to let me hold them. He gave them up with an agreeable smile and did battle with the door as if it were a wild beast. It yielded so suddenly that he staggered back into me, and I staggered back against the opposite door, and we both laughed. But still I felt as if my eyes must pop out of my head, and as if this must be a dream.

"Please come in," said Mr. Pocket Junior. "Allow me to lead the way. I am rather bare here, but I hope you'll manage tolerably well till Monday. My father thought you would get on more comfortably through tomorrow with me than with him, and might like to take a walk about London. I shall be very happy to show you London. As to our table, you won't find that bad, I hope, as it will be supplied from our coffee house here, and — it's only right I should add — at your expense, such being Mr. Jaggers's directions. As to our lodging, it's not by any means splendid, because I have my own living to earn, and my father hasn't anything to give me, and I shouldn't be willing to take it if he had. This is our sitting room — just such chairs and tables and carpet and so forth, you see, as they could spare from home. You mustn't give me credit for the tablecloth and spoons and casters, because they come from the coffee house for you. This is my little bedroom — rather musty, but Barnard's is musty. This is your bedroom — the furniture's hired for the occasion, but I trust it will serve. If you should want anything, I'll go and fetch it. The chambers are quiet, and we shall be alone together, but we shan't fight, I dare say. But dear me, I beg your pardon — you're holding the fruit all this time. Please let me take these bags from you. I'm quite ashamed."
As I stood opposite Mr. Pocket Junior, handing him the bags — one, two — I saw the same startled recognition come into his eyes that I knew to be in mine. He said, falling back:
"Lord bless me, you're the prowling boy!"
"And you," said I, "are the pale young gentleman!"

chapters.title: Chapter 22
paragraphs: The pale young gentleman and I stood staring at one another in Barnard's Inn, until we both burst out laughing. "The idea of it being you!" said he. "The idea of it being you!" said I. And then we stared at one another afresh and laughed again. "Well!" said the pale young gentleman, reaching out his hand good-naturedly, "it's all over now, I hope, and it will be very generous of you if you'll forgive me for having knocked you about so."

I gathered from this speech that Mr. Herbert Pocket — for Herbert was the pale young gentleman's name — still rather confused his intentions with his results. But I made a modest reply, and we shook hands warmly.
"You hadn't come into your good fortune at that time?" said Herbert Pocket.
"No," said I.
"No," he agreed. "I heard it had happened very recently. I was rather hoping for good fortune myself then."
"Indeed?"
"Yes. Miss Havisham had sent for me, to see if she could take a fancy to me. But she couldn't — or at any rate, she didn't."
I thought it polite to say I was surprised to hear that.

"Bad taste," said Herbert, laughing, "but a fact. Yes, she had sent for me on a trial visit, and if I had come through it successfully, I suppose I should have been provided for. Perhaps I should have been what-you-may-call-it to Estella."
"What's that?" I asked, with sudden gravity.

He was arranging his fruit on plates while we talked, which divided his attention, and was the cause of this vague phrasing. "Affianced," he explained, still busy with the fruit. "Betrothed. Engaged. What's-his-name. Any word of that sort."
"How did you bear your disappointment?" I asked.
"Pooh!" said he. "I didn't care much for it. She's a Tartar."
"Miss Havisham?"
"I don't say no to that, but I meant Estella. That girl's hard and haughty and changeable to the last degree, and has been brought up by Miss Havisham to wreak revenge on all the male sex."
"What relation is she to Miss Havisham?"
"None," said he. "Only adopted."
"Why should she wreak revenge on all the male sex? What revenge?"
"Lord, Mr. Pip!" said he. "Don't you know?"
"No," said I.
"Dear me! It's quite a story, and shall be saved till dinner time. And now let me take the liberty of asking you a question. How did you come there that day?"

I told him, and he listened attentively until I had finished, then burst out laughing again and asked me if I was sore afterward. I didn't ask if he was, for my conviction on that point was perfectly established.
"Mr. Jaggers is your guardian, I understand?" he went on.
"Yes."
"You know he is Miss Havisham's man of business and solicitor, and has her confidence when nobody else does?"

This was steering me toward dangerous ground, I felt. I answered with a constraint I made no attempt to hide: that I had seen Mr. Jaggers in Miss Havisham's house on the very day of our fight, but never at any other time, and that I believed he had no memory of having seen me there.

"He was kind enough to suggest my father for your tutor, and he called on my father to propose it. Of course he knew about my father from his connection with Miss Havisham. My father is Miss Havisham's cousin — not that that implies close contact between them, for he is a bad courtier and will not flatter her."

Herbert Pocket had a frank and easy manner that was very appealing. I had never met anyone then, and I have never met anyone since, who more plainly showed, in every look and tone, a natural inability to do anything secretive or mean. There was something wonderfully hopeful about his whole air, and something that at the same time whispered to me he would never be very successful or rich. I don't know how this was. I became convinced of it that first day before we sat down to dinner, but I cannot explain by what means.

He was still a pale young gentleman, and had a certain graceful weariness about him amid his spirit and energy that did not suggest natural strength. He did not have a handsome face, but it was better than handsome — being extremely friendly and cheerful. His figure was a little ungainly, as in the days when my knuckles had taken such liberties with it, but it looked as if it would always be light and young. Whether Mr. Trabb's local tailoring would have sat more gracefully on him than on me may be a question. But I am certain he carried off his rather old clothes much better than I carried off my new suit.

Since he was so open with me, I felt that holding back would be a poor return and unsuited to our ages. So I told him my small story and stressed that I was forbidden to ask who my benefactor was. I also mentioned that, having been brought up as a blacksmith in the country and knowing very little of polite manners, I would take it as a great kindness if he would give me a hint whenever he saw me making a mistake.

"With pleasure," said he, "though I predict you'll need very few hints. I dare say we shall be together often, and I should like to get rid of any needless awkwardness between us. Will you do me the favor of calling me by my first name, Herbert?"
I thanked him and said I would. I informed him in return that my first name was Philip.

"I don't take to Philip," said he, smiling, "for it sounds like a moral boy out of the spelling book, who was so lazy that he fell into a pond, or so fat that he couldn't see out of his eyes, or so greedy that he locked up his cake till the mice ate it, or so determined to go bird-nesting that he got himself eaten by bears who lived handily in the neighborhood. I tell you what I should like. We get along so well, and you have been a blacksmith — would you mind it?"
"I shouldn't mind anything you suggest," I answered, "but I don't understand you."
"Would you mind Handel for a familiar name? There's a charming piece of music by Handel called the Harmonious Blacksmith."
"I should like it very much."
"Then, my dear Handel," said he, turning round as the door opened, "here is the dinner, and I must beg you to take the head of the table, because the dinner is of your providing."

This I would not hear of, so he took the head and I sat opposite. It was a nice little dinner — it seemed to me then a very Lord Mayor's feast — and it gained extra flavor from being eaten under those independent circumstances, with no old people around, and with London all about us. This was heightened further by a certain gypsy quality to the proceedings. For while the table was, as Mr. Pumblechook might have said, the lap of luxury — being entirely furnished from the coffee house — the surrounding sitting room was of a comparatively bare and makeshift nature. The waiter was forced into the wandering habit of putting the covers on the floor (where he tripped over them), the melted butter in the armchair, the bread on the bookshelves, the cheese in the coal scuttle, and the boiled fowl into my bed in the next room — where I found much of its parsley and butter in a state of congealment when I retired for the night. All this made the feast delightful, and when the waiter was not there to watch me, my pleasure was complete.
We had made some progress in the dinner when I reminded Herbert of his promise to tell me about Miss Havisham.

"True," he replied. "I'll keep my word at once. Let me introduce the topic, Handel, by mentioning that in London it is not the custom to put the knife in the mouth — for fear of accidents — and that while the fork is reserved for that use, it is not put in further than necessary. It is scarcely worth mentioning, only it's best to do as other people do. Also, the spoon is not generally used overhand but under. This has two advantages. You get at your mouth better — which after all is the object — and you save a good deal of the attitude of opening oysters, on the part of the right elbow."
He offered these friendly suggestions in such a lively way that we both laughed and I scarcely blushed.

"Now," he went on, "concerning Miss Havisham. Miss Havisham, you must know, was a spoiled child. Her mother died when she was a baby, and her father denied her nothing. Her father was a country gentleman down in your part of the world, and was a brewer. I don't know why it should be a respectable thing to be a brewer, but it is indisputable that while you cannot possibly be genteel and bake, you may be as genteel as anything and brew. You see it every day."
"Yet a gentleman may not keep a public house, may he?" said I.
"Not on any account," returned Herbert. "But a public house may keep a gentleman. Well! Mr. Havisham was very rich and very proud. So was his daughter."
"Miss Havisham was an only child?" I ventured.
"Stop a moment, I'm coming to that. No, she was not an only child. She had a half-brother. Her father privately married again — his cook, I rather think."
"I thought he was proud," said I.

"My good Handel, so he was. He married his second wife privately because he was proud, and in time she died. When she was dead, I believe he first told his daughter what he had done, and then the son became part of the family, living in the house you know. As the son grew to be a young man, he turned out wild, extravagant, undutiful — altogether bad. At last his father disinherited him. But he softened when he was dying, and left him well off, though not nearly so well off as Miss Havisham. — Take another glass of wine, and excuse my mentioning that society as a whole does not expect one to be so strictly thorough in emptying one's glass as to turn it upside down with the rim on one's nose."
I had been doing this, in my excessive attention to his story. I thanked him and apologized. He said, "Not at all," and went on.

"Miss Havisham was now an heiress, and you may imagine was pursued as a great catch. Her half-brother had ample means again, but what with debts and what with new follies, he wasted them most frightfully. There were worse quarrels between him and her than there had been between him and his father, and it is suspected that he nursed a deep and deadly grudge against her for having influenced their father's anger. Now, I come to the cruel part of the story — merely breaking off, my dear Handel, to note that a dinner napkin will not fit into a tumbler."

Why I was trying to pack mine into my tumbler, I am wholly unable to say. I only know that I found myself, with a persistence worthy of a much better cause, making the most strenuous efforts to squeeze it in. Again I thanked him and apologized, and again he said in the cheeriest manner, "Not at all, I'm sure!" and continued.

"There appeared on the scene — say at the races, or the public balls, or anywhere else you like — a certain man, who began courting Miss Havisham. I never saw him, for this happened twenty-five years ago, before you and I existed, Handel. But I have heard my father say that he was a showy man, and the right kind of man for the purpose. But that he was not to be, without ignorance or prejudice, mistaken for a gentleman, my father firmly maintains. Because it is a principle of his that no man who was not a true gentleman at heart, ever was, since the world began, a true gentleman in manner. He says no varnish can hide the grain of the wood, and the more varnish you put on, the more the grain shows through. Well! This man pursued Miss Havisham closely and professed to be devoted to her. I believe she had not shown much susceptibility until then. But all the susceptibility she possessed certainly came out, and she fell passionately in love with him. There is no doubt she absolutely idolized him. He worked on her feelings so systematically that he got great sums of money from her. He also persuaded her to buy her brother out of his share in the brewery — which had been weakly left him by their father — at a huge price, on the grounds that when he was her husband he must control and manage it all. Your guardian was not at that time in Miss Havisham's counsels, and she was too proud and too much in love to be advised by anyone. Her relations were poor and scheming, with the exception of my father. He was poor enough, but not self-serving or jealous. The only independent one among them, he warned her that she was doing too much for this man and placing herself too completely in his power. She took the first opportunity to angrily order my father out of the house, in the man's presence, and my father has never seen her since."
I thought of her having said, "Matthew will come and see me at last when I am laid dead upon that table," and I asked Herbert whether his father was so set against her.

"It's not that," said he, "but she accused him, in the presence of her intended husband, of being disappointed in the hope of flattering her for his own advancement. And if he were to go to her now, it would look true — even to him — and even to her. To return to the man and have done with him. The wedding day was fixed, the wedding dresses were bought, the wedding tour was planned, the wedding guests were invited. The day came, but not the bridegroom. He wrote her a letter—"
"Which she received," I broke in, "when she was dressing for her wedding? At twenty minutes to nine?"

"At the hour and minute," said Herbert, nodding, "at which she afterward stopped all the clocks. What was in the letter, beyond the fact that it most heartlessly broke off the marriage, I can't tell you, because I don't know. When she recovered from a serious illness that followed, she laid the whole place to waste, as you have seen it, and she has never since looked upon the light of day."
"Is that the whole story?" I asked, after thinking it over.

"All I know of it. And indeed I only know this much through piecing it together myself. My father always avoids the subject, and even when Miss Havisham invited me to visit, told me no more than I absolutely needed to understand. But I have forgotten one thing. It has been supposed that the man to whom she gave her misplaced trust acted throughout in league with her half-brother. That it was a conspiracy between them, and that they shared the profits."
"I wonder he didn't marry her and get all the property," said I.
"He may have been married already, and her cruel humiliation may have been part of her half-brother's scheme," said Herbert. "Mind! I don't know that."
"What became of the two men?" I asked, after further reflection.
"They fell into deeper shame and degradation — if there can be deeper — and ruin."
"Are they alive now?"
"I don't know."
"You said just now that Estella was not related to Miss Havisham, but adopted. When was she adopted?"

Herbert shrugged his shoulders. "There has always been an Estella, as long as I have heard of a Miss Havisham. I know no more. And now, Handel," said he, finally shaking off the story, "there is a perfectly open understanding between us. All that I know about Miss Havisham, you know."
"And all that I know," I replied, "you know."

"I fully believe it. So there can be no competition or confusion between you and me. And as to the condition on which you hold your advancement in life — namely, that you are not to ask or discuss to whom you owe it — you may be sure that it will never be trespassed on, or even approached, by me, or by anyone belonging to me."

In truth, he said this with such delicacy that I felt the subject was settled, even though I should live under his father's roof for years to come. Yet he said it with such meaning, too, that I felt he understood Miss Havisham to be my benefactress just as clearly as I did myself.

It had not occurred to me before that he had steered toward this topic for the purpose of clearing it out of our way. But we were so much lighter and easier for having addressed it that I now saw this was the case. We were very cheerful and sociable, and in the course of conversation I asked him what his profession was. He replied, "A capitalist — an insurer of ships." I suppose he saw me glancing around the room for some sign of shipping or capital, for he added, "In the City."

I had grand ideas of the wealth and importance of insurers of ships in the City, and I began to think with awe of having laid a young insurer on his back, blackened his enterprising eye, and cut his responsible head open. But again there came over me, for my relief, that odd impression that Herbert Pocket would never be very successful or rich.

"I shall not be content with merely employing my capital in insuring ships. I shall buy up some good life assurance shares and get onto the board. I shall also do a little in the mining way. None of these things will interfere with my chartering a few thousand tons on my own account. I think I shall trade," said he, leaning back in his chair, "to the East Indies, for silks, shawls, spices, dyes, drugs, and precious woods. It's an interesting trade."
"And the profits are large?" said I.
"Tremendous!" said he.
I wavered again, and began to think here were greater expectations than my own.
"I think I shall also trade," said he, putting his thumbs in his waistcoat pockets, "to the West Indies, for sugar, tobacco, and rum. Also to Ceylon, especially for elephants' tusks."
"You will want a good many ships," said I.
"A perfect fleet," said he.
Quite overwhelmed by the magnificence of these transactions, I asked him where the ships he insured mostly traded to at present.
"I haven't begun insuring yet," he replied. "I am looking about me."
Somehow, that pursuit seemed more in keeping with Barnard's Inn. I said, in a tone of conviction, "Ah!"
"Yes. I am in a counting house, and looking about me."
"Is a counting house profitable?" I asked.
"Do you mean — to the young fellow who's in it?" he asked in reply.
"Yes. To you."

"Why, n-no. Not to me." He said this with the air of one carefully adding up figures and striking a balance. "Not directly profitable. That is, it doesn't pay me anything, and I have to — keep myself."
This certainly did not have a profitable appearance, and I shook my head as if to suggest it would be difficult to save much from such a source of income.
"But the thing is," said Herbert Pocket, "that you look about you. That's the grand thing. You are in a counting house, you know, and you look about you."
It struck me as a peculiar notion that you couldn't be out of a counting house, you know, and look about you. But I silently deferred to his experience.

"Then the time comes," said Herbert, "when you see your opening. And you go in, and you swoop upon it, and you make your capital, and then there you are! When you have once made your capital, you have nothing to do but employ it."

This was very like his way of conducting that fight in the garden — very like. His manner of bearing his poverty, too, exactly matched his manner of bearing that defeat. It seemed to me that he took all blows and setbacks now with just the same air as he had taken mine then. It was obvious that he had nothing around him but the simplest necessities, for everything I remarked on turned out to have been sent in on my account from the coffee house or somewhere else.

Yet, having already made his fortune in his own mind, he was so modest about it that I felt quite grateful to him for not being conceited. It was a pleasant addition to his naturally pleasant ways, and we got on famously. In the evening we went out for a walk in the streets, then went half-price to the theater. Next day we went to church at Westminster Abbey, and in the afternoon we walked in the parks. I wondered who shod all the horses there, and wished Joe did.

By a fair estimate, it was many months, that Sunday, since I had left Joe and Biddy. The distance between myself and them had that kind of expansion, and our marshes seemed impossibly far off. That I could have been at our old church in my old church-going clothes, on the very last Sunday that ever was, seemed a combination of impossibilities — geographical and social, solar and lunar. Yet in the London streets, so crowded with people and so brilliantly lit in the evening dusk, there were depressing hints of reproach for having put the poor old kitchen at home so far away. And in the dead of night, the footsteps of some useless pretender of a porter drifting about Barnard's Inn, under pretense of watching it, fell hollow on my heart.

On Monday morning at a quarter to nine, Herbert went to the counting house to report himself — to look about him, too, I suppose — and I went along with him. He was to come away in an hour or two to accompany me to Hammersmith, and I was to wait for him. It appeared to me that the eggs from which young insurers were hatched were incubated in dust and heat, like ostrich eggs, judging from the places to which those budding giants made their way on a Monday morning. Nor did the counting house where Herbert worked look, to my eyes, like much of an observatory — being a dingy back room on the second floor up a yard, with a view into another dingy back room rather than a view out.

I waited about until noon, and went to the Exchange, where I saw pale men sitting under the bills about shipping, whom I took for great merchants, though I couldn't understand why they should all be so gloomy. When Herbert came, we went and had lunch at a celebrated establishment that I then quite revered, but now believe to have been the most appalling fraud in Europe. I could not help noticing, even then, that there was much more gravy on the tablecloths and knives and waiters' clothes than in the steaks. This meal disposed of at a moderate price — considering the grease, which was not charged for — we went back to Barnard's Inn for my little portmanteau, and then took a coach for Hammersmith. We arrived there around two or three in the afternoon and had very little way to walk to Mr. Pocket's house. Lifting the latch of a gate, we passed directly into a little garden overlooking the river, where Mr. Pocket's children were playing. And unless I deceive myself on a point where I have no personal stake, I saw that Mr. and Mrs. Pocket's children were not growing up or being brought up, but were tumbling up.

Mrs. Pocket was sitting on a garden chair under a tree, reading, with her feet up on another garden chair. Mrs. Pocket's two nursemaids were looking about them while the children played. "Mama," said Herbert, "this is young Mr. Pip." Mrs. Pocket received me with an appearance of gracious dignity.

"Master Alick and Miss Jane," cried one of the nurses to two of the children, "if you go bouncing up against them bushes, you'll fall over into the river and be drowned, and what'll your pa say then?"

At the same time, this nurse picked up Mrs. Pocket's handkerchief and said, "If that don't make six times you've dropped it, ma'am!" Mrs. Pocket laughed and said, "Thank you, Flopson," and settling herself in one chair only, resumed her book. Her face immediately assumed a knitted and intent expression as if she had been reading for a week. But before she could have read half a dozen lines, she fixed her eyes on me and said, "I hope your mama is quite well?" This unexpected question put me in such difficulty that I began saying in the most absurd way that if there had been any such person, I had no doubt she would have been quite well and would have been very much obliged and would have sent her compliments — when the nurse came to my rescue.

"Well!" she cried, picking up the handkerchief. "If that don't make seven times! What are you doing this afternoon, ma'am?" Mrs. Pocket received her property, at first with a look of utter surprise as if she had never seen it before, and then with a laugh of recognition, and said, "Thank you, Flopson," and forgot me, and went on reading.

I found, now that I had leisure to count them, that there were no fewer than six little Pockets present, in various stages of tumbling up. I had scarcely arrived at the total when a seventh was heard, as if from the upper air, wailing dolefully.
"If there ain't Baby!" said Flopson, appearing to think it most surprising. "Hurry up, Millers."

Millers, who was the other nurse, went into the house, and by degrees the child's wailing was hushed and stopped, as if it were a young ventriloquist with something in its mouth. Mrs. Pocket read the entire time, and I was curious to know what the book could be.

We were waiting, I supposed, for Mr. Pocket to come out to us. At any rate, we waited there, and I had an opportunity to observe a remarkable family phenomenon: whenever any of the children strayed near Mrs. Pocket in their play, they always tripped and tumbled over her — always very much to her momentary astonishment, and their own more lasting distress. I was at a loss to explain this surprising circumstance and could not help puzzling over it, until by and by Millers came down with the baby. The baby was handed to Flopson, and Flopson was handing it to Mrs. Pocket, when she too went headlong over Mrs. Pocket — baby and all — and was caught by Herbert and me.
"Gracious me, Flopson!" said Mrs. Pocket, looking up from her book for a moment. "Everybody's tumbling!"
"Gracious you, indeed, ma'am!" returned Flopson, very red in the face. "What have you got there?"
"I got here, Flopson?" asked Mrs. Pocket.
"Why, if it ain't your footstool!" cried Flopson. "And if you keep it under your skirts like that, who's to help tumbling? Here! Take the baby, ma'am, and give me your book."

Mrs. Pocket acted on this advice, and inexpertly bounced the infant a little on her lap while the other children played around it. This had lasted only a very short time when Mrs. Pocket issued summary orders that they were all to be taken into the house for a nap. Thus I made the second discovery on that first visit: that the raising of the little Pockets consisted of alternately tumbling up and lying down.

Under these circumstances, when Flopson and Millers had herded the children into the house like a little flock of sheep, and Mr. Pocket came out to make my acquaintance, I was not much surprised to find that Mr. Pocket was a gentleman with a rather bewildered expression, and with his very gray hair in disorder on his head, as if he didn't quite see his way to putting anything straight.

chapters.title: Chapter 23
paragraphs: Mr. Pocket said he was glad to see me, and he hoped I was not sorry to see him. "For I really am not," he added, with his son's smile, "an alarming person." He was a young-looking man, despite his troubles and very gray hair, and his manner seemed quite natural. I use the word natural in the sense of unaffected. There was something comical in his distracted way, as though it would have been outright laughable but for his own awareness that it very nearly was. When he had talked with me a little, he said to Mrs. Pocket, with a rather anxious furrowing of his eyebrows, which were black and handsome: "Belinda, I hope you have welcomed Mr. Pip?" She looked up from her book and said, "Yes." She then smiled at me in an absent-minded way and asked me if I liked the taste of orange-flower water. As the question had no bearing whatsoever on any past or future subject, I took it to have been tossed out, like her previous remarks, as general conversational small talk.

I found out within a few hours — and may mention at once — that Mrs. Pocket was the only daughter of a certain accidentally deceased knight. This knight had invented for himself a conviction that his own deceased father would have been made a baronet but for someone's determined opposition arising from entirely personal motives — I forget whose, if I ever knew — the Sovereign's, the Prime Minister's, the Lord Chancellor's, the Archbishop of Canterbury's, anybody's — and had attached himself to the nobility on the strength of this entirely imaginary fact. I believe he had been knighted himself for assaulting the English language with his pen in a desperate address written on vellum, on the occasion of the laying of the first stone of some building or other, and for handing some Royal Personage either the trowel or the mortar. Be that as it may, he had directed Mrs. Pocket to be brought up from her cradle as one who must naturally marry a title, and who was to be shielded from acquiring any common domestic knowledge.

So successful a guard had been kept over the young lady by this wise parent that she had grown up highly ornamental, but perfectly helpless and useless. With her character thus happily formed, in the first bloom of her youth she had met Mr. Pocket, who was also in the first bloom of youth and not quite decided whether to aim for the Lord Chancellor's seat or a bishop's mitre. As achieving either was a mere question of time, he and Mrs. Pocket had seized the moment — when, to judge from its length, it would seem to have needed cutting — and had married without the wise parent's knowledge. The wise parent, having nothing to give or withhold but his blessing, had handsomely settled that gift on them after a brief struggle, and had informed Mr. Pocket that his wife was "a treasure for a prince." Mr. Pocket had invested the prince's treasure in the ways of the world ever since, and it was generally thought to have brought him poor returns. Still, Mrs. Pocket was the object of a peculiar sort of respectful pity, because she had not married a title. While Mr. Pocket was the object of a peculiar sort of forgiving reproach, because he had never gotten one.

Mr. Pocket took me into the house and showed me my room, which was pleasant and so furnished that I could use it comfortably as my own private sitting room. He then knocked at the doors of two other similar rooms and introduced me to their occupants, named Drummle and Startop. Drummle, an old-looking young man of a heavy build, was whistling. Startop, younger in years and appearance, was reading and holding his head, as if he thought himself in danger of exploding it with too strong a charge of knowledge.

Both Mr. and Mrs. Pocket had such a noticeable air of being in somebody else's hands that I wondered who really possessed the house and merely let them live there, until I found this unknown power to be the servants. It was a smooth way of running things, perhaps, in terms of saving trouble. But it had the appearance of being expensive, for the servants felt it a duty they owed themselves to be particular about their food and drink, and to keep a great deal of company downstairs. They allowed a very generous table to Mr. and Mrs. Pocket. Yet it always seemed to me that by far the best part of the house to have boarded in would have been the kitchen — provided the boarder was capable of self-defense. For before I had been there a week, a neighboring lady with whom the family had no acquaintance wrote in to say she had seen Millers slapping the baby. This greatly distressed Mrs. Pocket, who burst into tears on receiving the note and said it was an extraordinary thing that the neighbors couldn't mind their own business.

Gradually I learned, chiefly from Herbert, that Mr. Pocket had been educated at Harrow and at Cambridge, where he had distinguished himself. But when he had had the happiness of marrying Mrs. Pocket very early in life, he had damaged his prospects and taken up work as a tutor. After grinding a number of dull blades — whose fathers, when influential, were always going to help him get a better position, but always forgot to do it once the blades had left the grindstone — he had tired of that poor work and come to London. Here, after gradually failing in loftier hopes, he had tutored various young men who had missed opportunities or wasted them, had polished up others for special occasions, and had turned his learning to literary editing and compilation. On such income, added to some very modest private resources, he still maintained the house I saw.

Mr. and Mrs. Pocket had a fawning neighbor — a widow lady of such a sympathetic nature that she agreed with everybody, blessed everybody, and shed smiles and tears on everybody, as circumstances required. This lady's name was Mrs. Coiler, and I had the honor of taking her in to dinner on the day of my arrival. She let me know on the stairs that it was a blow to dear Mrs. Pocket that dear Mr. Pocket should have to take in gentlemen to tutor. That did not extend to me, she told me in a gush of love and confidence (at that point, I had known her for less than five minutes). If they were all like me, it would be quite another thing.
"But dear Mrs. Pocket," said Mrs. Coiler, "after her early disappointment — not that dear Mr. Pocket was to blame in that — requires so much luxury and elegance—"
"Yes, ma'am," I said, to stop her, for I was afraid she was going to cry.
"And she is of so aristocratic a nature—"
"Yes, ma'am," I said again, with the same aim as before.
"That it is hard," said Mrs. Coiler, "to have dear Mr. Pocket's time and attention diverted from dear Mrs. Pocket."

I could not help thinking that it might be harder if the butcher's time and attention were diverted from dear Mrs. Pocket. But I said nothing, and indeed had enough to do keeping a careful watch on my table manners.

I gathered, from what passed between Mrs. Pocket and Drummle while I was preoccupied with my knife and fork, spoon, glasses, and other instruments of self-destruction, that Drummle — whose first name was Bentley — was actually the next heir but one to a baronetcy. It also appeared that the book I had seen Mrs. Pocket reading in the garden was all about titles, and that she knew the exact date at which her grandfather would have appeared in it, if he ever had appeared at all. Drummle didn't say much, but in his limited way — he struck me as a sulky sort of fellow — he spoke as one of the chosen, and acknowledged Mrs. Pocket as a woman and a sister. No one but themselves and Mrs. Coiler the fawning neighbor showed any interest in this branch of conversation, and it appeared to me that Herbert found it painful. But it promised to last a long time, when the page came in with the announcement of a domestic catastrophe. It was, in effect, that the cook had lost the beef. To my unspeakable amazement, I now saw Mr. Pocket, for the first time, relieve his feelings by going through a performance that struck me as very extraordinary, but which made no impression on anyone else, and which I soon became as familiar with as the rest. He laid down the carving knife and fork — being in the middle of carving — put both hands into his disordered hair, and appeared to make an extraordinary effort to lift himself up by it. When he had done this, and had not lifted himself up at all, he quietly went on with what he was doing.

Mrs. Coiler then changed the subject and began to flatter me. I liked it for a few moments, but she laid it on so thickly that the pleasure was soon over. She had a serpentine way of coming close to me when she pretended to be fascinated by the friends and places I had left, which was altogether snaky and forked-tongued. And when she made an occasional pounce upon Startop — who said very little to her — or upon Drummle — who said even less — I rather envied them for being on the other side of the table.

After dinner the children were brought in, and Mrs. Coiler made admiring comments on their eyes, noses, and legs — a clever method of improving their minds. There were four little girls and two little boys, besides the baby who might have been either, and the baby's next successor who was as yet neither. They were brought in by Flopson and Millers, much as though those two officers had been out recruiting for children and had enlisted these. Meanwhile, Mrs. Pocket looked at the young nobles who ought to have been hers, as if she rather thought she had had the pleasure of inspecting them before, but wasn't quite sure what to make of them.
"Here! Give me your fork, ma'am, and take the baby," said Flopson. "Don't take it that way, or you'll get its head under the table."
Thus advised, Mrs. Pocket took it the other way, and got its head upon the table — which was announced to all present by a tremendous crash.
"Dear, dear! Give it back, ma'am," said Flopson. "And Miss Jane, come and dance to baby, do!"

One of the little girls, a tiny thing who seemed to have prematurely taken charge of the others, stepped out of her place by me and danced to and from the baby until it stopped crying and laughed. Then all the children laughed, and Mr. Pocket — who had in the meantime twice tried to lift himself up by the hair — laughed, and we all laughed and were glad.

Flopson, by dint of doubling the baby at the joints like a Dutch doll, got it safely into Mrs. Pocket's lap and gave it the nutcrackers to play with. At the same time, she recommended Mrs. Pocket to take notice that the handles of that instrument were unlikely to agree with its eyes, and sharply charged Miss Jane to watch out for the same. Then the two nurses left the room and had a lively scuffle on the staircase with a disreputable page who had waited at dinner and had clearly lost half his buttons at gambling.

I was made very uneasy by Mrs. Pocket's falling into a discussion with Drummle about two baronetcies, while she ate a sliced orange steeped in sugar and wine, and forgetting all about the baby on her lap — which did the most alarming things with the nutcrackers. At length little Jane, seeing its young brains to be in danger, softly left her place and with many small tricks coaxed the dangerous weapon away. Mrs. Pocket, finishing her orange at about the same time and not approving of this, said to Jane:
"You naughty child, how dare you? Go and sit down this instant!"
"Mama dear," lisped the little girl, "baby would have put his eyes out."
"How dare you tell me so?" retorted Mrs. Pocket. "Go and sit down in your chair this moment!"
Mrs. Pocket's dignity was so crushing that I felt quite ashamed, as if I myself had done something to provoke it.
"Belinda," protested Mr. Pocket from the other end of the table, "how can you be so unreasonable? Jane only interfered to protect baby."
"I will not allow anybody to interfere," said Mrs. Pocket. "I am surprised, Matthew, that you should expose me to the insult of interference."
"Good God!" cried Mr. Pocket, in an outburst of desolate desperation. "Are infants to be nutcrackered into their tombs, and is nobody to save them?"
"I will not be interfered with by Jane," said Mrs. Pocket, with a majestic glance at that innocent little offender. "I hope I know my poor grandfather's position. Jane, indeed!"

Mr. Pocket got his hands in his hair again, and this time really did lift himself some inches out of his chair. "Hear this!" he helplessly exclaimed to the elements. "Babies are to be nutcrackered dead, for people's poor grandfather's positions!" Then he let himself down again and became silent.

We all looked awkwardly at the tablecloth while this was going on. A pause followed, during which the honest and irrepressible baby made a series of leaps and crows at little Jane, who appeared to me to be the only member of the family — servants aside — with whom it had any real acquaintance.
"Mr. Drummle," said Mrs. Pocket, "will you ring for Flopson? Jane, you undutiful little thing, go and lie down. Now, baby darling, come with mama!"

The baby was the soul of honor and protested with all its might. It doubled itself up the wrong way over Mrs. Pocket's arm, exhibited a pair of knitted shoes and dimpled ankles to the company in place of its soft face, and was carried out in the highest state of mutiny. And it gained its point after all, for I saw it through the window within a few minutes, being nursed by little Jane.

It happened that the other five children were left behind at the dinner table, through Flopson's having some private engagement, and their not being anybody else's business. I thus became aware of the relationship between them and Mr. Pocket, which went like this. Mr. Pocket, with his usual bewildered expression heightened and his hair rumpled, looked at them for some minutes, as if he couldn't figure out how they came to be boarding and lodging in that establishment, and why they hadn't been assigned by Nature to somebody else. Then, in a distant missionary sort of way, he asked them certain questions — as why little Joe had that hole in his frill (who said, Pa, Flopson was going to mend it when she had time) and how little Fanny came by that whitlow (who said, Pa, Millers was going to poultice it when she didn't forget). Then he melted into parental tenderness, gave them a shilling each, and told them to go and play. And then, as they went out, with one very strong effort to lift himself up by the hair, he dismissed the hopeless subject.

In the evening there was rowing on the river. As Drummle and Startop each had a boat, I resolved to get one of my own and beat them both. I was pretty good at most exercises that country boys are skilled in, but being aware that I lacked elegance of style for the Thames — not to say for other waters — I at once arranged to take lessons from a prize-winning oarsman who worked at our stairs, to whom I was introduced by my new companions. This practical authority embarrassed me greatly by remarking that I had the arm of a blacksmith. If he had known how nearly the compliment lost him his student, I doubt he would have paid it.

There was a supper tray after we got home at night, and I think we should all have enjoyed ourselves, but for a rather unpleasant domestic incident. Mr. Pocket was in good spirits when a housemaid came in and said, "If you please, sir, I should wish to speak to you."
"Speak to your master?" said Mrs. Pocket, whose dignity was roused again. "How can you think of such a thing? Go and speak to Flopson. Or speak to me — at some other time."
"Begging your pardon, ma'am," returned the housemaid, "I should wish to speak at once, and to speak to master."
At this, Mr. Pocket went out of the room, and we made the best of things until he came back.

"This is a pretty business, Belinda!" said Mr. Pocket, returning with a face full of grief and despair. "Here's the cook lying dead drunk on the kitchen floor, with a large bundle of fresh butter packed up in the cupboard ready to sell for grease!"
Mrs. Pocket instantly showed much feeling and said, "This is that odious Sophia's doing!"
"What do you mean, Belinda?" demanded Mr. Pocket.
"Sophia has told you," said Mrs. Pocket. "Did I not see her with my own eyes and hear her with my own ears, come into the room just now and ask to speak to you?"
"But has she not taken me downstairs, Belinda," returned Mr. Pocket, "and shown me the woman, and the bundle too?"
"And do you defend her, Matthew," said Mrs. Pocket, "for making trouble?"
Mr. Pocket uttered a dismal groan.

"Am I, grandfather's granddaughter, to count for nothing in the house?" said Mrs. Pocket. "Besides, the cook has always been a very nice respectful woman, and said in the most natural manner when she came to apply for the position that she felt I was born to be a duchess."

There was a sofa where Mr. Pocket stood, and he dropped onto it in the attitude of the Dying Gladiator. Still in that pose, he said, in a hollow voice, "Good night, Mr. Pip" — at which point I thought it wise to go to bed and leave him.

chapters.title: Chapter 24
paragraphs: After two or three days, when I had settled into my room and had gone back and forth to London several times and had ordered everything I needed from my tradesmen, Mr. Pocket and I had a long talk. He knew more about my intended career than I did myself, for he mentioned having been told by Mr. Jaggers that I was not destined for any profession, and that I should be well enough educated for my purpose if I could "hold my own" with the average young man in prosperous circumstances. I agreed, of course, knowing nothing to the contrary.

He advised me to attend certain places in London to acquire what basic knowledge I lacked, and to appoint him as the explainer and director of all my studies. He hoped that with intelligent guidance I should find little to discourage me, and would soon be able to manage with no help but his. Through his way of saying this, and much more to the same effect, he put himself on confidential terms with me in an admirable way. And I may say at once that he was always so dedicated and honorable in fulfilling his compact with me that he made me dedicated and honorable in fulfilling mine with him. If he had shown indifference as a teacher, I have no doubt I should have returned it as a student. He gave me no such excuse, and each of us did the other justice. Nor did I ever regard him as having anything laughable about him — or anything but what was serious, honest, and good — in his role as my tutor.

When these points were settled, and so far carried out that I had begun to work in earnest, it occurred to me that if I could keep my bedroom in Barnard's Inn, my life would be pleasantly varied, while my manners would benefit from Herbert's company. Mr. Pocket did not object to this arrangement, but urged that before any step could be taken, it must be submitted to my guardian. I felt that this delicacy arose from the thought that the plan would save Herbert some expense, so I went off to Little Britain and put my wish to Mr. Jaggers.
"If I could buy the furniture now rented for me," said I, "and one or two other little things, I should be quite at home there."
"Go for it!" said Mr. Jaggers, with a short laugh. "I told you you'd get on. Well! How much do you want?"
I said I didn't know how much.
"Come!" retorted Mr. Jaggers. "How much? Fifty pounds?"
"Oh, not nearly so much."
"Five pounds?" said Mr. Jaggers.
This was such a drop that I said in dismay, "Oh, more than that."
"More than that, eh!" retorted Mr. Jaggers, lying in wait for me with his hands in his pockets, his head on one side, and his eyes on the wall behind me. "How much more?"
"It is so difficult to fix a sum," said I, hesitating.
"Come!" said Mr. Jaggers. "Let's get at it. Twice five — will that do? Three times five — will that do? Four times five — will that do?"
I said I thought that would do nicely.
"Four times five will do nicely, will it?" said Mr. Jaggers, knitting his brows. "Now, what do you make of four times five?"
"What do I make of it?"
"Ah!" said Mr. Jaggers. "How much?"
"I suppose you make it twenty pounds," said I, smiling.
"Never mind what I make it, my friend," observed Mr. Jaggers, with a knowing and contradictory toss of his head. "I want to know what you make it."
"Twenty pounds, of course."
"Wemmick!" said Mr. Jaggers, opening his office door. "Take Mr. Pip's written order, and pay him twenty pounds."

This strongly marked way of doing business made a strong impression on me, and not an agreeable one. Mr. Jaggers never laughed, but he wore great bright creaking boots. In poising himself on these boots, with his large head bent down and his eyebrows drawn together, awaiting an answer, he sometimes made the boots creak, as if they were laughing in a dry and suspicious way. As he happened to go out just then, and as Wemmick was cheerful and talkative, I said to Wemmick that I hardly knew what to make of Mr. Jaggers's manner.

"Tell him that, and he'll take it as a compliment," answered Wemmick. "He doesn't mean you should know what to make of it. — Oh!" for I looked surprised. "It's not personal. It's professional. Only professional."
Wemmick was at his desk, lunching — and crunching — on a dry hard biscuit, pieces of which he threw from time to time into his slit of a mouth, as if he were posting letters.
"Always seems to me," said Wemmick, "as if he had set a man-trap and was watching it. Suddenly — click — you're caught!"
Without remarking that man-traps were not among life's pleasures, I said I supposed he was very skillful.

"Deep," said Wemmick, "as Australia." He pointed with his pen at the office floor, to indicate that Australia was understood, for the purposes of the figure, to be directly on the opposite side of the globe. "If there was anything deeper," added Wemmick, bringing his pen to paper, "he'd be it."
Then I said I supposed he had a good business, and Wemmick said, "Capital!" Then I asked if there were many clerks, to which he replied:
"We don't go in much for clerks, because there's only one Jaggers, and people won't have him secondhand. There are only four of us. Would you like to see them? You are one of us, as I may say."

I accepted the offer. When Mr. Wemmick had finished posting his biscuit and had paid me from a cash box in a safe — the key of which he kept somewhere down his back and produced from his coat collar like an iron pigtail — we went upstairs. The house was dark and shabby, and the greasy shoulders that had left their marks in Mr. Jaggers's room seemed to have been shuffling up and down the staircase for years. On the first floor front, a clerk who looked something between a publican and a rat catcher — a large, pale, puffy, swollen man — was attentively engaged with three or four shabby people, whom he treated as unceremoniously as everybody seemed to be treated who contributed to Mr. Jaggers's income. "Getting evidence together," said Mr. Wemmick, as we came out, "for the Old Bailey." In the room above, a little flabby terrier of a clerk with dangling hair — his grooming seemed to have been forgotten when he was a puppy — was similarly engaged with a man with weak eyes, whom Mr. Wemmick introduced as a metalworker who kept his pot always boiling, and who would melt me anything I pleased. This man was in an excessive white sweat, as if he had been trying his art on himself. In a back room, a high-shouldered man with a face-ache tied up in dirty flannel, dressed in old black clothes that appeared to have been waxed, was stooping over his work of making fair copies of the other two gentlemen's notes, for Mr. Jaggers's own use.
This was the entire establishment. When we went downstairs again, Wemmick led me into my guardian's room and said, "This you've seen already."
"Please," said I, as the two hideous casts with their twitching leer caught my eye again, "whose likenesses are those?"

"These?" said Wemmick, climbing on a chair and blowing the dust off the horrible heads before bringing them down. "These are two celebrated ones. Famous clients of ours that got us a world of credit. This fellow" — he said, addressing the cast — "why, you must have come down in the night and been peeping into the inkstand, to get that blot on your eyebrow, you old rascal! — he murdered his master, and considering that he wasn't brought up in the trade of evidence, didn't plan it badly."
"Is it like him?" I asked, shrinking from the brute as Wemmick spat on his eyebrow and rubbed it with his sleeve.

"Like him? It is him, you know. The cast was made in Newgate, directly after he was taken down. You had a particular fancy for me, didn't you, Old Artful?" said Wemmick. He then explained this affectionate address by touching his brooch — the one depicting the lady and the weeping willow at the tomb with the urn — and saying, "Had it made for me, express!"
"Is the lady anybody?" said I.

"No," returned Wemmick. "Only his game. You liked your bit of game, didn't you? No, not a bit of a lady in the case, Mr. Pip, except one — and she wasn't of this slender ladylike sort, and you wouldn't have caught her looking after this urn unless there was something to drink in it." Wemmick's attention being thus directed to his brooch, he put down the cast and polished the brooch with his handkerchief.
"Did that other creature come to the same end?" I asked. "He has the same look."

"You're right," said Wemmick. "It's the genuine look. As if one nostril was hooked up with a horsehair and a little fish hook. Yes, he came to the same end — quite the natural end here, I assure you. He forged wills, this one did, if he didn't also put the supposed will-makers to sleep as well. You were a gentlemanly fellow, though" — Mr. Wemmick was again addressing the cast — "and you said you could write Greek. Yah, bounceable! What a liar you were! I never met such a liar as you!" Before putting his late friend back on the shelf, Wemmick touched the largest of his mourning rings and said, "Sent out to buy it for me, only the day before."

While he was putting up the other cast and climbing down from the chair, it crossed my mind that all his personal jewelry came from similar sources. As he had shown no embarrassment about it, I ventured to ask him the question when he stood before me, dusting his hands.

"Oh yes," he returned, "these are all gifts of that kind. One brings another, you see — that's how it goes. I always take them. They're curiosities. And they're property. They may not be worth much, but after all, they're property and portable. It doesn't matter to you with your brilliant prospects, but as for myself, my guiding principle is always: 'Get hold of portable property.'"
Having paid tribute to this philosophy, he went on in a friendly manner:

"If at any odd time when you have nothing better to do, you wouldn't mind coming over to see me at Walworth, I could offer you a bed, and I should consider it an honor. I haven't much to show you, but I've got two or three curiosities you might like to look over, and I am fond of a bit of garden and a summer house."
I said I should be delighted to accept his hospitality.
"Thanks," said he. "Then we'll consider that settled, whenever it's convenient for you. Have you dined with Mr. Jaggers yet?"
"Not yet."
"Well," said Wemmick, "he'll give you wine, and good wine. I'll give you punch, and not bad punch. And now I'll tell you something. When you go to dine with Mr. Jaggers, look at his housekeeper."
"Shall I see something very unusual?"

"Well," said Wemmick, "you'll see a wild beast tamed. Not so very unusual, you'll tell me. I reply: that depends on the original wildness of the beast, and the amount of taming. It won't lower your opinion of Mr. Jaggers's powers. Keep your eye on it."
I told him I would do so, with all the interest and curiosity that his hint awakened. As I was leaving, he asked me if I would like to devote five minutes to seeing Mr. Jaggers "at it."

For several reasons — not least because I didn't clearly know what Mr. Jaggers would be found to be "at" — I said yes. We dived into the City and came up in a crowded police court, where a blood relation (in the murderous sense) of the deceased — the one with the fanciful taste in brooches — was standing at the bar, uncomfortably chewing something. Meanwhile my guardian had a woman under examination, and was striking her, and the bench, and everyone present, with awe. If anybody, of whatever standing, said a word he didn't approve of, he instantly demanded to have it "taken down." If anybody wouldn't make an admission, he said, "I'll have it out of you!" And if anybody did make an admission, he said, "Now I have got you!" The magistrates shivered under a single bite of his finger. Thieves and thief-takers hung on his words in fearful rapture, and shrank when a hair of his eyebrows turned in their direction. Which side he was on I couldn't make out, for he seemed to be grinding the whole place in a mill. I only know that when I crept out on tiptoe, he was not on the side of the bench — for he was making the legs of the old gentleman who presided quite convulsive under the table, by his denunciations of that gentleman's conduct as the representative of British law and justice in that chair that day.

chapters.title: Chapter 25
paragraphs: Bentley Drummle, who was so sulky a fellow that he even picked up a book as if its author had done him an injury, did not take up an acquaintance in a more agreeable spirit. Heavy in build, movement, and comprehension — in the sluggish complexion of his face, and in the large, awkward tongue that seemed to loll about in his mouth as he himself lolled about in a room — he was idle, proud, stingy, reserved, and suspicious. He came from wealthy people down in Somersetshire, who had nurtured this combination of qualities until they made the discovery that it was just of age and a blockhead. Thus Bentley Drummle had come to Mr. Pocket when he was a head taller than that gentleman and half a dozen heads thicker than most.

Startop had been spoiled by a weak mother and kept at home when he ought to have been at school, but he was devotedly attached to her and admired her beyond measure. He had a woman's delicacy of feature and was — "as you may see, though you never saw her," said Herbert to me — "exactly like his mother." It was only natural that I should take to him much more warmly than to Drummle, and that even in the earliest evenings of our rowing, he and I should pull homeward side by side, talking from boat to boat, while Bentley Drummle came up in our wake alone, under the overhanging banks and among the rushes. He would always creep along the shore like some uncomfortable amphibious creature, even when the tide would have carried him fast on his way. I always think of him as coming after us in the dark or by the backwater, when our own two boats were breaking the sunset or the moonlight in midstream.

Herbert was my closest companion and friend. I gave him a half-share in my boat, which was the reason he often came down to Hammersmith. And my possession of a half-share in his chambers often took me up to London. We used to walk between the two places at all hours. I still have an affection for that road — though it is not so pleasant now as it was then — formed in the impressionable days of untried youth and hope.

When I had been in Mr. Pocket's family a month or two, Mr. and Mrs. Camilla appeared. Camilla was Mr. Pocket's sister. Georgiana, whom I had seen at Miss Havisham's on the same occasion, also appeared. She was a cousin — an indigestible single woman who called her rigidity religion and her liver love. These people hated me with the hatred of greed and disappointment. As a matter of course, they fawned on me in my prosperity with the basest flattery. Toward Mr. Pocket, as a grown-up infant with no sense of his own interests, they showed the condescending tolerance I had heard them express. Mrs. Pocket they held in contempt, but they allowed the poor soul to have been heavily disappointed in life, because that cast a feeble reflected glow on themselves.

These were the surroundings in which I settled down and applied myself to my education. I soon developed expensive habits and began to spend amounts of money that a few short months before I would have thought almost fabulous. But through good and bad I stuck to my books. There was no special virtue in this, beyond having sense enough to feel my deficiencies. Between Mr. Pocket and Herbert I progressed fast. And with one or the other always at my elbow to give me the push I needed and clear obstacles from my path, I must have been as great a dolt as Drummle if I had done less.

I had not seen Mr. Wemmick for some weeks when I thought I would write him a note and propose going home with him on a certain evening. He replied that it would give him much pleasure and that he would expect me at the office at six o'clock. I went there and found him putting the key of his safe down his back as the clock struck.
"Did you think of walking down to Walworth?" said he.
"Certainly," said I, "if you approve."

"Very much," was Wemmick's reply. "I've had my legs under the desk all day and shall be glad to stretch them. Now, I'll tell you what I've got for supper, Mr. Pip. I've got a stewed steak — which is of home preparation — and a cold roast fowl — which is from the cook's shop. I think it's tender, because the master of the shop was a juror in one of our cases the other day, and we let him off easy. I reminded him of it when I bought the fowl and said, 'Pick us out a good one, old man, because if we had chosen to keep you in the box another day or two, we could easily have done it.' He said to that, 'Let me make you a present of the best fowl in the shop.' I let him, of course. As far as it goes, it's property and portable. You don't object to an aged parent, I hope?"
I really thought he was still speaking of the fowl, until he added, "Because I have got an aged parent at my place." I then said what politeness required.
