"So, you haven't dined with Mr. Jaggers yet?" he went on as we walked.
"Not yet."
"He told me so this afternoon when he heard you were coming. I expect you'll get an invitation tomorrow. He's going to ask your friends too. Three of them, aren't there?"
Although I was not in the habit of counting Drummle as one of my close friends, I answered, "Yes."

"Well, he's going to ask the whole gang" — I hardly felt complimented by the word — "and whatever he gives you, he'll give you good. Don't look for variety, but you'll have excellence. And there's another curious thing in his house," Wemmick went on, after a moment's pause, as if the remark followed naturally from the housekeeper. "He never lets a door or window be fastened at night."
"Is he never robbed?"

"That's it!" returned Wemmick. "He says, and puts it about publicly, 'I want to see the man who'll rob me.' Lord bless you, I have heard him a hundred times say to professional burglars in our front office, 'You know where I live; now, not a bolt is ever drawn there; why don't you try your hand? Come, can't I tempt you?' Not a man of them, sir, would be bold enough to try it, for love or money."
"They dread him so much?" said I.
"Dread him," said Wemmick. "I should say they dread him. Not that he isn't artful, even in his defiance of them. No silver, sir. Cheap metal, every spoon."
"So they wouldn't have much," I observed, "even if they—"

"Ah! But he would have much," said Wemmick, cutting me short. "And they know it. He'd have their lives, and the lives of scores of them. He'd have all he could get. And it's impossible to say what he couldn't get, if he put his mind to it."
I was falling into a meditation on my guardian's greatness when Wemmick remarked:
"As to the absence of silver, that's only his natural depth, you know. A river has its natural depth, and he has his. Look at his watch chain. That's real enough."
"It's very massive," said I.

"Massive?" repeated Wemmick. "I should think so. And his watch is a gold repeater, and worth a hundred pounds if it's worth a penny. Mr. Pip, there are about seven hundred thieves in this town who know all about that watch. There's not a man, woman, or child among them who wouldn't recognize the smallest link in that chain, and drop it as if it were red hot, if tricked into touching it."
With such talk at first, and afterward with conversation of a more general kind, Mr. Wemmick and I passed the time and the road until he let me know we had arrived in the district of Walworth.

It appeared to be a collection of back lanes, ditches, and little gardens, presenting the aspect of a rather dull retirement. Wemmick's house was a little wooden cottage in the midst of garden plots, and the top of it was cut out and painted to look like a battery mounted with guns.
"My own doing," said Wemmick. "Looks pretty, doesn't it?"
I highly praised it. I think it was the smallest house I ever saw, with the quaintest gothic windows — most of them fake — and a gothic door almost too small to get in through.
"That's a real flagstaff, you see," said Wemmick, "and on Sundays I run up a real flag. Then look here. After I have crossed this bridge, I hoist it up — so — and cut off the communication."

The bridge was a plank, and it crossed a chasm about four feet wide and two deep. But it was very pleasant to see the pride with which he hoisted it up and made it fast, smiling as he did so with genuine relish and not merely mechanically.
"At nine o'clock every night, Greenwich time," said Wemmick, "the gun fires. There he is, you see! And when you hear him go, I think you'll say he's a Stinger."

The piece of artillery in question was mounted in a separate fortress, constructed of latticework. It was protected from the weather by an ingenious little tarpaulin device in the form of an umbrella.

"Then, at the back," said Wemmick, "out of sight, so as not to spoil the idea of fortifications — for it's a principle of mine, if you have an idea, carry it out and keep it up — I don't know whether that's your view—"
I said, firmly, that it was.

"At the back, there's a pig, and there are fowls and rabbits. Then I knock together my own little frame, you see, and grow cucumbers. And you'll judge at supper what sort of salad I can raise. So, sir," said Wemmick, smiling again, but seriously too, as he shook his head, "if you can imagine the little place besieged, it would hold out a devil of a time in point of provisions."

Then he conducted me to a bower about a dozen yards off, but which was approached by such ingenious twists of path that it took quite a long time to reach. In this retreat, our glasses were already set out. Our punch was cooling in an ornamental lake, on whose margin the bower was raised. This body of water — with an island in the middle that might have been the salad for supper — was circular in shape, and he had built a fountain in it, which, when you set a little mill going and took a cork out of a pipe, played with such force that it made the back of your hand quite wet.

"I am my own engineer, and my own carpenter, and my own plumber, and my own gardener, and my own jack of all trades," said Wemmick, acknowledging my compliments. "Well, it's a good thing, you know. It brushes the Newgate cobwebs away and pleases the Aged. You wouldn't mind being introduced to the Aged right away, would you? It wouldn't put you out?"
I expressed my readiness, and we went into the castle. There we found, sitting by a fire, a very old man in a flannel coat — clean, cheerful, comfortable, and well cared for, but intensely deaf.
"Well, aged parent," said Wemmick, shaking hands with him in a cordial and jovial way, "how am you?"
"All right, John! All right!" replied the old man.
"Here's Mr. Pip, aged parent," said Wemmick, "and I wish you could hear his name. Nod away at him, Mr. Pip — that's what he likes. Nod away at him, if you please, like mad!"

"This is a fine place of my son's, sir," cried the old man, while I nodded as hard as I possibly could. "This is a pretty pleasure ground, sir. This spot and these beautiful works upon it ought to be kept together by the Nation, after my son's time, for the people's enjoyment."

"You're as proud of it as Punch, aren't you, Aged?" said Wemmick, gazing at the old man with his hard face genuinely softened. "There's a nod for you" — giving him a tremendous one. "There's another for you" — giving him a still more tremendous one. "You like that, don't you? If you're not tired, Mr. Pip — though I know it's tiring for visitors — will you give him one more? You can't think how it pleases him."

I gave him several more, and he was in great spirits. We left him busying himself feeding the fowls, and we sat down to our punch in the arbor. There Wemmick told me, as he smoked a pipe, that it had taken him a good many years to bring the property up to its present state of perfection.
"Is it your own, Mr. Wemmick?"
"Oh yes," said Wemmick. "I have got hold of it, a bit at a time. It's a freehold, by George!"
"Is it indeed? I hope Mr. Jaggers admires it?"

"Never seen it," said Wemmick. "Never heard of it. Never seen the Aged. Never heard of him. No — the office is one thing, and private life is another. When I go into the office, I leave the Castle behind me, and when I come into the Castle, I leave the office behind me. If it's not disagreeable to you, you'll oblige me by doing the same. I don't wish it spoken about professionally."

Of course I felt my good faith bound up in respecting his request. The punch being very good, we sat there drinking it and talking until it was almost nine o'clock. "Getting near gun-fire," said Wemmick then, as he laid down his pipe. "It's the Aged's treat."

Going back into the castle, we found the Aged heating the poker, with expectant eyes, as a preliminary to the great nightly ceremony. Wemmick stood with his watch in his hand until the moment came for him to take the red-hot poker from the Aged and go to the battery. He took it, went out, and presently the Stinger went off with a Bang that shook the rickety little box of a cottage as if it must fall to pieces, and made every glass and teacup in it ring. At this, the Aged — who I believe would have been blown out of his armchair but for holding on by the elbows — cried out joyfully, "He's fired! I heard him!" And I nodded at the old gentleman until it is no figure of speech to say that I absolutely could not see him.

The time between then and supper, Wemmick devoted to showing me his collection of curiosities. They were mostly criminal in nature, comprising the pen with which a celebrated forgery had been committed, a distinguished razor or two, some locks of hair, and several confessions written under sentence of death — upon which Mr. Wemmick set particular value as being, to use his own words, "every one of them lies, sir." These were agreeably scattered among small specimens of china and glass, various neat trifles made by the proprietor of the museum, and some tobacco stoppers carved by the Aged. They were all displayed in the chamber of the castle where I had first been received, which served not only as the general sitting room but as the kitchen too, judging by a saucepan on the stove and a brass fixture over the fireplace designed for hanging a roasting jack.

There was a neat little girl in attendance who looked after the Aged during the day. When she had laid the supper cloth, the bridge was lowered to let her out, and she withdrew for the night. The supper was excellent. And though the castle was rather subject to dry rot, so much so that it tasted like a bad nut, and though the pig might have been farther off, I was heartily pleased with the whole entertainment. Nor was there any drawback to my little turret bedroom, beyond there being such a thin ceiling between me and the flagstaff that when I lay on my back in bed, it felt as if I had to balance that pole on my forehead all night.

Wemmick was up early in the morning, and I am afraid I heard him cleaning my boots. After that, he fell to gardening, and I saw him from my gothic window pretending to employ the Aged, nodding at him in the most devoted manner. Our breakfast was as good as the supper, and at precisely half past eight we started for Little Britain. By degrees, Wemmick got dryer and harder as we went along, and his mouth tightened into a post office again. At last, when we got to his place of business and he pulled out his key from his coat collar, he looked as unconscious of his Walworth property as if the Castle and the drawbridge and the arbor and the lake and the fountain and the Aged had all been blown into space together by the last discharge of the Stinger.

chapters.title: Chapter 26
paragraphs: Things turned out just as Wemmick had predicted. I soon got the chance to compare my guardian's home with his clerk's. My guardian was in his office washing his hands with scented soap when I arrived from Walworth. He called me over and gave me the invitation for myself and my friends that Wemmick had mentioned. "No ceremony," he said. "No dinner dress. No nonsense."

Some people were lurking outside as usual when we stepped into the street, clearly eager to speak with him. But there was something so final about the halo of scented soap surrounding him that they gave up for the day. As we walked westward, he was recognized and greeted by two people, and started on the subjects of capital punishment and flogging. When I challenged his opinions, he defended them thoroughly, then unexpectedly pulled off what felt like a trick, making me argue against my own earlier points.

He led us to Gerrard Street, Soho, to a house on the south side. It was a rather grand house of its kind, but desperately in need of paint, with dirty windows. He took out his key and opened the door. We all walked into a stone entrance hall that was bare, gloomy, and seldom used. Then up a dark staircase we went to a set of three rooms on the first floor, connected to each other. The front and largest room was barely furnished as a sitting room. The other two rooms were smaller.

Dinner was laid in the best of these rooms. The second was his dressing room, the third his bedroom. He told us he rented the whole house but rarely used more of it than we saw. The table was comfortably set — no silver service, of course — and beside his chair stood a large dumb-waiter, stocked with bottles and condiments. Everything had that half-dead, half-alive quality, just like the forced-growth fruit I'd seen at Mr. Pumblechook's shop. The room was so oppressively heated that I couldn't help comparing it to a hothouse.

There was a bookcase in the room. I could see from the spines that the books were about evidence, criminal law, criminal biography, trials, acts of Parliament, and similar subjects. The furniture was all very solid and good, like his watch chain. It had an official look, though, and there was nothing merely ornamental anywhere. In a corner stood a little table holding a peculiar set: a deadly-looking gun case, a sword in a scabbard, several strange-looking boxes and packages, and two dreadful plaster casts on a shelf above, showing faces with swollen noses. Mr. Jaggers's own tall dark armchair was the most imposing piece in the room.

Since he had barely seen my three companions until now — he and I had walked together — he stood on the hearthrug after ringing the bell and gave them a searching look. To my surprise, he seemed at once to be mainly, if not solely, interested in Drummle.
"Pip," he said, placing his large hand on my shoulder and steering me to the window. "I can't tell one from another. Who's the Spider?"
"The spider?" I said.
"The blotchy, sprawling, sulky fellow."
"That's Bentley Drummle," I replied. "The one with the delicate face is Startop."
Taking no notice at all of "the one with the delicate face," he said, "Bentley Drummle is his name, is it? I like the look of that fellow."

He immediately began talking to Drummle. He wasn't at all put off by Drummle's heavy, reluctant replies. In fact, they seemed to spur him on to screw more conversation out of him. I was watching the two of them when the housekeeper appeared between us, carrying the first dish for the table.

She was a woman of about forty, I supposed — though I may have thought her younger than she was. Rather tall, with a lithe, nimble figure, extremely pale, with large faded eyes and a mass of streaming hair. I couldn't say whether some affliction of the heart made her lips part as if she were gasping, or whether her face simply had that expression. Her knees had a peculiar look, as though they'd been frequently clenched. I noticed that she always had her eyes on her master. I also noticed that Jaggers found something to criticize in her whenever she came near — some trivial thing about the arrangement of the table, the dishes, or the room — to make her show her hands. Whether he intended me to notice these things or not, I couldn't be sure. I noticed them, and Wemmick's words were fresh in my mind.

She set the dish down, touched my guardian quietly on the arm with a finger to signal that dinner was ready, and vanished. We took our seats at the round table. My guardian kept Drummle on one side of him and Startop on the other. It was a noble fish dish that the housekeeper had put on, and it was followed by a joint of equally fine mutton and then an equally fine bird. Sauces, wines, everything we needed stood on the dumb-waiter ready for us. We all seemed to manage the food and drink well, and my guardian took the lead. It was not at all a talkative dinner, and yet it wasn't dull either. He directed the conversation against us whenever it flagged — which it did occasionally, when we grew rather drunk and reckless — and urged the drinks on us, making steady progress toward his goal of getting us thoroughly intoxicated.

Having been persuaded to pay close attention to the housekeeper, both by her own striking appearance and by Wemmick's briefing, I noticed that whenever she was in the room she kept her eyes fixed on my guardian. I also noticed that she would remove her hands from any dish she set before him hesitantly, as if she dreaded his calling her back. She was a most docile creature, like the obedient dogs in the happy-family show. But her hands drew my attention, and I compared them with other hands around the table. Her fingers were thin, but strong and muscular, and they bore signs of having been deeply lined and scratched. Mr. Jaggers seemed to notice my watchfulness, for a new and surprising expression appeared on his face — I only noticed it because I was watching closely.

Dinner went off cheerfully. Although my guardian seemed to follow subjects rather than start them, I knew he was pulling our weakest traits out of us. I found myself revealing my tendency toward lavish spending, my habit of patronizing Herbert, and my boasting about my great expectations. It was both a mercy and a disgrace that nothing of a tender nature could possibly be confided to this man, though I strongly suspected Herbert of getting dangerously close to admitting some tender feelings about someone.

It was when we'd reached the cheese, not before, that our conversation turned to our rowing exploits. Drummle was teased about creeping up behind us at night in that slow, amphibious way of his. At this, Drummle informed our host that he greatly preferred our room to our company, and that as for our strength, he could handle any of us with one hand. My guardian was thoroughly pleased with this remark. He told him so and said, "Come! I like that!" Then he called for more wine and leaned back in his chair, biting his forefinger sideways at Drummle.

At that moment, the housekeeper was clearing the table. My guardian, taking no notice of her but with the side of his face turned away from her, was leaning back in his chair biting his forefinger and showing an interest in Drummle that I found utterly baffling. Suddenly he clapped his large hand on the housekeeper's, like a trap, as she stretched it across the table. She trembled and turned white, struggling to pull her hand free.
"If you're talking about strength," said Mr. Jaggers, "I'll show you a wrist. Molly, let them see your wrist."
Her trapped hand was on the table, but she had already put her other hand behind her back. "Master," she said in a low voice, her eyes fixed on him with attention and entreaty. "Don't."
"I'll show you a wrist," Mr. Jaggers repeated with an unmovable determination. "Molly, let them see your wrist."
"Master," she murmured again. "Please!"
"Molly," said Mr. Jaggers, not looking at her but obstinately staring at the opposite wall, "let them see both your wrists. Show them. Come!"

He released her hand and turned that wrist face-up on the table. She brought her other hand from behind her and held both out side by side. The second wrist was badly disfigured — deeply scarred, crisscrossed with scars. When she held her hands out, she took her eyes off Mr. Jaggers and turned them watchfully on every one of us in succession. Her demeanor was so quiet that it made the house quiet too. It was like the cases of those dreadful people I'd waited for at the prison gate on my very first morning in London. They had that same look of belonging to the jail, as if they were never to get free of it.

"There's power here," said Mr. Jaggers, coolly tracing the sinews with his forefinger. "Very few men have the wrist strength this woman has. It's remarkable what sheer force of grip there is in these hands. I've had occasion to examine many hands, but I never saw stronger ones in that respect, man's or woman's, than these."

While he said these words in a leisurely, appraising way, she continued looking at each of us in turn. The moment he stopped, she looked at him again. "That'll do, Molly," said Mr. Jaggers, giving her a slight nod. "You've been admired, and you can go." She withdrew her hands, dropped them at her sides, and left the room. Since Mr. Jaggers and Drummle were clearly very well suited to each other, I felt I'd fallen rather into the background during dinner. But now I slipped in a word.
"At half past nine, gentlemen," he said, deliberately setting down his glass and hauling out his gold pocket watch by its massive chain, "I am extremely sorry to announce that it's half past nine."

Taking this hint, we all rose to leave. Before we reached the street door, Startop was cheerfully calling Drummle "old boy" as if nothing had happened. But the old boy was so far from responding that he refused even to walk to Hammersmith on the same side of the street. So Herbert and I, who were staying in town, slipped away together and went home through Temple. As we walked, Herbert told me about his Blackfriars adventure, and I told him lightly about Mr. Jaggers's housekeeper. I had no idea then that the topic would ever come back to me, but it came back before long, as everything in life kept coming back.

In our boyish lack of discretion, I dare say we drank too much, and I know we talked too much. We became particularly heated over some boorish sneer of Drummle's, to the effect that we were too free with our money. It led to my remarking, with more zeal than discretion, that it came badly from him, who borrowed money from Herbert and me at a time when he could barely have had it from anyone else.
"Well," retorted Drummle. "He'll be paid."
"I don't mean to imply that he won't," I said. "But it might make you hold your tongue about us and our money, I should think."
"You should think!" retorted Drummle. "Oh Lord!"
"I dare say," I went on, meaning to be very severe, "that you wouldn't lend money to any of us if we wanted it."
"You are right," said Drummle. "I wouldn't lend one of you a sixpence. I wouldn't lend anybody a sixpence."
"Rather mean to borrow under those circumstances, I should say."
"You should say," repeated Drummle. "Oh Lord!"
This was so very aggravating — the more so as I found myself making no headway against his surly stubbornness — that I said, disregarding Herbert's efforts to check me —
"Come, Mr. Drummle, since we are on the subject, I'll tell you what passed between Herbert here and me when you borrowed that money."
"I don't want to know what passed between Herbert there and you," growled Drummle. And I think he added in a lower growl that we might both go to the devil and shake ourselves.

"I'll tell you, however," I said, "whether you want to know or not. We said that as you put it in your pocket very glad to get it, you seemed to be immensely amused at his being so weak as to lend it."

Drummle laughed outright and sat laughing in our faces, with his hands in his pockets and his round shoulders raised, plainly signifying that it was quite true and that he despised us as fools, all of us.

At this, Startop took him in hand, though with a much better grace than I had shown, and urged him to be a little more agreeable. Startop being a lively, bright young fellow, and Drummle being the exact opposite, the latter was always disposed to resent him as a direct personal insult. He now retorted with some rude remark, and Startop tried to turn the discussion. But Drummle wouldn't hear of it. Startop protested mildly and Drummle scowled heavily at him.
"Gentlemen," said Mr. Jaggers, deliberately putting down his glass and hauling out his gold pocket watch by its massive chain, "I am extremely sorry to announce that it's half past nine."

Taking this hint, we all rose to leave. Before we reached the street door, Startop was cheerfully calling Drummle "old boy" as if nothing had happened. But the old boy was so far from responding that he refused even to walk to Hammersmith on the same side of the street. So Herbert and I, who were staying in town, slipped away together and went home through Temple. As we walked, Herbert told me about his Blackfriars adventure, and I told him lightly about Mr. Jaggers's housekeeper. I had no idea then that the topic would ever come back to me, but it came back before long, as everything in life kept coming back.

Since I was not going home to supper just yet, and since Herbert had hardly enough powder in the barrel for his own supper, I thought I'd leave Herbert there for a moment and run back upstairs to say a word to my guardian. I found him in his dressing room surrounded by his boots, already hard at work washing his hands of us.
I told him I'd come back up to say how sorry I was that anything unpleasant had occurred, and that I hoped he wouldn't blame me much.
"Pooh!" he said, sluicing his face and speaking through the water drops. "It's nothing, Pip. I like that Spider, though."
He had turned toward me now and was shaking his head, blowing, and toweling himself.
"I'm glad you like him, sir," I said, "but I don't."
"No, no," my guardian agreed. "Don't have too much to do with him. Keep as clear of him as you can. But I like the fellow, Pip. He's one of the true sort. Why, if I were a fortune-teller —"
Looking out of the towel, he caught my eye.
"But I am not a fortune-teller," he said, letting his head drop into a festoon of towel and rubbing away at his ears. "You know what I am, don't you? Good night, Pip."
"Good night, sir."
About a month after that, the Spider's time with Mr. Pocket was up for good. To the great relief of everyone in the house except Mrs. Pocket, he went home to the family estate.

chapters.title: Chapter 27
paragraphs: "MY DEAR MR PIP:—

"I write this at the request of Mr. Gargery, to let you know that he is coming to London with Mr. Wopsle and would be glad, if agreeable, to be allowed to see you. He would call at Barnard's Hotel on Tuesday morning at nine o'clock. If not agreeable, please leave word. Your poor sister is much the same as when you left. We talk of you in the kitchen every night and wonder what you are saying and doing. If this is now considered a liberty, please excuse it for the love of the old days. No more, dear Mr. Pip, from
"Your ever obliged and affectionate servant, BIDDY."

"P.S. He wishes me most particularly to write what larks. He says you will understand. I hope and do not doubt it will be agreeable to see him, even though you are a gentleman, for you always had a good heart, and he is a worthy, worthy man. I have read him all of this, except only the last little sentence, and he wishes me most particularly to write again what larks."
I received this letter by the post on Monday morning, so the appointment was for the next day. Let me confess exactly what feelings I had about Joe's coming.

Not pleasure, though I was bound to him by so many ties. No — considerable disturbance, some mortification, and a sharp sense of incongruity. If I could have kept him away by paying money, I certainly would have paid. My greatest reassurance was that he was coming to Barnard's Inn, not to Hammersmith, and so would not cross paths with Bentley Drummle. I had little objection to his being seen by Herbert or his father, for both of whom I had respect. But I felt the sharpest sensitivity about his being seen by Drummle, whom I held in contempt. So it goes throughout life — our worst weaknesses and meannesses are usually committed for the sake of the people we most despise.

I had begun to constantly decorate the rooms in some quite unnecessary and inappropriate way, and very expensive those battles with Barnard proved to be. By this time, the rooms were vastly different from what I'd found them, and I enjoyed the honor of occupying a few prominent pages in a nearby upholsterer's account books. I had advanced so quickly of late that I'd even hired a boy in boots — top boots — to whom I might be said to have been in bondage and slavery. For after I had created this monster from the refuse of my washerwoman's family and clothed him in a blue coat, canary waistcoat, white cravat, cream breeches, and the boots already mentioned, I had to find him a little to do and a great deal to eat. Both of those horrible requirements haunted my existence.

This avenging phantom was ordered on duty at eight on Tuesday morning in the hall (it was two feet square, as charged for floor-cloth). Herbert suggested certain things for breakfast that he thought Joe would like. While I felt genuinely grateful to him for being so thoughtful and considerate, I had an odd, half-irritated suspicion that if Joe had been coming to see him, he wouldn't have been quite so eager about it.

Still, I came into town on Monday night to be ready for Joe. I got up early in the morning and made the sitting room and breakfast table assume their most splendid appearance. Unfortunately, the morning was drizzly, and an angel could not have hidden the fact that Barnard was shedding sooty tears outside the window, like some feeble giant of a chimney sweep.

As the time approached, I wanted to run away. But the Avenger, following orders, was in the hall, and soon I heard Joe on the staircase. I knew it was Joe by his clumsy way of climbing — his best boots were always too big for him — and by the time he took to read the names on the other floors as he came up. When at last he stopped outside our door, I could hear his finger tracing over the painted letters of my name. I distinctly heard him breathing in at the keyhole. Finally he gave a faint single knock, and Pepper — such was the compromising name of the avenging boy — announced "Mr. Gargery!" I thought he would never be done wiping his feet, and that I'd have to go out and lift him off the mat. But at last he came in.
"Joe, how are you, Joe?"
"Pip, how AIR you, Pip?"
With his good honest face all glowing and shining, and his hat set down on the floor between us, he caught both my hands and worked them straight up and down, as if I were the latest patented pump.
"I'm glad to see you, Joe. Give me your hat."

But Joe, picking it up carefully with both hands like a bird's nest with eggs in it, wouldn't hear of parting with that piece of property. He persisted in standing and talking over it in the most uncomfortable way.

"Which you have that growed," said Joe, "and that swelled, and that gentle-folked" — Joe considered a little before he discovered this word — "as to be sure you are an honor to your king and country."
"And you, Joe, look wonderfully well."

"Thank God," said Joe, "I'm ekerval to most. And your sister, she's no worse than she were. And Biddy, she's ever right and ready. And all friends is no backerder, if not no forarder. 'Ceptin Wopsle; he's had a drop."
All this time, still taking great care of the bird's nest with both hands, Joe was rolling his eyes round and round the room and round and round the flowered pattern of my dressing gown.
"Had a drop, Joe?"

"Why yes," said Joe, lowering his voice. "He's left the Church and went into the playacting. Which the playacting have likeways brought him to London along with me. And his wish were," said Joe, getting the bird's nest under his left arm for the moment and groping in it for an egg with his right, "if no offence, as I would 'and you that."

I took what Joe gave me and found it to be the crumpled playbill of a small London theatre, announcing the first appearance that very week of "the celebrated Provincial Amateur of Roscian renown, whose unique performance in the highest tragic walk of our National Bard has lately occasioned so great a sensation in local dramatic circles."
"Were you at his performance, Joe?" I asked.
"I were," said Joe, with emphasis and solemnity.
"Was there a great sensation?"

"Why," said Joe, "yes, there certainly were a peck of orange peel. Partickler when he see the ghost. Though I put it to yourself, sir, whether it were calc'lated to keep a man up to his work with a good hart, to be continiwally cutting in betwixt him and the Ghost with 'Amen!' A man may have had a misfortun' and been in the Church," said Joe, lowering his voice to an argumentative and feeling tone, "but that is no reason why you should put him out at such a time. Which I meantersay, if the ghost of a man's own father cannot be allowed to claim his attention, what can, Sir? Still more, when his mourning 'at is unfortunately made so small as that the weight of the black feathers brings it off, try to keep it on how you may."

A ghost-seeing expression in Joe's own face told me that Herbert had entered the room. So I introduced Joe to Herbert, who held out his hand. But Joe backed away from it and held on to the bird's nest.

"Your servant, Sir," said Joe, "which I hope as you and Pip" — here his eye fell on the Avenger, who was putting some toast on the table, and so plainly showed an intention to include that young gentleman in the family that I frowned it down and confused him more — "I meantersay, you two gentlemen — which I hope as you get your elths in this close spot? For the present may be a werry good inn, according to London opinions," said Joe confidentially, "and I believe its character do stand it; but I wouldn't keep a pig in it myself — not in the case that I wished him to fatten wholesome and to eat with a meller flavour on him."

Having delivered this flattering testimony to our dwelling place, and having incidentally shown his tendency to call me "sir," Joe was invited to sit down at the table. He looked all round the room for a suitable spot to deposit his hat — as if only a few rare substances in nature could serve as its resting place — and finally stood it on an extreme corner of the mantelpiece, from which it fell off at intervals ever after.
"Do you take tea or coffee, Mr. Gargery?" asked Herbert, who always presided in the morning.
"Thankee, Sir," said Joe, stiff from head to foot. "I'll take whichever is most agreeable to yourself."
"What do you say to coffee?"

"Thankee, Sir," returned Joe, evidently disheartened by the proposal. "Since you are so kind as to make chice of coffee, I will not run contrairy to your own opinions. But don't you never find it a little 'eating?"
"Say tea then," said Herbert, pouring it out.

Here Joe's hat tumbled off the mantelpiece, and he started out of his chair, picked it up, and fitted it to the same exact spot — as if it were an absolute point of good breeding that it should tumble off again soon.
"When did you come to town, Mr. Gargery?"

"Were it yesterday afternoon?" said Joe, after coughing behind his hand as if he'd had time to catch the whooping cough since he arrived. "No it were not. Yes it were. Yes. It were yesterday afternoon" — with an appearance of mingled wisdom, relief, and strict impartiality.
"Have you seen anything of London yet?"

"Why, yes, Sir," said Joe. "Me and Wopsle went off straight to look at the Blacking Ware'us. But we didn't find that it come up to its likeness in the red bills at the shop doors; which I meantersay," added Joe in an explanatory manner, "as it is there drawd too architectooralooral."

I truly believe Joe would have prolonged this word — mightily expressive to my mind of some architecture I know — into a perfect chorus, had his attention not been providentially attracted by his hat, which was toppling. Indeed, it demanded constant attention from him, and a quickness of eye and hand very like that required by wicket-keeping. He made extraordinary play with it and showed the greatest skill. Now rushing at it and catching it neatly as it dropped. Now merely stopping it midway, batting it up, and chasing it around various parts of the room and against a good deal of the wallpaper, before he felt it safe to close with it. Finally he splashed it into the slop basin, where I took the liberty of laying hands on it.

As for his shirt collar and coat collar, they were perplexing to reflect on — insoluble mysteries both. Why should a man scrape himself to that extent before he could consider himself fully dressed? Why should he suppose it necessary to be purified by suffering for his holiday clothes? Then he fell into such unaccountable fits of meditation, with his fork midway between his plate and his mouth. His eyes were attracted in such strange directions. He was afflicted with such remarkable coughs. He sat so far from the table and dropped so much more than he ate, pretending he hadn't dropped it. I was heartily glad when Herbert left us for the City.

I had neither the good sense nor the good feeling to know that this was all my fault, and that if I had been easier with Joe, Joe would have been easier with me. I felt impatient with him and out of temper. In which condition he heaped coals of fire on my head.
"Us two being now alone, sir —" Joe began.
"Joe," I interrupted irritably, "how can you call me sir?"
Joe looked at me for a single instant with something faintly like reproach. Utterly absurd as his cravat was, and as his collars were, I was conscious of a sort of dignity in the look.

"Us two being now alone," Joe resumed, "and me having the intentions and abilities to stay not many minutes more, I will now conclude — leastways begin — to mention what has led to my having had the present honor. For was it not," said Joe, with his old air of lucid explanation, "that my only wish were to be useful to you, I should not have had the honor of breaking victuals in the company and abode of gentlemen."
I was so unwilling to see that look again that I made no objection to this tone.

"Well, sir," Joe continued, "this is how it were. I were at the Bargemen t'other night, Pip" — whenever he subsided into affection he called me Pip, and whenever he relapsed into politeness he called me sir — "when there come up in his shay-cart, Pumblechook. Which that same identical," said Joe, going off on a new track, "do comb my 'air the wrong way sometimes, awful, by giving out up and down town as it were him which ever had your infant companionation and were looked upon as a playfellow by yourself."
"Nonsense. It was you, Joe."

"Which I fully believed it were, Pip," said Joe, slightly tossing his head, "though it signify little now, sir. Well, Pip; this same identical, which his manners is given to blusterous, come to me at the Bargemen (wot a pipe and a pint of beer do give refreshment to the workingman, sir, and do not over stimilate), and his word were, 'Joseph, Miss Havisham she wish to speak to you.'"
"Miss Havisham, Joe?"
"'She wish,' were Pumblechook's word, 'to speak to you.'" Joe sat and rolled his eyes at the ceiling.
"Yes, Joe? Go on, please."
"Next day, sir," said Joe, looking at me as if I were a long way off, "having cleaned myself, I go and I see Miss A."
"Miss A., Joe? Miss Havisham?"

"Which I say, sir," replied Joe with an air of legal formality, as if he were making his will, "Miss A., or otherways Havisham. Her expression air then as follering: 'Mr. Gargery. You air in correspondence with Mr. Pip?' Having had a letter from you, I were able to say 'I am.' (When I married your sister, sir, I said 'I will;' and when I answered your friend, Pip, I said 'I am.') 'Would you tell him, then,' said she, 'that which Estella has come home and would be glad to see him.'"
I felt my face fire up as I looked at Joe. I hope one remote cause of its firing may have been my awareness that if I had known his errand, I would have given him more encouragement.

"Biddy," Joe continued, "when I got home and asked her fur to write the message to you, a little hung back. Biddy says, 'I know he will be very glad to have it by word of mouth, it is holiday time, you want to see him, go!' I have now concluded, sir," said Joe, rising from his chair, "and, Pip, I wish you ever well and ever prospering to a greater and a greater height."
"But you're not going now, Joe?"
"Yes I am," said Joe.
"But you're coming back to dinner, Joe?"
"No I am not," said Joe.
Our eyes met, and all the "Sir" melted out of that manly heart as he gave me his hand.

"Pip, dear old chap, life is made of ever so many partings welded together, as I may say, and one man's a blacksmith, and one's a whitesmith, and one's a goldsmith, and one's a coppersmith. Diwisions among such must come, and must be met as they come. If there's been any fault at all today, it's mine. You and me is not two figures to be together in London; nor yet anywheres else but what is private, and beknown, and understood among friends. It ain't that I am proud, but that I want to be right, as you shall never see me no more in these clothes. I'm wrong in these clothes. I'm wrong out of the forge, the kitchen, or off th' meshes. You won't find half so much fault in me if you think of me in my forge dress, with my hammer in my hand, or even my pipe. You won't find half so much fault in me if, supposing as you should ever wish to see me, you come and put your head in at the forge window and see Joe the blacksmith, there, at the old anvil, in the old burnt apron, sticking to the old work. I'm awful dull, but I hope I've beat out something nigh the rights of this at last. And so GOD bless you, dear old Pip, old chap, GOD bless you!"

I had not been mistaken in my sense that there was a simple dignity in him. The fashion of his dress could no more get in its way when he spoke these words than it could get in its way in Heaven. He touched me gently on the forehead and went out. As soon as I could recover myself enough, I hurried out after him and looked for him in the nearby streets. But he was gone.

chapters.title: Chapter 28
paragraphs: It was clear I must go to our town the next day. In the first rush of my repentance, it was equally clear I must stay at Joe's. But after I'd booked my seat on tomorrow's coach and gone down to Mr. Pocket's and back, I was no longer convinced on that last point. I began inventing reasons and making excuses to stay at the Blue Boar instead. I would be an inconvenience at Joe's. I wasn't expected, and my bed wouldn't be ready. I'd be too far from Miss Havisham's, and she was demanding and mightn't like it. All other swindlers on earth are nothing compared to the self-swindlers, and with such pretenses I cheated myself. A curious thing, surely. That I should innocently accept a bad half-crown from someone else is reasonable enough. But that I should knowingly count the counterfeit coins of my own making as real money! A helpful stranger, pretending to fold up my banknotes for safekeeping, switches the notes for nutshells. But what is his sleight of hand compared to mine, when I fold up my own nutshells and pass them off to myself as notes!

Having settled that I must go to the Blue Boar, my mind was much disturbed by indecision over whether to take the Avenger. It was tempting to imagine that expensive mercenary publicly airing his boots in the archway of the Blue Boar's posting yard. It was almost thrilling to picture him casually produced in the tailor's shop, confounding the disrespectful senses of Trabb's boy. On the other hand, Trabb's boy might worm his way into the Avenger's confidence and tell him things. Or, reckless and desperate wretch that I knew he could be, he might jeer at him in the High Street. My patroness, too, might hear of him and not approve. On the whole, I resolved to leave the Avenger behind.

It was the afternoon coach I'd booked, and since winter had now come round, I wouldn't arrive at my destination until two or three hours after dark. Our departure time from the Cross Keys was two o'clock. I arrived with a quarter of an hour to spare, attended by the Avenger — if I may use that expression for one who never attended on me if he could possibly help it.

At that time it was customary to transport convicts down to the dockyards by stagecoach. I had often heard of them riding as outside passengers and had more than once seen them on the highway dangling their ironed legs over the coach roof. So I had no cause to be surprised when Herbert, meeting me in the yard, told me there were two convicts going down with me. But I had a reason — an old reason now — for instinctively faltering whenever I heard the word "convict."
"You don't mind them, Handel?" said Herbert.
"Oh no!"
"I thought you seemed as if you didn't like them?"
"I can't pretend I do like them, and I suppose you don't particularly. But I don't mind them."
"See! There they are," said Herbert, "coming out of the Tap. What a degraded and vile sight it is!"

They had been treating their guard, I suppose, for they had a jailer with them, and all three came out wiping their mouths on their hands. The two convicts were handcuffed together, with irons on their legs — irons of a pattern I knew well. They wore the dress I likewise knew well. Their keeper had a brace of pistols and carried a thick-knobbed club under his arm. But he was on good terms with them and stood beside them watching the horses being hitched, rather as if the convicts were an interesting exhibit not formally open to the public, and he the curator. One was a taller and stouter man than the other, and appeared, as a matter of course according to the mysterious ways of the world, both convict and free, to have been given the smaller suit of clothes. His arms and legs were like great pincushions of those shapes, and his outfit disguised him absurdly. But I knew his half-closed eye at one glance. There stood the man I had seen on the settle at the Three Jolly Bargemen on a Saturday night, the man who had aimed at me with his invisible gun!

It was easy to confirm that he didn't recognize me any more than if he'd never seen me in his life. He looked across at me, appraised my watch chain, then casually spat and said something to the other convict. They laughed and swung around with a clink of their coupling manacle, and looked at something else. The great numbers on their backs, as if they were street doors. Their coarse, mangy, ungainly outer surface, as if they were animals. Their ironed legs, apologetically garlanded with pocket handkerchiefs. And the way everyone present looked at them and kept away. All this made them, as Herbert had said, a most disagreeable and degraded spectacle.

But this was not the worst of it. It turned out that the whole back of the coach had been taken by a family moving from London, and there were no places for the two prisoners but on the front seat behind the coachman. At this, a choleric gentleman who had taken the fourth seat flew into a violent passion. He said it was a breach of contract to mix him up with such villainous company, that it was poisonous, pernicious, infamous, shameful, and I don't know what else. By now the coach was ready and the coachman impatient. We were all preparing to climb up, and the prisoners had come over with their keeper, bringing with them that peculiar flavor of bread poultice, baize, rope yarn, and hearthstone that accompanies the convict presence.

"Don't take it so much amiss, sir," the keeper pleaded with the angry passenger. "I'll sit next to you myself. I'll put them on the outside of the row. They won't interfere with you, sir. You needn't know they're there."
"And don't blame me," growled the convict I had recognized. "I don't want to go. I'm quite ready to stay behind. As far as I'm concerned, anyone's welcome to my place."

"Or mine," said the other gruffly. "I wouldn't have inconvenienced any of you if I'd had my way." Then they both laughed and began cracking nuts and spitting the shells about — as I really think I would have liked to do myself, if I'd been in their place and so despised.

At length, it was decided there was no help for the angry gentleman. He must either go in his chance company or remain behind. So he got into his place, still complaining. The keeper got in next to him, and the convicts hauled themselves up as best they could. The convict I had recognized sat behind me with his breath on the back of my head.
"Goodbye, Handel!" Herbert called out as we started. I thought what a blessed fortune it was that he'd found another name for me than Pip.

It is impossible to describe how acutely I felt the convict's breathing — not only on the back of my head but all along my spine. The sensation was like being touched in my marrow with some pungent, searching acid. It set my very teeth on edge. He seemed to have more breathing business to do than other men and to make more noise doing it. I was conscious of growing high-shouldered on one side in my shrinking efforts to fend him off.

The weather was miserably raw, and the two cursed the cold. It made us all lethargic before we had gone far. When we had left the Halfway House behind, we habitually dozed, shivered, and were silent. I dozed off myself while considering whether I ought to give a couple of pounds to this creature before losing sight of him, and how it could best be done. In the act of pitching forward as if I were about to dive among the horses, I woke in a fright and took up the question again.

But I must have lost consciousness longer than I thought, since, although I couldn't recognize anything in the darkness and the fitful lights and shadows of our lamps, I could sense marsh country in the cold damp wind blowing at us. Huddling forward for warmth and using me as a screen against the wind, the convicts were closer to me than before. The very first words I heard them exchange as I came to were the words of my own thought: "Two one-pound notes."
"How did he get them?" said the convict I had never seen.
"How should I know?" returned the other. "He had them stowed away somehow. Given to him by friends, I expect."
"I wish," said the other, with a bitter curse on the cold, "that I had them here."
"Two one-pound notes, or friends?"
"Two one-pound notes. I'd sell all the friends I ever had for one, and think it a blessed good bargain. Well? So he says —?"

"So he says," the convict I had recognized resumed — "it was all said and done in half a minute, behind a pile of timber in the dockyard — 'You're going to be discharged?' Yes, I was. Would I find out that boy who had fed him and kept his secret, and give him those two one-pound notes? Yes, I would. And I did."
"More fool you," growled the other. "I'd have spent them on a man, in food and drink. He must have been a green one. Mean to say he knew nothing of you?"
"Not a halfpenny's worth. Different gangs and different ships. He was tried again for prison-breaking and got made a lifer."
"And was that — honor! — the only time you served out in this part of the country?"
"The only time."
"What might have been your opinion of the place?"
"A most beastly place. Mudbank, mist, swamp, and work. Work, swamp, mist, and mudbank."
They both cursed the place in very strong language, then gradually growled themselves out and had nothing left to say.

After overhearing this conversation, I would certainly have climbed down and been left in the solitude and darkness of the highway, if not for feeling certain that the man had no suspicion of my identity. Indeed, I was not only so changed by the course of nature but so differently dressed and so differently situated that it was very unlikely he could have known me without some accidental clue. Still, the coincidence of our being together on the coach was strange enough to fill me with dread that some other coincidence might at any moment connect me, within his hearing, with my name. For this reason, I resolved to get off as soon as we reached the town and get out of his hearing. This I managed successfully. My small portmanteau was in the boot under my feet. I had only to turn a hinge to get it out. I threw it down before me, climbed down after it, and was left at the first lamp on the first stones of the town pavement. As for the convicts, they went their way with the coach, and I knew at what point they would be spirited off to the river. In my imagination, I saw the boat with its convict crew waiting for them at the slime-washed stairs — again heard the gruff "Give way, you!" like an order to dogs — again saw the wicked Noah's Ark lying out on the black water.

I could not have said what I was afraid of, for my fear was completely undefined and vague. But there was great fear upon me. As I walked to the hotel, I felt that a dread far exceeding the mere worry of a painful or disagreeable recognition made me tremble. I am sure it took no distinct shape, and that it was the revival, for a few minutes, of the terror of childhood.

The coffee room at the Blue Boar was empty. I had not only ordered my dinner there but had sat down to it before the waiter recognized me. As soon as he had apologized for his lapse of memory, he asked me if he should send Boots for Mr. Pumblechook.
"No," I said. "Certainly not."

The waiter — the same one who had brought up the Great Remonstrance from the Commercials on the day I was bound apprentice — appeared surprised. He took the earliest opportunity of placing a dirty old copy of a local newspaper so directly in my way that I picked it up and read this paragraph:

Our readers will learn, not altogether without interest, in reference to the recent romantic rise in fortune of a young artificer in iron of this neighbourhood (what a theme, by the way, for the magic pen of our as yet not universally acknowledged townsman TOOBY, the poet of our columns!) that the youth's earliest patron, companion, and friend, was a highly respected individual not entirely unconnected with the corn and seed trade, and whose eminently convenient and commodious business premises are situate within a hundred miles of the High Street. It is not wholly irrespective of our personal feelings that we record HIM as the Mentor of our young Telemachus, for it is good to know that our town produced the founder of the latter's fortunes. Does the thought-contracted brow of the local Sage or the lustrous eye of local Beauty inquire whose fortunes? We believe that Quintin Matsys was the BLACKSMITH of Antwerp. VERB. SAP.

I hold a conviction, based on extensive experience, that if in the days of my prosperity I had gone to the North Pole, I would have met somebody there — wandering Eskimo or civilized man — who would have told me that Pumblechook was my earliest patron and the founder of my fortunes.

chapters.title: Chapter 29
paragraphs: Early in the morning I was up and out. It was too early yet to go to Miss Havisham's, so I wandered into the country on Miss Havisham's side of town — which was not Joe's side; I could go there tomorrow — thinking about my patroness and painting brilliant pictures of her plans for me.

She had adopted Estella. She had as good as adopted me. It could not fail to be her intention to bring us together. She reserved it for me to restore the desolate house, let the sunshine into the dark rooms, set the clocks going and the cold hearths blazing, tear down the cobwebs, destroy the vermin — in short, to do all the shining deeds of the young knight of romance and marry the princess. I had stopped to look at the house as I passed. Its seared red brick walls, blocked windows, and strong green ivy clasping even the chimney stacks with its twigs and tendons, as if with sinewy old arms, had made up a rich attractive mystery of which I was the hero. Estella was the inspiration and the heart of it, of course. But though she had taken such strong possession of me, though my fancy and my hope were so set upon her, though her influence on my boyish life and character had been all-powerful, I did not, even that romantic morning, invest her with any qualities beyond those she actually possessed. I mention this here with a fixed purpose, because it is the key to my poor labyrinth. In my experience, the conventional notion of a lover cannot always be true. The plain truth is that when I loved Estella with the love of a man, I loved her simply because I found her irresistible. Once for all: I knew to my sorrow, often and often if not always, that I loved her against reason, against promise, against peace, against hope, against happiness, against every discouragement there could be. Once for all: I loved her none the less because I knew it, and it had no more power to restrain me than if I had devoutly believed her to be human perfection.

I timed my walk so as to arrive at the gate at my old hour. When I had rung the bell with an unsteady hand, I turned my back on the gate while I tried to get my breath and keep the beating of my heart reasonably quiet. I heard the side door open and steps come across the courtyard. But I pretended not to hear, even when the gate swung on its rusty hinges.

When at last I was touched on the shoulder, I started and turned. I started much more naturally then, to find myself confronted by a man in a sober grey suit. The last man I should have expected to see as porter at Miss Havisham's door.
"Orlick!"
"Ah, young master, there's more changes than yours. But come in, come in. It's against my orders to hold the gate open."
I entered, and he swung it shut, locked it, and took the key out. "Yes!" he said, turning round after doggedly preceding me a few steps toward the house. "Here I am!"
"How did you come here?"
"I come here," he retorted, "on my legs. I had my box brought alongside me in a barrow."
"Are you here for good?"
"I ain't here for harm, young master, I suppose?"
I was not so sure of that. I had time to consider the retort in my mind while he slowly lifted his heavy glance from the pavement, up my legs and arms, to my face.
"Then you've left the forge?" I said.
"Do this look like a forge?" replied Orlick, sending his glance around with an air of injury. "Now, do it look like it?"
I asked him how long ago he had left Gargery's forge.
"One day is so like another here," he replied, "that I don't know without adding it up. But I came here some time after you left."
"I could have told you that, Orlick."
"Ah!" he said dryly. "But then you've got to be a scholar."

By this time we had reached the house. I found his room to be one just within the side door, with a little window looking onto the courtyard. In its small proportions, it was not unlike the sort of place usually given to a gatekeeper in Paris. Certain keys hung on the wall, to which he now added the gate key. His patchwork-covered bed was in a little inner alcove. The whole place had a slovenly, cramped, and sleepy look, like a cage for a human dormouse. And he, looming dark and heavy in the shadow of a corner by the window, looked like the human dormouse it was made for — as indeed he was.
"I never saw this room before," I remarked. "But there used to be no porter here."

"No," he said. "Not till it got about that there was no protection on the premises, and it came to be considered dangerous, with convicts and all sorts going up and down. And then I was recommended for the place as a man who could give as good as he got, and I took it. It's easier than working the bellows and hammering. That's loaded, that is."
My eye had been caught by a gun with a brass-bound stock over the chimney piece, and his eye had followed mine.
"Well," I said, not wanting more conversation, "shall I go up to Miss Havisham?"

"Burn me if I know!" he retorted, first stretching himself and then shaking himself. "My orders end here, young master. I give this bell a rap with this hammer, and you go on along the passage till you meet somebody."
"I am expected, I believe?"
"Burn me twice over if I can say!" he said.

At that, I turned down the long passage I had first walked in my thick boots, and he rang his bell. At the end of the passage, while the bell was still echoing, I found Sarah Pocket, who appeared to have now become permanently green and yellow on my account.
"Oh!" she said. "You, is it, Mr. Pip?"
"It is, Miss Pocket. I'm glad to tell you that Mr. Pocket and family are all well."
"Are they any wiser?" said Sarah, with a dismal shake of the head. "They had better be wiser than well. Ah, Matthew, Matthew! You know your way, sir?"

Well enough, for I had gone up the staircase in the dark many a time. I climbed it now in lighter boots than before and tapped in my old way at the door of Miss Havisham's room. "Pip's knock," I heard her say immediately. "Come in, Pip."

She was in her chair near the old table, in the old dress, with her two hands crossed on her stick, her chin resting on them, and her eyes on the fire. Sitting near her, with the white shoe that had never been worn in her hand, her head bent as she looked at it, was an elegant lady I had never seen.
"Come in, Pip," Miss Havisham continued to mutter, without looking round or up. "Come in, Pip, how do you do, Pip? So you kiss my hand as if I were a queen, eh? — Well?"
She looked up at me suddenly, only moving her eyes, and repeated in a grimly playful manner —
"Well?"
"I heard, Miss Havisham," I said, rather at a loss, "that you were so kind as to wish me to come and see you, and I came directly."
"Well?"

The lady I had never seen before lifted her eyes and looked archly at me, and then I saw that the eyes were Estella's eyes. But she was so much changed, so much more beautiful, so much more womanly, so winning in every way, had made such wonderful progress, that I seemed to have made none. As I looked at her, I felt I had slipped hopelessly back into the coarse and common boy again. Oh, the sense of distance and disparity that came upon me, and the inaccessibility that surrounded her!
She gave me her hand. I stammered something about the pleasure I felt in seeing her again, and about having looked forward to it for a long, long time.
"Do you find her much changed, Pip?" asked Miss Havisham, with her greedy look, striking her stick on a chair between them as a sign for me to sit down.
"When I came in, Miss Havisham, I thought there was nothing of Estella in the face or figure. But now it all settles down so curiously into the old —"
"What? You are not going to say into the old Estella?" Miss Havisham interrupted. "She was proud and insulting, and you wanted to go away from her. Don't you remember?"

I said confusedly that that was long ago, and that I knew no better then, and so on. Estella smiled with perfect composure and said she had no doubt I had been quite right, and that she had been very disagreeable.
"Is he changed?" Miss Havisham asked her.
"Very much," said Estella, looking at me.
"Less coarse and common?" said Miss Havisham, playing with Estella's hair.
Estella laughed, looked at the shoe in her hand, laughed again, looked at me, and put the shoe down. She treated me as a boy still, but she lured me on.

We sat in the dreamy room among the old strange influences that had so worked upon me. I learned that she had just come home from France and was going to London. Proud and willful as ever, she had brought those qualities into such subjection to her beauty that it was impossible — or I thought so — to separate them from it. Truly, it was impossible to disconnect her presence from all those wretched longings for money and gentility that had disturbed my boyhood. From all those misguided aspirations that had first made me ashamed of home and Joe. From all those visions that had raised her face in the glowing fire, struck it out of the iron on the anvil, summoned it from the darkness of night to look in at the forge window and flit away. In a word, it was impossible for me to separate her, in the past or the present, from the innermost life of my life.

It was settled that I should stay there all the rest of the day, return to the hotel at night, and go to London tomorrow. When we had conversed for a while, Miss Havisham sent us two out to walk in the neglected garden. When we came back in, she said, I should wheel her about a little, as in the old days.

So Estella and I went out into the garden by the gate through which I had strayed to my encounter with the pale young gentleman, now Herbert. I trembled in spirit and worshipped the very hem of her dress. She was quite composed and most decidedly not worshipping the hem of mine. As we drew near the place of our encounter, she stopped and said —
"I must have been a strange little creature to hide and watch that fight that day. But I did, and I enjoyed it very much."
"You rewarded me very generously."
"Did I?" she replied in an offhand and forgetful way. "I remember I had a great objection to your opponent, because I resented him being brought here to pester me with his company."
"He and I are great friends now."
"Are you? I think I remember, though, that you study with his father?"
"Yes."
I made the admission reluctantly, for it seemed boyish, and she already treated me more than enough like a boy.
"Since your change of fortune and prospects, you have changed your companions," said Estella.
"Naturally," I said.
"And necessarily," she added in a haughty tone. "What was fit company for you once would be quite unfit company for you now."
In my conscience, I very much doubt whether I had any lingering intention left of going to see Joe. But if I had, this remark put it to flight.
"You had no idea of your coming good fortune in those times?" said Estella, with a slight wave of her hand meaning the fighting times.
"Not the least."

The air of completeness and superiority with which she walked at my side, and the air of youthfulness and submission with which I walked at hers, made a contrast I strongly felt. It would have stung me more if I had not regarded myself as singled out for her and assigned to her.

The garden was too overgrown and wild for comfortable walking, and after we had gone round it twice or three times, we came out again into the brewery yard. I showed her exactly where I had seen her walking on the casks that first old day. She said with a cold, careless look in that direction, "Did I?" I reminded her where she had come out of the house and given me my food and drink. She said, "I don't remember." "Not remember that you made me cry?" I said. "No," she said, and shook her head and looked about her. I truly believe that her not remembering and not caring in the least made me cry again, inwardly — and that is the sharpest crying of all.
"You must know," said Estella, condescending to me as a brilliant and beautiful woman might, "that I have no heart — if that has anything to do with my memory."
I got through some clumsy words to the effect that I doubted that. That I knew better. That there could be no such beauty without a heart.

"Oh! I have a heart to be stabbed in or shot in, I have no doubt," said Estella, "and of course if it ceased to beat I would cease to be. But you know what I mean. I have no softness there, no — sympathy — sentiment — nonsense."

What was it that impressed itself on my mind when she stood still and looked attentively at me? Anything I had seen in Miss Havisham? No. In some of her looks and gestures there was that hint of resemblance to Miss Havisham which may often be noticed in children who have been much with a certain grown person, and which, when childhood has passed, produces a remarkable occasional likeness of expression between otherwise quite different faces. And yet I could not trace this to Miss Havisham. I looked again, and though she was still looking at me, the suggestion was gone.
What was it?

"I am serious," said Estella, not so much with a frown — for her brow was smooth — as with a darkening of her face. "If we are to be thrown much together, you had better believe it at once. No!" she said imperiously, stopping me as I opened my lips. "I have not bestowed my tenderness anywhere. I have never had any such thing."

In another moment we were in the brewery, so long abandoned. She pointed to the high gallery where I had seen her going out on that same first day, and told me she remembered being up there and seeing me standing scared below. As my eyes followed her white hand, again the same dim suggestion I could not grasp crossed my mind. My involuntary start made her lay her hand on my arm. Instantly the ghost passed once more and was gone.
What was it?
"What is the matter?" asked Estella. "Are you scared again?"
"I should be, if I believed what you said just now," I replied, to turn it off.

"Then you don't? Very well. It is said, at any rate. Miss Havisham will soon be expecting you at your old post, though I think that might be set aside now, along with other old things. Let us make one more round of the garden and then go in. Come! You shall not shed tears for my cruelty today. You shall be my page, and give me your shoulder."

Her handsome dress had trailed on the ground. She held it in one hand now, and with the other lightly touched my shoulder as we walked. We went round the ruined garden twice or three times more, and it was all in bloom for me. If the green and yellow growth of weeds in the cracks of the old wall had been the most precious flowers that ever bloomed, it could not have been more cherished in my memory.

There was no gap of years between us to remove her far from me. We were of nearly the same age, though of course the age counted for more in her case than in mine. But the air of inaccessibility that her beauty and her manner gave her tormented me in the midst of my delight, and at the height of my certainty that our patroness had chosen us for one another. Wretched boy!

At last we went back into the house. There I heard, with surprise, that my guardian had come down to see Miss Havisham on business and would stay for dinner. The old wintry branches of chandeliers in the room where the moldering table was spread had been lit while we were out, and Miss Havisham was in her chair, waiting for me.

It was like pushing the chair itself back into the past when we began the old slow circuit around the ashes of the bridal feast. But in the funeral room, with that figure of the grave fallen back in the chair fixing its eyes upon her, Estella looked more bright and beautiful than before, and I was under stronger enchantment.

The time melted away so quickly that our early dinner hour drew near. Estella left us to prepare herself. We had stopped near the center of the long table, and Miss Havisham, with one of her withered arms stretched out of the chair, rested that clenched hand on the yellow cloth. As Estella looked back over her shoulder before going out at the door, Miss Havisham kissed that hand to her with a ravenous intensity that was, in its way, quite dreadful.
Then, Estella being gone and we two left alone, she turned to me and said in a whisper —
"Is she beautiful, graceful, well-grown? Do you admire her?"
"Everybody must who sees her, Miss Havisham."
She drew an arm round my neck and pulled my head close down to hers as she sat in the chair. "Love her, love her, love her! How does she treat you?"

Before I could answer — if I could have answered so difficult a question at all — she repeated, "Love her, love her, love her! If she favors you, love her. If she wounds you, love her. If she tears your heart to pieces — and as it gets older and stronger it will tear deeper — love her, love her, love her!"
Never had I seen such passionate eagerness as was joined to her speaking of these words. I could feel the muscles of the thin arm round my neck swell with the vehemence that possessed her.
"Hear me, Pip! I adopted her to be loved. I bred her and educated her to be loved. I developed her into what she is, that she might be loved. Love her!"

She said the word often enough, and there could be no doubt she meant to say it. But if the often-repeated word had been hate instead of love — despair — revenge — dire death — it could not have sounded from her lips more like a curse.

"I'll tell you," she said in the same hurried, passionate whisper, "what real love is. It is blind devotion, unquestioning self-humiliation, utter submission, trust and belief against yourself and against the whole world, giving up your whole heart and soul to the one who strikes you — as I did!"

When she came to that, and to the wild cry that followed, I caught her round the waist. For she rose up in the chair in her shroud of a dress and struck at the air as if she would as soon have struck herself against the wall and fallen dead.
All this passed in a few seconds. As I drew her down into her chair, I was conscious of a scent I knew, and turning, saw my guardian in the room.

He always carried — I have not yet mentioned it, I think — a silk pocket handkerchief of imposing proportions, which was of great value to him in his profession. I have seen him so terrify a client or a witness by ceremoniously unfolding this handkerchief as if he were about to blow his nose, and then pausing as if he knew he shouldn't have time to do it before the client or witness committed himself, that the self-incrimination followed directly, as a matter of course. When I saw him in the room, he had this expressive handkerchief in both hands and was looking at us. On meeting my eye, he said plainly, by a momentary silent pause in that attitude, "Indeed? Singular!" and then put the handkerchief to its proper use with wonderful effect.
Miss Havisham had seen him as soon as I had, and was — like everybody else — afraid of him. She made a strong attempt to compose herself and stammered that he was as punctual as ever.
"As punctual as ever," he repeated, coming up to us. "How do you do, Pip? Shall I give you a ride, Miss Havisham? Once round? And so you are here, Pip?"

I told him when I had arrived and how Miss Havisham had wished me to come and see Estella. To which he replied, "Ah! Very fine young lady!" Then he pushed Miss Havisham in her chair before him with one of his large hands, and put the other in his trouser pocket as if it were full of secrets.
"Well, Pip! How often have you seen Miss Estella before?" he said when he came to a stop.
"How often?"
"Ah! How many times? Ten thousand times?"
"Oh! Certainly not so many."
"Twice?"
"Jaggers," interposed Miss Havisham, much to my relief, "leave my Pip alone and go with him to your dinner."

He obeyed, and we groped our way down the dark stairs together. While we were still making our way to those separate rooms across the paved yard at the back, he asked me how often I had seen Miss Havisham eat and drink, offering me his usual range of choices between a hundred times and once.
I considered and said, "Never."

"And never will, Pip," he retorted with a frowning smile. "She has never allowed herself to be seen doing either since she began living this present life of hers. She wanders about at night and then lays hands on whatever food she takes."
"Pray, sir," I said, "may I ask you a question?"
"You may," he said, "and I may decline to answer it. Ask your question."
"Estella's name. Is it Havisham or —?" I had nothing to add.
"Or what?" he said.
"Is it Havisham?"
"It is Havisham."

This brought us to the dinner table, where she and Sarah Pocket awaited us. Mr. Jaggers presided. Estella sat opposite him. I faced my green and yellow friend. We dined very well and were waited on by a maidservant I had never seen in all my comings and goings, but who, for all I knew, had been in that mysterious house the whole time. After dinner, a bottle of fine old port was placed before my guardian — he was evidently well acquainted with the vintage — and the two ladies left us.

I never saw anything to equal the determined reticence of Mr. Jaggers under that roof, even from him. He kept his very looks to himself and scarcely directed his eyes to Estella's face once during dinner. When she spoke to him, he listened and in due course answered, but never looked at her, as far as I could see. She, on the other hand, often looked at him with interest and curiosity, if not distrust. But his face never showed the least awareness. Throughout dinner, he took a dry delight in making Sarah Pocket greener and yellower by often referring in conversation with me to my expectations. But here again he showed no consciousness, and even made it appear that he extracted — and even did extract, though I don't know how — those references from my innocent self.

And when he and I were left alone together, he sat with an air of generally holding back because of information he possessed, which really was too much for me. He cross-examined his very wine when he had nothing else at hand. He held it between himself and the candle, tasted the port, rolled it in his mouth, swallowed it, looked at his glass again, smelled the port, tried it, drank it, filled again, and cross-examined the glass again, until I was as nervous as if I'd known the wine to be telling him something to my disadvantage. Three or four times I feebly thought I would start a conversation. But whenever he saw me about to ask him something, he looked at me with his glass in his hand, rolling his wine about in his mouth, as if requesting me to take notice that it was no use, because he couldn't answer.

I think Miss Pocket was aware that the sight of me put her in danger of being goaded to madness, and perhaps tearing off her cap — which was a very hideous one, a sort of muslin mop — and strewing the ground with her hair, which surely had never grown on her head. She did not appear when we afterwards went up to Miss Havisham's room, and we four played at whist. In the interval, Miss Havisham, in a fantastical way, had put some of the most beautiful jewels from her dressing table into Estella's hair and about her bosom and arms. I saw even my guardian look at her from under his thick eyebrows and raise them a little when her loveliness was before him, with those rich flashes of glitter and color in it.

Of the way he took our trump cards into custody, and came out with mean little cards at the ends of hands before which the glory of our kings and queens was utterly humbled, I say nothing. Nor of the feeling I had that he regarded us personally as three very obvious and poor riddles he had solved long ago. What I suffered from was the incompatibility between his cold presence and my feelings toward Estella. It was not that I knew I could never bear to speak to him about her, that I knew I could never bear to hear him creak his boots at her, that I knew I could never bear to see him wash his hands of her. It was that my adoration should be within a foot or two of him — that my feelings should be in the same place with him — that was the agonizing thing.

We played until nine o'clock. Then it was arranged that when Estella came to London, I should be warned of her coming and should meet her at the coach. I took leave of her, touched her hand, and left her.

My guardian stayed at the Boar in the next room to mine. Far into the night, Miss Havisham's words — "Love her, love her, love her!" — sounded in my ears. I adapted them for my own use and said to my pillow, "I love her, I love her, I love her!" hundreds of times. Then a burst of gratitude came over me that she should be destined for me, once the blacksmith's boy. Then I thought: if she were, as I feared, by no means rapturously grateful for that destiny yet, when would she begin to take an interest in me? When would I awaken the heart within her that was mute and sleeping now?

Ah me! I thought those were high and great emotions. But I never thought there was anything low and small in my keeping away from Joe, because I knew she would be contemptuous of him. It was but a day gone, and Joe had brought tears to my eyes. They had soon dried — God forgive me! — soon dried.

chapters.title: Chapter 30
paragraphs: After careful consideration while dressing at the Blue Boar that morning, I resolved to tell my guardian that I doubted Orlick was the right sort of man for a position of trust at Miss Havisham's. "Why of course he's not the right sort of man, Pip," said my guardian, comfortably satisfied on the general point, "because the man who fills a post of trust never is the right sort of man." It seemed to cheer him up to find that this particular post was not exceptionally held by the right sort of man. He listened in a satisfied manner while I told him what I knew of Orlick.
