"Very good, Pip," he observed when I had finished. "I'll go round presently and pay our friend off." Rather alarmed by this swift action, I was for a little delay and even hinted that our friend himself might be difficult to deal with. "Oh no he won't," said my guardian, making his pocket-handkerchief point with perfect confidence. "I should like to see him argue the question with me."

Since we were going back together to London by the midday coach, and since I breakfasted under such terror of Pumblechook that I could scarcely hold my cup, this gave me an opportunity to say I wanted a walk. I would go on along the London road while Mr. Jaggers was occupied, if he would let the coachman know that I would get into my seat when overtaken. This allowed me to flee from the Blue Boar immediately after breakfast. By then making a loop of about two miles into the open country behind Pumblechook's premises, I got back to the High Street a little beyond that trap and felt myself in comparative safety.

It was interesting to be in the quiet old town once more, and it was not disagreeable to be here and there suddenly recognized and stared at. One or two shopkeepers even darted out of their shops and walked a little way down the street ahead of me, so they might turn around as if they'd forgotten something and pass me face to face. On those occasions, I don't know whether they or I made the worse pretense — they of not doing it, or I of not seeing it. Still, my position was a distinguished one, and I was not at all dissatisfied with it, until Fate threw me in the way of that unlimited scoundrel, Trabb's boy.

Casting my eyes along the street at a certain point in my progress, I saw Trabb's boy approaching, lashing himself with an empty blue bag. Deciding that a serene and unconscious contemplation of him would suit me best and be most likely to quell his evil mind, I advanced with that expression and was rather congratulating myself on my success when suddenly Trabb's boy's knees smacked together, his hair stood on end, his cap fell off, he trembled violently in every limb, staggered out into the road, and crying to the passersby, "Hold me! I'm so frightened!" pretended to be in a fit of terror and contrition, occasioned by the dignity of my appearance. As I passed him, his teeth loudly chattered in his head, and with every mark of extreme humiliation, he prostrated himself in the dust.

This was a hard thing to bear, but it was nothing. I had not gone another two hundred yards when, to my inexpressible terror, amazement, and indignation, I again saw Trabb's boy approaching. He was coming round a narrow corner. His blue bag was slung over his shoulder. Honest industry beamed in his eyes. A determination to proceed to Trabb's with cheerful briskness was clear in his walk. With a shock he became aware of me and was severely afflicted as before. But this time his motion was rotary. He staggered round and round me with knees even more afflicted, and with uplifted hands as if begging for mercy. His sufferings were hailed with the greatest joy by a group of spectators, and I felt utterly confounded.

I had not got much further down the street than the post office when I again saw Trabb's boy shooting round by a back way. This time he was entirely changed. He wore the blue bag in the manner of my greatcoat and was strutting along the pavement toward me on the opposite side of the street, attended by a company of delighted young friends to whom he exclaimed from time to time, with a wave of his hand, "Don't know yah!" Words cannot express the aggravation and injury inflicted on me by Trabb's boy when, passing alongside me, he pulled up his shirt collar, twirled his side hair, stuck an arm on his hip, and smirked extravagantly by, wriggling his elbows and body and drawling to his attendants, "Don't know yah, don't know yah, 'pon my soul don't know yah!" The disgrace of his immediately afterwards taking to crowing and pursuing me across the bridge with crows, as from an exceedingly dejected fowl who had known me when I was a blacksmith, completed the disgrace with which I left the town and was, so to speak, ejected by it into the open country.

But unless I had taken the life of Trabb's boy on that occasion, I really do not even now see what I could have done but endure. To have struggled with him in the street, or to have demanded any lesser payment than his heart's best blood, would have been futile and degrading. Moreover, he was a boy whom no man could catch — an invulnerable and dodging serpent who, when chased into a corner, flew out again between his captor's legs, scornfully yelping. I wrote, however, to Mr. Trabb by next day's post, to say that Mr. Pip must decline to deal further with one who could so far forget what he owed to the best interests of society as to employ a boy who excited loathing in every respectable mind.

The coach, with Mr. Jaggers inside, came up on time, and I took my seat again and arrived in London safe — but not sound, for my heart was gone. As soon as I arrived, I sent a penitential codfish and barrel of oysters to Joe as reparation for not having gone myself, and then went on to Barnard's Inn.

I found Herbert dining on cold meat and delighted to welcome me back. Having sent the Avenger to the coffee house for an addition to the dinner, I felt I must open my heart that very evening to my friend and companion. Since confidential conversation was out of the question with the Avenger in the hall, which could only be regarded as an antechamber to the keyhole, I sent him to the theater. A better proof of my bondage to that taskmaster could scarcely be found than the degrading lengths to which I was constantly driven to find him employment. So low is desperation that I sometimes sent him to Hyde Park Corner to see what time it was.
Dinner done and our feet on the fender, I said to Herbert, "My dear Herbert, I have something very particular to tell you."
"My dear Handel," he returned, "I shall value and respect your confidence."
"It concerns myself, Herbert," I said, "and one other person."
Herbert crossed his feet, looked at the fire with his head on one side, and having looked at it in vain for some time, looked at me because I didn't go on.
"Herbert," I said, laying my hand on his knee, "I love — I adore — Estella."
Instead of being transfixed, Herbert replied in an easy, matter-of-fact way, "Exactly. Well?"
"Well, Herbert? Is that all you say? Well?"
"What next, I mean?" said Herbert. "Of course I know that."
"How do you know it?" I said.
"How do I know it, Handel? Why, from you."
"I never told you."

"Told me! You have never told me when you've had your hair cut, but I've had senses to notice it. You have always adored her, ever since I have known you. You brought your adoration and your portmanteau here together. Told me! Why, you have always told me all day long. When you told me your own story, you told me plainly that you began adoring her the first time you saw her, when you were very young indeed."

"Very well, then," I said, to whom this was a new and not unwelcome light. "I have never left off adoring her. And she has come back, a most beautiful and most elegant creature. And I saw her yesterday. And if I adored her before, I now doubly adore her."

"Lucky for you then, Handel," said Herbert, "that you are picked out for her and assigned to her. Without trespassing on forbidden ground, we may venture to say there can be no doubt between ourselves of that fact. Have you any idea yet of Estella's views on the adoration question?"
I shook my head gloomily. "Oh! She is thousands of miles away from me," I said.
"Patience, my dear Handel. Time enough, time enough. But you have something more to say?"

"I am ashamed to say it," I returned, "and yet it's no worse to say it than to think it. You call me a lucky fellow. Of course I am. I was a blacksmith's boy but yesterday. I am — what shall I say I am — today?"

"Say a good fellow, if you want a phrase," returned Herbert, smiling and clapping his hand on the back of mine. "A good fellow, with impetuosity and hesitation, boldness and diffidence, action and dreaming, curiously mixed in him."
I stopped for a moment to consider whether this mixture really was in my character. On the whole, I by no means recognized the analysis, but thought it not worth disputing.

"When I ask what I am to call myself today, Herbert," I went on, "I suggest what I have in my thoughts. You say I am lucky. I know I have done nothing to raise myself in life, and that fortune alone has raised me. That is being very lucky. And yet, when I think of Estella —"
"And when don't you, you know?" Herbert threw in, with his eyes on the fire, which I thought kind and sympathetic of him.

"— Then, my dear Herbert, I cannot tell you how dependent and uncertain I feel, and how exposed to hundreds of chances. Avoiding forbidden ground, as you did just now, I may still say that on the constancy of one person — naming no person — all my expectations depend. And at best, how vague and unsatisfying, only to know so indefinitely what they are!" In saying this, I relieved my mind of what had always been there, more or less, though no doubt especially since yesterday.

"Now, Handel," Herbert replied in his cheerful, hopeful way, "it seems to me that in the despondency of the tender passion, we are looking into our gift horse's mouth with a magnifying glass. Likewise, it seems to me that, concentrating our attention on the examination, we are altogether overlooking one of the best points of the animal. Didn't you tell me that your guardian, Mr. Jaggers, told you at the beginning that you were not endowed with expectations only? And even if he had not told you so — though that is a very large if, I grant — could you believe that of all men in London, Mr. Jaggers is the man to hold his present relations toward you unless he were sure of his ground?"
I said I could not deny that this was a strong point. I said it — as people often do in such cases — like a rather reluctant concession to truth and justice, as if I wanted to deny it!

"I should think it was a strong point," said Herbert, "and I should think you'd be hard pressed to imagine a stronger. As for the rest, you must wait for your guardian's time, and he must wait for his client's time. You'll be twenty-one before you know it, and then perhaps you'll get some further enlightenment. At any rate, you'll be nearer to getting it, for it must come at last."
"What a hopeful disposition you have!" I said, gratefully admiring his cheery ways.

"I ought to have," said Herbert, "for I don't have much else. I must acknowledge, by the way, that the good sense of what I've just said is not my own but my father's. The only remark I ever heard him make on your story was his final one: 'The thing is settled and done, or Mr. Jaggers would not be in it.' And now, before I say anything more about my father or my father's son, and repay confidence with confidence, I want to make myself seriously disagreeable to you for a moment — positively repulsive."
"You won't succeed," I said.

"Oh yes I shall!" he said. "One, two, three, and now I'm in for it. Handel, my good fellow" — though he spoke in this light tone, he was very much in earnest — "I have been thinking since we've been talking with our feet on this fender, that Estella surely cannot be a condition of your inheritance, if she was never referred to by your guardian. Am I right in understanding from what you've told me that he never referred to her, directly or indirectly, in any way? Never even hinted, for instance, that your patron might have plans regarding your marriage eventually?"
"Never."
"Now, Handel, I am quite free from sour grapes, upon my soul and honor! Not being bound to her, can you not detach yourself from her? — I told you I should be disagreeable."

I turned my head aside, for with a rush and a sweep, like the old marsh winds coming up from the sea, a feeling like the one that had overcome me on the morning when I left the forge, when the mists were solemnly rising and I laid my hand upon the village signpost, struck my heart again. There was silence between us for a little while.

"Yes. But my dear Handel," Herbert went on, as if we had been talking instead of silent, "its having been so strongly rooted in the heart of a boy whom nature and circumstances made so romantic makes it very serious. Think of her upbringing, and think of Miss Havisham. Think of what she is herself — now I am repulsive and you hate me. This may lead to miserable things."
"I know it, Herbert," I said, with my head still turned away. "But I can't help it."
"You can't detach yourself?"
"No. Impossible!"
"You can't try, Handel?"
"No. Impossible!"
"Well!" said Herbert, getting up with a lively shake as if he had been asleep and stirring the fire. "Now I'll try to make myself agreeable again!"

So he went round the room, shook the curtains out, put the chairs in their places, tidied the books and other things lying about, looked into the hall, peeped into the letter box, shut the door, and came back to his chair by the fire, where he sat down nursing his left leg in both arms.

"I was going to say a word or two, Handel, concerning my father and my father's son. I am afraid it is scarcely necessary for my father's son to remark that my father's establishment is not particularly brilliant in its housekeeping."
"There is always plenty, Herbert," I said, trying to say something encouraging.

"Oh yes! And so the dustman says, I believe, with the strongest approval, and so does the secondhand shop in the back street. But seriously, Handel, for the subject is serious enough, you know how it is as well as I do. I suppose there was a time once when my father had not given matters up. But if there ever was, the time is gone. May I ask you if you have ever had an opportunity of noticing, down in your part of the country, that the children of not exactly suitable marriages are always most particularly anxious to be married?"
This was such a peculiar question that I asked him in return, "Is it so?"

"I don't know," said Herbert. "That's what I want to know. Because it is decidedly the case with us. My poor sister Charlotte, who was next to me and died before she was fourteen, was a striking example. Little Jane is the same. In her desire to be married, you might suppose she had passed her short existence in the perpetual contemplation of domestic bliss. Little Alick in a frock has already made arrangements for his union with a suitable young person at Kew. And indeed, I think we are all engaged, except the baby."
"Then you are?" I said.
"I am," said Herbert. "But it's a secret."
I assured him I would keep the secret and asked for further details. He had spoken so sensibly and feelingly of my weakness that I wanted to know something about his strength.
"May I ask the name?" I said.
"Name of Clara," said Herbert.
"Lives in London?"

"Yes. Perhaps I ought to mention," said Herbert, who had become curiously crestfallen and meek since we entered on this interesting subject, "that she is rather below my mother's nonsensical family notions. Her father had to do with the provisioning of passenger ships. I think he was a species of purser."
"What is he now?" I said.
"He's an invalid now," replied Herbert.
"Living on —?"

"On the first floor," said Herbert. Which was not at all what I meant, for I had intended my question to apply to his income. "I have never seen him, for he has always kept his room upstairs since I have known Clara. But I have heard him constantly. He makes tremendous rows — roars and bangs at the floor with some frightful instrument." In looking at me and then laughing heartily, Herbert for the time recovered his usual lively manner.
"Don't you expect to see him?" I said.
"Oh yes, I constantly expect to see him," returned Herbert, "because I never hear him without expecting him to come tumbling through the ceiling. But I don't know how long the rafters may hold."

When he had once more laughed heartily, he became meek again and told me that the moment he began to accumulate capital, it was his intention to marry this young lady. He added, as a self-evident proposition that produced low spirits, "But you can't marry, you know, while you're looking about you."

As we contemplated the fire, and as I thought what a difficult vision to realize this same capital sometimes was, I put my hands in my pockets. A folded piece of paper in one of them caught my attention. I opened it and found it to be the playbill I had received from Joe, about the celebrated provincial amateur of Roscian renown. "And bless my heart," I involuntarily added aloud, "it's tonight!"

This changed the subject instantly and made us hurriedly resolve to go to the play. So when I had pledged myself to comfort and support Herbert in the affair of his heart by all practicable and impracticable means, and when Herbert had told me that his fiancee already knew me by reputation and that I should be introduced to her, and when we had warmly shaken hands on our mutual confidence, we blew out our candles, made up our fire, locked our door, and set forth in quest of Mr. Wopsle and Denmark.

chapters.title: Chapter 31
paragraphs: On our arrival in Denmark, we found the king and queen of that country elevated in two armchairs on a kitchen table, holding court. The whole of the Danish nobility was in attendance, consisting of a noble boy in the wash-leather boots of a gigantic ancestor, a venerable peer with a dirty face who seemed to have risen from the people late in life, and the Danish chivalry with a comb in its hair and a pair of white silk legs, presenting on the whole a feminine appearance. My gifted townsman stood gloomily apart with folded arms, and I could have wished that his curls and forehead had been more convincing.

Several curious little details emerged as the action proceeded. The late king of the country not only appeared to have been troubled with a cough at the time of his death but to have taken it with him to the tomb and brought it back. The royal phantom also carried a ghostly manuscript round its staff, to which it had the appearance of occasionally referring, with an air of anxiety and a tendency to lose its place that suggested mortality. This, I believe, led to the ghost's being advised by the gallery to "turn over!" — a recommendation it took extremely badly. It was likewise worth noting that whereas this majestic spirit always appeared with an air of having been out a long time and walked an immense distance, it perceptibly came from a closely neighboring wall. This caused its terrors to be received with derision. The Queen of Denmark, a very buxom lady, though no doubt historically brazen, was considered by the public to have too much brass about her. Her chin was attached to her diadem by a broad band of that metal, as if she had a gorgeous toothache. Her waist was encircled by another band, and each of her arms by another, so that she was openly referred to as "the kettledrum." The noble boy in the ancestral boots was inconsistent, representing himself — as it were in one breath — as an able seaman, a strolling actor, a gravedigger, a clergyman, and a person of the utmost importance at a court fencing match, on the authority of whose practiced eye the finest strokes were judged. This gradually led to a lack of tolerance for him, and even — on his being detected in holy orders and declining to perform the funeral service — to the general indignation taking the form of nuts. Lastly, Ophelia was prey to such slow musical madness that when, in the course of time, she had taken off her white muslin scarf, folded it up, and buried it, a sulky man who had been long cooling his impatient nose against an iron bar in the front row of the gallery growled, "Now the baby's put to bed, let's have supper!" Which, to say the least, was out of keeping.

Upon my unfortunate townsman all these incidents accumulated with playful effect. Whenever that undecided prince had to ask a question or state a doubt, the public helped him out with it. For example, on the question whether it was nobler in the mind to suffer, some roared yes and some no, and some, inclined to both opinions, said "Toss up for it" — and quite a debating society arose. When he asked what such fellows as he should do crawling between earth and heaven, he was encouraged with loud cries of "Hear, hear!" When he appeared with his stocking disordered — its disorder expressed, according to custom, by one very neat fold in the top, which I suppose was always pressed with a flat iron — a conversation took place in the gallery about the paleness of his leg and whether it was caused by the turn the ghost had given him. On his taking the recorders — very like a little black flute that had just been played in the orchestra and handed out at the door — he was called upon unanimously for Rule Britannia. When he recommended the player not to saw the air, the sulky man said, "And don't you do it, neither. You're a deal worse than him!" And I grieve to add that peals of laughter greeted Mr. Wopsle on every one of these occasions.

But his greatest trials were in the churchyard, which had the appearance of a primeval forest, with a sort of small ecclesiastical wash house on one side and a turnpike gate on the other. Mr. Wopsle, in a comprehensive black cloak, being spotted entering at the turnpike, the gravedigger was warned in a friendly way, "Look out! Here's the undertaker coming to see how you're getting on with your work!" I believe it is well known in a constitutional country that Mr. Wopsle could not possibly have returned the skull, after philosophizing over it, without dusting his fingers on a white napkin taken from his breast. But even that innocent and necessary action did not pass without the comment, "Waiter!" The arrival of the body for burial — in an empty black box with the lid tumbling open — was the signal for general joy, which was much enhanced by the discovery, among the bearers, of someone particularly worth identifying. The joy attended Mr. Wopsle through his struggle with Laertes on the brink of the orchestra pit and the grave, and did not slacken until he had tumbled the king off the kitchen table and had died by inches from the ankles upward.

We had made some feeble efforts at the beginning to applaud Mr. Wopsle, but they were too hopeless to continue. So we had sat, feeling keenly for him, but laughing nonetheless from ear to ear. I laughed in spite of myself the whole time, the whole thing was so absurd. And yet I had a lingering impression that there was something decidedly fine in Mr. Wopsle's elocution — not for old associations' sake, I'm afraid, but because it was very slow, very dreary, very uphill and downhill, and very unlike any way in which any man in any natural circumstances of life or death ever expressed himself about anything. When the tragedy was over and he had been called for and booed, I said to Herbert, "Let us go at once, or perhaps we shall meet him."

We hurried downstairs as fast as we could, but we were not quick enough. Standing at the door was a Jewish man with an unnaturally heavy smear of eyebrow, who caught my eye as we approached and said when we reached him —
"Mr. Pip and friend?"
Identity of Mr. Pip and friend confessed.
"Mr. Waldengarver," said the man, "would be glad to have the honor."
"Waldengarver?" I repeated — when Herbert murmured in my ear, "Probably Wopsle."
"Oh!" I said. "Yes. Shall we follow you?"
"A few steps, please." When we were in a side alley, he turned and asked, "How did you think he looked? — I dressed him."

I didn't know what he had looked like, except a funeral — with the addition of a large Danish sun or star hanging round his neck by a blue ribbon, giving him the appearance of being insured in some extraordinary fire office. But I said he had looked very nice.

"When he come to the grave," said our guide, "he showed his cloak beautiful. But judging from the wing, it looked to me that when he see the ghost in the queen's apartment, he might have made more of his stockings."

I modestly agreed, and we all fell through a little dirty swing door into a sort of hot packing case immediately behind it. Here Mr. Wopsle was removing his Danish garments, and here there was just room for us to look at him over one another's shoulders by keeping the packing case door, or lid, wide open.

"Gentlemen," said Mr. Wopsle, "I am proud to see you. I hope, Mr. Pip, you will excuse my sending round. I had the happiness to know you in former times, and the drama has ever had a claim — which has ever been acknowledged — on the noble and the affluent."
Meanwhile, Mr. Waldengarver, in a frightful perspiration, was trying to get himself out of his princely sables.

"Skin the stockings off Mr. Waldengarver," said the owner of that property, "or you'll bust 'em. Bust 'em, and you'll bust five and thirty shillings. Shakespeare never was complimented with a finer pair. Keep quiet in your chair now and leave 'em to me."
With that, he went upon his knees and began to flay his victim, who, on the first stocking coming off, would certainly have fallen over backward with his chair, had there been any room to fall.
I had been afraid until then to say a word about the play. But then Mr. Waldengarver looked up at us with satisfaction and said —
"Gentlemen, how did it seem to you, to go, out front?"
Herbert said from behind, at the same time poking me, "Capitally." So I said, "Capitally."
"How did you like my reading of the character, gentlemen?" said Mr. Waldengarver, almost, if not quite, with condescension.
Herbert said from behind, again poking me, "Massive and concrete." So I said boldly, as if I had invented it and must insist upon it, "Massive and concrete."
"I am glad to have your approval, gentlemen," said Mr. Waldengarver with an air of dignity, despite being pressed against the wall at the time and holding on by the seat of the chair.

"But I'll tell you one thing, Mr. Waldengarver," said the man on his knees, "in which you're out in your reading. Now mind! I don't care who says otherwise. I tell you so. You're out in your reading of Hamlet when you get your legs in profile. The last Hamlet I dressed made the same mistakes in his reading at rehearsal, till I got him to put a large red wafer on each of his shins, and then at that rehearsal — which was the last — I went out front, sir, to the back of the pit, and whenever his reading brought him into profile, I called out 'I don't see no wafers!' And at night his reading was lovely."

Mr. Waldengarver smiled at me, as much as to say "a faithful dependent — I overlook his foolishness," and then said aloud, "My approach is a little classical and thoughtful for them here, but they will improve. They will improve."
Herbert and I said together, "Oh, no doubt they would improve."
"Did you observe, gentlemen," said Mr. Waldengarver, "that there was a man in the gallery who tried to cast scorn on the service — I mean the performance?"
We basely replied that we rather thought we had noticed such a man. I added, "He was drunk, no doubt."
"Oh dear no, sir," said Mr. Wopsle. "Not drunk. His employer would see to that, sir. His employer would not allow him to be drunk."
"You know his employer?" I said.

Mr. Wopsle shut his eyes and opened them again, performing both ceremonies very slowly. "You must have observed, gentlemen," he said, "an ignorant and blatant ass, with a rasping throat and a face expressing low malice, who went through — I will not say sustained — the role (if I may use a French expression) of Claudius, King of Denmark. That is his employer, gentlemen. Such is the profession!"

Without clearly knowing whether I should have been sorrier for Mr. Wopsle if he had been in despair, I was so sorry for him as it was that I took the opportunity of his turning round to have his braces put on — which jostled us out at the doorway — to ask Herbert what he thought of having him home to supper. Herbert said he thought it would be kind to do so. Therefore I invited him, and he went to Barnard's with us, wrapped up to the eyes. We did our best for him, and he sat until two o'clock in the morning, reviewing his success and developing his plans. I forget the details, but I have a general recollection that he was to begin by reviving the drama and end with crushing it, since his death would leave it utterly bereft and without a chance or hope.

Miserably I went to bed after all, and miserably thought of Estella, and miserably dreamed that my expectations were all canceled, and that I had to give my hand in marriage to Herbert's Clara, or play Hamlet to Miss Havisham's ghost, before twenty thousand people, without knowing twenty words of it.

chapters.title: Chapter 32
paragraphs: One day when I was busy with my books and Mr. Pocket, I received a note by the post, the mere outside of which threw me into a great flutter. For though I had never seen the handwriting it was addressed in, I guessed whose hand it was. It had no set beginning — no Dear Mr. Pip, or Dear Pip, or Dear Sir, or Dear Anything — but ran thus:

"I am to come to London the day after tomorrow by the midday coach. I believe it was settled you should meet me? At all events Miss Havisham has that impression, and I write in obedience to it. She sends you her regard.
"Yours, ESTELLA."

If there had been time, I should probably have ordered several suits of clothes for the occasion. But since there was not, I had to be content with what I had. My appetite vanished instantly, and I knew no peace or rest until the day arrived. Not that its arrival brought me either, for then I was worse than ever, and began haunting the coach office in Wood Street, Cheapside, before the coach had even left the Blue Boar in our town. Although I knew this perfectly well, I still felt as if it were not safe to let the coach office out of my sight for longer than five minutes at a time. In this condition of unreason, I had completed the first half hour of a four- or five-hour watch when Wemmick ran into me.
"Hello, Mr. Pip," he said. "How do you do? I should hardly have thought this was your area."
I explained that I was waiting to meet somebody coming up by coach, and I asked after the Castle and the Aged.

"Both flourishing, thank you," said Wemmick, "and particularly the Aged. He's in wonderful form. He'll be eighty-two next birthday. I have a notion of firing eighty-two times, if the neighborhood shouldn't complain and that cannon of mine proves equal to the pressure. However, this is not London talk. Where do you think I am going to?"
"To the office?" I said, for he was heading in that direction.

"Next thing to it," returned Wemmick. "I am going to Newgate. We are in a banker's-parcel case just at present, and I have been down the road taking a look at the scene of action. Now I must have a word or two with our client."
"Did your client commit the robbery?" I asked.
"Bless your soul and body, no," answered Wemmick very drily. "But he is accused of it. So might you or I be. Either of us might be accused of it, you know."
"Only neither of us is," I remarked.
"Yah!" said Wemmick, touching me on the chest with his forefinger. "You're a deep one, Mr. Pip! Would you like to have a look at Newgate? Have you time to spare?"

I had so much time to spare that the proposal came as a relief, despite its being at odds with my desire to keep my eye on the coach office. Muttering that I would check whether I had time to walk with him, I went into the office and ascertained from the clerk, with the nicest precision and much to the trying of his temper, the earliest moment at which the coach could be expected — which I knew beforehand quite as well as he. I then rejoined Mr. Wemmick and, pretending to consult my watch and be surprised by the information I had received, accepted his offer.

We were at Newgate in a few minutes and passed through the lodge, where some fetters hung on the bare walls among the prison rules, into the interior of the jail. At that time, jails were much neglected, and the period of exaggerated reaction that follows all public wrongdoing — and which is always its heaviest and longest punishment — was still far off. So felons were not housed and fed better than soldiers, to say nothing of paupers, and seldom set fire to their prisons with the excusable object of improving the flavor of their soup. It was visiting time when Wemmick took me in, and a potman was making his rounds with beer. The prisoners, behind bars in yards, were buying beer and talking to friends. A grimy, ugly, disorderly, depressing scene it was.

It struck me that Wemmick walked among the prisoners much as a gardener might walk among his plants. This was first put into my head by his noticing a new arrival and saying, "What, Captain Tom? Are you there? Ah, indeed!" and also, "Is that Black Bill behind the cistern? Why, I didn't look for you these two months. How do you find yourself?" Equally, in his stopping at the bars and attending to anxious whisperers — always one at a time — Wemmick, with his post office in an immovable state, looked at them as if he were taking particular notice of the progress they had made since last observed, toward coming out in full bloom at their trial.

He was highly popular, and I found that he handled the familiar side of Mr. Jaggers's business, though something of the authority of Mr. Jaggers hung about him too, forbidding approach beyond certain limits. His personal recognition of each successive client consisted of a nod, a settling of his hat a little easier on his head with both hands, then tightening the post office and putting his hands in his pockets. In one or two instances there was a difficulty about the raising of fees. Then Mr. Wemmick, backing as far as possible from the insufficient money produced, said, "It's no use, my boy. I'm only a subordinate. I can't take it. Don't go on in that way with a subordinate. If you are unable to make up your amount, my boy, you had better apply to a principal. There are plenty of principals in the profession, you know, and what is not worth the while of one may be worth the while of another. That's my recommendation to you, speaking as a subordinate. Don't try useless measures. Why should you? Now, who's next?"
So we walked through Wemmick's greenhouse, until he turned to me and said, "Notice the man I shall shake hands with." I would have done so without the warning, as he had shaken hands with no one yet.

Almost as soon as he had spoken, a portly upright man — whom I can see now as I write — in a well-worn olive-colored frock coat, with a peculiar paleness overlaying the redness of his complexion, and eyes that wandered about when he tried to fix them, came up to a corner of the bars and put his hand to his hat, which had a greasy and fatty surface like cold broth, with a half-serious and half-joking military salute.
"Colonel, to you!" said Wemmick. "How are you, Colonel?"
"All right, Mr. Wemmick."
"Everything was done that could be done, but the evidence was too strong for us, Colonel."
"Yes, it was too strong, sir — but I don't care."
"No, no," said Wemmick coolly. "You don't care." Then, turning to me, "Served His Majesty, this man. Was a soldier in the line and bought his discharge."
I said, "Indeed?" and the man's eyes looked at me, then over my head, then all round me, and then he drew his hand across his lips and laughed.
"I think I shall be out of this on Monday, sir," he said to Wemmick.
"Perhaps," returned my friend. "But there's no knowing."
"I am glad to have the chance of bidding you goodbye, Mr. Wemmick," said the man, stretching out his hand between two bars.
"Thank you," said Wemmick, shaking hands with him. "Same to you, Colonel."

"If what I had upon me when taken had been real, Mr. Wemmick," said the man, unwilling to let his hand go, "I should have asked the favor of your wearing another ring — in acknowledgment of your attentions."

"I'll accept the will for the deed," said Wemmick. "By the way, you were quite a pigeon fancier." The man looked up at the sky. "I am told you had a remarkable breed of tumblers. Could you commission any friend of yours to bring me a pair, if you've no further use for them?"
"It shall be done, sir."

"All right," said Wemmick. "They shall be taken care of. Good afternoon, Colonel. Goodbye!" They shook hands again, and as we walked away Wemmick said to me, "A counterfeiter. A very good workman. The Recorder's report is made today, and he is sure to be executed on Monday. Still, you see, as far as it goes, a pair of pigeons is portable property all the same." With that, he looked back and nodded at this dead plant, and then cast his eyes about as we walked out of the yard, as if he were considering what other pot would go best in its place.

As we came out of the prison through the lodge, I found that my guardian's great importance was appreciated by the turnkeys no less than by those they held in charge. "Well, Mr. Wemmick," said the turnkey who kept us between the two studded and spiked lodge gates, and who carefully locked one before unlocking the other, "what's Mr. Jaggers going to do with that waterside murder? Is he going to make it manslaughter, or what's he going to make of it?"
"Why don't you ask him?" returned Wemmick.
"Oh yes, I dare say!" said the turnkey.

"Now that's the way with them here, Mr. Pip," remarked Wemmick, turning to me with his post office stretched out. "They don't mind what they ask of me, the subordinate. But you'll never catch them asking any questions of my principal."
"Is this young gentleman one of the apprentices or articled clerks of your office?" asked the turnkey, with a grin at Mr. Wemmick's humor.
"There he goes again, you see!" cried Wemmick. "I told you so! Asks another question of the subordinate before his first is dry! Well, suppose Mr. Pip is one of them?"
"Why then," said the turnkey, grinning again, "he knows what Mr. Jaggers is."

"Yah!" cried Wemmick, suddenly taking a playful swing at the turnkey. "You're dumb as one of your own keys when you have to do with my principal, you know you are. Let us out, you old fox, or I'll get him to bring an action against you for false imprisonment."
The turnkey laughed, wished us good day, and stood laughing at us over the spikes of the wicket as we descended the steps into the street.

"Mind you, Mr. Pip," said Wemmick, gravely in my ear, as he took my arm to be more confidential, "I don't know that Mr. Jaggers does a better thing than the way he keeps himself so high. He's always so high. His constant height is of a piece with his immense abilities. That colonel dared no more take leave of him than that turnkey dared ask him his intentions regarding a case. Then, between his height and them, he slips in his subordinate — don't you see? — and so he has them, soul and body."

I was very much impressed, and not for the first time, by my guardian's subtlety. To confess the truth, I very heartily wished, and not for the first time, that I had had some other guardian of lesser abilities.

Mr. Wemmick and I parted at the office in Little Britain, where people hoping for Mr. Jaggers's notice were lingering about as usual. I returned to my watch in the street of the coach office with some three hours on hand. I spent the whole time thinking how strange it was that I should be surrounded by all this taint of prison and crime. That in my childhood out on our lonely marshes on a winter evening, I should have first encountered it. That it should have reappeared on two occasions, starting out like a stain that was faded but not gone. That it should in this new way pervade my fortune and advancement. While my mind was so occupied, I thought of the beautiful young Estella, proud and refined, coming toward me, and I thought with absolute horror of the contrast between the jail and her. I wished Wemmick had not met me, or that I had not yielded to him and gone with him, so that on this day of all days I might not have had Newgate in my breath and on my clothes. I beat the prison dust off my feet as I paced to and fro. I shook it out of my clothing. I exhaled its air from my lungs. So contaminated did I feel, remembering who was coming, that the coach came quickly after all, and I was not yet free from the soiling awareness of Mr. Wemmick's conservatory when I saw her face at the coach window and her hand waving to me.
What was the nameless shadow which again in that one instant had passed?

chapters.title: Chapter 33
paragraphs: In her fur traveling dress, Estella seemed more delicately beautiful than she had ever seemed yet, even to my eyes. Her manner was more welcoming than she had cared to let it be to me before, and I thought I saw Miss Havisham's influence in the change.

We stood in the inn yard while she pointed out her luggage to me. When it was all collected, I remembered — having forgotten everything but herself in the meanwhile — that I knew nothing of her destination.

"I am going to Richmond," she told me. "Our lesson is that there are two Richmonds, one in Surrey and one in Yorkshire, and that mine is the Surrey Richmond. The distance is ten miles. I am to have a carriage, and you are to take me. This is my purse, and you are to pay my charges out of it. Oh, you must take the purse! We have no choice, you and I, but to obey our instructions. We are not free to follow our own wishes, you and I."
As she looked at me while giving me the purse, I hoped there was a deeper meaning in her words. She said them lightly, but not with displeasure.
"A carriage will have to be sent for, Estella. Will you rest here a little?"
"Yes, I am to rest here a little, and I am to drink some tea, and you are to take care of me in the meantime."

She drew her arm through mine, as if it must be done, and I asked a waiter — who had been staring at the coach like a man who had never seen such a thing in his life — to show us a private sitting room. At this, he pulled out a napkin, as if it were a magic thread without which he couldn't find the way upstairs, and led us to the black hole of the establishment, fitted up with a shrinking mirror — quite a superfluous article considering the hole's proportions — an anchovy sauce cruet, and somebody's pattens. On my objecting to this retreat, he took us into another room with a dinner table for thirty, and in the grate a scorched page from a copybook under a bushel of coal dust. Having looked at this dead fire and shaken his head, he took my order. It proved to be merely "Some tea for the lady," which sent him out of the room in very low spirits.

I was, and I am, aware that the air of this room, in its strong combination of stable with soup stock, might have led one to suspect that the coaching department was not doing well and that the enterprising owner was boiling down the horses for the refreshment department. Yet the room was everything to me, Estella being in it. I thought that with her I could have been happy there for life. (I was not at all happy there at the time, observe, and I knew it well.)
"Where are you going to, at Richmond?" I asked Estella.
"I am going to live," she said, "at great expense, with a lady there who has the power — or says she has — of taking me about, introducing me, and showing people to me and showing me to people."
"I suppose you will be glad of variety and admiration?"
"Yes, I suppose so."
She answered so carelessly that I said, "You speak of yourself as if you were someone else."

"Where did you learn how I speak of others? Come, come," said Estella, smiling delightfully, "you must not expect me to go to school to you. I must talk in my own way. How do you get on with Mr. Pocket?"
"I live quite pleasantly there; at least —" It occurred to me that I was losing an opportunity.
"At least?" repeated Estella.
"As pleasantly as I could anywhere, away from you."
"You silly boy," said Estella quite composedly. "How can you talk such nonsense? Your friend Mr. Matthew, I believe, is superior to the rest of his family?"
"Very superior indeed. He is nobody's enemy —"
"Don't add 'but his own,'" interposed Estella, "for I hate that sort of man. But he really is unselfish, and above small jealousy and spite, I have heard?"
"I am sure I have every reason to say so."

"You have not every reason to say so of the rest of his people," said Estella, nodding at me with an expression that was at once serious and teasing. "For they besiege Miss Havisham with reports and accusations to your disadvantage. They watch you, misrepresent you, write letters about you — anonymous sometimes — and you are the torment and the occupation of their lives. You can scarcely imagine the hatred those people feel for you."
"They do me no harm, I hope?"

Instead of answering, Estella burst out laughing. This was very strange to me, and I looked at her in considerable bewilderment. When she stopped — and she had not laughed languidly but with real enjoyment — I said, in my diffident way with her —
"I hope I may suppose that you would not be amused if they did me any harm."

"No, no, you may be sure of that," said Estella. "You may be certain that I laugh because they fail. Oh, those people with Miss Havisham, and the tortures they undergo!" She laughed again, and even now, when she had told me why, her laughter struck me as strange. For I could not doubt it was genuine, and yet it seemed too much for the occasion. I thought there must really be something more here than I knew. She saw the thought in my mind and answered it.

"It is not easy for even you," said Estella, "to know what satisfaction it gives me to see those people thwarted, or what an enjoyable sense of the ridiculous I have when they are made ridiculous. For you were not brought up in that strange house from a mere baby. I was. You had not your little wits sharpened by their scheming against you, suppressed and defenseless, under the mask of sympathy and pity and whatnot that is soft and soothing. I had. You did not gradually open your round childish eyes wider and wider to the discovery of that fraud of a woman who stores up her peace of mind for when she wakes up in the night. I did."
It was no laughing matter with Estella now, nor was she drawing these memories from any shallow place. I would not have been the cause of that look of hers for all my expectations in a heap.

"Two things I can tell you," said Estella. "First, despite the proverb that constant dropping will wear away a stone, you may rest assured that these people never will — never would in a hundred years — undermine your standing with Miss Havisham, in any particular, great or small. Second, I am grateful to you as the cause of their being so busy and so mean in vain, and there is my hand upon it."

As she gave it to me playfully — for her darker mood had been only momentary — I held it and put it to my lips. "You ridiculous boy," said Estella. "Will you never take warning? Or do you kiss my hand in the same spirit in which I once let you kiss my cheek?"
"What spirit was that?" I said.
"I must think a moment. A spirit of contempt for the fawners and plotters."
"If I say yes, may I kiss the cheek again?"
"You should have asked before you touched the hand. But yes, if you like."
I leaned down, and her calm face was like a statue's. "Now," said Estella, gliding away the instant I touched her cheek, "you are to see that I have some tea, and you are to take me to Richmond."

Her returning to this tone, as if our association were forced upon us and we were mere puppets, gave me pain. But everything in our dealings did give me pain. Whatever her tone with me happened to be, I could put no trust in it and build no hope on it. And yet I went on, against trust and against hope. Why repeat it a thousand times? So it always was.

I rang for the tea, and the waiter, reappearing with his magic thread, brought in by degrees some fifty items related to that refreshment, but of tea itself not a glimpse. A tea board, cups and saucers, plates, knives and forks including carvers, spoons of various kinds, salt cellars, a meek little muffin confined with the utmost caution under a heavy iron cover, Moses in the bulrushes represented by a soft bit of butter in a quantity of parsley, a pale loaf with a powdered top, two burnt impressions of the bars of the kitchen fireplace on triangular bits of bread, and finally a fat family urn, which the waiter staggered in with, expressing in his face a burden of suffering. After a prolonged absence at this stage of the entertainment, he at length came back with a casket of precious appearance containing twigs. These I steeped in hot water, and so from all these appliances extracted one cup of I don't know what for Estella.

The bill paid, and the waiter remembered, and the ostler not forgotten, and the chambermaid taken into account — in a word, the whole house bribed into a state of contempt and hostility, and Estella's purse much lightened — we got into our carriage and drove away. Turning into Cheapside and rattling up Newgate Street, we were soon under the walls of which I was so ashamed.
"What place is that?" Estella asked me.

I made a foolish pretense of not at first recognizing it, and then told her. As she looked at it and drew in her head again, murmuring, "Wretches!" I would not have confessed to my visit for anything.
"Mr. Jaggers," I said, by way of neatly shifting it onto someone else, "has the reputation of being more in the secrets of that dismal place than any man in London."
"He is more in the secrets of every place, I think," said Estella in a low voice.
"You have been accustomed to seeing him often, I suppose?"

"I have been accustomed to seeing him at uncertain intervals, ever since I can remember. But I know him no better now than I did before I could speak clearly. What is your own experience of him? Do you make progress with him?"
"Once accustomed to his distrustful manner," I said, "I have done very well."
"Are you close?"
"I have dined with him at his private house."
"I imagine," said Estella, with a shudder, "that must be a curious place."
"It is a curious place."

I would have been cautious about discussing my guardian too freely even with her. But I should have gone on far enough to describe the dinner in Gerrard Street if we had not then come into a sudden glare of gaslight. It seemed, while it lasted, to be all alight and alive with that inexplicable feeling I had had before. And when we were out of it, I was as dazed for a few moments as if I had been in lightning.

So we fell into other conversation, and it was mainly about the road we were traveling, and what parts of London lay on this side and what on that. The great city was almost new to her, she told me, for she had never left Miss Havisham's neighborhood until she had gone to France, and she had merely passed through London then, going and returning. I asked her if my guardian had any charge of her while she remained here. To that she emphatically said, "God forbid!" and no more.

It was impossible for me to avoid seeing that she cared to attract me, that she made herself charming and would have won me even if the task had needed effort. Yet this made me no happier. For even if she had not taken that tone of our being disposed of by others, I would have felt that she held my heart in her hand because she willfully chose to hold it, and not because it would have pained any tenderness in her to crush it and throw it away.
When we passed through Hammersmith, I showed her where Mr. Matthew Pocket lived and said it was no great distance from Richmond, and that I hoped I should see her sometimes.
"Oh yes, you are to see me. You are to come when you think proper. You are to be mentioned to the family. Indeed, you are already mentioned."
I asked whether it was a large household she was going to join.
"No, there are only two — mother and daughter. The mother is a lady of some standing, though not opposed to increasing her income."
"I wonder Miss Havisham could part with you again so soon."

"It is part of Miss Havisham's plans for me, Pip," said Estella with a sigh, as if she were tired. "I am to write to her constantly and see her regularly and report how I go on — I and the jewels — for they are nearly all mine now."
It was the first time she had ever called me by my name. Of course she did so on purpose, and knew that I should treasure it up.

We came to Richmond all too soon. Our destination there was a house by the green — a stately old house where hoops and powder and patches, embroidered coats, rolled stockings, ruffles, and swords had had their court days many a time. Some ancient trees before the house were still trimmed into shapes as formal and unnatural as the hoops and wigs and stiff skirts. But their own allotted places in the great procession of the dead were not far off, and they would soon sink into them and go the silent way of the rest.

A bell with an old voice — which I dare say in its time had often said to the house, "Here is the green farthingale, here is the diamond-hilted sword, here are the shoes with red heels and the blue solitaire" — sounded gravely in the moonlight. Two cherry-colored maids came fluttering out to receive Estella. The doorway soon swallowed her boxes, and she gave me her hand and a smile and said good night and was swallowed likewise. And still I stood looking at the house, thinking how happy I should be if I lived there with her, and knowing that I never was happy with her, but always miserable.

I got into the carriage to be taken back to Hammersmith. I got in with a bad heartache, and I got out with a worse heartache. At our own door, I found little Jane Pocket coming home from a little party escorted by her little lover. I envied her little lover, despite his being subject to Flopson.

Mr. Pocket was out lecturing, for he was a most delightful lecturer on domestic economy, and his treatises on the management of children and servants were considered the very best textbooks on those subjects. But Mrs. Pocket was at home and was in a little difficulty, on account of the baby's having been given a needle case to keep him quiet during the unexplained absence — with a relative in the Foot Guards — of Millers. And more needles were missing than it could be regarded as quite wholesome for a patient of such tender years either to apply externally or to take as a tonic.

Mr. Pocket being justly celebrated for giving most excellent practical advice, and for having a clear and sound perception of things and a highly judicious mind, I had some thought in my heartache of asking him to accept my confidence. But happening to look up at Mrs. Pocket as she sat reading her book of dignities after prescribing bed as a sovereign remedy for baby, I thought — well — no, I wouldn't.

chapters.title: Chapter 34
paragraphs: As I had grown accustomed to my expectations, I had gradually begun to notice their effect on myself and those around me. I disguised their influence on my own character as much as possible, but I knew very well that it was not all good. I lived in a state of chronic unease about my behavior toward Joe. My conscience was not at all comfortable about Biddy. When I woke up in the night — like Camilla — I used to think, with a weariness on my spirits, that I should have been happier and better if I had never seen Miss Havisham's face, and had risen to manhood content to be partners with Joe in the honest old forge. Many an evening, when I sat alone looking at the fire, I thought that after all there was no fire like the forge fire and the kitchen fire at home.

Yet Estella was so inseparable from all my restlessness and disquiet of mind that I fell into genuine confusion about the limits of my own part in producing it. That is to say, supposing I had had no expectations and yet had had Estella to think of, I could not satisfy myself that I should have done much better. Now, concerning the influence of my position on others, I was in no such difficulty. I perceived — though dimly enough perhaps — that it was not beneficial to anybody, and above all, that it was not beneficial to Herbert. My lavish habits led his easy nature into expenses he could not afford, corrupted the simplicity of his life, and disturbed his peace with anxieties and regrets. I was not at all remorseful for having unwittingly set those other branches of the Pocket family to the petty tricks they practiced, because such littleness was their natural bent and would have been drawn out by anybody else if I had left them sleeping. But Herbert's was a very different case, and it often caused me a pang to think that I had done him a disservice by crowding his sparsely furnished rooms with incongruous upholstery and placing the canary-breasted Avenger at his disposal.

So now, as an infallible way of making little unease into great unease, I began to run up a quantity of debt. I could hardly begin without Herbert beginning too, so he soon followed. At Startop's suggestion, we put ourselves down for election into a club called The Finches of the Grove. The object of this institution I have never worked out, if it were not that the members should dine expensively once a fortnight, quarrel among themselves as much as possible after dinner, and cause six waiters to get drunk on the stairs. I know that these gratifying social ends were so invariably accomplished that Herbert and I understood nothing else to be meant by the first standing toast of the society, which ran: "Gentlemen, may the present promotion of good feeling ever reign predominant among the Finches of the Grove."

The Finches spent their money foolishly (the hotel we dined at was in Covent Garden), and the first Finch I saw when I had the honor of joining the Grove was Bentley Drummle, at that time blundering about town in a cab of his own and doing a great deal of damage to the posts at street corners. Occasionally he shot himself out of his carriage headfirst over the front. I saw him on one occasion deliver himself at the door of the Grove in this unintentional way — like a load of coals. But here I am getting ahead of myself, for I was not a Finch and could not be, according to the sacred laws of the society, until I came of age.

In my confidence in my own resources, I would willingly have taken Herbert's expenses on myself. But Herbert was proud, and I could make no such offer to him. So he got into difficulties in every direction and continued to look about him. When we gradually fell into keeping late hours and late company, I noticed that he looked about him with a desponding eye at breakfast time. He began to look about him more hopefully around midday. He drooped when he came in to dinner. He seemed to spot Capital in the distance, rather clearly, after dinner. He all but seized Capital toward midnight. And at about two o'clock in the morning, he became so deeply despondent again as to talk of buying a rifle and going to America, with a general purpose of compelling buffaloes to make his fortune.

I was usually at Hammersmith about half the week, and when I was at Hammersmith I haunted Richmond — whereof more separately by and by. Herbert would often come to Hammersmith when I was there, and I think at those times his father would occasionally have some passing awareness that the opening he was looking for had not appeared yet. But in the general tumble of the family, his tumbling out in life somewhere was a thing to work itself out somehow. In the meantime, Mr. Pocket grew greyer and tried more often to lift himself out of his perplexities by the hair. While Mrs. Pocket tripped up the family with her footstool, read her book of dignities, lost her handkerchief, told us about her grandfather, and taught the young idea how to shoot by shooting it into bed whenever it attracted her notice.
As I am now summarizing a period of my life with the aim of clearing my way before me, I can scarcely do so better than by at once completing the description of our usual habits at Barnard's Inn.

We spent as much money as we could and got as little for it as people could bring themselves to give us. We were always more or less miserable, and most of our acquaintance were in the same state. There was a cheerful fiction among us that we were constantly enjoying ourselves, and a skeleton truth that we never did. To the best of my belief, our situation was, in that last respect, a rather common one.

Every morning, with an air ever fresh, Herbert went into the City to look about him. I often paid him a visit in the dark back room where he kept company with an ink jar, a hat peg, a coal box, a string box, an almanac, a desk and stool, and a ruler. I do not remember that I ever saw him do anything else but look about him. If we all did what we undertake to do as faithfully as Herbert did, we might live in a Republic of the Virtues. He had nothing else to do, poor fellow, except at a certain hour every afternoon to "go to Lloyd's" — to observe a ceremony of seeing his principal, I think. He never did anything else in connection with Lloyd's that I could discover, except come back again. When he felt his case unusually serious and that he positively must find an opening, he would go on the Exchange at a busy time and walk in and out in a kind of gloomy country-dance figure among the assembled magnates. "For," said Herbert to me, coming home to dinner on one of those special occasions, "I find the truth to be, Handel, that an opening won't come to one, but one must go to it — so I have been."

If we had been less attached to one another, I think we must have hated one another regularly every morning. I detested the rooms beyond expression at that period of repentance and could not endure the sight of the Avenger's livery, which had a more expensive and less profitable appearance then than at any other time in the twenty-four hours. As we got more and more into debt, breakfast became a hollower and hollower form. On one occasion, being threatened at breakfast time by letter with legal proceedings "not wholly unconnected," as my local paper might put it, "with jewelry," I went so far as to seize the Avenger by his blue collar and shake him off his feet — so that he was actually in the air, like a booted Cupid — for presuming to suppose that we wanted a roll.
At certain times — meaning at uncertain times, for they depended on our mood — I would say to Herbert, as if it were a remarkable discovery —
"My dear Herbert, we are getting on badly."
"My dear Handel," Herbert would say to me in all sincerity, "if you will believe me, those very words were on my lips, by a strange coincidence."
"Then, Herbert," I would respond, "let us look into our affairs."

We always derived profound satisfaction from making an appointment for this purpose. I always thought this was business, this was the way to confront the thing, this was the way to take the enemy by the throat. And I know Herbert thought so too.

We ordered something rather special for dinner, with a bottle of something similarly out of the ordinary, in order that our minds might be fortified for the occasion and we might come well up to the mark. Dinner over, we produced a bundle of pens, a generous supply of ink, and a fine show of writing and blotting paper. For there was something very comfortable in having plenty of stationery.

I would then take a sheet of paper and write across the top of it, in a neat hand, the heading "Memorandum of Pip's debts," with Barnard's Inn and the date very carefully added. Herbert would also take a sheet of paper and write across it with similar formalities, "Memorandum of Herbert's debts."

Each of us would then consult a confused heap of papers at his side, which had been thrown into drawers, worn into holes in pockets, half burned in lighting candles, stuck for weeks into the looking glass, and otherwise damaged. The sound of our pens going refreshed us exceedingly, so much so that I sometimes found it difficult to distinguish between this edifying business proceeding and actually paying the money. In point of merit, the two things seemed about equal.

When we had written for a little while, I would ask Herbert how he was getting on. Herbert probably would have been scratching his head in a most rueful manner at the sight of his accumulating figures.
"They are mounting up, Handel," Herbert would say. "Upon my life, they are mounting up."
"Be firm, Herbert," I would retort, plying my own pen with great diligence. "Look the thing in the face. Look into your affairs. Stare them out of countenance."
"So I would, Handel, only they are staring me out of countenance."

However, my determined manner would have its effect, and Herbert would fall to work again. After a time he would give up once more, on the plea that he had not got Cobbs's bill, or Lobbs's, or Nobbs's, as the case might be.
"Then, Herbert, estimate. Estimate it in round numbers, and put it down."
"What a fellow of resource you are!" my friend would reply with admiration. "Really, your business powers are very remarkable."

I thought so too. I established with myself, on these occasions, the reputation of a first-rate man of business — prompt, decisive, energetic, clear, cool-headed. When I had got all my responsibilities down upon my list, I compared each with the bill and ticked it off. My self-approval when I ticked an entry was quite a luxurious sensation. When I had no more ticks to make, I folded all my bills up uniformly, labeled each on the back, and tied the whole into a symmetrical bundle. Then I did the same for Herbert, who modestly said he had not my administrative genius, and felt that I had brought his affairs into focus for him.

My business habits had one other bright feature, which I called "leaving a margin." For example, supposing Herbert's debts to be one hundred and sixty-four pounds four and twopence, I would say, "Leave a margin, and put them down at two hundred." Or, supposing my own to be four times as much, I would leave a margin and put them down at seven hundred. I had the highest opinion of the wisdom of this same margin. But I am bound to acknowledge that on looking back, I consider it to have been an expensive device. For we always ran into new debt immediately, to the full extent of the margin, and sometimes, in the sense of freedom and solvency it gave us, got pretty far into another margin.

But there was a calm, a rest, a virtuous hush, following these examinations of our affairs that gave me, for the time, an admirable opinion of myself. Soothed by my exertions, my method, and Herbert's compliments, I would sit with his symmetrical bundle and my own on the table before me among the stationery, and feel like a bank of some sort rather than a private individual.

We shut our outer door on these solemn occasions, so that we might not be interrupted. I had fallen into my serene state one evening when we heard a letter dropped through the slit in the door and fall on the ground. "It's for you, Handel," said Herbert, going out and coming back with it, "and I hope there is nothing the matter." This was in reference to its heavy black seal and border.

The letter was signed Trabb & Co., and its contents were simply that I was an honored sir, and that they begged to inform me that Mrs. J. Gargery had departed this life on Monday last at twenty minutes past six in the evening, and that my attendance was requested at the interment on Monday next at three o'clock in the afternoon.

chapters.title: Chapter 35
paragraphs: It was the first time that a grave had opened in my road of life, and the gap it made in the smooth ground was extraordinary. The figure of my sister in her chair by the kitchen fire haunted me night and day. That the place could possibly exist without her was something my mind seemed unable to grasp. And whereas she had seldom or never been in my thoughts of late, I now had the strangest ideas that she was coming toward me in the street, or that she would presently knock at the door. In my rooms too, with which she had never been associated, there was at once the blankness of death and a perpetual suggestion of the sound of her voice or the turn of her face or figure, as if she were still alive and had been often there.

Whatever my fortunes might have been, I could scarcely have recalled my sister with much tenderness. But I suppose there is a shock of regret which may exist without much tenderness. Under its influence — and perhaps to make up for the lack of the softer feeling — I was seized with a violent anger against the assailant from whom she had suffered so much. I felt that on sufficient proof I could have vengefully pursued Orlick, or anyone else, to the last extremity.

Having written to Joe to offer him consolation and to assure him that I would come to the funeral, I passed the days in between in the curious state of mind I have described. I went down early in the morning and got off at the Blue Boar in good time to walk over to the forge.

It was fine summer weather again, and as I walked along, the times when I was a little helpless creature and my sister did not spare me came vividly back. But they returned with a gentle tone upon them that softened even the edge of Tickler. For now, the very breath of the beans and clover whispered to my heart that the day must come when it would be well for my memory that others walking in the sunshine should be softened as they thought of me.

At last I came within sight of the house and saw that Trabb and Co. had put in a funereal occupation and taken possession. Two dismally absurd persons, each ostentatiously exhibiting a crutch done up in a black bandage — as if that instrument could possibly communicate any comfort to anybody — were posted at the front door. In one of them I recognized a postboy dismissed from the Boar for turning a young couple into a sawpit on their bridal morning, as a consequence of intoxication making it necessary for him to ride his horse clasped round the neck with both arms. All the children of the village and most of the women were admiring these sable wardens and the closed windows of the house and forge. As I came up, one of the two wardens — the postboy — knocked at the door, implying that I was far too exhausted by grief to have strength remaining to knock for myself.

Another sable warden — a carpenter who had once eaten two geese for a bet — opened the door and showed me into the best parlor. Here Mr. Trabb had commandeered the best table and got all the leaves up and was holding a kind of black bazaar with the aid of a quantity of black pins. At the moment I arrived, he had just finished putting somebody's hat into black mourning clothes, like an African baby. So he held out his hand for mine. But I, misled by the action and confused by the occasion, shook hands with him with every display of warm affection.

Poor dear Joe, tangled in a little black cloak tied in a large bow under his chin, was seated apart at the upper end of the room, where, as chief mourner, he had evidently been stationed by Trabb. When I bent down and said to him, "Dear Joe, how are you?" he said, "Pip, old chap, you knowed her when she were a fine figure of a —" and clasped my hand and said no more.

Biddy, looking very neat and modest in her black dress, went quietly here and there and was very helpful. When I had spoken to Biddy, thinking it not a time for talking, I went and sat down near Joe. There I began to wonder in what part of the house it — she — my sister — was. The air of the parlor being faint with the smell of sweet cake, I looked about for the table of refreshments. It was scarcely visible until one's eyes adjusted to the gloom, but there was a cut-up plum cake upon it, and there were cut-up oranges, and sandwiches, and biscuits, and two decanters that I knew very well as ornaments but had never seen used in all my life — one full of port and one of sherry. Standing at this table, I became conscious of the servile Pumblechook in a black cloak and several yards of hatband, who was alternately stuffing himself and making obsequious gestures to catch my attention. The moment he succeeded, he came over to me — breathing sherry and crumbs — and said in a subdued voice, "May I, dear sir?" and did. I then noticed Mr. and Mrs. Hubble, the latter in a decent speechless fit in a corner. We were all going to "follow" and were all in the course of being tied up separately by Trabb into ridiculous bundles.

"Which I meantersay, Pip," Joe whispered to me, as we were being what Mr. Trabb called "formed" in the parlor, two and two — and it was dreadfully like a preparation for some grim kind of dance — "which I meantersay, sir, as I would in preference have carried her to the church myself, along with three or four friendly ones wot come to it with willing harts and arms, but it were considered wot the neighbours would look down on such and would be of opinions as it were wanting in respect."
"Pocket handkerchiefs out, all!" cried Mr. Trabb at this point, in a depressed businesslike voice. "Pocket handkerchiefs out! We are ready!"

So we all put our pocket handkerchiefs to our faces, as if our noses were bleeding, and filed out two and two: Joe and I, Biddy and Pumblechook, Mr. and Mrs. Hubble. The remains of my poor sister had been brought round by the kitchen door, and, it being a point of undertaking ceremony that the six bearers must be stifled and blinded under a horrible black velvet housing with a white border, the whole looked like a blind monster with twelve human legs, shuffling and blundering along under the guidance of two keepers — the postboy and his comrade.

The neighborhood, however, highly approved of these arrangements, and we were much admired as we went through the village. The more youthful and vigorous part of the community made dashes now and then to cut us off and lay in wait to intercept us at points of advantage. At such times, the more enthusiastic among them called out in an excited manner on our emergence round some corner of anticipation, "Here they come! Here they are!" and we were all but cheered. In this procession I was much annoyed by the abject Pumblechook, who, being behind me, persisted the whole way in arranging my streaming hatband and smoothing my cloak as a delicate attention. My thoughts were further distracted by the excessive pride of Mr. and Mrs. Hubble, who were surpassingly conceited and vainglorious at being members of so distinguished a procession.

And now the range of marshes lay clear before us, with the sails of the ships on the river growing out of it. We went into the churchyard, close to the graves of my unknown parents, Philip Pirrip, late of this parish, and Also Georgiana, Wife of the Above. And there my sister was laid quietly in the earth, while the larks sang high above it and the light wind scattered beautiful shadows of clouds and trees.

Of the conduct of the worldly-minded Pumblechook while this was happening, I desire to say no more than that it was all directed at me. Even when those noble passages were read which remind humanity how it brought nothing into the world and can take nothing out, and how it flees like a shadow and never continues long in one place, I heard him cough a reservation for the case of a young gentleman who came unexpectedly into large property. When we got back, he had the nerve to tell me he wished my sister could have known I had done her so much honor, and to hint that she would have considered it reasonably purchased at the price of her death. After that, he drank all the rest of the sherry, and Mr. Hubble drank the port, and the two talked — as I have since observed to be customary in such cases — as if they were of quite another race from the deceased, and were notoriously immortal. Finally he went away with Mr. and Mrs. Hubble — to make an evening of it, I felt sure, and to tell the Jolly Bargemen that he was the founder of my fortunes and my earliest benefactor.

When they were all gone, and when Trabb and his men — but not his boy; I looked for him — had crammed their costumes into bags and were gone too, the house felt healthier. Soon afterwards, Biddy, Joe, and I had a cold dinner together. But we dined in the best parlor, not in the old kitchen, and Joe was so exceedingly particular about what he did with his knife and fork and the salt cellar and whatnot that there was great restraint upon us. But after dinner, when I made him take his pipe and when I had loitered with him about the forge and when we sat down together on the great block of stone outside it, we got on better. I noticed that after the funeral Joe changed his clothes so far as to make a compromise between his Sunday dress and working dress, in which the dear fellow looked natural and like the man he was.

He was very pleased by my asking if I might sleep in my own little room, and I was pleased too, for I felt that I had done rather a great thing in making the request. When the shadows of evening were closing in, I took an opportunity of getting into the garden with Biddy for a little talk.
"Biddy," I said, "I think you might have written to me about these sad matters."
"Do you, Mr. Pip?" said Biddy. "I should have written if I had thought that."
"Don't suppose that I mean to be unkind, Biddy, when I say I think you ought to have thought that."
"Do you, Mr. Pip?"

She was so quiet and had such an orderly, good, and pretty way with her that I did not like the thought of making her cry again. After looking a little at her downcast eyes as she walked beside me, I gave up that point.
"I suppose it will be difficult for you to remain here now, Biddy dear?"

"Oh! I can't do so, Mr. Pip," said Biddy, in a tone of regret but still of quiet conviction. "I have been speaking to Mrs. Hubble, and I am going to her tomorrow. I hope we shall be able to take some care of Mr. Gargery, together, until he settles down."
"How are you going to live, Biddy? If you want any mo —"

"How am I going to live?" repeated Biddy, breaking in with a momentary flush on her face. "I'll tell you, Mr. Pip. I am going to try to get the place of mistress in the new school nearly finished here. I can be well recommended by all the neighbors, and I hope I can be hardworking and patient, and teach myself while I teach others. You know, Mr. Pip," Biddy went on with a smile, raising her eyes to my face, "the new schools are not like the old, but I learned a good deal from you after that time, and have had time since then to improve."
"I think you would always improve, Biddy, under any circumstances."
"Ah! Except in my bad side of human nature," murmured Biddy.
It was not so much a reproach as an irresistible thinking aloud. Well! I thought I would give up that point too. So I walked a little further with Biddy, looking silently at her downcast eyes.
"I have not heard the details of my sister's death, Biddy."

"They are very slight, poor thing. She had been in one of her bad states — though they had gotten better of late rather than worse — for four days, when she came out of it in the evening, just at teatime, and said quite plainly, 'Joe.' As she had not said any word for a long while, I ran and fetched Mr. Gargery from the forge. She made signs to me that she wanted him to sit down close to her, and wanted me to put her arms round his neck. So I put them round his neck, and she laid her head down on his shoulder, quite content and satisfied. And so she presently said 'Joe' again, and once 'Pardon,' and once 'Pip.'
