When I had gone into Herbert's room and had shut off any other connection between it and the staircase except through the room where our conversation had taken place, I sat down by the fire. I would have sat longer but could not feel safe there either. In a dazed, grief-stricken way, I looked at the room around me and, finding the place empty and cheerless, went out again to be alone in the corridors.

I got away from him, without knowing how I did it, and mended the fire in the room where we had been together, and sat down by it, afraid to go to bed. For an hour or more, I remained too stunned to think. It was then beginning to occur to me that I would be in great danger from the man who had put me in this position if I stopped his allowance. All of this slowly sank into me.

Miss Havisham's intentions toward me — all a mere dream. Estella not designed for me. I had only suffered in Satis House as a convenience, a sting for the greedy relations, a model with a mechanical heart to practice on when no other practice was at hand. Those were the first smarts I had. But sharper and deeper than any was this — it was for the convict, guilty of I knew not what crimes, and liable to be taken and hanged, that I had deserted Joe.

I would not have gone back to Joe now. I would not have gone back to Biddy now, for any consideration. Simply, I suppose, because my sense of my own worthless conduct toward them was greater than every consideration. No wisdom on earth could have given me the comfort that I should have derived from their simplicity and fidelity. But I could never, never, never undo what I had done.

In every gust of wind and rush of rain, I heard pursuers. Twice I could have sworn there was a knocking and whispering at the outer door. With these fears upon me, I began either to imagine or recall that I had had mysterious warnings of this man's approach. That for weeks gone by, I had passed faces in the streets which I had thought like his. That they had first come at me since the stormy nights in November, and had reappeared among the faces in the streets, and that some dread of this coming must have caused me to start so many times.

Crowding in with these thoughts came the reflection that I had seen him with my childish eyes to be a desperately violent man. That I had heard that other convict accuse him of attempted murder. That I had seen him struggle in the ditch like a wild beast. That I had a reason to believe he had been tried for some capital offense. And that he had been in prison, and had returned to me in the dead of night.

He had rolled a handkerchief round his head, and his face was set and lowering in his sleep. But he was asleep, and quietly too, though he had a pistol lying on the pillow. Assured of this, I softly removed the key of his room to my own pocket and turned the lock upon him, then sat down by my fire again and fell asleep before it.
THIS IS THE END OF THE SECOND STAGE OF PIP'S EXPECTATIONS.

chapters.title: Chapter 40
paragraphs: It was lucky for me that I had to think about keeping my dreaded visitor safe. That concern, pressing on me when I woke, held all other thoughts at a confused distance.

The impossibility of hiding him in the chambers was obvious. It couldn't be done, and trying would only arouse suspicion. True, I no longer had the Avenger in my service, but I was looked after by a fiery old woman, assisted by an animated ragbag she called her niece. Keeping a room secret from them would only invite curiosity and wild exaggeration. They both had weak eyes, which I had long blamed on their habit of looking through keyholes, and they were always underfoot when not wanted. Indeed, that was their only reliable quality besides thievery. Not wanting to create a mystery for these people, I decided to announce in the morning that my uncle had unexpectedly arrived from the country.

I settled on this plan while still groping in the darkness for a way to get a light. Unable to find one, I had to go out to the adjacent Lodge and get the watchman to come with his lantern. Now, groping my way down the black staircase, I stumbled over something. That something was a man crouching in a corner.

The man made no answer when I asked what he was doing there, but slipped away from my touch in silence. I ran to the Lodge and urged the watchman to come quickly, telling him about the incident on the way back. The wind was as fierce as ever, so we didn't risk the lantern light on the extinguished staircase lamps. Instead we examined the staircase from bottom to top and found no one. It then occurred to me that the man might have slipped into my rooms. So, lighting my candle from the watchman's lantern and leaving him at the door, I searched them carefully, including the room where my dreaded guest lay asleep. All was quiet, and certainly no other man was in those chambers.

It troubled me that someone had been lurking on the stairs, on that night of all nights. I asked the watchman, hoping for some reassuring explanation as I handed him a drink at the door, whether he had admitted any gentleman who had obviously been dining out. Yes, he said — at different times of the night, three. One lived in Fountain Court, and the other two lived in the Lane, and he had seen them all go home. The only other man who lived in the house of which my chambers were part had been in the country for weeks, and he certainly had not returned, because we had seen his door still sealed as we came upstairs.

"The night being so bad, sir," said the watchman, handing back my glass, "very few have come in at my gate. Besides those three gentlemen I've named, I can't recall another since about eleven o'clock, when a stranger asked for you."
"My uncle," I muttered. "Yes."
"You saw him, sir?"
"Yes. Oh yes."
"And the person with him?"
"Person with him!" I repeated.
"I took the person to be with him," the watchman replied. "The person stopped when he stopped to ask me for directions, and the person went this way when he went this way."
"What sort of person?"

The watchman hadn't particularly noticed. He'd say a working person. To the best of his belief, the man wore dust-coloured clothes under a dark coat. The watchman made less of the matter than I did, naturally — he didn't have my reasons for attaching weight to it.

When I'd got rid of him — which I thought wise to do without prolonging explanations — my mind was deeply troubled by these two facts taken together. Separately, they were easy enough to explain innocently. Some diner who hadn't passed this watchman's gate might have strayed onto my staircase and fallen asleep. And my nameless visitor might have brought someone along to show him the way. But taken together, they had an ugly look to someone as prone to distrust and fear as the last few hours had made me.

I lit my fire, which burned with a raw, pale flare at that hour of the morning, and dozed in front of it. I seemed to have been dozing a whole night when the clocks struck six. Since there was still an hour and a half until daylight, I dozed again — now waking uneasily with rambling conversations about nothing in my ears, now imagining the wind in the chimney as thunder — until at length I fell into a deep sleep, from which the daylight woke me with a start.

All this time I had never been able to consider my own situation, and I still couldn't. I didn't have the power to focus on it. I was deeply dejected and distressed, but in a confused, wholesale sort of way. As for forming any plan for the future, I might as well have tried to form an elephant. When I opened the shutters and looked out at the wet, wild morning, all in shades of lead, when I walked from room to room, when I sat down again shivering before the fire, waiting for my cleaning woman to appear — I thought how miserable I was, but hardly knew why, or how long I had been so, or what day it was, or even who I was.

At last the old woman and the niece came in — the niece with a head barely distinguishable from her dusty broom — and showed surprise at seeing me and the fire. I told them how my uncle had come in the night and was now asleep, and how the breakfast preparations should be adjusted accordingly. Then I washed and dressed while they knocked the furniture about and made a dust. And so, in a sort of dream or half-waking state, I found myself sitting by the fire again, waiting for — Him — to come to breakfast.
Before long, his door opened and he came out. I could not bring myself to look at him, and I thought he looked even worse by daylight.
"I don't even know," I said, speaking quietly as he took his seat at the table, "what name to call you. I've told people you are my uncle."
"That's it, dear boy! Call me uncle."
"You took some name, I suppose, on the ship?"
"Yes, dear boy. I took the name of Provis."
"Do you mean to keep that name?"
"Why, yes, dear boy, it's as good as another — unless you'd like another."
"What is your real name?" I asked him in a whisper.
"Magwitch," he answered, in the same low tone. "Christened Abel."
"What were you brought up to be?"
"A varmint, dear boy."
He answered quite seriously, and used the word as if it meant some profession.
"When you came into the Temple last night —" I said, pausing to wonder whether that could really have been last night, which seemed so long ago.
"Yes, dear boy?"
"When you came in at the gate and asked the watchman the way here, did you have anyone with you?"
"With me? No, dear boy."
"But there was someone there?"
"I didn't take particular notice," he said doubtfully, "not knowing the ways of the place. But I think there was a person who came in along with me."
"Are you known in London?"
"I hope not!" he said, giving his neck a jerk with his forefinger that made me turn hot and sick.
"Were you known in London once?"
"Not especially, dear boy. I was in the provinces mostly."
"Were you — tried — in London?"
"Which time?" he said, with a sharp look.
"The last time."
He nodded. "First knew Mr. Jaggers that way. Jaggers was my lawyer."

It was on the tip of my tongue to ask what he'd been tried for, but he picked up a knife, gave it a flourish, and with the words, "And what I done is worked out and paid for!" fell upon his breakfast.

He ate in a ravenous way that was very disagreeable, and all his actions were rough, noisy, and greedy. Some of his teeth had failed him since I'd seen him eat on the marshes, and as he turned his food in his mouth, tilting his head sideways to bring his strongest teeth to bear on it, he looked terribly like a hungry old dog. If I'd had any appetite to begin with, he would have destroyed it. I sat as I did — repelled by an overwhelming aversion, gloomily staring at the tablecloth.

"I'm a heavy eater, dear boy," he said, by way of polite apology when he'd finished his meal, "but I always was. If it had been in my nature to eat less, I might have got into lighter trouble. Likewise, I must have my smoke. When I was first hired out as a shepherd on the other side of the world, I believe I'd have gone mad with misery if I hadn't had my pipe."

As he said this, he got up from the table, reached into the breast of his pea-coat, and brought out a short black pipe and a handful of loose tobacco of the kind called Negro-head. Having filled his pipe, he put the rest back as if his pocket were a drawer. Then he took a live coal from the fire with the tongs, lit his pipe, and turned round on the hearthrug with his back to the fire. He went through his favourite gesture of holding out both his hands for mine.

"And this," he said, rocking my hands up and down in his as he puffed at his pipe, "and this is the gentleman what I made! The real genuine one! It does me good to look at you, Pip. All I ask is to stand by and look at you, dear boy!"

I freed my hands as soon as I could, and found that I was beginning slowly to settle into contemplating my situation. What I was chained to, and how heavily, became clear to me as I heard his hoarse voice and sat looking up at his furrowed bald head with its iron-grey hair at the sides.

"I can't have my gentleman trudging through the mud of the streets. There can't be no mud on his boots. My gentleman must have horses, Pip! Horses to ride, and horses to drive, and horses for his servant to ride and drive too. Shall colonists have their horses — and thoroughbreds, if you please, good Lord! — and not my London gentleman? No, no. We'll show them a different pair of shoes than that, Pip, won't we?"
He pulled a great thick pocketbook from his coat, bursting with papers, and tossed it on the table.

"There's something worth spending in that book, dear boy. It's yours. All I've got isn't mine — it's yours. Don't you be afraid of it. There's more where that came from. I've come to the old country to see my gentleman spend his money like a gentleman. That'll be my pleasure. My pleasure will be to see him do it. And blast you all!" he wound up, looking round the room and snapping his fingers with a loud crack. "Blast every one of you, from the judge in his wig to the colonist stirring up the dust — I'll show a better gentleman than the whole lot of you put together!"

"Stop!" I said, almost frantic with fear and disgust. "I want to speak to you. I want to know what is to be done. I want to know how you are to be kept out of danger, how long you're going to stay, what your plans are."

"Look here, Pip," he said, laying his hand on my arm in a suddenly altered and subdued manner. "First of all, look here. I forgot myself half a minute ago. What I said was low — that's what it was — low. Look here, Pip. Forgive it. I ain't going to be low."
"First," I resumed, half groaning, "what precautions can be taken against your being recognised and seized?"

"No, dear boy," he said in the same tone as before, "that don't come first. Lowness comes first. I ain't spent so many years making a gentleman without knowing what's due to him. Look here, Pip. I was low — that's what I was — low. Forgive it, dear boy."
Some sense of the grimly comical moved me to a fretful laugh as I replied, "I have forgiven it. In Heaven's name, don't harp upon it!"
"Yes, but look here," he persisted. "Dear boy, I ain't come so far just to be low. Now, go on, dear boy. You was saying —"
"How are you to be guarded from the danger you've brought on yourself?"
"Well, dear boy, the danger ain't so great. Unless I was informed against, the danger ain't much to worry about. There's Jaggers, and there's Wemmick, and there's you. Who else is there to inform?"
"Is there no chance someone might recognise you in the street?" I said.

"Well," he returned, "there ain't many. And I don't intend to advertise myself in the newspapers as A.M. come back from Botany Bay. Years have rolled by, and who's to gain by it? Still, look here, Pip. If the danger had been fifty times as great, I'd have come to see you just the same."
"And how long do you mean to remain?"
"How long?" he said, taking the black pipe from his mouth and dropping his jaw as he stared at me. "I'm not going back. I've come for good."
"Where are you to live?" I said. "What is to be done with you? Where will you be safe?"

"Dear boy," he returned, "there's wigs that can be bought for money, and there's hair powder, and spectacles, and black clothes — shorts and what not. Others have done it safely before, and what others have done before, others can do again. As to the where and how of living, dear boy, give me your own opinions on it."
"You talk calmly enough now," I said, "but you were very serious last night, when you swore it was Death."

"And so I swear it is Death," he said, putting his pipe back in his mouth, "and Death by the rope, in the open street not far from this. And it's serious that you should fully understand it. What then, once that's understood? Here I am. To go back now would be as bad as standing my ground — worse. Besides, Pip, I'm here because I've intended it for years and years. As for what I dare, I'm an old bird now who's faced all manner of traps since I was first fledged, and I'm not afraid to perch on a scarecrow. If Death is hiding inside it, so be it — let him come out, and I'll face him, and then I'll believe in him, not before. And now let me have another look at my gentleman."
Once more, he took me by both hands and surveyed me with an air of admiring ownership, smoking with great satisfaction all the while.

It seemed to me that I could do no better than find him some quiet lodging nearby, which he could move into when Herbert returned. I expected Herbert in two or three days. That the secret must be shared with Herbert as an unavoidable necessity — even setting aside the immense relief I would feel in sharing it — was plain to me. But it was by no means plain to Mr. Provis (I resolved to call him by that name), who withheld his consent to Herbert's involvement until he should have seen him and formed a favourable opinion of his face. "And even then, dear boy," he said, pulling a greasy little clasped black Testament from his pocket, "we'll have him on his oath."

To say that my terrible patron carried this little black book about the world solely to swear people on in emergencies would be to state what I never quite proved. But this I can say: I never knew him put it to any other use. The book itself looked as though it had been stolen from some court of justice, and perhaps his knowledge of its history, combined with his own experience in such places, gave him a faith in its powers as a sort of legal spell or charm. When he first produced it, I remembered how he had made me swear loyalty in the churchyard long ago, and how he had described himself last night as always swearing to his resolutions in his solitude.

Since he was currently dressed in a seafaring outfit — in which he looked as if he had parrots and cigars to sell — I next discussed with him what he should wear. He cherished an extraordinary faith in the virtues of "shorts" as a disguise, and had in his own mind designed an outfit that would have made him something between a dean and a dentist. It was with considerable difficulty that I persuaded him to adopt a style more like a prosperous farmer's. We agreed that he should cut his hair short and wear a little powder. Lastly, since the cleaning woman and her niece hadn't yet seen him, he was to keep out of their sight until the change of dress was complete.

It might seem simple enough to settle on these precautions. But in my dazed — not to say distracted — state, it took so long that I didn't get out to arrange things until two or three in the afternoon. He was to stay locked in the chambers while I was gone, and was on no account to open the door.

There being, to my knowledge, a respectable lodging-house in Essex Street, the back of which looked into the Temple and was almost within calling distance of my windows, I went there first and was fortunate enough to secure the second floor for my uncle, Mr. Provis. I then went from shop to shop, buying everything necessary for his change in appearance. With that done, I turned my steps, on my own account, to Little Britain. Mr. Jaggers was at his desk but, seeing me enter, got up immediately and stood before his fire.
"Now, Pip," he said, "be careful."
"I will, sir," I returned. For, on my way there, I had thought carefully about what I was going to say.
"Don't commit yourself," said Mr. Jaggers, "and don't commit anyone. You understand — anyone. Don't tell me anything. I don't want to know anything. I am not curious."
Of course I saw that he knew the man had come.
"I merely want, Mr. Jaggers," I said, "to confirm that what I've been told is true. I have no hope of it being untrue, but at least I may verify it."

Mr. Jaggers nodded. "But did you say 'told' or 'informed'?" he asked, with his head tilted to one side, not looking at me but listening in the direction of the floor. "'Told' would seem to imply verbal communication. You can't have verbal communication with a man in New South Wales, you know."
"I will say 'informed,' Mr. Jaggers."
"Good."
"I have been informed by a person named Abel Magwitch that he is the benefactor so long unknown to me."
"That is the man," said Mr. Jaggers, "in New South Wales."
"And only he?" I said.
"And only he," said Mr. Jaggers.
"I am not so unreasonable, sir, as to hold you responsible for my mistakes and wrong conclusions. But I always supposed it was Miss Havisham."
"As you say, Pip," returned Mr. Jaggers, turning his cool eyes on me and biting his forefinger, "I am not at all responsible for that."
"And yet it looked so much like it, sir," I pleaded, downhearted.
"Not a particle of evidence, Pip," said Mr. Jaggers, shaking his head and gathering up his coat-tails. "Take nothing on its looks. Take everything on evidence. There's no better rule."
"I have nothing more to say," I said with a sigh, after standing silent for a moment. "I've verified my information, and there's an end of it."

"And Magwitch — in New South Wales — having at last revealed himself," said Mr. Jaggers, "you will understand, Pip, how rigidly throughout my dealings with you, I have always kept to the strict line of fact. There has never been the least departure from the strict line of fact. You are quite aware of that?"
"Quite, sir."

"I communicated to Magwitch — in New South Wales — when he first wrote to me — from New South Wales — the warning that he must never expect me to deviate from the strict line of fact. I also communicated another warning. He appeared to me to have vaguely hinted in his letter at some distant idea of seeing you in England. I warned him that I must hear no more of that — that he was not at all likely to obtain a pardon, that he was transported for life, and that his appearing in this country would be an act of felony, liable to the extreme penalty of the law. I gave Magwitch that warning," said Mr. Jaggers, looking hard at me. "I wrote it to New South Wales. He guided himself by it, no doubt."
"No doubt," I said.
"I have been informed by Wemmick," continued Mr. Jaggers, still looking hard at me, "that he has received a letter, dated from Portsmouth, from a colonist by the name of Purvis, or —"
"Or Provis," I suggested.
"Or Provis — thank you, Pip. Perhaps it is Provis? Perhaps you know it's Provis?"
"Yes," I said.

"You know it's Provis. A letter, dated from Portsmouth, from a colonist named Provis, asking for the details of your address, on behalf of Magwitch. Wemmick sent him the details, I understand, by return of post. Presumably it is through Provis that you have received the explanation of Magwitch — in New South Wales?"
"It came through Provis," I replied.

"Good day, Pip," said Mr. Jaggers, offering his hand. "Glad to have seen you. In writing by post to Magwitch — in New South Wales — or in communicating with him through Provis, have the goodness to mention that the details and vouchers of our long account shall be sent to you, together with the balance — for there is still a balance remaining. Good day, Pip!"

We shook hands, and he looked hard at me as long as he could see me. I turned at the door, and he was still staring at me, while the two hideous death-mask casts on the shelf seemed to be trying to get their eyelids open and to force out of their swollen throats, "Oh, what a man he is!"

Wemmick was out, and even if he'd been at his desk, he could have done nothing for me. I went straight back to the Temple, where I found the terrible Provis drinking rum and water and smoking negro-head tobacco, safe and sound.

The next day all the clothes I'd ordered arrived, and he put them on. Whatever he wore looked worse on him — it dismally seemed to me — than what he'd had on before. To my thinking, there was something about him that made it hopeless to try to disguise him. The more I dressed him and the better I dressed him, the more he looked like the slouching fugitive on the marshes. This effect on my anxious imagination was partly due, no doubt, to his old face and manner growing more familiar to me. But I believe too that he dragged one leg as if there were still a weight of iron on it, and that from head to foot there was Convict in the very grain of the man.

The marks of his solitary hut-life were on him besides, giving him a savage air that no clothes could tame. Added to these were the marks of his years as a branded man among other men. And crowning all was his awareness that he was dodging and hiding now. In all his ways of sitting and standing, eating and drinking — his brooding about in a high-shouldered, reluctant style — his pulling out his great horn-handled jackknife and wiping it on his trousers before cutting his food — his lifting delicate glasses and cups to his lips as if they were clumsy tin mugs — his chopping a wedge off his bread and soaking up the last traces of gravy round and round his plate, as if making the most of a prison ration, and then drying his fingertips on it, and then swallowing it — in these ways and a thousand other small instances arising every minute of the day, there was Prisoner, Felon, Bondsman, plain as plain could be.

It had been his own idea to wear that touch of powder, and I had agreed to the powder only after defeating the shorts. But the effect of it, once on, was like rouge on a dead man's face. Everything in him that I most wanted to suppress seemed to start through that thin layer of pretence and come blazing out at the crown of his head. It was abandoned as soon as tried, and he wore his grizzled hair cut short.

Words cannot describe the sense I had, at the same time, of the dreadful mystery he was to me. When he fell asleep of an evening, with his knotted hands gripping the sides of the easy-chair, and his bald head tattooed with deep wrinkles falling forward on his chest, I would sit and stare at him, wondering what he had done, loading him with every crime in the calendar, until the urge to leap up and flee from him was almost overpowering. Every hour increased my loathing of him so much that I think I might have given in to this impulse in the first agony of being so haunted — despite all he had done for me and the risk he ran — but for the knowledge that Herbert must soon come back. Once, I actually did start out of bed in the night and begin dressing in my worst clothes, frantically intending to leave him there with everything else I possessed and enlist for India as a private soldier.

I doubt that a ghost could have been more terrible to me, up in those lonely rooms through the long evenings and long nights, with the wind and rain always rushing by. A ghost couldn't have been arrested and hanged on my account, and knowing that he could be — dreading that he would be — added considerably to my horrors. When he was not asleep, or playing a complicated kind of Patience with a ragged pack of his own cards — a game I'd never seen before or since, in which he recorded his winnings by sticking his jackknife into the table — when he was not occupied with either of these pursuits, he would ask me to read to him. "Foreign language, dear boy!" While I obliged, he would stand before the fire surveying me with the air of a showman, not comprehending a single word. Between the fingers of the hand I used to shade my face, I would see him gesturing in silent appeal to the furniture to take notice of my accomplishments. The imaginary student pursued by the misshapen creature he had wickedly made was not more wretched than I, pursued by the creature who had made me, recoiling from him with a stronger revulsion the more he admired me and the fonder he grew of me.

I am aware that I write of this as though it lasted a year. It lasted about five days. Expecting Herbert the whole time, I dared not go out except to take Provis for a walk after dark. At length, one evening when dinner was over and I had dropped into a doze, quite worn out — for my nights had been restless and my sleep broken by fearful dreams — I was roused by the welcome footstep on the staircase. Provis, who had been asleep too, staggered up at the noise I made, and in an instant I saw his jackknife gleaming in his hand.
"Quiet! It's Herbert!" I said. And Herbert came bursting in, with the airy freshness of six hundred miles of France upon him.

"Handel, my dear fellow, how are you? And again, how are you? And again, how are you? I seem to have been gone a whole year! Why, so I must have been, for you've grown quite thin and pale! Handel, my — Hullo! I beg your pardon."
He was stopped in his rush to shake my hand by the sight of Provis. Provis, regarding him with a fixed stare, was slowly putting up his jackknife and groping in another pocket for something else.
"Herbert, my dear friend," I said, shutting the double doors while Herbert stood staring in amazement, "something very strange has happened. This is — a visitor of mine."

"It's all right, dear boy!" said Provis, coming forward with his little clasped black book and then addressing Herbert. "Take it in your right hand. Lord strike you dead on the spot if ever you breathe a word! Kiss it!"

"Do as he asks," I said to Herbert. So Herbert, looking at me with friendly bewilderment and amazement, obeyed. Provis immediately shook hands with him and said, "Now you're on your oath, you know. And never believe me on mine, if Pip shan't make a gentleman of you!"

chapters.title: Chapter 41
paragraphs: It would be useless to try to describe Herbert's astonishment and distress when he, Provis, and I sat down before the fire, and I told him the whole secret. It is enough to say that I saw my own feelings reflected in Herbert's face — not least among them, my revulsion toward the man who had done so much for me.

What alone would have set a barrier between that man and us, even if there had been no other dividing circumstance, was his triumph in my story. Apart from his nagging sense of having been "low" on one occasion since his return — on which point he began lecturing Herbert the moment my revelation was finished — he had no idea that I might find any fault with my good fortune. His boast that he had made me a gentleman, and had come to see me live up to the part on his ample resources, was made for my benefit quite as much as for his own. And that this was a highly agreeable boast to both of us, and that we must both be very proud of it, was a conclusion firmly established in his own mind.

"Though, look here, Pip's comrade," he said to Herbert, after talking for some time, "I know very well that once since I come back — for half a minute — I've been low. I said to Pip, I knew I had been low. But don't you worry yourself about that. I ain't made Pip a gentleman, and Pip ain't going to make you a gentleman, not for me not to know what's due to both of you. Dear boy, and Pip's comrade, you two may count on me always keeping a genteel muzzle on. Muzzled I have been since that half minute when I was betrayed into lowness, muzzled I am at the present time, muzzled I ever will be."

Herbert said, "Certainly," but looked as if he found no particular comfort in this, and remained perplexed and dismayed. We were anxious for the time when he would go to his lodging and leave us alone, but he was clearly jealous of leaving us together and sat late. It was midnight before I walked him round to Essex Street and saw him safely in at his own dark door. When it closed behind him, I felt the first moment of relief I had known since the night of his arrival.

Never entirely free from an uneasy memory of the man on the stairs, I had always looked carefully around me when taking my guest out after dark and when bringing him back. I looked around me now. Difficult as it is in a large city to shake the suspicion of being watched, when the mind is conscious of danger on that score, I could not persuade myself that any of the people in sight cared about my movements. The few who were passing went on their separate ways, and the street was empty when I turned back into the Temple. Nobody had come out at the gate with us, and nobody went in at the gate with me. As I crossed by the fountain, I saw his lit windows looking bright and quiet. When I stood for a few moments in the doorway of my building before going up, Garden Court was as still and lifeless as the staircase was when I climbed it.

Herbert received me with open arms, and I had never so deeply felt what a blessing it is to have a friend. When he had spoken some kind words of sympathy and encouragement, we sat down to consider the question: What was to be done?

The chair that Provis had occupied still stood where it had been — for he had a soldier's way of camping in one spot, in one restless manner, and cycling through one round of rituals with his pipe and his negro-head tobacco and his jackknife and his pack of cards and whatnot, as if it were all laid out for him on a schedule. As I say, his chair remaining where it had stood, Herbert unconsciously sat in it, but the next moment jumped out of it, pushed it away, and took another. He had no need to say after that that he had developed a disgust for my patron, nor had I any need to confess my own. We exchanged that understanding without shaping a single word.
"What," I said to Herbert, when he was safe in another chair, "what is to be done?"
"My poor dear Handel," he replied, holding his head, "I am too stunned to think."
"So was I, Herbert, when the blow first fell. Still, something must be done. He is set on various new expenses — horses, and carriages, and lavish displays of all kinds. He must be stopped somehow."
"You mean that you can't accept —"
"How can I?" I broke in, as Herbert paused. "Think of him! Look at him!"
An involuntary shudder passed over both of us.
"Yet I am afraid the dreadful truth is, Herbert, that he is attached to me — strongly attached to me. Was there ever such a fate!"
"My poor dear Handel," Herbert repeated.

"Then," I said, "after all, even stopping short here, never taking another penny from him — think what I owe him already! Then again, I am heavily in debt — very heavily for someone who now has no expectations — and I have been trained to no trade, and I am fit for nothing."
"Well, well, well!" Herbert protested. "Don't say fit for nothing."
"What am I fit for? I know only one thing I'm fit for, and that is to go for a soldier. And I might have gone, my dear Herbert, but for the hope of taking counsel with your friendship and affection."
Of course I broke down there. And of course Herbert, beyond seizing a warm grip of my hand, pretended not to notice.

"Anyhow, my dear Handel," he said presently, "soldiering won't do. If you were to renounce this patronage and these favours, I suppose you would do so with some faint hope of one day repaying what you've already had. Not very strong, that hope, if you went soldiering! Besides, it's absurd. You would be infinitely better off in Clarriker's house, small as it is. I am working my way toward a partnership, you know."
Poor fellow! He had no idea whose money was behind it.

"But there is another question," said Herbert. "This is an ignorant, determined man who has long had one fixed idea. More than that, he seems to me — I may be wrong about him — to be a man of desperate and fierce character."
"I know he is," I returned. "Let me tell you what I've seen of it." And I told him what I had left out of my account — the encounter with the other convict.

"See, then," said Herbert. "Think of this! He comes here at the risk of his life, for the fulfilment of his fixed idea. In the moment of fulfilment, after all his toil and waiting, you pull the ground from under his feet, destroy his idea, and make his gains worthless to him. Do you see nothing he might do, in his disappointment?"
"I have seen it, Herbert, and dreamed of it, ever since the fatal night of his arrival. Nothing has been in my thoughts so clearly as his putting himself in the way of being caught."

"Then you may be sure," said Herbert, "that there would be great danger of his doing exactly that. That is his power over you as long as he remains in England, and that would be his reckless course if you abandoned him."

I was so struck by the horror of this idea — which had weighed on me from the first, and the working out of which would make me regard myself, in some sense, as his murderer — that I could not sit still, but began pacing back and forth. I said to Herbert, meanwhile, that even if Provis were recognised and arrested in spite of himself, I should be wretched as the cause, however innocently. Yes — even though I was so wretched in having him at large and near me, and even though I would far rather have worked at the forge all the days of my life than have ever come to this!
But there was no escaping the question: What was to be done?
"The first and main thing to be done," said Herbert, "is to get him out of England. You will have to go with him, and then he may be persuaded to go."
"But wherever I take him, could I prevent him from coming back?"

"My good Handel, isn't it obvious that with Newgate prison in the next street, there must be far greater risk in telling him your feelings and making him reckless here than elsewhere? If a pretext to get him away could be found in that other convict, or in anything else in his life, now."

"There again!" I said, stopping in front of Herbert, with my open hands held out as if they contained the desperation of the case. "I know nothing of his life. It has almost driven me mad to sit here night after night and see him before me, so bound up with my fortunes and misfortunes, and yet so unknown to me — except as the miserable wretch who terrified me two days in my childhood!"
Herbert got up and linked his arm in mine, and we slowly walked back and forth together, studying the carpet.
"Handel," said Herbert, stopping, "you feel convinced that you can take no further benefits from him — do you?"
"Entirely. Surely you would too, if you were in my place?"
"And you feel convinced that you must break with him?"
"Herbert, can you ask me that?"

"And you have, and are bound to have, that tenderness for the life he has risked on your account, that you must save him, if possible, from throwing it away. Then you must get him out of England before you lift a finger to free yourself. That done, free yourself, in Heaven's name, and we'll see it through together, dear old boy."
It was a comfort to shake hands on it and walk up and down again, with only that much settled.
"Now, Herbert," I said, "about learning something of his history. There is only one way that I know of. I must ask him directly."
"Yes. Ask him," said Herbert, "when we sit at breakfast in the morning." For he had said, on taking leave of Herbert, that he would come to breakfast with us.

With this plan formed, we went to bed. I had the wildest dreams about him and woke unrefreshed. I woke, too, to recover the fear I had lost in the night — the fear of his being discovered as a returned convict. Once awake, I never lost that fear.

He came round at the appointed time, took out his jackknife, and sat down to his meal. He was full of plans "for his gentleman's coming out strong, and like a gentleman," and urged me to begin spending from the pocketbook he had left in my possession. He considered the chambers and his own lodging as temporary quarters, and advised me to look at once for a "fashionable place" near Hyde Park, where he could have a bed. When he had finished his breakfast and was wiping his knife on his trouser leg, I said to him, without any preamble —
"After you left last night, I told my friend about the struggle the soldiers found you in on the marshes, when we came upon you. You remember?"
"Remember!" he said. "I should think so!"

"We want to know something about that man — and about you. It is strange to know no more about either, and particularly you, than I was able to tell last night. Isn't this as good a time as any for knowing more?"
"Well!" he said, after thinking it over. "You're on your oath, you know, Pip's comrade?"
"Assuredly," replied Herbert.
"As to anything I say, you know," he pressed. "The oath applies to all."
"I understand it to."
"And look here! Whatever I done is worked out and paid for," he insisted again.
"So be it."

He took out his black pipe and was about to fill it with negro-head tobacco, when, looking at the tangle of tobacco in his hand, he seemed to think it might tangle the thread of his story too. He put it back, stuck his pipe in a buttonhole of his coat, spread a hand on each knee, and after turning an angry eye on the fire for a few silent moments, looked round at us and said what follows.

chapters.title: Chapter 42
paragraphs: "Dear boy and Pip's comrade. I'm not going to tell you my life like a song or a storybook. But to give it to you short and simple, I'll put it in a mouthful of English. In jail and out of jail, in jail and out of jail, in jail and out of jail. There, you've got it. That's my life, pretty much, down to the time I got shipped off — after Pip stood my friend.

"I've had everything done to me, pretty well — except hanging. I've been locked up as often as a silver teakettle. I've been carted here and carted there, put out of this town and put out of that, stuck in the stocks, whipped and harried and driven. I've no more idea where I was born than you have — if that much. I first became aware of myself down in Essex, stealing turnips to live on. Someone had run away from me — a man — a tinker — and he'd taken the fire with him and left me very cold.

"I knew my name to be Magwitch, christened Abel. How did I know it? Same way I knew the birds' names in the hedges to be chaffinch, sparrow, thrush. I might have thought it was all lies together, only since the birds' names turned out true, I supposed mine did too.

"So far as I could tell, there wasn't a soul that saw young Abel Magwitch, with as little on him as in him, who didn't take fright and either drove him off or locked him up. I was taken up, taken up, taken up, to such a degree that I literally grew up taken up.

"This is how it was. When I was a ragged little creature as much to be pitied as any I ever saw — not that I looked in the mirror much, for there weren't many furnished houses open to me — I got the name of being hardened. 'This is a terribly hardened one,' they'd say to prison visitors, pointing me out. 'You might say this boy lives in jails.' Then they looked at me and I looked at them, and some of them measured my head — they'd have done better to measure my stomach — and others gave me religious pamphlets I couldn't read and made me speeches I couldn't understand. They always went on at me about the Devil. But what the Devil was I supposed to do? I had to put something in my stomach, didn't I? — But I'm getting low, and I know what's proper. Dear boy and Pip's comrade, don't you worry about me being low.

"Tramping, begging, thieving, working sometimes when I could — though that wasn't as often as you might think, until you ask yourself whether you'd have been eager to give me work yourselves — a bit of a poacher, a bit of a labourer, a bit of a wagoner, a bit of a haymaker, a bit of a peddler, a bit of most things that don't pay and lead to trouble, I grew to be a man. A deserting soldier in a traveller's rest, hiding up to his chin under a pile of potatoes, taught me to read. And a travelling giant who signed his name at a penny a time taught me to write. I wasn't locked up as often as before, but I still wore out my good share of prison keys.

"At Epsom races, more than twenty years ago, I got acquainted with a man whose skull I'd crack with this poker, like the claw of a lobster, if I had it on this hearth. His real name was Compeyson. And that's the man, dear boy, that you saw me pounding in the ditch, according to what you told your comrade after I left last night.

"He set himself up as a gentleman, this Compeyson, and he'd been to a public boarding school and had an education. He was smooth talker and knew the ways of well-born people. He was good-looking too. It was the night before the big race when I found him on the heath, in a booth I knew. He and some others were sitting among the tables when I went in, and the landlord — who knew me and was a sporting type — called him aside and said, 'I think this is a man that might suit you' — meaning me.
"Compeyson looks at me very carefully, and I look at him. He's got a watch and a chain and a ring and a breast-pin and a handsome suit of clothes.
"'Judging from appearances, you're out of luck,' says Compeyson to me.
"'Yes, master, and I've never been much in it.' I had just come out of Kingston Jail on a vagrancy charge. Not that it mightn't have been for something else — but it wasn't.
"'Luck changes,' says Compeyson. 'Perhaps yours is about to change.'
"I says, 'I hope it may. There's room.'
"'What can you do?' says Compeyson.
"'Eat and drink,' I says, 'if you'll provide the materials.'
"Compeyson laughed, looked at me again very carefully, gave me five shillings, and told me to come the next night. Same place.

"I went to Compeyson the next night, same place, and Compeyson took me on as his man and partner. And what was Compeyson's line of business, which we were to be partners in? Compeyson's business was swindling, handwriting forging, passing stolen banknotes, and the like. Every kind of trap that Compeyson could set with his brain, while keeping his own legs out of it and getting the profits and letting another man take the fall — that was Compeyson's business. He had no more heart than an iron file. He was as cold as death. And he had the cunning of the Devil I mentioned.

"There was another man in with Compeyson, called Arthur — not as a Christian name, but a surname. He was in a decline, and was a shadow to look at. He and Compeyson had been involved in a bad scheme with a rich lady some years before, and they'd made a fortune from it. But Compeyson gambled and bet it all away, so Arthur was dying, dying poor, and dying with the horrors on him. Compeyson's wife — whom Compeyson mostly kicked — was showing him some pity when she could, and Compeyson was showing pity to nothing and nobody.

"I might have taken warning from Arthur, but I didn't, and I won't pretend I was particular — for where would be the good of that, dear boy and comrade? So I went in with Compeyson, and a poor tool I was in his hands. Arthur lived at the top of Compeyson's house — over near Brentford it was — and Compeyson kept a careful account against him for board and lodging, in case he should ever get better and could work it off. But Arthur soon settled the account. The second or third time I ever saw him, he came tearing down into Compeyson's parlour late at night, in nothing but a flannel gown, his hair drenched in sweat, and he says to Compeyson's wife, 'Sally, she really is upstairs with me now, and I can't get rid of her. She's all in white,' he says, 'with white flowers in her hair, and she's terribly mad, and she's got a shroud hanging over her arm, and she says she'll put it on me at five in the morning.'
"Says Compeyson: 'Why, you fool, don't you know she's got a living body? And how could she be up there without coming through the door or in at the window and up the stairs?'

"'I don't know how she's there,' says Arthur, shivering dreadfully with the horrors, 'but she's standing in the corner at the foot of the bed, terribly mad. And over where her heart's broken — you broke it! — there's drops of blood.'
"Compeyson spoke boldly, but he was always a coward. 'Go up with this drivelling sick man,' he says to his wife, 'and Magwitch, lend her a hand, will you?' But he never went near the room himself.

"Compeyson's wife and I took him back up to bed, and he raved most dreadfully. 'Why, look at her!' he cries out. 'She's shaking the shroud at me! Don't you see her? Look at her eyes! Isn't it awful to see her so mad?' Then he cries, 'She'll put it on me, and then I'm done for! Take it away from her, take it away!' And then he grabbed hold of us and kept on talking to her and answering her, until I half believed I could see her myself.

"Compeyson's wife, being used to him, gave him some liquor to drive the horrors off, and by and by he quieted. 'Oh, she's gone! Has her keeper come for her?' he says. 'Yes,' says Compeyson's wife. 'Did you tell him to lock her in and bar her in?' 'Yes.' 'And to take that ugly thing away from her?' 'Yes, yes, all right.' 'You're a good creature,' he says, 'don't leave me, whatever you do, and thank you!'

"He rested pretty quiet until what must have been a few minutes before five, and then he starts up with a scream. 'Here she is! She's got the shroud again. She's unfolding it. She's coming out of the corner. She's coming to the bed. Hold me, both of you — one on each side — don't let her touch me with it. Ha! She missed me that time. Don't let her throw it over my shoulders. Don't let her lift me up to get it round me. She's lifting me up. Keep me down!' Then he lifted himself up hard, and was dead.

"Compeyson took it easy, as a good riddance for both sides. He and I were soon busy, and first he swore me — being ever cunning — on my own book: this here little black book, dear boy, what I swore your comrade on.

"Not to go into the things that Compeyson planned and I carried out — which would take a week — I'll simply say to you, dear boy, and Pip's comrade, that that man got me into such nets as made me his black slave. I was always in debt to him, always under his thumb, always working, always getting into danger. He was younger than me, but he had cunning and he had learning, and he outmatched me five hundred times over with no mercy. My missus that I had the hard time with — Stop, though! I haven't brought her into it —"

He looked about him in a confused way, as if he had lost his place in the book of his memory. He turned his face to the fire, spread his hands broader on his knees, lifted them off, and put them on again.

"There's no need to go into it," he said, looking round once more. "The time with Compeyson was about as hard a time as I ever had. That said, all's said. Did I tell you I was tried on my own for a lesser offence, while I was with Compeyson?"
I answered, No.

"Well!" he said, "I was, and I was convicted. As for being picked up on suspicion, that happened two or three times in the four or five years it lasted, but the evidence was never enough. At last, me and Compeyson were both charged with felony — for passing stolen banknotes — and there were other charges behind it. Compeyson says to me, 'Separate defences, no communication,' and that was all. And I was so miserably poor that I sold every piece of clothing I had, except what was on my back, before I could afford Jaggers.

"When we were put in the dock, I noticed first of all what a gentleman Compeyson looked, with his curly hair and his black clothes and his white pocket-handkerchief, and what a common sort of wretch I looked. When the prosecution opened and the evidence was laid out, I noticed how heavy it all fell on me and how light on him. When the testimony was given, I noticed how it was always me who had come forward and could be identified under oath, always me the money had been paid to, always me who had seemed to work the scheme and take the profit. But when the defence came on, then I saw the plan more clearly. For Compeyson's lawyer says, 'My lord and gentlemen, here you have before you, side by side, two persons your eyes can tell apart at a glance. One, the younger, well brought up, who will be spoken of as such. One, the elder, ill brought up, who will be spoken of as such. One, the younger, seldom if ever seen in these transactions, and only suspected. The other, the elder, always seen in them and always with his guilt brought home. Can you doubt, if only one is in it, which is the one? And if two are in it, which is by far the worst one?' And so on. And when it came to character, wasn't it Compeyson who'd been to the school? Wasn't it his school friends who were in this position and that? Wasn't it him who'd been known by witnesses at such clubs and societies, with nothing against him? And wasn't it me who'd been tried before, who'd been known up hill and down dale in jails and lock-ups? And when it came to speeches, wasn't it Compeyson who could address them with his face drooping now and then into his white pocket-handkerchief — ah, and with lines of verse in his speech, too — and wasn't it me who could only say, 'Gentlemen, this man at my side is a most precious rascal'? And when the verdict came, wasn't it Compeyson who was recommended to mercy on account of good character and bad company and giving up all the information he could against me, and wasn't it me who got nothing but Guilty? And when I says to Compeyson, 'Once out of this court, I'll smash that face of yours!' wasn't it Compeyson who begs the Judge for protection and gets two guards stood between us? And when we're sentenced, isn't it him that gets seven years and me fourteen, and isn't it him the Judge feels sorry for because he might have done so well, and isn't it me the Judge sees as an old offender of violent temper, likely to come to worse?"

He had worked himself into a state of great excitement, but he checked it, took two or three short breaths, swallowed as often, and stretching his hand toward me said, in a reassuring manner, "I ain't going to be low, dear boy!"
He had so overheated himself that he took out his handkerchief and wiped his face and head and neck and hands before he could go on.

"I had said to Compeyson that I'd smash that face of his, and I swore to God to do it. We were in the same prison-ship, but I couldn't get at him for a long time, though I tried. At last I came up behind him and hit him on the cheek to spin him round and land a real blow, when I was seen and seized. The punishment hold of that ship wasn't strong enough to hold a man who could swim and dive. I escaped to the shore, and I was hiding among the graves there, envying those who were in them and all done with life, when I first saw my boy!"
He looked at me with such affection that it made him almost repulsive to me again, though I had felt great pity for him.

"From my boy, I understood that Compeyson was out on those marshes too. Upon my soul, I half believe he escaped in his terror just to get away from me, not knowing it was me who'd got ashore. I hunted him down. I smashed his face. 'And now,' says I, 'as the worst thing I can do, caring nothing for myself, I'll drag you back.' And I'd have swum off towing him by the hair, if it had come to that, and I'd have got him back on board without the soldiers.

"Of course he had much the best of it to the last — his character was so good. He had escaped when he was made half wild by me and my murderous intentions, and his punishment was light. I was put in irons, brought to trial again, and sent away for life. I didn't stay for life, dear boy and Pip's comrade, seeing as I'm here."
He wiped himself again, as he had done before, and then slowly took his tangle of tobacco from his pocket, plucked his pipe from his buttonhole, slowly filled it, and began to smoke.
"Is he dead?" I asked, after a silence.
"Is who dead, dear boy?"
"Compeyson."
"He hopes I am, if he's alive, you may be sure," he said with a fierce look. "I never heard any more of him."
Herbert had been writing with his pencil in the cover of a book. He quietly pushed the book over to me, as Provis stood smoking with his eyes on the fire, and I read in it:
"Young Havisham's name was Arthur. Compeyson is the man who pretended to be Miss Havisham's lover."
I shut the book and nodded slightly to Herbert, and put the book aside. But neither of us said anything, and both looked at Provis as he stood smoking by the fire.

chapters.title: Chapter 43
paragraphs: Why should I pause to ask how much of my recoiling from Provis might be traced to Estella? Why should I linger to compare the state of mind in which I had tried to rid myself of the stain of prison before meeting her at the coach-office, with the state of mind in which I now reflected on the gulf between Estella in her pride and beauty, and the returned convict I was sheltering? The road would be no smoother for it, the end no better, he would not be helped, nor I excused.

A new fear had been born in my mind from his story — or rather, his story had given shape and purpose to a fear that was already there. If Compeyson were alive and should discover his return, I could hardly doubt the consequence. That Compeyson lived in mortal fear of him, neither of them could know better than I. And that such a man as Compeyson had been described to be would hesitate to free himself once and for all from a dreaded enemy by the safe means of becoming an informer was scarcely imaginable.

Never had I breathed, and never would I breathe — or so I resolved — a word of Estella to Provis. But I said to Herbert that, before I could go abroad, I must see both Estella and Miss Havisham. This was when we were left alone on the night of the day Provis told us his story. I resolved to go out to Richmond the next day, and I went.

When I presented myself at Mrs. Brandley's, Estella's maid was called to say that Estella had gone into the country. Where? To Satis House, as usual. Not as usual, I said, for she had never yet gone there without me. When was she coming back? There was a guarded quality in the answer that increased my confusion, and the answer was that her maid believed she was only coming back at all for a short while. I could make nothing of this, except that it was meant that I should make nothing of it, and I went home in complete bewilderment.

Another night's discussion with Herbert after Provis had gone home — I always walked him home and always kept a careful watch around me — led us to conclude that nothing should be said about going abroad until I came back from Miss Havisham's. In the meantime, Herbert and I were to consider separately what would be best to say: whether we should invent some pretence of fearing he was under suspicious observation, or whether I, who had never yet been abroad, should propose a trip. We both knew that I had only to suggest anything and he would agree. We also agreed that his remaining many days in his present danger was not to be thought of.

The next day I had the meanness to pretend that I was under a binding promise to go down to Joe. But I was capable of almost any meanness toward Joe or his name. Provis was to be strictly careful while I was gone, and Herbert was to watch over him as I had done. I was to be absent only one night, and on my return, the gratification of his eagerness for me to begin living as a gentleman on a grander scale was to begin. It occurred to me then — and, as I later found, to Herbert as well — that the best way to get him away across the water might be on that pretext: as if to make purchases, or the like.

Having cleared the way for my trip to Miss Havisham's, I set off by the early morning coach before it was yet light. I was out on the open country road when the day came creeping on, halting and whimpering and shivering, wrapped in patches of cloud and rags of mist, like a beggar. When we drove up to the Blue Boar after a drizzly ride, who should I see come out under the gateway, toothpick in hand, to look at the coach, but Bentley Drummle!

As he pretended not to see me, I pretended not to see him. It was a very feeble pretence on both sides — all the more feeble because we both went into the coffee-room, where he had just finished his breakfast and where I ordered mine. It was poison to me to see him in the town, for I knew very well why he had come.

Pretending to read a smeared newspaper long out of date, which had nothing half so legible in its local news as the foreign matter of coffee, pickles, fish sauces, gravy, melted butter, and wine with which it was spattered all over — as if it had taken measles in a highly irregular form — I sat at my table while he stood before the fire. By degrees it became an enormous offence to me that he stood before the fire. I got up, determined to have my share of it. I had to reach behind his legs for the poker when I went up to stir the fire, but still pretended not to know him.
"Is this a snub?" said Mr. Drummle.
"Oh!" I said, poker in hand. "It's you, is it? How do you do? I was wondering who it was, blocking the fire."
With that, I poked the fire vigorously, and having done so, planted myself side by side with Mr. Drummle, my shoulders squared and my back to the fire.
"You've just come down?" said Mr. Drummle, edging me slightly away with his shoulder.
"Yes," I said, edging him slightly away with mine.
"Beastly place," said Drummle. "Your part of the country, I think?"
"Yes," I agreed. "I'm told it's very like your Shropshire."
"Not in the least like it," said Drummle.
Here Mr. Drummle looked at his boots and I looked at mine, and then Mr. Drummle looked at my boots, and I looked at his.
"Have you been here long?" I asked, determined not to yield an inch of the fire.
"Long enough to be tired of it," returned Drummle, pretending to yawn but equally determined.
"Do you stay here long?"
"Can't say," answered Mr. Drummle. "Do you?"
"Can't say," said I.

I felt, through a tingling in my blood, that if Mr. Drummle's shoulder had claimed another hair's breadth of room, I should have shoved him into the window. Equally, if my own shoulder had pressed a similar claim, Mr. Drummle would have shoved me into the nearest box. He whistled a little. So did I.
"Large tract of marshes about here, I believe?" said Drummle.
"Yes. What of it?" said I.
Mr. Drummle looked at me, and then at my boots, and then said, "Oh!" and laughed.
"Are you amused, Mr. Drummle?"

"No," he said, "not particularly. I'm going out for a ride. I mean to explore those marshes for amusement. Out-of-the-way villages, they tell me. Curious little public-houses — and smithies — and that. Waiter!"
"Yes, sir."
"Is that horse of mine ready?"
"Brought round to the door, sir."
"I say. Look here, you sir. The lady won't ride today — the weather won't do."
"Very good, sir."
"And I don't dine, because I'm going to dine at the lady's."
"Very good, sir."

Then Drummle glanced at me with an insolent triumph on his heavy-jowled face that cut me to the heart. Dull as he was, it so infuriated me that I felt inclined to seize him bodily — as the robber in the storybook is said to have seized the old lady — and plant him on the fire.

One thing was clear to both of us: until relief came, neither could abandon the fire. There we stood, well squared up before it, shoulder to shoulder and foot to foot, with our hands behind us, not budging an inch. The horse was visible outside in the drizzle at the door, my breakfast was put on the table, Drummle's was cleared away, the waiter invited me to begin, I nodded — and we both held our ground.
"Have you been to the Grove since?" said Drummle.
"No," I said. "I had quite enough of the Finches the last time I was there."
"Was that when we had a difference of opinion?"
"Yes," I replied, very curtly.
"Come, come! They let you off easily enough," sneered Drummle. "You shouldn't have lost your temper."
"Mr. Drummle," I said, "you are not qualified to give advice on that subject. When I lose my temper — not that I admit having done so on that occasion — I don't throw glasses."
"I do," said Drummle.
After glancing at him once or twice, in a rising state of smouldering fury, I said —
"Mr. Drummle, I did not seek this conversation, and I don't find it an agreeable one."
"I'm sure it's not," he said superciliously, over his shoulder. "I don't think anything about it."
"And therefore," I went on, "with your leave, I will suggest that we have no further communication."
"Quite my opinion," said Drummle, "and what I should have suggested myself, or done — more likely — without suggesting. But don't lose your temper. Haven't you lost enough without that?"
"What do you mean, sir?"
"Waiter!" said Drummle, by way of answering me.
The waiter reappeared.
"Look here, you sir. You quite understand that the young lady doesn't ride today, and that I dine at the young lady's?"
"Quite so, sir!"

When the waiter had felt my fast-cooling teapot with the palm of his hand and had looked imploringly at me and had gone out, Drummle — careful not to move the shoulder nearest me — took a cigar from his pocket and bit the end off, but showed no sign of stirring. Choking and boiling as I was, I felt that we could not exchange another word without bringing up Estella's name, which I could not bear to hear him speak. So I stared stonily at the opposite wall as if no one were present, and forced myself into silence. How long we might have remained in this absurd position it is impossible to say, had it not been for the arrival of three hearty farmers — sent in by the waiter, I think — who came into the coffee-room unbuttoning their greatcoats and rubbing their hands, and before whom, as they charged at the fire, we were forced to give way.

I saw him through the window, seizing his horse's mane and mounting in his clumsy, brutal manner, then sidling and backing away. I thought he was gone, when he came back, calling for a light for the cigar in his mouth, which he had forgotten. A man in a dust-coloured coat appeared with what was needed — I couldn't have said from where, whether from the inn yard or the street or elsewhere — and as Drummle leaned down from the saddle and lit his cigar and laughed, jerking his head toward the coffee-room windows, the slouching shoulders and ragged hair of this man whose back was toward me reminded me of Orlick.

Too heavily out of sorts to care much at the time whether it was him or not, or even to touch my breakfast, I washed the weather and the journey from my face and hands, and went out to the memorable old house that it would have been so much the better for me never to have entered, never to have seen.

chapters.title: Chapter 44
paragraphs: In the room where the dressing-table stood and the wax candles burned on the wall, I found Miss Havisham and Estella. Miss Havisham sat on a settee near the fire, and Estella on a cushion at her feet. Estella was knitting, and Miss Havisham was looking on. They both raised their eyes as I came in, and both saw a change in me. I gathered as much from the look they exchanged.
"And what wind," said Miss Havisham, "blows you here, Pip?"

Though she looked steadily at me, I saw that she was rather flustered. Estella paused a moment in her knitting with her eyes on me, then went on. I fancied I could read in the movement of her fingers, as plainly as if she had told me in sign language, that she had guessed I had discovered my real benefactor.
"Miss Havisham," I said, "I went to Richmond yesterday to speak to Estella. Finding that some wind had blown her here, I followed."

Miss Havisham motioned me for the third or fourth time to sit down. I took the chair by the dressing-table, which I had often seen her occupy. With all that ruin at my feet and about me, it seemed a natural place for me that day.

"What I had to say to Estella, Miss Havisham, I will say before you, presently — in a few moments. It will not surprise you, it will not displease you. I am as unhappy as you can ever have meant me to be."
Miss Havisham continued to look steadily at me. I could see in the movement of Estella's fingers as they worked that she was listening to what I said, but she did not look up.

"I have found out who my patron is. It is not a fortunate discovery, and is not likely ever to enrich me in reputation, standing, fortune, or anything. There are reasons why I must say no more. It is not my secret, but another's."
As I was silent for a while, looking at Estella and considering how to go on, Miss Havisham repeated, "It is not your secret, but another's. Well?"

"When you first had me brought here, Miss Havisham — when I belonged to the village over yonder, which I wish I had never left — I suppose I really did come here as any other chance boy might have come: as a kind of servant, to gratify a want or a whim, and to be paid for it?"
"Yes, Pip," replied Miss Havisham, steadily nodding her head. "You did."
"And that Mr. Jaggers —"

"Mr. Jaggers," said Miss Havisham, cutting me off in a firm tone, "had nothing to do with it, and knew nothing of it. His being my lawyer and his being the lawyer of your patron is a coincidence. He holds the same relation to numbers of people, and it might easily have occurred. Be that as it may, it did occur, and was not arranged by anyone."
Anyone might have seen in her haggard face that there was no suppression or evasion so far.
"But when I fell into the mistake I have so long remained in — at least you encouraged me in it?" I said.
"Yes," she returned, nodding steadily again. "I let you go on."
"Was that kind?"
"Who am I," cried Miss Havisham, striking her stick upon the floor and flashing into rage so suddenly that Estella glanced up at her in surprise — "who am I, for God's sake, that I should be kind?"
It was a weak complaint to have made, and I had not meant to make it. I told her so, as she sat brooding after this outburst.
"Well, well, well!" she said. "What else?"

"I was generously paid for my old attendance here," I said, to soothe her, "in being apprenticed, and I have asked these questions only for my own understanding. What follows has another — and I hope more selfless — purpose. In encouraging my mistake, Miss Havisham, you punished — practised upon — perhaps you will supply whatever term expresses your intention, without offence — your self-seeking relatives?"

"I did. Why, they would have it so! So would you. What has my history been, that I should take the trouble of begging either them or you not to have it so! You made your own traps. I never made them."
Waiting until she was calm again — for this, too, had flashed out of her in a wild and sudden way — I went on.

"I have been thrown among one branch of your relations, Miss Havisham, and have been constantly among them since I went to London. I know them to have been as honestly deceived as I was myself. And I should be false and base if I did not tell you — whether you accept it or not, whether you believe it or not — that you deeply wrong both Mr. Matthew Pocket and his son Herbert if you suppose them to be anything but generous, upright, open, and incapable of anything scheming or mean."
"They are your friends," said Miss Havisham.
"They made themselves my friends," I said, "when they supposed me to have displaced them. And when Sarah Pocket, Miss Georgiana, and Mistress Camilla were not my friends, I think."
This contrasting of them with the rest seemed, I was glad to see, to do them good in her eyes. She looked at me keenly for a little while, then said quietly —
"What do you want for them?"
"Only," I said, "that you would not lump them together with the others. They may be of the same blood, but believe me, they are not of the same nature."
Still looking at me keenly, Miss Havisham repeated —
"What do you want for them?"

"I am not so cunning, you see," I said in answer, conscious that I was blushing slightly, "as to be able to hide from you, even if I wished to, that I do want something. Miss Havisham, if you would spare the money to do my friend Herbert a lasting service in life — but one which, by its nature, must be done without his knowledge — I could show you how."
"Why must it be done without his knowledge?" she asked, settling her hands on her stick so she might study me more closely.

"Because," I said, "I began the service myself more than two years ago, without his knowledge, and I don't want to be exposed. Why I am unable to finish it, I cannot explain. It is part of the secret which belongs to another person, not to me."

She gradually withdrew her eyes from me and turned them on the fire. After watching it for what seemed, in the silence and the light of the slowly wasting candles, a long time, she was roused by the collapse of some of the red coals and looked toward me again — at first vacantly, then with a gradually focusing attention. All this time Estella knitted on. When Miss Havisham had fixed her attention on me, she said, speaking as if there had been no pause in our conversation —
"What else?"
"Estella," I said, turning to her now and trying to steady my trembling voice, "you know I love you. You know that I have loved you long and dearly."

She raised her eyes to my face on being addressed this way, and her fingers kept working, and she looked at me with an unmoved expression. I saw that Miss Havisham glanced from me to her and from her to me.

"I should have said this sooner, but for my long mistake. It led me to hope that Miss Havisham meant us for one another. While I thought you could not help yourself, as it were, I held back from saying it. But I must say it now."
Keeping her expression unchanged, her fingers still going, Estella shook her head.

"I know," I said, in answer to that gesture. "I know. I have no hope that I shall ever call you mine, Estella. I have no idea what may become of me very soon — how poor I may be, or where I may go. Still, I love you. I have loved you ever since I first saw you in this house."
Looking at me perfectly unmoved, her fingers busy, she shook her head again.

"It would have been cruel of Miss Havisham — horribly cruel — to play upon the feelings of a poor boy and to torture me through all these years with a vain hope and an idle pursuit, if she had considered the weight of what she did. But I think she did not. I think that, in the endurance of her own suffering, she forgot mine, Estella."
I saw Miss Havisham put her hand to her heart and hold it there, as she sat looking by turns at Estella and at me.

"It seems," said Estella, very calmly, "that there are sentiments, fancies — I don't know what to call them — which I am not able to understand. When you say you love me, I know what you mean as a form of words, but nothing more. You reach nothing in my heart. You touch nothing there. I don't care for what you say at all. I have tried to warn you of this. Now, have I not?"
I said in a miserable tone, "Yes."
"Yes. But you would not be warned, because you thought I didn't mean it. Now, didn't you think so?"
"I thought and hoped you could not mean it. You, so young, untried, and beautiful, Estella! Surely it is not in Nature."

"It is in my nature," she returned. And then she added, with emphasis on the words, "It is in the nature formed within me. I make a great distinction between you and all other people when I say so much. I can do no more."
"Is it not true," I said, "that Bentley Drummle is in town here, and pursuing you?"
"It is quite true," she replied, referring to him with the indifference of utter contempt.
"That you encourage him, and ride out with him, and that he dines with you this very day?"
She seemed a little surprised that I should know it, but again replied, "Quite true."
"You cannot love him, Estella!"
Her fingers stopped for the first time, as she retorted rather angrily, "What have I told you? Do you still think, in spite of it, that I don't mean what I say?"
"You would never marry him, Estella?"
She looked toward Miss Havisham and considered for a moment with her work in her hands. Then she said, "Why not tell you the truth? I am going to be married to him."

I dropped my face into my hands, but managed to control myself better than I might have expected, considering the agony it gave me to hear her say those words. When I raised my face again, there was such a ghastly look on Miss Havisham's that it struck me even through my passionate grief.

"Estella, dearest Estella, do not let Miss Havisham lead you into this fatal step. Put me aside forever — you have done so, I know — but give yourself to some worthier person than Drummle. Miss Havisham is giving you to him as the greatest insult and injury that could be dealt to the many far better men who admire you, and to the few who truly love you. Among those few there may be one who loves you even as dearly, though he has not loved you as long, as I. Take him, and I can bear it better, for your sake!"
My earnestness stirred a wonder in her that seemed as though it would have been touched with compassion, if she could have made any sense of me at all.

"I am going," she said again, in a gentler voice, "to be married to him. The preparations for my marriage are underway, and I shall be married soon. Why do you insultingly bring in the name of my mother by adoption? It is my own decision."
"Your own decision, Estella, to throw yourself away on a brute?"

"On whom should I throw myself away?" she retorted, with a smile. "Should I throw myself away on the man who would soonest feel — if people do feel such things — that I brought nothing to him? There! It is done. I shall do well enough, and so will my husband. As for leading me into what you call this fatal step, Miss Havisham would have had me wait and not marry yet. But I am tired of the life I have led, which has very few charms for me, and I am willing enough to change it. Say no more. We shall never understand each other."
"Such a mean brute, such a stupid brute!" I urged, in despair.
"Don't be afraid of my being a blessing to him," said Estella. "I shall not be that. Come! Here is my hand. Do we part on this, you visionary boy — or man?"

"Oh, Estella!" I answered, as my bitter tears fell fast on her hand, do what I would to hold them back. "Even if I remained in England and could hold my head up with the rest, how could I see you as Drummle's wife?"
"Nonsense," she returned. "Nonsense. This will pass in no time."
"Never, Estella!"
"You will get me out of your thoughts in a week."

"Out of my thoughts! You are part of my existence, part of myself. You have been in every line I have ever read since I first came here, the rough common boy whose poor heart you wounded even then. You have been in every view I have ever seen since — on the river, on the sails of the ships, on the marshes, in the clouds, in the light, in the darkness, in the wind, in the woods, in the sea, in the streets. You have been the embodiment of every graceful idea that my mind has ever known. The stones of which the strongest London buildings are made are not more real, or more impossible to be moved by your hands, than your presence and influence have been to me, there and everywhere, and will be. Estella, to the last hour of my life, you cannot choose but remain part of my character, part of the little good in me, part of the evil. But in this separation, I associate you only with the good, and I will faithfully hold you to that always, for you must have done me far more good than harm, whatever sharp pain I may feel now. Oh God bless you, God forgive you!"

In what agony of unhappiness I got these broken words out of myself, I don't know. The outpouring welled up within me like blood from an inward wound, and gushed out. I held her hand to my lips for some lingering moments, and so I left her. But ever afterwards I remembered — and soon afterwards with stronger reason — that while Estella looked at me merely with incredulous wonder, the spectral figure of Miss Havisham, her hand still covering her heart, seemed entirely dissolved into a ghastly stare of pity and remorse.

All done, all gone! So much was done and gone that when I went out at the gate, the light of the day seemed darker than when I went in. For a while I hid myself among lanes and byways, and then struck off to walk all the way to London.
