For I had by that time recovered myself enough to realise that I could not go back to the inn and see Drummle there, that I could not bear to sit on the coach and be spoken to, that I could do nothing half so good for myself as tire myself out.

It was past midnight when I crossed London Bridge. Following the narrow winding streets which at that time ran westward near the Middlesex shore of the river, my nearest way to the Temple was close by the riverside, through Whitefriars. I was not expected until tomorrow, but I had my keys, and if Herbert had gone to bed, I could get to bed myself without disturbing him.

Since it rarely happened that I came in at the Whitefriars gate after the Temple was closed, and since I was very muddy and weary, I did not take offence when the night-porter examined me closely as he held the gate slightly open for me to pass through. To help his memory, I mentioned my name.
"I was not quite sure, sir, but I thought so. Here's a note, sir. The messenger that brought it said would you be so good as to read it by my lantern?"

Much surprised by the request, I took the note. It was addressed to Philip Pip, Esquire, and on the top of the address were the words, "PLEASE READ THIS, HERE." I opened it, the watchman holding up his light, and read inside, in Wemmick's handwriting —
"DON'T GO HOME."

chapters.title: Chapter 45
paragraphs: Turning from the Temple gate as soon as I had read the warning, I made the best of my way to Fleet Street, where I got a late hackney cab and drove to the Hummums in Covent Garden. In those times a bed could always be had there at any hour of the night. The chamberlain, letting me in at his ready wicket, lit the next candle on his shelf and showed me straight into the next bedroom on his list. It was a sort of vault on the ground floor at the back, with a monstrous four-poster bed straddling over the whole space, thrusting one of its arbitrary legs into the fireplace and another into the doorway, and squeezing the wretched little washstand into a corner with tyrannical authority.

Since I had asked for a night-light, the chamberlain had brought me, before he left, the trusty old rushlight of those virtuous days — an object like the ghost of a walking-cane, which instantly snapped in half if touched, which nothing could ever be lit from, and which was placed in solitary confinement at the bottom of a tall tin tower, pierced with round holes that cast a strikingly wide-awake pattern on the walls. When I had got into bed and lay there footsore, weary, and wretched, I found that I could no more close my own eyes than I could close the eyes of this foolish Argus. And so, in the gloom and death of the night, we stared at one another.

What a wretched night! How anxious, how dismal, how long! There was an inhospitable smell in the room of cold soot and hot dust. As I looked up into the corners of the canopy above my head, I thought what a number of bluebottle flies from the butchers', and earwigs from the market, and grubs from the country, must be clinging up there, lying in wait for next summer. This led me to wonder whether any of them ever fell down, and then I imagined I felt light drops on my face — a disagreeable turn of thought, suggesting other and more objectionable visitors crawling up my back. When I had lain awake a little while, those extraordinary voices with which silence teems began to make themselves heard. The closet whispered, the fireplace sighed, the little washstand ticked, and one guitar-string played occasionally in the chest of drawers. At about the same time, the holes in the wall acquired a new expression, and in every one of those staring circles I saw written: DON'T GO HOME.

Whatever night-terrors and night-noises crowded in on me, they never drove off this DON'T GO HOME. It wove itself into whatever I thought of, as bodily pain would have done. Not long before, I had read in the newspapers how an unknown gentleman had come to the Hummums in the night, gone to bed, and killed himself, and been found in the morning drenched in blood. It came into my head that he must have occupied this very vault of mine, and I got out of bed to make sure there were no red marks about. Then I opened the door to look out into the passage and cheer myself with the companionship of a distant light, near which I knew the chamberlain to be dozing. But all this time, why I was not to go home, and what had happened at home, and when I should go home, and whether Provis was safe at home, were questions occupying my mind so intensely that you might have thought there was no room for any other subject. Even when I thought of Estella — how we had parted that day forever — and when I recalled every detail of our parting, all her looks and tones, the movement of her fingers while she knitted — even then I was pursuing, here and there and everywhere, the warning: Don't go home. When at last I dozed, in sheer exhaustion of mind and body, it became a vast shadowy verb which I had to conjugate. Imperative mood, present tense: Do not thou go home, let him not go home, let us not go home, do not ye or you go home, let not them go home. Then potentially: I may not and I cannot go home; and I might not, could not, would not, and should not go home — until I felt I was going mad, and rolled over on the pillow, and stared at the round holes on the wall again.

I had left instructions to be called at seven, for it was plain that I must see Wemmick before seeing anyone else, and equally plain that this was a case where only his Walworth feelings could be trusted. It was a relief to escape the room where the night had been so miserable, and I needed no second knock at the door to start me from my restless bed.

The Castle battlements rose into view at eight o'clock. The little servant happened to be entering the fortress with two hot rolls, so I passed through the gate and crossed the drawbridge in her company, and came unannounced into the presence of Wemmick as he was making tea for himself and the Aged. An open door offered a view of the Aged in bed.
"Hullo, Mr. Pip!" said Wemmick. "You did come home, then?"
"Yes," I returned, "but I didn't go home."
"That's all right," he said, rubbing his hands. "I left a note for you at each of the Temple gates, on the chance. Which gate did you come to?"
I told him.

"I'll go round to the others during the day and destroy the notes," said Wemmick. "It's a good rule never to leave documentary evidence if you can help it, because you don't know when it may be produced. I'm going to take a liberty with you. Would you mind toasting this sausage for the Aged P.?"
I said I should be delighted.
"Then you can go about your work, Mary Anne," said Wemmick to the little servant. "Which leaves us to ourselves, don't you see, Mr. Pip?" he added, winking, as she disappeared.
I thanked him for his friendship and caution, and our conversation proceeded in a low tone while I toasted the Aged's sausage and he buttered the crust of the Aged's roll.

"Now, Mr. Pip, you know," said Wemmick, "you and I understand one another. We are in our private and personal capacities, and we have been involved in a confidential matter before today. Official sentiments are one thing. We are extra-official."
I heartily agreed. I was so nervous that I had already set the Aged's sausage ablaze like a torch and been forced to blow it out.
"I happened to hear, yesterday morning," said Wemmick, "being in a certain place where I once took you — even between you and me, it's best not to mention names when avoidable —"
"Much better not," I said. "I understand you."

"I heard there by chance, yesterday morning," said Wemmick, "that a certain person not entirely unconnected with colonial pursuits, and not without portable property — I don't know who it may really be — we won't name this person —"
"Not necessary," I said.
"— Had caused some little stir in a certain part of the world where a good many people go, not always by their own choice, and not entirely without government funding —"
In watching his face, I turned the Aged's sausage into quite a firework, and greatly disturbed both my own attention and Wemmick's, for which I apologised.

"— By disappearing from such place and being no more heard of there. From which," said Wemmick, "guesses had been made and theories formed. I also heard that you, at your chambers in Garden Court, Temple, had been watched, and might be watched again."
"By whom?" I said.

"I wouldn't go into that," said Wemmick evasively. "It might conflict with official responsibilities. I heard it, as I have heard other curious things in my time in the same place. I don't tell you this on information received. I heard it."

He took the toasting-fork and sausage from me as he spoke, and neatly laid out the Aged's breakfast on a little tray. Before placing it in front of him, he went into the Aged's room with a clean white cloth, tied it under the old gentleman's chin, propped him up, set his nightcap at a jaunty angle, and gave him quite a rakish air. Then he placed the breakfast before him with great care and said, "All right, aren't you, Aged P.?" To which the cheerful Aged replied, "All right, John, my boy, all right!" Since there seemed to be an unspoken understanding that the Aged was not in a presentable state and was therefore to be considered invisible, I pretended to be completely unaware of these proceedings.
"This watching of me at my chambers — which I have once had reason to suspect," I said to Wemmick when he came back, "is connected to the person you've referred to, is it?"
Wemmick looked very grave. "I couldn't say that from my own knowledge. I mean, I couldn't say it was so at first. But it either is, or it will be, or it's in great danger of being."

Since I could see he was held back by his loyalty to Little Britain from saying as much as he could, and since I knew with gratitude how far out of his way he had gone to say what he did, I could not press him. But I told him, after a little reflection by the fire, that I would like to ask him a question, subject to his answering or not as he thought right, trusting that his judgment would be sound. He paused in his breakfast and, crossing his arms and pinching his shirt-sleeves — his idea of indoor comfort was to sit without any coat — he nodded once, for me to put my question.
"You have heard of a man of bad character whose real name is Compeyson?"
He answered with a single nod.
"Is he living?"
Another nod.
"Is he in London?"
He gave me one more nod, compressed his lips extremely tight, gave me one final nod, and went on with his breakfast.

"Now," said Wemmick, "questioning being over" — which he emphasised and repeated for my guidance — "I come to what I did after hearing what I heard. I went to Garden Court to find you. Not finding you, I went to Clarriker's to find Mr. Herbert."
"And you found him?" I said, with great anxiety.

"And I found him. Without mentioning any names or going into any details, I gave him to understand that if he was aware of anybody — Tom, Jack, or Richard — being about the chambers or the immediate neighbourhood, he had better get Tom, Jack, or Richard out of the way while you were out of the way."
"He must have been greatly puzzled about what to do?"

"He was puzzled what to do — all the more because I gave him my opinion that it was not safe to try to get Tom, Jack, or Richard too far away at present. Mr. Pip, I'll tell you something. Under the circumstances, there is no place like a great city when you're once in it. Don't break cover too soon. Lie low. Wait until things calm down before you try the open, even for foreign air."
I thanked him for his valuable advice and asked what Herbert had done.

"Mr. Herbert," said Wemmick, "after being in a state of shock for half an hour, came up with a plan. He mentioned to me as a secret that he is courting a young lady who has, as no doubt you are aware, a bedridden father. Which father, having been in the shipping business, lies in bed in a bow-window where he can watch the ships sail up and down the river. You are acquainted with the young lady, most probably?"
"Not personally," I said.

The truth was that she had objected to me as an expensive friend who did Herbert no good. When Herbert had first proposed to introduce me, she had received the idea with such lukewarm enthusiasm that Herbert had felt obliged to tell me privately, suggesting we wait a little before I made her acquaintance. When I had begun to advance Herbert's prospects in secret, I had been able to accept this philosophically. He and his fiancée, for their part, had naturally not been eager to introduce a third person into their time together. So, although I was assured that I had risen in Clara's esteem, and although she and I had long exchanged messages and greetings through Herbert, I had never met her. However, I did not trouble Wemmick with these details.

"The house with the bow-window," said Wemmick, "being by the riverside, down the Pool between Limehouse and Greenwich, and being kept, it seems, by a very respectable widow who has a furnished upper floor to let — Mr. Herbert put it to me, what did I think of that as a temporary lodging for Tom, Jack, or Richard? Now, I thought very well of it, for three reasons I'll give you. Firstly, it's completely outside all your usual areas, and well away from the common heap of streets great and small. Secondly, without going near it yourself, you could always hear of the safety of Tom, Jack, or Richard through Mr. Herbert. Thirdly, after a while, when it might be safe, if you should want to slip Tom, Jack, or Richard aboard a foreign ship — there he is, ready."
Much comforted by these points, I thanked Wemmick again and again, and begged him to continue.

"Well, sir! Mr. Herbert threw himself into it with a will, and by nine o'clock last night he had housed Tom, Jack, or Richard — whichever it may be — you and I don't want to know — quite successfully. At the old lodgings it was understood that he had been summoned to Dover, and in fact he was taken down the Dover road and diverted off it. Now, another great advantage of all this is that it was done without you, and at a time when, if anyone was watching your movements, you must have been known to be miles away and otherwise occupied. This diverts suspicion and confuses it. And for the same reason I suggested that, even if you came back last night, you should not go home. It adds more confusion, and you want confusion."
Wemmick, having finished his breakfast, looked at his watch and began putting on his coat.

"And now, Mr. Pip," he said, with his hands still in the sleeves, "I have probably done the most I can do. But if I can ever do more — from a Walworth point of view, and in a strictly private and personal capacity — I shall be glad to. Here's the address. There can be no harm in your going there tonight and seeing for yourself that all is well with Tom, Jack, or Richard, before you go home — which is another reason for your not going home last night. But after you have gone home, don't go back there. You are very welcome, I am sure, Mr. Pip" — his hands were now out of his sleeves, and I was shaking them — "and let me finally impress one important point upon you." He laid his hands upon my shoulders and added in a solemn whisper: "Get hold of his portable property while you can. You don't know what may happen to him. Don't let anything happen to the portable property."
Quite despairing of making Wemmick understand my feelings on this point, I gave up trying.

"Time's up," said Wemmick, "and I must be off. If you had nothing more pressing to do than to stay here till dark, that's what I'd advise. You look very worn, and it would do you good to have a perfectly quiet day with the Aged — he'll be up presently — and a little bit of — you remember the pig?"
"Of course," I said.

"Well, and a little bit of him. That sausage you toasted was his, and he was in all respects a first-rate animal. Do try him, if only for old acquaintance's sake. Goodbye, Aged Parent!" in a cheery shout.
"All right, John! All right, my boy!" piped the old man from within.

I soon fell asleep before Wemmick's fire, and the Aged and I enjoyed one another's company by dozing before it more or less all day. We had loin of pork for dinner, with greens grown on the estate. I nodded kindly at the Aged whenever I failed to do it drowsily. When it was quite dark, I left the Aged preparing the fire for toast. And I guessed, from the number of teacups as well as from his glances at the two little doors in the wall, that Miss Skiffins was expected.

chapters.title: Chapter 46
paragraphs: It was past eight o'clock before I got into the air, which was scented, not unpleasantly, by the chips and shavings of the riverside boat-builders and makers of masts, oars, and blocks. All that waterside region of the upper and lower Pool below Bridge was unknown ground to me. When I struck down by the river, I found that the spot I wanted was not where I'd supposed it to be, and was anything but easy to find. It was called Mill Pond Bank, Chinks's Basin, and I had no other guide to Chinks's Basin than the Old Green Copper Rope-walk.

It doesn't matter what stranded ships repairing in dry docks I lost myself among, what old hulls in the process of being broken up, what ooze and slime and other dregs of the tide, what shipbuilders' and ship-breakers' yards, what rusty anchors blindly biting into the ground though off duty for years, what mountainous country of stacked casks and timber, how many rope-walks that were not the Old Green Copper. After several times falling short of my destination and as often overshooting it, I came unexpectedly round a corner upon Mill Pond Bank. It was a surprisingly fresh kind of place, all things considered, where the wind from the river had room to turn itself around. There were two or three trees in it, and the stump of a ruined windmill, and the Old Green Copper Rope-walk — whose long, narrow vista I could trace in the moonlight along a series of wooden frames set in the ground, looking like ancient haymaking-rakes that had grown old and lost most of their teeth.

Selecting from the few odd houses on Mill Pond Bank one with a wooden front and three stories of bow-window — not bay-window, which is a different thing — I looked at the nameplate on the door and read Mrs. Whimple. That being the name I wanted, I knocked, and an elderly woman of pleasant and prosperous appearance answered. She was immediately replaced, however, by Herbert, who silently led me into the parlour and shut the door. It was a strange sensation to see his very familiar face so perfectly at home in that very unfamiliar room and neighbourhood. I found myself looking at him much as I looked at the corner-cupboard with its glass and china, the shells on the chimney-piece, and the coloured prints on the wall showing the death of Captain Cook, a ship-launch, and His Majesty King George the Third in a coachman's wig, leather breeches, and top-boots, on the terrace at Windsor.

"All is well, Handel," said Herbert, "and he is quite settled, though eager to see you. My dear girl is with her father. If you'll wait till she comes down, I'll introduce you, and then we'll go upstairs. That's her father."
I had become aware of an alarming growling overhead, and had probably shown it in my expression.
"I'm afraid he is a terrible old rogue," said Herbert, smiling, "but I have never seen him. Don't you smell rum? He's always at it."
"At rum?" I said.

"Yes," returned Herbert, "and you can imagine how that helps his gout. He also insists on keeping all the provisions upstairs in his room and doling them out. He keeps them on shelves over his head and insists on weighing everything. His room must be like a chandler's shop."
While he was speaking, the growling noise became a prolonged roar, and then died away.

"What else can you expect," said Herbert, by way of explanation, "if he insists on cutting the cheese? A man with gout in his right hand — and everywhere else — can't expect to get through a Double Gloucester without hurting himself."
He seemed to have hurt himself badly, for he gave another furious roar.
"Having Provis for an upstairs lodger is a godsend to Mrs. Whimple," said Herbert, "because of course most people won't put up with that noise. A curious place, Handel, isn't it?"
It was indeed a curious place, but remarkably well kept and clean.

"Mrs. Whimple," said Herbert, when I told him so, "is the best of housewives, and I really don't know what my Clara would do without her motherly help. For Clara has no mother of her own, Handel, and no relation in the world but old Gruffandgrim."
"Surely that's not his name, Herbert?"

"No, no," said Herbert. "That's my name for him. His name is Mr. Barley. But what a blessing it is for the son of my father and mother to love a girl who has no relations and who can never bother herself or anybody else about her family!"

Herbert had told me before, and now reminded me, that he had first known Miss Clara Barley when she was finishing her education at a school in Hammersmith. When she was called home to nurse her father, he and she had entrusted their affection to the motherly Mrs. Whimple, who had fostered and managed it with equal kindness and discretion ever since. It was understood that nothing of a romantic nature could possibly be confided to old Barley, since he was completely incapable of considering any subject more complex than Gout, Rum, and Stores.

As we were conversing in low tones while Old Barley's steady growl vibrated in the beam that crossed the ceiling, the door opened and a very pretty, slight, dark-eyed girl of about twenty came in with a basket in her hand. Herbert tenderly relieved her of the basket and introduced her, blushing, as "Clara." She really was a most charming girl and might have passed for a captive fairy whom that brutal ogre, Old Barley, had pressed into his service.

"Look here," said Herbert, showing me the basket with a tender and sympathetic smile, after we had talked a little. "Here's poor Clara's supper, served out every night. Here's her allowance of bread, and here's her slice of cheese, and here's her rum — which I drink. This is Mr. Barley's breakfast for tomorrow, served out to be cooked. Two mutton-chops, three potatoes, some split peas, a little flour, two ounces of butter, a pinch of salt, and all this black pepper. It's stewed up together and eaten hot, and it must be a fine thing for the gout, I should think!"

There was something so natural and winning in Clara's resigned way of looking at these supplies as Herbert pointed them out, something so trusting, loving, and innocent in her modest manner of yielding herself to Herbert's embracing arm, and something so gentle in her — so much needing protection on Mill Pond Bank, by Chinks's Basin and the Old Green Copper Rope-walk, with Old Barley growling in the beam — that I would not have undone the engagement between her and Herbert for all the money in the pocketbook I had never opened.

I was looking at her with pleasure and admiration when suddenly the growl swelled into a roar again, and a frightful thumping noise was heard above, as if a giant with a wooden leg were trying to bore it through the ceiling to reach us. At this, Clara said to Herbert, "Papa wants me, darling!" and ran away.
"There's an outrageous old shark for you!" said Herbert. "What do you suppose he wants now, Handel?"
"I don't know," I said. "Something to drink?"

"That's it!" cried Herbert, as if I had made a guess of extraordinary brilliance. "He keeps his grog ready-mixed in a little tub on the table. Wait a moment and you'll hear Clara lift him up to take some. There he goes!" Another roar, with a prolonged shudder at the end. "Now," said Herbert, as silence followed, "he's drinking. Now," said Herbert, as the growl resounded in the beam once more, "he's down again on his back!"

Clara returned soon afterwards, and Herbert accompanied me upstairs to see our charge. As we passed Mr. Barley's door, he could be heard hoarsely muttering within, in a rhythm that rose and fell like wind, the following refrain, in which I substitute blessings for something quite the reverse:

"Ahoy! Bless your eyes, here's old Bill Barley. Here's old Bill Barley, bless your eyes. Here's old Bill Barley on the flat of his back, by the Lord. Lying on the flat of his back like a drifting old dead flounder, here's your old Bill Barley, bless your eyes. Ahoy! Bless you."

In this vein of self-consolation, Herbert informed me, the invisible Barley would converse with himself by the day and night together. Often, while it was light, he would have one eye at a telescope that was mounted on his bed for the convenience of surveying the river.

In his two cabin-like rooms at the top of the house, which were fresh and airy, and in which Mr. Barley was less audible than below, I found Provis comfortably settled. He showed no alarm and seemed to feel none worth mentioning. But it struck me that he was softened — in some indefinable way, for I could not have said how, and could never afterwards recall how when I tried — but softened, certainly.

The day's rest had given me time to reflect, and I had firmly decided to say nothing to him about Compeyson. For all I knew, his hatred of the man might otherwise lead him to seek Compeyson out and rush headlong to his own destruction. Therefore, when Herbert and I sat down with him by his fire, I asked him first whether he trusted Wemmick's judgment and sources of information.
"Ay, ay, dear boy!" he answered, with a grave nod. "Jaggers knows."
"Then I have talked with Wemmick," I said, "and have come to tell you what warnings and advice he gave me."

This I did accurately, with the one reservation I've mentioned. I told him how Wemmick had heard, in Newgate prison — whether from officers or prisoners I could not say — that he was under some suspicion, and that my chambers had been watched. I told him how Wemmick had advised him to lie low for a time, and me to keep away from him, and what Wemmick had said about getting him abroad. I added that of course, when the time came, I would go with him, or follow close behind, as might be safest in Wemmick's judgment. What was to follow beyond that I did not touch upon. Indeed, I was not at all clear or comfortable about it in my own mind, now that I saw him in this softer state, in declared danger on my account. As for changing my lifestyle by spending more lavishly, I put it to him whether, in our present unsettled and difficult circumstances, it would not be simply absurd, if not worse.

He could not disagree, and indeed was very reasonable throughout. His coming back was a gamble, he said, and he had always known it to be one. He would do nothing to make it a desperate gamble, and he had very little fear for his safety with such good help.

Herbert, who had been staring at the fire and thinking, said that something had occurred to him arising from Wemmick's suggestion, which might be worth pursuing. "We are both good oarsmen, Handel, and could take him down the river ourselves when the right time comes. No boat would then be hired for the purpose, and no boatmen. That would eliminate at least one chance of suspicion, and every chance is worth saving. Never mind the season — don't you think it might be a good idea if you began at once to keep a boat at the Temple stairs, and got into the habit of rowing up and down the river? You fall into that habit, and then who notices or cares? Do it twenty or fifty times, and there's nothing remarkable about doing it the twenty-first or fifty-first."

I liked this plan, and Provis was thrilled by it. We agreed it should be put into action, and that Provis should never acknowledge us if we came below Bridge and rowed past Mill Pond Bank. But we further agreed that he should pull down the blind on the east-facing part of his window whenever he saw us and all was well.

Our conference being over and everything arranged, I rose to go, remarking to Herbert that he and I had better not go home together and that I would take half an hour's head start. "I don't like leaving you here," I said to Provis, "though I cannot doubt you are safer here than near me. Goodbye!"
"Dear boy," he answered, clasping my hands, "I don't know when we may meet again, and I don't like goodbye. Say good-night!"
"Good-night! Herbert will go regularly between us, and when the time comes you may be certain I shall be ready. Good-night, good-night!"

We thought it best that he should stay in his rooms. We left him on the landing outside his door, holding a light over the stair-rail to light us downstairs. Looking back at him, I thought of the first night of his return, when our positions were reversed, and when I little imagined my heart could ever be as heavy and anxious at parting from him as it was now.

Old Barley was growling and swearing when we passed his door again, with no sign of having stopped or meaning to. When we reached the foot of the stairs, I asked Herbert whether he had given the name of Provis. He said certainly not — the lodger was Mr. Campbell. He also explained that all Mrs. Whimple knew of Mr. Campbell was that Herbert had him in his charge and felt a strong personal interest in his being well cared for and living a secluded life. So when we went into the parlour where Mrs. Whimple and Clara were seated at their work, I said nothing of my own interest in Mr. Campbell but kept it to myself.

When I had said goodbye to the pretty, gentle, dark-eyed girl, and to the motherly woman who had not outgrown her honest sympathy with a little affair of true love, I felt as if the Old Green Copper Rope-walk had become quite a different place. Old Barley might be as old as the hills and might swear like a regiment of soldiers, but there was enough redeeming youth and trust and hope in Chinks's Basin to fill it to overflowing. And then I thought of Estella, and of our parting, and went home very sadly.

All was as quiet in the Temple as I had ever seen it. The windows of the rooms on that side, lately occupied by Provis, were dark and still, and there was no one loitering in Garden Court. I walked past the fountain two or three times before I went down the steps to my rooms, but I was quite alone. Herbert, coming to my bedside when he got in — for I went straight to bed, dispirited and exhausted — reported the same. Opening a window, he looked out into the moonlight and told me that the pavement was as solemnly empty as the pavement of any cathedral at that same hour.

The next day I set about getting the boat. It was soon done, and the boat was brought round to the Temple stairs, where I could reach her within a minute or two. Then I began going out as if for training and practice — sometimes alone, sometimes with Herbert. I was often out in cold, rain, and sleet, but nobody took much notice of me after the first few times. At first I stayed above Blackfriars Bridge, but as the hours of the tide changed, I moved toward London Bridge. It was Old London Bridge in those days, and at certain states of the tide there was a rush and fall of water there that gave it a dangerous reputation. But I soon learned to shoot the bridge after watching it done, and so began to row about among the shipping in the Pool and down to Erith. The first time I passed Mill Pond Bank, Herbert and I were pulling a pair of oars, and both going and returning, we saw the east-facing blind come down. Herbert was rarely there less than three times a week, and he never brought me a single piece of news that was at all alarming. Still, I knew there was cause for alarm, and I could not shake the feeling of being watched. Once that idea takes hold, it haunts you. How many innocent people I suspected of watching me, it would be hard to count.

In short, I was always full of fears for the reckless man who was in hiding. Herbert had sometimes said to me that he found it pleasant to stand at one of our windows after dark, when the tide was running out, and to think that it was flowing, with everything it carried, toward Clara. But I thought with dread that it was flowing toward Magwitch, and that any dark shape on its surface might be his pursuers, going swiftly, silently, and surely, to take him.

chapters.title: Chapter 47
paragraphs: Some weeks passed without any change. We waited for Wemmick, and he gave no sign. If I had never known him outside Little Britain, and had never enjoyed the privilege of being on familiar terms at the Castle, I might have doubted him. But knowing him as I did, I did not doubt him for a moment.

My financial affairs began to look grim, and I was pressed for money by more than one creditor. Even I myself began to feel the want of ready cash in my own pocket, and to relieve it by converting some easily spared items of jewellery into money. But I had firmly decided that it would be a heartless fraud to take more money from my patron in the current state of my uncertain thoughts and plans. So I had sent him the unopened pocketbook through Herbert, to hold in his own keeping, and I felt a kind of satisfaction — whether false or true, I hardly know — in not having profited from his generosity since his revelation of himself.

As time wore on, a heavy conviction settled upon me that Estella was married. Afraid of having it confirmed, though it was all but certain, I avoided the newspapers and begged Herbert — to whom I had confided the details of our last meeting — never to speak of her to me. Why I clung to this last wretched shred of hope, how can I say? Why did you who read this commit that not dissimilar inconsistency of your own, last year, last month, last week?

It was an unhappy life that I lived, and its one dominant anxiety, towering over all the others like a high mountain above a range of mountains, never disappeared from view. Still, no new cause for fear arose. Let me start from my bed as I might, with the terror fresh upon me that he was discovered. Let me sit listening, as I did with dread, for Herbert's returning step at night, fearing it might be faster than usual and winged with bad news. For all that, and much more to the same effect, the round of things went on. Condemned to inaction and a state of constant restlessness and suspense, I rowed about in my boat and waited, waited, waited, as best I could.

There were states of the tide when, having gone down the river, I could not get back through the churning arches and supports of old London Bridge. Then I left my boat at a wharf near the Custom House, to be brought up later to the Temple stairs. I did not mind doing this, as it made me and my boat a more familiar sight among the waterside people there. From this small circumstance came two encounters that I have now to tell of.

One afternoon, late in February, I came ashore at the wharf at dusk. I had rowed down as far as Greenwich with the ebb tide and had turned back with the flood. It had been a fine, bright day, but had turned foggy as the sun dropped, and I had had to feel my way back among the shipping fairly carefully. Both going and returning, I had seen the signal in his window: All well.

As it was a raw evening and I was cold, I thought I would treat myself to dinner at once. Since I had hours of gloom and solitude ahead if I went home to the Temple, I thought I would go to the theatre afterwards. The theatre where Mr. Wopsle had achieved his questionable success was in that waterside neighbourhood — it is gone now — and to that theatre I resolved to go. I was aware that Mr. Wopsle had not succeeded in reviving the Drama but had rather shared in its decline. He had been ominously advertised as a faithful Black, in connection with a little girl of noble birth and a monkey. And Herbert had seen him as a comic predatory Tartar, with a face like a red brick and an outrageous hat covered in bells.

I dined at what Herbert and I used to call a geographical chophouse, where there were maps of the world in beer-mug rings on every half-yard of the tablecloth, and charts of gravy on every knife — to this day there is scarcely a single chophouse in the City which is not geographical — and I killed time dozing over crumbs, staring at the gaslight, and baking in a hot blast of dinners. Eventually I roused myself and went to the play.

There I found a virtuous boatswain in His Majesty's service — a most excellent man, though I could have wished his trousers not quite so tight in some places and not quite so loose in others — who knocked all the little men's hats over their eyes, though he was very generous and brave, and who would not hear of anybody paying taxes, though he was very patriotic. He had a bag of money in his pocket like a pudding in a cloth, and on that fortune married a young person dressed in bedding, with great celebrations. The whole population of Portsmouth — nine at the last census — turned out on the beach to rub their own hands and shake everybody else's and sing "Fill, fill!" A certain dark-complexioned villain, however, who would not fill or do anything else that was suggested, and whose heart was openly stated by the boatswain to be as black as his figurehead, proposed to two other villains that they get all mankind into trouble. This was so effectively done — the villain family having considerable political influence — that it took half the evening to set things right. And then it was only managed through an honest little grocer with a white hat, black gaiters, and a red nose, who got into a clock with a gridiron, listened, came out, and knocked down from behind with the gridiron everyone he couldn't defeat with what he had overheard. This led to Mr. Wopsle — who had never been heard of before — coming in wearing a star and garter, as an all-powerful representative direct from the Admiralty, to announce that the villains were all to go to prison on the spot, and that he had brought the boatswain the Union Jack as a small token of gratitude for his public services. The boatswain, overcome for the first time, respectfully dried his eyes on the Jack, and then, cheering up and addressing Mr. Wopsle as Your Honour, asked permission to shake him by the hand. Mr. Wopsle, extending his hand with gracious dignity, was immediately shoved into a dusty corner while everybody danced a hornpipe. And from that corner, surveying the audience with a discontented eye, he became aware of me.

The second piece was the latest grand comic Christmas pantomime. In its first scene I was pained to suspect that I detected Mr. Wopsle with red woollen legs under a hugely magnified glowing face and a shock of red curtain-fringe for his hair, making thunderbolts in a mine and showing great cowardice when his gigantic master came home — very hoarse — to dinner. But he presently appeared in worthier circumstances. For, the Genius of Youthful Love being in need of help — on account of the parental brutality of an ignorant farmer who opposed his daughter's choice of sweetheart by purposely jumping on the young man, in a flour-sack, from a first-floor window — summoned a solemn Enchanter. This Enchanter, arriving from the antipodes rather unsteadily after an apparently violent journey, proved to be Mr. Wopsle in a tall pointed hat, with a book of magic under his arm. Since the enchanter's main business on earth was to be talked at, sung at, butted at, danced at, and blasted with fireworks of various colours, he had a good deal of time on his hands. And I noticed, with great surprise, that he devoted it to staring in my direction as if he were lost in amazement.

There was something so striking in the growing intensity of Mr. Wopsle's gaze, and he seemed to be turning so many things over in his mind and to grow so confused, that I could not work it out. I sat thinking about it long after he had ascended to the clouds in a large watch-case, and still I could not work it out. I was still puzzling over it when I came out of the theatre an hour later and found him waiting for me near the door.
"How do you do?" I said, shaking hands with him as we turned down the street together. "I saw that you saw me."
"Saw you, Mr. Pip!" he returned. "Yes, of course I saw you. But who else was there?"
"Who else?"
"It is the strangest thing," said Mr. Wopsle, drifting into his bewildered look again, "and yet I could swear to him."
Growing alarmed, I begged Mr. Wopsle to explain himself.
"Whether I should have noticed him at first if you hadn't been there," said Mr. Wopsle, continuing in the same dazed way, "I can't be sure. But I think I would have."
Instinctively I looked around me, as I was accustomed to do on my way home, for these mysterious words gave me a chill.
"Oh! He can't be in sight," said Mr. Wopsle. "He went out before I went off. I saw him go."
Having the reasons I had for being suspicious, I even suspected this poor actor. I distrusted a scheme to trick me into some admission. So I glanced at him as we walked on together but said nothing.
"I had a silly idea that he must be with you, Mr. Pip, until I saw that you were completely unaware of him, sitting behind you there like a ghost."

My earlier chill crept over me again, but I was determined not to speak yet, for it was perfectly consistent with his words that he might have been sent to lure me into connecting these references with Provis. Of course, I was perfectly sure and certain that Provis had not been there.
"I dare say you wonder at me, Mr. Pip. Indeed, I see you do. But it is so very strange! You'll hardly believe what I'm going to tell you. I could hardly believe it myself, if you told me."
"Indeed?" I said.
"No, indeed. Mr. Pip, you remember in old times a certain Christmas Day, when you were quite a child, and I dined at Gargery's, and some soldiers came to the door to get a pair of handcuffs mended?"
"I remember it very well."

"And you remember that there was a chase after two convicts, and that we joined in it, and that Gargery carried you on his back, and that I took the lead, and you kept up with me as well as you could?"
"I remember it all very well." Better than he thought — except that last part.
"And you remember that we came upon the two in a ditch, and that there was a struggle between them, and that one of them had been severely handled and badly beaten about the face by the other?"
"I see it all before me."

"And that the soldiers lit torches and put the two in the centre, and that we went on to see the last of them over the black marshes, with the torchlight shining on their faces — I am particular about that — with the torchlight shining on their faces, when there was an outer ring of dark night all about us?"
"Yes," I said. "I remember all that."
"Then, Mr. Pip, one of those two prisoners sat behind you tonight. I saw him over your shoulder."
"Steady!" I thought. I asked him then, "Which of the two do you suppose you saw?"
"The one who had been beaten," he answered at once, "and I'll swear I saw him! The more I think of him, the more certain I am."
"This is very curious!" I said, with the best pretence I could manage of its being nothing more to me. "Very curious indeed!"

I cannot overstate the heightened alarm this conversation threw me into, or the special and particular terror I felt at Compeyson's having been behind me "like a ghost." For if he had ever been out of my thoughts for a few moments together since the hiding began, it was in those very moments when he was closest to me. To think that I could have been so unaware and off my guard after all my care was as if I had shut a hundred doors to keep him out and then found him at my elbow. I could not doubt, either, that he was there because I was there, and that however slight the appearance of danger around us, danger was always near and active.

I put such questions to Mr. Wopsle as: When did the man come in? He could not tell me. He saw me, and over my shoulder he saw the man. It was not until he had seen him for some time that he began to recognise him, but he had from the first vaguely connected him with me and known him as somehow belonging to me in the old village days. How was he dressed? Prosperously, but not noticeably otherwise; he thought in black. Was his face at all disfigured? No, he believed not. I believed not either, for although in my brooding state I had taken no special notice of the people behind me, I thought it likely that a disfigured face would have caught my attention.

When Mr. Wopsle had told me everything he could recall or I could draw from him, and when I had treated him to a little refreshment after the exertions of the evening, we parted. It was between twelve and one o'clock when I reached the Temple, and the gates were shut. No one was near me when I went in and went home.

Herbert had come in, and we held a very serious discussion by the fire. But there was nothing to be done except to tell Wemmick what I had discovered that night and to remind him that we were waiting for his signal. Since I thought I might draw attention to him if I went to the Castle too often, I sent this information by letter. I wrote it before I went to bed and went out and posted it. Again, no one was near me. Herbert and I agreed that we could do nothing but be very cautious. And we were very cautious indeed — more cautious than before, if that were possible — and I for my part never went near Chinks's Basin except when I rowed past, and then I only glanced at Mill Pond Bank as I glanced at anything else.

chapters.title: Chapter 48
paragraphs: The second of the two encounters mentioned in the last chapter occurred about a week after the first. I had again left my boat at the wharf below Bridge. The time was an hour earlier in the afternoon, and, undecided where to eat, I had wandered up into Cheapside and was strolling along it — surely the most unsettled person in all that busy throng — when a large hand was laid upon my shoulder by someone coming up behind me. It was Mr. Jaggers's hand, and he passed it through my arm.
"As we are going in the same direction, Pip, we may walk together. Where are you headed?"
"For the Temple, I think," I said.
"Don't you know?" said Mr. Jaggers.
"Well," I returned, glad for once to get the better of him in cross-examination, "I do not know, for I haven't made up my mind."
"You are going to dine?" said Mr. Jaggers. "You don't mind admitting that, I suppose?"
"No," I returned, "I don't mind admitting that."
"And are not engaged?"
"I don't mind admitting also that I am not engaged."
"Then," said Mr. Jaggers, "come and dine with me."

I was about to make an excuse when he added, "Wemmick's coming." So I changed my excuse into an acceptance — the few words I had begun served for the start of either — and we went along Cheapside and turned off to Little Britain, while the lights were springing up brilliantly in the shop windows and the lamplighters, scarcely finding ground enough to plant their ladders in the bustle of the afternoon, were darting up and down and in and out, opening more red eyes in the gathering fog than my rushlight tower at the Hummums had opened white eyes in the ghostly wall.

At the office in Little Britain there was the usual letter-writing, hand-washing, candle-snuffing, and safe-locking that closed the business of the day. As I stood idle by Mr. Jaggers's fire, its rising and falling flame made the two death-mask casts on the shelf look as if they were playing a diabolical game of peekaboo with me, while the pair of coarse, fat office candles that dimly lit Mr. Jaggers as he wrote in a corner were dressed in dirty melted-wax shrouds, as if in memory of a host of hanged clients.

We went to Gerrard Street, all three together, in a cab. As soon as we arrived, dinner was served. Although I would not have dreamed of making, in that place, the slightest reference by so much as a look to Wemmick's Walworth feelings, I should not have minded catching his eye now and then in a friendly way. But it was not to be. He fixed his eyes on Mr. Jaggers whenever he raised them from the table, and was as dry and distant to me as if there were twin Wemmicks and this was the wrong one.
"Did you send that note of Miss Havisham's to Mr. Pip, Wemmick?" Mr. Jaggers asked, soon after we began dinner.
"No, sir," returned Wemmick. "It was about to go by post when you brought Mr. Pip into the office. Here it is." He handed it to his principal instead of to me.

"It's a two-line note, Pip," said Mr. Jaggers, passing it on, "sent up to me by Miss Havisham because she wasn't sure of your address. She tells me she wants to see you about a little matter of business you mentioned to her. You'll go down?"
"Yes," I said, glancing over the note, which said exactly that.
"When do you think of going?"
"I have a pending commitment," I said, glancing at Wemmick, who was feeding fish into the post-office, "that makes me rather uncertain of my time. At once, I think."
"If Mr. Pip intends to go at once," said Wemmick to Mr. Jaggers, "he needn't write an answer, you know."
Taking this as a hint that it was best not to delay, I decided I would go tomorrow and said so. Wemmick drank a glass of wine and looked with a grimly satisfied air at Mr. Jaggers, but not at me.
"So, Pip! Our friend the Spider," said Mr. Jaggers, "has played his cards. He has won the pool."
It was as much as I could do to agree.
"Ha! He is a promising fellow — in his way — but he may not have it all his own way. The stronger will win in the end, but the stronger has to be found out first. If he should turn to and beat her —"
"Surely," I interrupted, with a burning face and heart, "you do not seriously think that he is scoundrel enough for that, Mr. Jaggers?"

"I didn't say so, Pip. I am putting a case. If he should turn to and beat her, he may possibly get the upper hand. If it should be a question of intellect, he certainly will not. It would be guesswork to predict how a fellow of that sort will turn out in such circumstances, because it's a toss-up between two outcomes."
"May I ask what they are?"
"A fellow like our friend the Spider," answered Mr. Jaggers, "either beats or cringes. He may cringe and growl, or cringe and not growl, but he either beats or cringes. Ask Wemmick his opinion."
"Either beats or cringes," said Wemmick, not addressing himself to me at all.

"So here's to Mrs. Bentley Drummle," said Mr. Jaggers, taking a decanter of finer wine from his side table and filling for each of us and for himself. "And may the question of supremacy be settled to the lady's satisfaction! To the satisfaction of the lady and the gentleman, it never will be. Now, Molly, Molly, Molly, Molly, how slow you are today!"

She was at his elbow when he spoke, setting a dish upon the table. As she withdrew her hands from it, she fell back a step or two, nervously muttering some excuse. And a certain movement of her fingers, as she spoke, arrested my attention.
"What's the matter?" said Mr. Jaggers.
"Nothing. Only the subject we were speaking of," I said, "was rather painful to me."

The movement of her fingers was like the action of knitting. She stood looking at her master, uncertain whether she was free to go or whether he had more to say and would call her back if she did. Her look was very intent. Surely, I had seen exactly such eyes and such hands on a memorable occasion very recently!

He dismissed her, and she glided out of the room. But she remained before me as plainly as if she were still there. I looked at those hands, I looked at those eyes, I looked at that flowing hair. And I compared them with other hands, other eyes, other hair that I knew, and with what those might look like after twenty years of a brutal husband and a stormy life. I looked again at the housekeeper's hands and eyes and thought of the inexplicable feeling that had come over me when I last walked — not alone — in the ruined garden and through the abandoned brewery. I thought how the same feeling had returned when I saw a face looking at me and a hand waving from a stagecoach window. And how it had come back again and flashed about me like lightning when I had passed in a carriage — not alone — through a sudden glare of light in a dark street. I thought how one link of association had helped that recognition in the theatre, and how such a link, missing before, had now been forged for me when I had passed in a flash from Estella's name to the fingers with their knitting action and the intent eyes. And I felt absolutely certain that this woman was Estella's mother.

Mr. Jaggers had seen me with Estella and was not likely to have missed the feelings I had made no effort to conceal. He nodded when I said the subject was painful to me, clapped me on the back, passed round the wine again, and went on with his dinner.

Only twice more did the housekeeper reappear, and then her stay in the room was very brief, and Mr. Jaggers was sharp with her. But her hands were Estella's hands and her eyes were Estella's eyes, and if she had appeared a hundred times I could have been neither more sure nor less sure that my conviction was the truth.

It was a dull evening, for Wemmick drank his wine when it came round purely as a matter of business — just as he might have drawn his salary when that came round — and with his eyes on his chief, sat in a state of perpetual readiness for cross-examination. As for the quantity of wine, his post-office was as indifferent and ready as any other post-office for its quantity of letters. From my point of view, he was the wrong twin the whole time, and only outwardly like the Wemmick of Walworth.

We took our leave early and left together. Even while we were groping among Mr. Jaggers's collection of boots for our hats, I felt that the right twin was on his way back. And we had not gone half a dozen yards down Gerrard Street in the Walworth direction before I found that I was walking arm in arm with the right twin, and that the wrong twin had evaporated into the evening air.
"Well!" said Wemmick. "That's over! He's a wonderful man, without his equal in the world. But I feel that I have to wind myself up tight when I dine with him — and I dine more comfortably unwound."
I felt that this was a fair description and told him so.
"Wouldn't say it to anybody but yourself," he answered. "I know that what is said between you and me goes no further."

I asked him if he had ever seen Miss Havisham's adopted daughter, Mrs. Bentley Drummle. He said no. To avoid being too abrupt, I then spoke of the Aged and of Miss Skiffins. He looked rather sly when I mentioned Miss Skiffins, and stopped in the street to blow his nose with a roll of the head and a flourish not quite free from hidden boastfulness.
"Wemmick," I said, "do you remember telling me, before I first went to Mr. Jaggers's private house, to notice that housekeeper?"
"Did I?" he replied. "Ah, I dare say I did. Confound it," he added suddenly, "I know I did. I find I'm not quite unwound yet."
"A wild beast tamed, you called her."
"And what do you call her?"
"The same. How did Mr. Jaggers tame her, Wemmick?"
"That's his secret. She has been with him many a long year."
"I wish you would tell me her story. I feel a particular interest in knowing it. You know that what is said between you and me goes no further."
"Well!" Wemmick replied. "I don't know her whole story. But what I do know, I'll tell you. We are in our private and personal capacities, of course."
"Of course."

"About twenty years ago, that woman was tried at the Old Bailey for murder, and was acquitted. She was a very handsome young woman, and I believe had some gypsy blood in her. At any rate, it was fierce enough when it was up, as you can imagine."
"But she was acquitted."

"Mr. Jaggers was her lawyer," continued Wemmick, with a look full of meaning, "and worked the case in a truly astonishing way. It was a desperate case, and it was relatively early in his career, and he worked it to universal admiration. In fact, it may almost be said to have made him. He worked it himself at the police court, day after day for many days, fighting even against a formal charge. And at the trial, where he couldn't lead the case himself, he sat under counsel, and — everyone knew — supplied all the fire and strategy. The murdered person was a woman — a woman a good ten years older, very much larger, and very much stronger. It was a case of jealousy. They both led wandering lives, and this woman in Gerrard Street here had been married very young, informally, to a travelling man, and was a perfect fury when it came to jealousy. The murdered woman — more a match for the man, certainly, in age — was found dead in a barn near Hounslow Heath. There had been a violent struggle, perhaps a fight. She was bruised and scratched and torn, and had been held by the throat at last and choked. Now, there was no reasonable evidence against anyone but this woman, and Mr. Jaggers based his defence principally on the improbability of her having been able to do it. You may be sure," said Wemmick, touching me on the sleeve, "that he never drew attention to the strength of her hands then, though he sometimes does now."
I had told Wemmick about him showing us her wrists that day at the dinner party.

"Well, sir!" Wemmick went on. "It happened — happened, mind you — that this woman was so cleverly dressed from the time of her arrest that she looked much slighter than she really was. In particular, her sleeves are always remembered to have been so skilfully made that her arms looked quite delicate. She had only a bruise or two about her — nothing remarkable for a woman of her rough life — but the backs of her hands were torn, and the question was: Was it from fingernails? Now, Mr. Jaggers showed that she had pushed through a large thicket of brambles which were not as high as her face but through which she could not have passed without her hands getting scratched. And bits of those brambles were actually found in her skin and presented as evidence, along with the fact that the brambles in question had been broken through and had little shreds of her dress and spots of blood on them. But the boldest point he made was this: it was attempted to be proved, as evidence of her jealousy, that she was strongly suspected of having, around the time of the murder, frantically destroyed her child by this man — a child of about three years old — to avenge herself on him. Mr. Jaggers worked that this way: 'We say these are not marks of fingernails but marks of brambles, and we show you the brambles. You say they are marks of fingernails, and you put forward the theory that she destroyed her child. You must accept all consequences of that theory. For anything we know, she may have destroyed her child, and the child in clinging to her may have scratched her hands. What then? You are not trying her for the murder of her child — why don't you? As to this case, if you insist on scratches, we say that, for anything we know, you may have accounted for them — assuming for the sake of argument that you have not invented them.' To sum up, sir," said Wemmick, "Mr. Jaggers was altogether too much for the jury, and they gave in."
"Has she been in his service ever since?"

"Yes, but not only that," said Wemmick. "She went into his service immediately after her acquittal, tamed as she is now. She has since been taught this and that about her duties, but she was tamed from the beginning."
"Do you remember the sex of the child?"
"Said to have been a girl."
"You have nothing more to say to me tonight?"
"Nothing. I got your letter and destroyed it. Nothing."
We exchanged a warm good-night, and I went home with new material for my thoughts, though with no relief from the old.

chapters.title: Chapter 49
paragraphs: Putting Miss Havisham's note in my pocket, so it might serve as my credentials for reappearing so soon at Satis House — in case her unpredictability should lead her to express surprise at seeing me — I went down again by coach the next day. But I got off at the Halfway House, breakfasted there, and walked the rest of the distance, for I wanted to enter the town quietly by the back roads and to leave it the same way.

The best light of the day was gone when I passed along the quiet echoing courts behind the High Street. The nooks of ruin where the old monks had once had their dining halls and gardens, and where the strong walls now served as humble sheds and stables, were almost as silent as the old monks in their graves. The cathedral chimes had a sadder and more distant sound to me, as I hurried on avoiding notice, than they had ever had before. The swell of the old organ reached my ears like funeral music, and the rooks, as they hovered about the grey tower and swung in the bare high trees of the priory garden, seemed to call to me that the place was changed, and that Estella was gone from it forever.

An elderly woman, whom I had seen before as one of the servants who lived in the house across the back courtyard, opened the gate. The lit candle stood in the dark passage within, as it always had, and I took it up and climbed the staircase alone. Miss Havisham was not in her own room but was in the larger room across the landing. Looking in at the door after knocking without answer, I saw her sitting on the hearth in a ragged chair, close to and lost in the contemplation of the ashy fire.

Doing as I had often done, I went in and stood by the old chimney-piece where she could see me when she raised her eyes. There was an air of utter loneliness about her that would have moved me to pity even if she had deliberately done me a deeper injury than I could accuse her of. As I stood there feeling sorry for her, and thinking how, in the course of time, I too had come to be part of the ruined fortunes of that house, her eyes rested on me. She stared and said in a low voice, "Is it real?"
"It is I, Pip. Mr. Jaggers gave me your note yesterday, and I have lost no time."
"Thank you. Thank you."
As I brought another of the ragged chairs to the hearth and sat down, I noticed a new expression on her face, as if she were afraid of me.

"I want," she said, "to take up that subject you mentioned when you were last here, and to show you that I am not all stone. But perhaps you can never believe, now, that there is anything human in my heart?"
When I said some reassuring words, she stretched out her trembling right hand as though she was going to touch me, but drew it back before I understood the gesture or knew how to receive it.
"You said, speaking for your friend, that you could tell me how to do something useful and good. Something that you would like done, is it not?"
"Something that I would like done very much."
"What is it?"

I began explaining the secret history of the partnership. I had not got far when I judged from her looks that she was thinking in a wandering way about me rather than about what I was saying. It seemed to be so, for when I stopped speaking, many moments passed before she showed that she had noticed.
"Do you stop," she asked then, with the same air of being afraid of me, "because you hate me too much to bear speaking to me?"
"No, no," I answered. "How can you think so, Miss Havisham! I stopped because I thought you weren't following what I said."
"Perhaps I wasn't," she answered, putting a hand to her head. "Begin again, and let me look at something else. Wait! Now tell me."

She set her hand upon her stick in the determined way that was sometimes habitual to her, and stared at the fire with a fierce expression of forcing herself to pay attention. I went on with my explanation and told her how I had hoped to complete the arrangement from my own funds, but had been disappointed. That part of the subject, I reminded her, involved matters that could form no part of my explanation, for they were the weighty secrets of another person.
"So!" she said, nodding but not looking at me. "And how much money is needed to complete the purchase?"
I was rather afraid to state it, for it sounded like a large sum. "Nine hundred pounds."
"If I give you the money for this purpose, will you keep my secret as you have kept your own?"
"Just as faithfully."
"And your mind will be more at rest?"
"Much more at rest."
"Are you very unhappy now?"

She asked this question still without looking at me, but in an unusual tone of sympathy. I could not answer at once, for my voice failed me. She put her left arm across the head of her stick and softly rested her forehead on it.
"I am far from happy, Miss Havisham. But I have other causes of distress besides any you know of. They are the secrets I have mentioned."
After a little while, she raised her head and looked at the fire again.
"It is noble in you to tell me that you have other causes of unhappiness. Is it true?"
"Too true."
"Can I only serve you, Pip, by serving your friend? Setting that aside as done, is there nothing I can do for you yourself?"
"Nothing. I thank you for the question. I thank you even more for the tone of the question. But there is nothing."

She presently rose from her seat and looked about the blighted room for writing materials. There were none, so she took from her pocket a yellow set of ivory tablets, mounted in tarnished gold, and wrote upon them with a pencil in a tarnished gold case that hung from her neck.
"You are still on good terms with Mr. Jaggers?"
"Quite. I dined with him yesterday."

"This is an authorisation to him to pay you that money, to use at your sole discretion for your friend. I keep no money here, but if you would rather Mr. Jaggers knew nothing of the matter, I will send it to you."
"Thank you, Miss Havisham. I have not the least objection to receiving it from him."

She read me what she had written, and it was direct and clear, evidently intended to free me from any suspicion of profiting from the money. I took the tablets from her hand, and it trembled again, and trembled more as she took off the chain to which the pencil was attached and placed it in mine. All this she did without looking at me.
"My name is on the first leaf. If you can ever write under my name, 'I forgive her,' though ever so long after my broken heart is dust — pray do it!"

"Oh, Miss Havisham," I said, "I can do it now. There have been painful mistakes, and my life has been a blind and thankless one, and I need forgiveness and guidance far too much to be bitter with you."

She turned her face to me for the first time since she had looked away and, to my amazement — I may even say to my terror — dropped on her knees at my feet, with her folded hands raised to me in the way in which, when her poor heart was young and fresh and whole, they must often have been raised to Heaven from her mother's side.

To see her with her white hair and her worn face kneeling at my feet sent a shock through my whole body. I begged her to rise and got my arms about her to help her up, but she only pressed the hand of mine that was nearest to her grasp and hung her head over it and wept. I had never seen her shed a tear before, and in the hope that the release might do her good, I bent over her without speaking. She was not kneeling now, but was down upon the ground.
"Oh!" she cried despairingly. "What have I done! What have I done!"
"If you mean, Miss Havisham, what have you done to injure me, let me answer. Very little. I should have loved her under any circumstances. Is she married?"
"Yes."
It was a needless question, for a new desolation in the desolate house had already told me so.
"What have I done! What have I done!" She wrung her hands and clutched her white hair and returned to this cry over and over again. "What have I done!"

I did not know how to answer or how to comfort her. That she had done a grievous thing in taking an impressionable child and shaping her into the instrument that her wild resentment, rejected love, and wounded pride found vengeance in — I knew full well. But that in shutting out the light of day she had shut out infinitely more; that in her seclusion she had cut herself off from a thousand natural and healing influences; that her mind, brooding in solitude, had grown diseased, as all minds do and must and will that reverse the order appointed by their Maker — I knew equally well. And could I look upon her without compassion, seeing her punishment in the ruin she was, in her profound unfitness for this earth, in the vanity of a sorrow that had become a ruling obsession, like the vanity of penitence, the vanity of remorse, the vanity of unworthiness, and other monstrous vanities that have been curses in this world?

"Until you spoke to her the other day, and until I saw in you a mirror that showed me what I once felt myself, I did not know what I had done. What have I done! What have I done!" And so again, twenty, fifty times over — What had she done!

"Miss Havisham," I said, when her cry had died away, "you may dismiss me from your mind and conscience. But Estella is a different case, and if you can ever undo any scrap of what you have done wrong in keeping a part of her true nature from her, it will be better to do that than to mourn the past through a hundred years."

"Yes, yes, I know it. But, Pip — my dear!" There was an earnest, womanly compassion for me in her new warmth. "My dear! Believe this: when she first came to me, I meant to save her from misery like my own. At first, I meant no more."
"Well, well!" I said. "I hope so."

"But as she grew, and promised to be very beautiful, I gradually did worse. With my praises, and with my jewels, and with my teachings, and with this figure of myself always before her as a warning to reinforce my lessons, I stole her heart away and put ice in its place."
"Better," I could not help saying, "to have left her a natural heart, even to be bruised or broken."
At that, Miss Havisham looked at me in a distracted way for a while, and then burst out again: What had she done!
"If you knew all my story," she pleaded, "you would have some compassion for me and a better understanding of me."

"Miss Havisham," I answered, as gently as I could, "I believe I may say that I do know your story, and have known it ever since I first left this neighbourhood. It has inspired me with great sympathy, and I hope I understand it and its effects. Does what has passed between us give me any right to ask you a question about Estella? Not as she is now, but as she was when she first came here?"
She was seated on the ground, with her arms on the ragged chair and her head resting on them. She looked full at me when I said this and replied, "Go on."
"Whose child was Estella?"
She shook her head.
"You don't know?"
She shook her head again.
"But Mr. Jaggers brought her here, or sent her here?"
"Brought her here."
"Will you tell me how that came about?"

She answered in a low whisper, cautiously: "I had been shut up in these rooms a long time — I don't know how long; you know what time the clocks keep here — when I told him that I wanted a little girl to raise and love and save from my fate. I had first seen him when I sent for him to lay this place waste for me, having read of him in the newspapers before I and the world parted. He told me that he would look about for such an orphan child. One night he brought her here asleep, and I called her Estella."
"Might I ask her age then?"
"Two or three. She herself knows nothing except that she was left an orphan and I adopted her."
So convinced was I that that woman was her mother, I needed no further evidence to establish the fact in my own mind. But to anyone, I thought, the connection here was clear and direct.

What more could I hope to accomplish by prolonging the visit? I had succeeded on Herbert's behalf. Miss Havisham had told me all she knew of Estella. I had said and done what I could to ease her mind. No matter with what other words we parted — we parted.

Twilight was closing in when I went downstairs into the natural air. I called to the woman who had opened the gate when I arrived, that I would not trouble her just yet but would walk round the place before leaving. For I had a presentiment that I should never be here again, and I felt that the dying light was suited to my last view of it.

Past the wilderness of casks that I had walked on long ago, and on which the rain of years had fallen since, rotting them in many places and leaving miniature swamps and pools of water on those that stood upright, I made my way to the ruined garden. I went all round it — round by the corner where Herbert and I had fought our battle, round by the paths where Estella and I had walked. So cold, so lonely, so dreary, all of it!

Taking the brewery on my way back, I raised the rusty latch of a little door at the garden end and walked through. I was going out at the opposite door — not easy to open now, for the damp wood had warped and swelled, and the hinges were giving way, and the threshold was choked with a growth of fungus — when I turned my head to look back. A childish association revived with wonderful force in the slight moment of that action, and I imagined I saw Miss Havisham hanging from the beam. So strong was the impression that I stood under the beam shuddering from head to foot before I knew it was only fancy — though to be sure I was there in an instant.

The mournfulness of the place and time, and the great terror of this illusion, though it was only momentary, filled me with an indescribable dread as I came out between the open wooden gates where I had once torn my hair after Estella had torn my heart. Passing on into the front courtyard, I hesitated whether to call the woman to let me out at the locked gate, of which she had the key, or first to go upstairs and make sure that Miss Havisham was as safe and well as I had left her. I chose the latter course and went up.

I looked into the room where I had left her, and I saw her seated in the ragged chair by the hearth, close to the fire, with her back to me. In the moment when I was pulling my head back to go quietly away, I saw a great flaming light spring up. In the same moment I saw her running at me, shrieking, with a whirl of fire blazing all about her, soaring at least as many feet above her head as she was tall.

I had a double-caped greatcoat on, and over my arm another thick coat. That I got them off, closed with her, threw her down, and got them over her; that I dragged the great cloth from the table for the same purpose, and with it dragged down the heap of rotting things in the middle and all the ugly stuff that sheltered there; that we were on the ground struggling like desperate enemies, and that the more closely I covered her the more wildly she shrieked and tried to free herself — all this I knew through the result, but not through anything I felt or thought or knew I did. I knew nothing until I knew that we were on the floor by the great table, and that patches of smouldering ash were floating in the smoky air which, a moment ago, had been her faded bridal dress.

Then I looked round and saw the disturbed beetles and spiders running away over the floor, and the servants coming in with breathless cries at the door. I still held her forcibly down with all my strength, like a prisoner who might escape. And I doubt if I even knew who she was, or why we had struggled, or that she had been on fire, or that the flames were out, until I saw the patches of ash that had been her garments no longer alight but falling in a black shower around us.

She was unconscious, and I was afraid to have her moved or even touched. Assistance was sent for, and I held her until it came, as if I unreasonably feared — I think I did — that if I let her go, the fire would break out again and consume her. When I got up, as the surgeon arrived with other help, I was astonished to see that both my hands were burned, for I had had no awareness of it through the sense of feeling.

On examination it was pronounced that she had received serious injuries, but that they were far from hopeless in themselves. The danger lay mainly in the nervous shock. By the surgeon's directions, her bed was carried into that room and laid upon the great table, which happened to be well suited for dressing her wounds. When I saw her again, an hour later, she lay indeed where I had seen her strike her stick and had heard her say she would lie one day.

Though every trace of her dress was burned away, as they told me, she still had something of her old ghostly bridal appearance. For they had covered her to the throat with white cotton-wool, and as she lay with a white sheet loosely over that, the phantom air of something that had been and was changed still hung about her.

I found, on questioning the servants, that Estella was in Paris. I got a promise from the surgeon that he would write to her by the next post. Miss Havisham's family I took upon myself, intending to contact Mr. Matthew Pocket only and leave him to inform the rest as he saw fit. This I did the next day, through Herbert, as soon as I returned to town.

There was a stage that evening when she spoke coherently of what had happened, though with a certain terrible intensity. Toward midnight she began to wander in her speech, and after that it gradually set in that she said innumerable times in a low, solemn voice, "What have I done!" And then, "When she first came, I meant to save her from misery like mine." And then, "Take the pencil and write under my name, 'I forgive her!'" She never changed the order of these three sentences, but she sometimes left out a word in one or another of them — never putting in a different word, but always leaving a blank and going on to the next.

As I could do no good there, and as I had, nearer home, that pressing reason for anxiety and fear which even her wandering words could not drive from my mind, I decided in the course of the night that I would return by the early morning coach, walking a mile or so and being picked up outside the town. At about six o'clock in the morning, therefore, I leaned over her and touched her lips with mine, just as they said, not pausing for my kiss, "Take the pencil and write under my name, 'I forgive her.'"

chapters.title: Chapter 50
paragraphs: My hands had been dressed twice or three times in the night and again in the morning. My left arm was badly burned to the elbow, and less severely up to the shoulder. It was very painful, but the flames had gone in that direction, and I felt thankful it was no worse. My right hand was not so badly burned that I couldn't move the fingers. It was bandaged, of course, but much less awkwardly than my left hand and arm, which I carried in a sling. I could only wear my coat like a cloak, loose over my shoulders and fastened at the neck. My hair had been caught by the fire, but not my head or face.

When Herbert had been down to Hammersmith and seen his father, he came back to me at our chambers and devoted the day to looking after me. He was the kindest of nurses, and at regular intervals he took off the bandages, soaked them in the cooling liquid that was kept ready, and put them on again with a patient tenderness for which I was deeply grateful.

At first, as I lay quietly on the sofa, I found it painfully difficult — impossible, I might say — to get rid of the impression of the glare of the flames, their rush and noise, and the fierce burning smell. If I dozed for a minute, I was woken by Miss Havisham's cries and by the sight of her running at me with all that height of fire above her head. This pain of the mind was much harder to fight than any physical pain I suffered, and Herbert, seeing that, did his utmost to keep my attention occupied.
