Neither of us spoke of the boat, but we both thought of it. That was clear from our avoidance of the subject, and from our agreeing — without saying so — to measure my recovery in hours, not weeks.

My first question when I saw Herbert had been, of course, whether all was well downriver. As he answered yes, with perfect confidence and cheerfulness, we did not return to the subject until the day was wearing on. But then, as Herbert changed the bandages, more by the light of the fire than by the fading daylight, he went back to it on his own.
"I sat with Provis last night, Handel, for two good hours."
"Where was Clara?"

"Dear little thing!" said Herbert. "She was up and down with Gruffandgrim all evening. He was banging his stick on the floor the moment she left his sight. I doubt he can hold on much longer, though. What with rum and pepper — and pepper and rum — I should think his banging must be nearly over."
"And then you will be married, Herbert?"

"How can I take care of the dear child otherwise? — Lay your arm out along the back of the sofa, my dear boy, and I'll sit down here and get the bandage off so gradually you won't feel it coming. I was speaking of Provis. Do you know, Handel, he improves?"
"I said to you I thought he was softened when I last saw him."
"So you did. And so he is. He was very talkative last night and told me more of his life. You remember his breaking off here about some woman he had had great trouble with. — Did I hurt you?"
I had started, but not from his touch. His words had given me a start.
"I had forgotten that, Herbert, but I remember it now that you mention it."
"Well! He went into that part of his life, and a dark, wild part it is. Shall I tell you? Or would it be too much for you just now?"
"Tell me by all means. Every word."
Herbert leaned forward to look at me more closely, as if my reply had been more hurried or eager than he could quite account for. "Your head is clear?" he said, touching it.
"Quite," I said. "Tell me what Provis said, my dear Herbert."

"It seems," said Herbert, "— there's a bandage off beautifully, and now comes the cool one — makes you flinch at first, my poor dear fellow, doesn't it? But it will be comfortable in a moment — it seems that the woman was a young woman, and a jealous woman, and a vengeful woman. Vengeful, Handel, to the last degree."
"To what last degree?"
"Murder. — Does it feel too cold on that sensitive spot?"
"I don't feel it. How did she murder? Whom did she murder?"

"Well, the deed may not have quite deserved so terrible a name," said Herbert, "but she was tried for it, and Mr. Jaggers defended her, and the fame of that defence first brought his name to Provis's attention. It was another and stronger woman who was the victim, and there had been a struggle — in a barn. Who started it, or how fair or unfair it was, may be doubtful. But how it ended is certainly not doubtful, for the victim was found strangled."
"Was the woman found guilty?"
"No. She was acquitted. — My poor Handel, I hurt you!"
"It is impossible to be gentler, Herbert. Yes? What else?"

"This acquitted young woman and Provis had a little child — a little child of whom Provis was extremely fond. On the evening of the very night when the object of her jealousy was strangled as I've described, the young woman appeared before Provis for one moment and swore that she would destroy the child — which was in her possession — and he would never see it again. Then she vanished. — There's the worst arm comfortably in the sling once more, and now there remains only the right hand, which is a far easier job. I can do it better by this light than by a stronger one, for my hand is steadiest when I don't see the poor blistered patches too clearly. — You don't think your breathing is affected, my dear boy? You seem to be breathing quickly."
"Perhaps I am, Herbert. Did the woman keep her oath?"
"There comes the darkest part of Provis's life. She did."
"That is, he says she did."
"Why, of course, my dear boy," returned Herbert, in a tone of surprise, bending forward again to get a closer look at me. "He says it all. I have no other information."
"No, to be sure."

"Now, whether," Herbert continued, "he had used the child's mother badly or used the child's mother well, Provis doesn't say. But she had shared some four or five years of the wretched life he described to us at this fireside, and he seems to have felt pity for her and shown her restraint. Therefore, fearing he might be called to testify about this supposedly destroyed child, and so be the cause of her death, he hid himself — much as he grieved for the child — kept himself dark, as he says, out of the way and out of the trial, and was only vaguely spoken of as a certain man called Abel, out of whom the jealousy arose. After the acquittal she disappeared, and so he lost the child and the child's mother."
"I want to ask —"

"A moment, my dear boy, and I'm done. That evil genius Compeyson, the worst of scoundrels among many scoundrels, knowing that he had kept out of the way at that time and knowing his reasons for doing so, of course afterwards held that knowledge over his head as a way of keeping him poorer and working him harder. It was clear last night that this sharpened the point of Provis's hatred."
"I want to know," I said, "and particularly, Herbert, whether he told you when this happened."

"Particularly? Let me remember, then, what he said about that. His words were, 'a round score of year ago, and almost directly after I took up with Compeyson.' How old were you when you came upon him in the little churchyard?"
"I think in my seventh year."
"Yes. It had happened some three or four years before that, he said, and you brought to his mind the little girl so tragically lost, who would have been about your age."
"Herbert," I said after a short silence, in a hurried way, "can you see me best by the light of the window, or the light of the fire?"
"By the firelight," answered Herbert, coming close again.
"Look at me."
"I do look at you, my dear boy."
"Touch me."
"I do touch you, my dear boy."
"You are not afraid that I am feverish, or that my head has been badly disordered by last night's accident?"
"N-no, my dear boy," said Herbert, after taking a moment to examine me. "You are rather excited, but you are quite yourself."
"I know I am quite myself. And the man we have in hiding down the river is Estella's father."

chapters.title: Chapter 51
paragraphs: What purpose I had in mind when I was so intent on tracing and proving Estella's parentage, I cannot say. It will presently be seen that the question was not clear to me until a wiser head than mine put it before me.

But when Herbert and I had held our momentous conversation, I was seized with a feverish conviction that I ought to pursue the matter — that I ought not to let it rest but ought to see Mr. Jaggers and get at the bare truth. I really do not know whether I did this for Estella's sake, or whether I was glad to transfer to the man whose safety was my chief concern some of the romantic interest that had so long surrounded me. Perhaps the latter possibility is nearer the truth.

In any case, I could scarcely be kept from going out to Gerrard Street that night. Only Herbert's argument that if I did, I should probably be laid up and useless at the very time when our fugitive's safety would depend on me alone held back my impatience. On the understanding, repeated again and again, that come what may I was to go to Mr. Jaggers tomorrow, I at last agreed to keep quiet, have my burns looked after, and stay at home. Early the next morning we went out together, and at the corner of Giltspur Street by Smithfield, I left Herbert to go his way into the City and took mine to Little Britain.

There were regular occasions when Mr. Jaggers and Wemmick went over the office accounts, checked off the vouchers, and put everything in order. On these occasions, Wemmick brought his books and papers into Mr. Jaggers's room, and one of the upstairs clerks came down to the outer office. Finding such a clerk at Wemmick's desk that morning, I knew what was going on. But I was not sorry to have Mr. Jaggers and Wemmick together, as Wemmick would then hear for himself that I said nothing to compromise him.

My appearance, with my arm bandaged and my coat loose over my shoulders, served my purpose. Although I had sent Mr. Jaggers a brief account of the accident as soon as I reached town, I still had to give him all the details now. And the unusual nature of the occasion made our conversation less dry and hard, and less strictly governed by the rules of evidence, than it had been before. While I described the disaster, Mr. Jaggers stood as usual before the fire. Wemmick leaned back in his chair, staring at me, with his hands in his trouser pockets and his pen placed horizontally into the post-office. The two brutal death-mask casts, always inseparable in my mind from official proceedings, seemed to be thickly considering whether they didn't smell fire at that moment.

When my account was finished and their questions exhausted, I produced Miss Havisham's authorisation to receive the nine hundred pounds for Herbert. Mr. Jaggers's eyes retreated a little deeper into his head when I handed him the tablets, but he presently passed them over to Wemmick with instructions to draw up the cheque for his signature. While that was being done, I looked on at Wemmick as he wrote, and Mr. Jaggers, rocking and swaying on his well-polished boots, looked on at me. "I am sorry, Pip," he said, as I put the cheque in my pocket after he had signed it, "that we do nothing for you."
"Miss Havisham was good enough to ask me," I returned, "whether she could do nothing for me, and I told her no."
"Everybody should know his own business," said Mr. Jaggers. And I saw Wemmick's lips form the words "portable property."
"I should not have told her no, if I had been you," said Mr. Jaggers. "But every man ought to know his own business best."
"Every man's business," said Wemmick, rather reproachfully in my direction, "is portable property."
As I thought the time had come to pursue the subject I had at heart, I said, turning to Mr. Jaggers —
"I did ask something of Miss Havisham, however, sir. I asked her for some information about her adopted daughter, and she gave me all she had."

"Did she?" said Mr. Jaggers, bending forward to look at his boots and then straightening up. "Ha! I don't think I should have done so, if I had been Miss Havisham. But she ought to know her own business best."
"I know more of the history of Miss Havisham's adopted child than Miss Havisham herself does, sir. I know her mother."
Mr. Jaggers looked at me with interest and repeated, "Mother?"
"I have seen her mother within the last three days."
"Yes?" said Mr. Jaggers.
"And so have you, sir. And you have seen her still more recently."
"Yes?" said Mr. Jaggers.
"Perhaps I know more of Estella's history than even you do," I said. "I know her father too."

A certain check that came into Mr. Jaggers's manner — he was too self-possessed to change his manner, but he could not help its being brought to an indefinably attentive halt — assured me that he did not know who her father was. This I had strongly suspected from Provis's account, as Herbert had repeated it, of his having kept himself hidden. I connected that to the fact that he himself had not become Mr. Jaggers's client until some four years later, when he would have had no reason for claiming his identity. But I could not be sure of this gap in Mr. Jaggers's knowledge before, though I was quite sure of it now.
"So! You know the young lady's father, Pip?" said Mr. Jaggers.
"Yes," I replied, "and his name is Provis — from New South Wales."

Even Mr. Jaggers started when I said those words. It was the slightest start that could escape a man — the most carefully suppressed and the soonest checked — but he did start, though he made it part of the movement of taking out his pocket-handkerchief. How Wemmick received the announcement I cannot say, for I was afraid to look at him just then, lest Mr. Jaggers's sharpness should detect that there had been some communication between us unknown to him.
"And on what evidence, Pip," asked Mr. Jaggers very coolly, pausing with his handkerchief halfway to his nose, "does Provis make this claim?"
"He does not make it," I said, "and has never made it, and has no knowledge or belief that his daughter is alive."

For once, the powerful pocket-handkerchief failed. My reply was so unexpected that Mr. Jaggers put the handkerchief back in his pocket without completing the usual routine, folded his arms, and looked at me with stern attention, though with an expressionless face.

Then I told him all I knew and how I knew it, with the single reservation that I let him think I had learned from Miss Havisham what I had actually learned from Wemmick. I was very careful about that. Nor did I look toward Wemmick until I had finished everything I had to say and had been for some time silently meeting Mr. Jaggers's gaze. When I did at last turn my eyes in Wemmick's direction, I found that he had removed his pen from the post-office and was studying the table before him intently.
"Ha!" said Mr. Jaggers at last, as he moved toward the papers on the table. "What item were you at, Wemmick, when Mr. Pip came in?"

But I refused to be brushed off in that way, and I made a passionate, almost indignant appeal to him to be more frank and honest with me. I reminded him of the false hopes I had fallen into, how long they had lasted, and the discovery I had made. I hinted at the danger that weighed upon my mind. I said I was surely worthy of some small confidence from him, in return for the confidence I had just shared. I said I did not blame him, or suspect him, or distrust him, but I wanted the truth confirmed by him. And if he asked why I wanted it and why I thought I had any right to it, I would tell him — little as he cared for such poor dreams — that I had loved Estella dearly and long, and that although I had lost her and must live a bereaved life, everything that concerned her was still nearer and dearer to me than anything else in the world. And seeing that Mr. Jaggers stood perfectly still and silent, and apparently unmoved by this appeal, I turned to Wemmick and said, "Wemmick, I know you to be a man with a gentle heart. I have seen your pleasant home, and your old father, and all the innocent, cheerful, playful ways with which you refresh your working life. And I beg you to say a word for me to Mr. Jaggers, and to point out to him that, all things considered, he ought to be more open with me!"

I have never seen two men look more oddly at one another than Mr. Jaggers and Wemmick did after this speech. At first I feared that Wemmick would be instantly dismissed from his position. But that fear melted as I saw Mr. Jaggers relax into something like a smile, and Wemmick grow bolder.
"What's all this?" said Mr. Jaggers. "You with an old father, and you with pleasant and playful ways?"
"Well!" returned Wemmick. "If I don't bring them here, what does it matter?"
"Pip," said Mr. Jaggers, laying his hand on my arm and smiling openly, "this man must be the most cunning impostor in all London."
"Not a bit of it," returned Wemmick, growing bolder and bolder. "I think you're another."
Again they exchanged those odd looks, each apparently still suspicious that the other was putting him on.
"You with a pleasant home?" said Mr. Jaggers.

"Since it doesn't interfere with business," returned Wemmick, "let it be. Now I look at you, sir, I shouldn't wonder if you might be planning and scheming to have a pleasant home of your own one of these days, when you're tired of all this work."

Mr. Jaggers nodded his head reflectively two or three times and actually sighed. "Pip," he said, "we won't talk about 'poor dreams.' You know more about such things than I, having much fresher experience of that kind. But now, about this other matter. I'll put a case to you. Mind! I admit nothing."
He waited for me to confirm that I fully understood he was expressly saying he admitted nothing.

"Now, Pip," said Mr. Jaggers, "put this case. Put the case that a woman, under such circumstances as you have mentioned, had hidden her child, and was forced to tell her legal adviser the facts, since he insisted he must know — with an eye to the scope of her defence — how things stood about that child. Put the case that at the same time he held a commission to find a child for an eccentric rich lady to adopt and raise."
"I follow you, sir."

"Put the case that he lived in an atmosphere of evil, and that all he saw of children was their being produced in great numbers for certain destruction. Put the case that he constantly saw children solemnly tried in a criminal court, where they were held up for all to see. Put the case that he routinely knew of their being imprisoned, whipped, transported, neglected, cast out, fitted in every way for the gallows, and growing up to be hanged. Put the case that nearly all the children he saw in his daily business life he had reason to view as so much spawn, destined to develop into the fish that would come to his net — to be prosecuted, defended, perjured, made orphans, ruined one way or another."
"I follow you, sir."

"Put the case, Pip, that here was one pretty little child out of the heap who could be saved. Whose father believed her dead and dared make no enquiry about her. As to whom, over the mother, the legal adviser had this power: 'I know what you did, and how you did it. You went here and there, you did such and such things to divert suspicion. I have tracked you through it all, and I tell it you all. Give up the child, unless it should be necessary to produce it to clear you, and then it shall be produced. Place the child in my hands, and I will do my best to save you. If you are saved, your child is saved too. If you are lost, your child is still saved.' Put the case that this was done, and that the woman was cleared."
"I understand you perfectly."
"But that I make no admissions?"
"That you make no admissions." And Wemmick repeated, "No admissions."

"Put the case, Pip, that passion and the terror of death had somewhat shaken the woman's mind, and that when she was set free, she was frightened out of the ways of the world and went to him for shelter. Put the case that he took her in, and that he kept down the old wild, violent nature whenever he saw a hint of it breaking out, by asserting his power over her in the old way. Do you follow the imaginary case?"
"Quite."

"Put the case that the child grew up and was married for money. That the mother was still living. That the father was still living. That the mother and father, unknown to one another, were dwelling within so many miles, furlongs, yards if you like, of one another. That the secret was still a secret, except that you had caught wind of it. Put that last case to yourself very carefully."
"I do."
"I ask Wemmick to put it to himself very carefully."
And Wemmick said, "I do."

"For whose sake would you reveal the secret? For the father's? I think he would not be much the better for the mother. For the mother's? I think if she had done such a deed, she would be safer where she was. For the daughter's? I think it would hardly help her to establish her parentage for the benefit of her husband, and to drag her back to disgrace after an escape of twenty years, fairly sure to last for life. But add the case that you had loved her, Pip, and had made her the subject of those 'poor dreams' which have, at one time or another, been in the heads of more men than you think likely — then I tell you that you had better, and would much sooner when you had thought it through, chop off that bandaged left hand of yours with your bandaged right hand, and then pass the blade to Wemmick there, to cut that off too."

I looked at Wemmick, whose face was very grave. He gravely touched his lips with his forefinger. I did the same. Mr. Jaggers did the same. "Now, Wemmick," said the latter then, resuming his usual manner, "what item were you at when Mr. Pip came in?"

Standing by for a little while as they worked, I noticed that the odd looks they had exchanged were repeated several times, with this difference now: each of them seemed uncomfortable, not to say self-conscious, about having shown himself in a weak and unprofessional light to the other. For this reason, I suppose, they were now rigid with one another — Mr. Jaggers being highly dictatorial, and Wemmick stubbornly defending himself whenever there was the smallest point in dispute. I had never seen them on such bad terms, for generally they got along very well.

But they were both happily rescued by the timely appearance of Mike, the client with the fur cap and the habit of wiping his nose on his sleeve, whom I had seen on the very first day of my coming to that office. This individual, who — either in his own person or in that of some family member — seemed to be always in trouble (which in that place meant Newgate), came to announce that his eldest daughter had been arrested on suspicion of shoplifting. As he conveyed this unhappy news to Wemmick, with Mr. Jaggers standing magisterially before the fire and taking no part in the proceedings, Mike's eye happened to glisten with a tear.
"What are you about?" demanded Wemmick with the utmost indignation. "What do you come snivelling here for?"
"I didn't go to do it, Mr. Wemmick."
"You did," said Wemmick. "How dare you? You're not in a fit state to come here if you can't come without sputtering like a bad pen. What do you mean by it?"
"A man can't help his feelings, Mr. Wemmick," pleaded Mike.
"His what?" demanded Wemmick, quite savagely. "Say that again!"
"Now look here, my man," said Mr. Jaggers, advancing a step and pointing to the door. "Get out of this office. I'll have no feelings here. Get out."
"It serves you right," said Wemmick. "Get out."

So the unfortunate Mike very humbly withdrew, and Mr. Jaggers and Wemmick appeared to have restored their good understanding, and went back to work with an air of refreshment about them, as if they had just had lunch.

chapters.title: Chapter 52
paragraphs: From Little Britain I went, with my cheque in my pocket, to Miss Skiffins's brother, the accountant. Miss Skiffins's brother, the accountant, went straight to Clarriker's and brought Clarriker to me, and I had the great satisfaction of completing that arrangement. It was the only good thing I had done, and the only completed thing I had done, since I was first told of my great expectations.

Clarriker told me on that occasion that the affairs of the House were progressing steadily, that he would now be able to establish a small branch-house in the East which was much needed for expanding the business, and that Herbert in his new partnership capacity would go out and take charge of it. I realised that I must have been preparing for a separation from my friend, even if my own affairs had been better settled. And now, indeed, I felt as if my last anchor were loosening its hold, and I should soon be drifting with the winds and waves.

But there was compensation in the joy with which Herbert would come home at night and tell me of these changes — little imagining that he was telling me no news — and would sketch airy pictures of himself escorting Clara Barley to the land of the Arabian Nights, and of me going out to join them (with a caravan of camels, I believe), and of our all going up the Nile and seeing wonders. Without being optimistic about my own part in those bright plans, I felt that Herbert's path was clearing fast, and that old Bill Barley had only to stick to his pepper and rum and his daughter would soon be happily provided for.

We were now in the month of March. My left arm, though it showed no bad symptoms, naturally took a long time to heal, and I was still unable to get a coat on. My right arm was reasonably restored — scarred, but fairly usable.
On a Monday morning, when Herbert and I were at breakfast, I received the following letter from Wemmick by post.
"Walworth. Burn this as soon as read. Early in the week, or say Wednesday, you might do what you know of, if you felt disposed to try it. Now burn."
When I had shown this to Herbert and put it in the fire — but not before we had both memorised it — we considered what to do. For, of course, my being disabled could no longer be kept out of account.

"I have thought it over again and again," said Herbert, "and I think I know a better course than hiring a Thames waterman. Take Startop. A good fellow, a skilled oarsman, fond of us, and trustworthy and honourable."
I had thought of him more than once.
"But how much would you tell him, Herbert?"

"It is necessary to tell him very little. Let him suppose it a mere whim, but a secret one, until the morning comes. Then let him know there is an urgent reason for getting Provis aboard and away. You go with him?"
"No doubt."
"Where?"

It had seemed to me, in the many anxious hours I had given the question, almost irrelevant what port we made for — Hamburg, Rotterdam, Antwerp — the place mattered little, so long as he was out of England. Any foreign steamer that crossed our path and would take us on board would do. I had always planned to get him well down the river in the boat, certainly well past Gravesend, which was a critical point for search or enquiry if suspicion were aroused. Since foreign steamers would leave London at about the time of high water, our plan would be to go down the river on a previous ebb-tide and wait in some quiet spot until we could row out to one. The time when a steamer would be due where we lay, wherever that might be, could be calculated fairly accurately if we made enquiries beforehand.

Herbert agreed to all this, and we went out immediately after breakfast to make our investigations. We found that a steamer for Hamburg was likely to suit our purpose best and focused mainly on that vessel. But we also noted what other foreign steamers would be leaving London on the same tide, and made sure we knew the shape and colour of each. We then separated for a few hours — I to get whatever passports were necessary, Herbert to see Startop at his lodgings. We both completed our tasks without any difficulty, and when we met again at one o'clock, reported it done. I had my passports ready. Herbert had seen Startop, and he was more than willing to join.

Those two would pull a pair of oars, we decided, and I would steer. Our charge would sit as a passenger and keep quiet. Since speed was not our aim, we should make good enough progress. We arranged that Herbert should not come home to dinner before going to Mill Pond Bank that evening; that he should not go there at all the next evening, Tuesday; that he should prepare Provis to come down to some stairs near the house on Wednesday, when he saw us approaching, and not before; that all the arrangements with him should be settled that Monday night; and that he should be contacted no more in any way until we took him on board.
With these precautions well understood by both of us, I went home.

On opening the outer door of our chambers with my key, I found a letter in the box, addressed to me — a very dirty letter, though not badly written. It had been delivered by hand, of course, since I had left home. Its contents were these:

"If you are not afraid to come to the old marshes tonight or tomorrow night at nine, and to come to the little sluice-house by the limekiln, you had better come. If you want information regarding your uncle Provis, you had much better come and tell no one, and lose no time. You must come alone. Bring this with you."

I had had load enough on my mind before receiving this strange letter. What to do now, I could not tell. And the worst was that I had to decide quickly, or I should miss the afternoon coach, which would get me down in time for tonight. Tomorrow night I could not think of going, for it would be too close to the time of the flight. And for all I knew, the offered information might have some important bearing on the flight itself.

If I had had plenty of time to think, I believe I would still have gone. Having almost no time to think — my watch showing me that the coach departed in half an hour — I resolved to go. I should certainly not have gone but for the reference to my Uncle Provis. That, coming on top of Wemmick's letter and the morning's busy preparations, tipped the balance.

It is so hard to properly absorb the contents of almost any letter in a violent hurry that I had to read this mysterious note twice more before its instruction to keep it secret lodged mechanically in my mind. Yielding to it in the same mechanical way, I left a pencilled note for Herbert, telling him that since I should be going away so soon, for how long I did not know, I had decided to make a quick trip down and back to check on Miss Havisham. I then barely had time to grab my greatcoat, lock up the chambers, and get to the coach office by the back streets. If I had taken a cab and gone by the main roads, I should have missed my goal. Going as I did, I caught the coach just as it came out of the yard. I was the only inside passenger, jolting along knee-deep in straw, when I came to my senses.

For I really had not been myself since receiving the letter; it had so bewildered me, following on the morning's rush. The morning's hurry and confusion had been intense, for long and anxiously as I had waited for Wemmick, his signal had come as a surprise at last. And now I began to wonder at myself for being in the coach, and to doubt whether I had sufficient reason for being there, and to consider whether I should get out presently and go back, and to argue against ever heeding an anonymous message — in short, to pass through all those phases of contradiction and indecision that I suppose very few people in a hurry are strangers to. Still, the reference to Provis by name overrode everything. I reasoned as I had already reasoned without knowing it — if that can be called reasoning — that should any harm befall him through my not going, how could I ever forgive myself!

It was dark before we arrived, and the journey seemed long and dreary to me, who could see little of it from inside and who could not ride on top in my injured state. Avoiding the Blue Boar, I put up at a lesser-known inn in the town and ordered some dinner. While it was being prepared, I went to Satis House and asked after Miss Havisham. She was still very ill, though considered somewhat better.

My inn had once been part of an ancient church building, and I dined in a little octagonal common-room, like a font. Since I could not cut my dinner with my injured arm, the old landlord, with a shining bald head, did it for me. This leading to conversation, he was kind enough to entertain me with my own story — of course featuring the popular version in which Pumblechook was my earliest benefactor and the founder of my fortunes.
"Do you know the young man?" I said.
"Know him!" repeated the landlord. "Ever since he was — no height at all."
"Does he ever come back to this neighbourhood?"
"Yes, he comes back," said the landlord, "to his great friends, now and again, and gives the cold shoulder to the man that made him."
"What man is that?"
"The one I'm speaking of," said the landlord. "Mr. Pumblechook."
"Is he ungrateful to no one else?"
"No doubt he would be, if he could," returned the landlord, "but he can't. And why? Because Pumblechook done everything for him."
"Does Pumblechook say so?"
"Say so!" replied the landlord. "He doesn't need to say so."
"But does he say so?"
"It would turn a man's blood to white wine vinegar to hear him tell of it, sir," said the landlord.
I thought, "Yet Joe, dear Joe, you never tell of it. Long-suffering and loving Joe, you never complain. Nor you, sweet-tempered Biddy!"
"Your appetite's been affected by your accident," said the landlord, glancing at the bandaged arm under my coat. "Try a tenderer piece."
"No, thank you," I replied, turning from the table to brood over the fire. "I can eat no more. Please take it away."
I had never been struck so sharply by my thanklessness to Joe as through the brazen impostor Pumblechook. The falser he, the truer Joe. The meaner he, the nobler Joe.

My heart was deeply and most deservedly humbled as I sat by the fire for an hour or more. The striking of the clock roused me, but not from my dejection or remorse. I got up and had my coat fastened round my neck and went out. I had previously searched my pockets for the letter, wanting to look at it again, but I could not find it, and was uneasy to think it must have been dropped in the straw of the coach. I knew very well, however, that the appointed place was the little sluice-house by the limekiln on the marshes, and the hour was nine. Toward the marshes I now went straight, having no time to spare.

chapters.title: Chapter 53
paragraphs: It was a dark night, though the full moon rose as I left the enclosed farmland and passed out upon the marshes. Beyond their dark line there was a ribbon of clear sky, barely broad enough to hold the red, large moon. In a few minutes she had risen out of that clear strip into the piled mountains of cloud.

There was a mournful wind, and the marshes were very dismal. A stranger would have found them unbearable, and even to me they were so oppressive that I hesitated, half inclined to go back. But I knew them well and could have found my way on a far darker night, and had no excuse for turning back now that I was here. So, having come against my inclination, I went on against it.

The direction I took was not toward my old home, nor the way we had chased the convicts. My back was turned toward the distant prison-ships as I walked on, and though I could see the old lights out on the spits of sand, I saw them over my shoulder. I knew the limekiln as well as I knew the old Battery, but they were miles apart. If a light had been burning at each point that night, there would have been a long strip of blank horizon between the two bright specks.

At first I had to shut some gates behind me, and now and then to stand still while the cattle lying in the raised pathway got up and blundered down among the grass and reeds. But after a little while I seemed to have the whole flat expanse to myself.

It was another half-hour before I drew near to the kiln. The lime was burning with a sluggish, suffocating smell, but the fires had been made up and left, and no workmen were visible. Nearby was a small stone quarry. It lay directly in my path and had been worked that day, as I could see from the tools and barrows lying about.

Coming up again to marsh level out of this excavation — for the rough path lay through it — I saw a light in the old sluice-house. I quickened my pace and knocked at the door with my hand. Waiting for an answer, I looked about me, noticing how the sluice was abandoned and broken, how the house — of wood with a tiled roof — would not withstand the weather much longer, if it even could now, and how the mud and ooze were coated with lime, and how the choking vapour of the kiln crept in a ghostly way toward me. Still there was no answer, and I knocked again. No answer still, and I tried the latch.

It rose under my hand and the door opened. Looking in, I saw a lit candle on a table, a bench, and a mattress on a low bedstead. Since there was a loft above, I called, "Is there anyone here?" but no voice answered. Then I checked my watch, and finding it was past nine, called again, "Is there anyone here?" There being still no answer, I went out at the door, uncertain what to do.

It was beginning to rain hard. Seeing nothing beyond what I had already seen, I turned back into the house and stood just within the shelter of the doorway, looking out into the night. While I was considering that someone must have been there recently and must soon return, or the candle would not be burning, it occurred to me to check if the wick was long. I turned round to do so and had taken up the candle in my hand when it was knocked out by some violent blow. The next thing I knew was that I had been caught in a strong running noose, thrown over my head from behind.
"Now," said a muffled voice with an oath, "I've got you!"
"What is this?" I cried, struggling. "Who is it? Help, help, help!"

Not only were my arms pulled tight to my sides, but the pressure on my bad arm caused me agonising pain. Sometimes a strong man's hand, sometimes a strong man's chest, was set against my mouth to stifle my cries, and with a hot breath always close to me, I struggled uselessly in the dark while I was fastened tight to the wall. "And now," said the muffled voice with another oath, "call out again, and I'll make short work of you!"

Faint and sick with the pain in my injured arm, bewildered by the ambush, and yet aware how easily this threat could be carried out, I stopped struggling and tried to ease my arm however slightly. But it was bound too tight for that. I felt as if, having been burned before, it were now being boiled.

The sudden shutting out of the night, and the replacement of darkness in its place, told me that the man had closed a shutter. After groping about for a little, he found the flint and steel he wanted and began to strike a light. I strained my eyes at the sparks that fell among the tinder, on which he breathed and breathed, match in hand, but I could only see his lips and the blue point of the match — and even those only fitfully. The tinder was damp — no wonder in that place — and one after another the sparks died out.

The man was in no hurry and struck again with the flint and steel. As the sparks fell thick and bright about him, I could see his hands and glimpses of his face, and could make out that he was seated and bending over the table, but nothing more. Presently I saw his blue lips again, breathing on the tinder, and then a flare of light flashed up and showed me Orlick.
Whom I had expected, I don't know. I had not expected him. Seeing him, I felt that I was in a truly dangerous situation, and I kept my eyes fixed on him.

He lit the candle from the flaring match with great deliberation, dropped the match, and trod it out. Then he put the candle on the far side of the table so its light fell on me, and sat with his arms folded on the table and looked at me. I made out that I was fastened to a stout vertical ladder a few inches from the wall — a fixture there — the means of climbing to the loft above.
"Now," he said, when we had surveyed one another for some time, "I've got you."
"Untie me. Let me go!"
"Ah!" he returned. "I'll let you go. I'll let you go to the moon. I'll let you go to the stars. All in good time."
"Why have you lured me here?"
"Don't you know?" he said, with a deadly look.
"Why have you attacked me in the dark?"
"Because I mean to do it all myself. One keeps a secret better than two. Oh, you enemy, you enemy!"

His enjoyment of the spectacle I presented, as he sat with his arms folded on the table, shaking his head at me and hugging himself, had a viciousness in it that made me tremble. As I watched him in silence, he put his hand into the corner at his side and took up a gun with a brass-bound stock.
"Do you know this?" he said, making as if to aim at me. "Do you know where you saw it before? Speak, wolf!"
"Yes," I answered.
"You cost me that place. You did. Speak!"
"What else could I do?"
"You did that, and that would be enough without more. How dared you come between me and a young woman I liked?"
"When did I?"
"When didn't you? It was you who always gave Old Orlick a bad name to her."
"You gave it to yourself. You earned it yourself. I could have done you no harm if you had done yourself none."

"You're a liar. And you'll take any pains, and spend any money, to drive me out of this country, will you?" he said, repeating my own words to Biddy from my last conversation with her. "Now I'll tell you a piece of information. It was never so worth your while to get me out of this country as it is tonight. Ah! If it were all your money twenty times over, to the last brass farthing!" As he shook his heavy hand at me, his mouth snarling like a tiger's, I felt that it was true.
"What are you going to do to me?"
"I'm going," he said, bringing his fist down on the table with a heavy blow and rising as the blow fell to give it greater force, "I'm going to have your life!"
He leaned forward staring at me, slowly unclenched his hand and drew it across his mouth as if it watered for me, and sat down again.
"You was always in Old Orlick's way since ever you was a child. You go out of his way this present night. He'll have no more of you. You're dead."
I felt that I had come to the brink of my grave. For a moment I looked wildly round my trap for any chance of escape, but there was none.

"More than that," he said, folding his arms on the table again, "I won't have a rag of you, I won't have a bone of you, left on earth. I'll put your body in the kiln — I could carry two of you to it, on my shoulders — and let people suppose what they like about you. They shall never know nothing."

My mind, with inconceivable speed, followed out all the consequences of such a death. Estella's father would believe I had deserted him, would be taken, would die accusing me. Even Herbert would doubt me, when he compared the letter I had left for him with the fact that I had called at Miss Havisham's gate for only a moment. Joe and Biddy would never know how sorry I had been that night. None would ever know what I had suffered, how true I had meant to be, what agony I had passed through. The death close before me was terrible, but far more terrible than death was the dread of being misremembered afterwards. And so swift were my thoughts that I saw myself despised by unborn generations — Estella's children and their children — while the wretch's words were still on his lips.
"Now, wolf," he said, "before I kill you like any other beast — which is what I mean to do and what I have tied you up for — I'll have a good look at you and a good goad at you. Oh, you enemy!"

It had crossed my mind to cry out for help again, though few could know better than I the solitary nature of the spot and the hopelessness of aid. But as he sat gloating over me, I was sustained by a scornful contempt for him that sealed my lips. Above all things, I resolved that I would not beg, and that I would die making some last poor resistance. Softened as my thoughts of all other people were in that dire extremity, humbly begging pardon of Heaven as I did, broken-hearted as I was at the thought that I had taken no farewell and never now could take farewell of those dear to me, or explain myself to them, or ask their compassion for my miserable mistakes — still, if I could have killed him, even in dying, I would have done it.

He had been drinking, and his eyes were red and bloodshot. Around his neck was slung a tin bottle, as I had often seen his food and drink slung about him in other days. He brought the bottle to his lips and took a fiery drink from it, and I smelled the strong spirits that I saw flash into his face.
"Wolf!" he said, folding his arms again. "Old Orlick's going to tell you something. It was you who did for your shrew sister."
Again my mind, with its former inconceivable speed, had exhausted the whole subject of the attack on my sister, her illness, and her death, before his slow, hesitating speech had formed those words.
"It was you, villain," I said.

"I tell you it was your doing — I tell you it was done through you," he retorted, snatching up the gun and making a blow with the stock at the empty air between us. "I came upon her from behind, as I come upon you tonight. I gave it to her! I left her for dead, and if there had been a limekiln as close to her as there is now to you, she wouldn't have come to life again. But it wasn't Old Orlick that did it — it was you. You were favoured, and he was bullied and beaten. Old Orlick bullied and beaten, eh? Now you pay for it. You done it, now you pay for it."

He drank again and became more savage. I saw by the tilting of the bottle that there was not much left in it. I clearly understood that he was working himself up with its contents to finish me off. I knew that every drop it held was a drop of my life. I knew that when I was changed into a part of the vapour that had crept toward me a little while before, like my own warning ghost, he would do as he had done in my sister's case — rush to the town and be seen slouching about there, drinking at the alehouses. My racing mind pursued him to the town, formed a picture of the street with him in it, and contrasted its lights and life with the lonely marsh and the white vapour creeping over it, into which I should have dissolved.

It was not only that I could have summed up years and years while he said a dozen words, but that what he said presented pictures to me, not mere words. In the excited and exalted state of my brain, I could not think of a place without seeing it, or of people without seeing them. It is impossible to overstate the vividness of these images, and yet I was so intent all the time upon him — who would not be intent on the tiger crouching to spring! — that I was aware of the slightest movement of his fingers.

When he had drunk this second time, he rose from the bench and pushed the table aside. Then he took up the candle and, shading it with his murderous hand so as to throw its light on me, stood before me, looking at me and savouring the sight.
"Wolf, I'll tell you something more. It was Old Orlick you stumbled over on your stairs that night."

I saw the staircase with its extinguished lamps. I saw the shadows of the heavy stair-rails cast by the watchman's lantern on the wall. I saw the rooms I was never to see again — here a door half open, there a door closed, all the articles of furniture around.

"And why was Old Orlick there? I'll tell you something more, wolf. You and her have pretty well hunted me out of this country, so far as making an easy living goes, and I've taken up with new companions and new masters. Some of them write my letters when I want them written — do you understand? — write my letters, wolf! They can write fifty different hands. They're not like sneaking you, who writes only one. I've had a firm mind and a firm will to have your life since you were down here at your sister's burying. I haven't seen a way to get you safe, and I've watched your comings and goings. For, says Old Orlick to himself, 'Somehow or other I'll have him!' What! When I look for you, I find your uncle Provis, eh?"

Mill Pond Bank and Chinks's Basin and the Old Green Copper Rope-walk, all so clear and plain! Provis in his rooms, the signal whose purpose was over, pretty Clara, the good motherly woman, old Bill Barley on his back — all drifting by, as on the swift stream of my life fast running out to sea!

"You with an uncle too! Why, I knew you at Gargery's when you were so small a wolf that I could have taken your throat between this finger and thumb and snapped you dead — as I thought of doing, odd times, when I saw you loitering among the pollard trees on a Sunday — and you hadn't found any uncles then. No, not you! But when Old Orlick came to hear that your uncle Provis had most likely worn the leg-iron that Old Orlick had picked up, filed apart, on these meshes ever so many years ago, and that he kept it by him till he struck down your sister with it, like an ox, as he means to strike down you — hey? — when he came to hear that — hey?"
In his savage taunting, he thrust the candle so close to my face that I turned aside to save it from the flame.

"Ah!" he cried, laughing, after doing it again. "The burnt child dreads the fire! Old Orlick knew you were burnt. Old Orlick knew you were smuggling your uncle Provis away. Old Orlick's a match for you and knew you'd come tonight! Now I'll tell you something more, wolf, and this ends it. There are those who are as good a match for your uncle Provis as Old Orlick has been for you. Let him beware of them when he's lost his nephew! Let him beware of them when no man can find a rag of his dear relation's clothes, nor yet a bone of his body. There are those who can't and who won't have Magwitch — yes, I know the name! — alive in the same land with them, and who've had such sure information of him when he was alive in another land that he couldn't and shouldn't leave it unknown and put them in danger. Perhaps it's those who write fifty hands, not like sneaking you who writes only one. Beware Compeyson, Magwitch, and the gallows!"

He thrust the candle at me again, smoking my face and hair and for an instant blinding me, and turned his powerful back as he replaced the light on the table. I had thought a prayer and had been with Joe and Biddy and Herbert before he turned toward me again.

There was a clear space of a few feet between the table and the opposite wall. Within this space he now slouched back and forth. His great strength seemed to sit heavier upon him than ever, as he did this with his hands hanging loose and heavy at his sides and his eyes glaring at me. I had not a grain of hope left. Wild as my inward rush was, and wonderful the force of the pictures that streamed past me instead of thoughts, I could clearly understand that unless he had resolved I was within a few moments of surely perishing from all human knowledge, he would never have told me what he had told.

Suddenly he stopped, took the cork out of his bottle, and tossed it away. Light as it was, I heard it fall like a weight. He swallowed slowly, tilting the bottle up little by little, and now he looked at me no more. The last few drops of liquor he poured into the palm of his hand and licked up. Then, with a sudden rush of violence and horrible swearing, he threw the bottle from him and stooped. And I saw in his hand a stone-hammer with a long heavy handle.

The resolution I had made did not desert me, for without uttering one useless word of appeal, I shouted out with all my might and struggled with all my might. It was only my head and my legs that I could move, but to that extent I struggled with all the force, until then unknown, that was in me. In the same instant I heard answering shouts, saw figures and a gleam of light dash in at the door, heard voices and tumult, and saw Orlick emerge from a tangle of men, as if it were churning water, clear the table at a leap, and fly out into the night.

After a blank, I found that I was lying unbound, on the floor, in the same place, with my head on someone's knee. My eyes were fixed on the ladder against the wall when I came to — had opened on it before my mind recognized it — and so, as I recovered consciousness, I knew that I was in the place where I had lost it.
Too dazed at first even to look round and see who supported me, I was lying staring at the ladder when a face came between me and it. The face of Trabb's boy!
"I think he's all right!" said Trabb's boy, in a serious voice. "But isn't he just pale though!"
At these words, the face of the one who supported me looked over into mine, and I saw my supporter to be —
"Herbert! Great Heaven!"
"Softly," said Herbert. "Gently, Handel. Don't be too eager."
"And our old comrade, Startop!" I cried, as he too bent over me.
"Remember what he is going to help us with," said Herbert, "and be calm."

The reference made me spring up, though I dropped again from the pain in my arm. "The time hasn't gone by, Herbert, has it? What night is tonight? How long have I been here?" For I had a strange and strong fear that I had been lying there a long time — a day and a night — two days and nights — more.
"The time has not gone by. It is still Monday night."
"Thank God!"
"And you have all of tomorrow, Tuesday, to rest in," said Herbert. "But you can't help groaning, my dear Handel. What injury have you got? Can you stand?"
"Yes, yes," I said. "I can walk. I have no hurt but in this throbbing arm."

They bared it and did what they could. It was violently swollen and inflamed, and I could scarcely bear to have it touched. But they tore up their handkerchiefs to make fresh bandages and carefully replaced it in the sling, until we could get to the town and find some cooling lotion. In a little while we had shut the door of the dark and empty sluice-house and were passing through the quarry on our way back. Trabb's boy — Trabb's overgrown young man now — went before us with a lantern, which was the light I had seen come in at the door. But the moon was a good two hours higher than when I had last seen the sky, and the night, though rainy, was much lighter. The white vapour of the kiln was drifting past us as we went by, and as I had thought a prayer before, I thought a thanksgiving now.

Begging Herbert to tell me how he had come to my rescue — which at first he flatly refused to do, insisting that I rest — I learned that I had in my hurry dropped the letter, open, in our chambers, where he, coming home to bring Startop whom he had met in the street on his way to me, found it very soon after I had gone. Its tone made him uneasy, and the more so because of the contradiction between it and the hasty note I had left for him. His uneasiness growing rather than fading after a quarter of an hour's thought, he set off for the coach office with Startop, who volunteered his company, to find out when the next coach went down. Discovering that the afternoon coach was already gone, and that his anxiety was turning into real alarm as obstacles arose, he resolved to follow in a post-chaise. So he and Startop arrived at the Blue Boar, fully expecting to find me or news of me. Finding neither, they went on to Miss Havisham's, where they lost my trail. They then went back to the hotel — doubtless at about the time I was hearing the popular local version of my own story — to refresh themselves and find someone to guide them out onto the marshes. Among the loiterers under the Boar's archway happened to be Trabb's boy — true to his ancient habit of being everywhere he had no business — and Trabb's boy had seen me passing from Miss Havisham's in the direction of my inn. So Trabb's boy became their guide, and with him they went out to the sluice-house, though by the town road to the marshes, which I had avoided. Now, as they went along, Herbert reflected that I might after all have been brought there on some genuine errand related to Provis's safety. Thinking that in that case an interruption would be harmful, he left his guide and Startop at the edge of the quarry and went on by himself, stealing round the house two or three times, trying to determine whether all was well within. Since he could hear nothing but the indistinct sounds of one deep rough voice — this was while my mind was so desperately busy — he had even begun to doubt whether I was there, when suddenly I cried out loudly. He answered the cries and rushed in, closely followed by the other two.

When I told Herbert what had happened inside the house, he was for our immediately going before a magistrate in the town, late as it was, and getting a warrant. But I had already considered that such a course, by keeping us there or obliging us to return, might be fatal to Provis. There was no arguing with this difficulty, and we abandoned all thought of pursuing Orlick for the time being. For the present, given the circumstances, we thought it wise to make rather light of the matter to Trabb's boy, who I am convinced would have been greatly disappointed if he had known that his arrival saved me from the limekiln. Not that Trabb's boy was malicious by nature, but he had too much restless energy, and it was in his character to crave variety and excitement at anybody's expense. When we parted, I gave him two guineas — which seemed to satisfy him — and told him I was sorry ever to have had a poor opinion of him, which made no impression on him at all.

Since Wednesday was so close, we decided to go back to London that night, three in the post-chaise — especially as we should then be well clear before the night's adventure began to be talked about. Herbert got a large bottle of medicine for my arm, and by having it dripped over the burn all night long, I was just able to bear the pain on the journey. It was daylight when we reached the Temple, and I went straight to bed, where I lay all day.

My terror, as I lay there, of falling ill and being unfit for tomorrow was so overwhelming that I am amazed it did not disable me on its own. It would have done so, almost certainly, combined with the mental strain I had endured, but for the unnatural tension of what tomorrow held. So anxiously looked forward to, charged with such consequences, its results so impenetrably hidden, though so near.

No precaution could have been more obvious than our avoiding all contact with him that day. Yet this only increased my restlessness. I started at every footstep and every sound, certain that he was discovered and taken, and that this was the messenger come to tell me so. I convinced myself that I knew he was taken — that there was something more on my mind than a fear or a premonition — that the thing had happened and I had a mysterious awareness of it. As the day wore on and no bad news came, as the day closed in and darkness fell, my overriding dread of being disabled by illness before tomorrow morning mastered me entirely. My burning arm throbbed, my burning head throbbed, and I fancied I was beginning to rave. I counted up to high numbers to test myself, and repeated passages I knew in prose and verse. It sometimes happened that in the mere escape of an exhausted mind I dozed for a few moments or lost my train of thought. Then I would say to myself with a start, "Now it has come, and I am turning delirious!"

They kept me very quiet all day and kept my arm constantly dressed and gave me cooling drinks. Whenever I fell asleep, I woke with the same conviction I had had in the sluice-house: that a long time had passed and the chance to save him was gone. Around midnight I got out of bed and went to Herbert, certain that I had slept for twenty-four hours and that Wednesday was past. It was the last self-exhausting effort of my fretfulness, for after that I slept soundly.

Wednesday morning was dawning when I looked out of the window. The twinkling lights on the bridges were already pale. The rising sun was like a marsh of fire on the horizon. The river, still dark and mysterious, was spanned by bridges turning coldly grey, with here and there a warm touch from the burning in the sky. As I looked along the clustered roofs, with church-towers and spires rising into the unusually clear air, the sun rose, and a veil seemed to be drawn from the river, and millions of sparkles burst out upon its waters. From me, too, a veil seemed to be drawn, and I felt strong and well.

Herbert lay asleep in his bed, and our old fellow-student lay asleep on the sofa. I could not dress myself without help, but I made up the fire, which was still burning, and got some coffee ready for them. In good time they too woke up, strong and well, and we let in the sharp morning air at the windows and watched the tide that was still flowing toward us.
"When it turns at nine o'clock," said Herbert cheerfully, "look out for us, and stand ready, you over there at Mill Pond Bank!"

chapters.title: Chapter 54
paragraphs: It was one of those March days when the sun shines hot and the wind blows cold — when it is summer in the light and winter in the shade. We had our pea-coats with us, and I took a bag. Of all my worldly possessions I took no more than the few necessities that filled it. Where I might go, what I might do, or when I might return were questions utterly unknown to me. Nor did I trouble my mind with them, for it was wholly fixed on Provis's safety. I only wondered for a passing moment, as I stopped at the door and looked back, under what changed circumstances I should next see those rooms, if ever.

We strolled down to the Temple stairs and stood loitering there, as if we weren't quite decided to go on the water at all. Of course I had taken care that the boat should be ready and everything in order. After a little show of indecision — which there was no one to see but the two or three amphibious creatures belonging to our Temple stairs — we got on board and cast off: Herbert in the bow, I steering. It was then about high-water — half-past eight.

Our plan was this. The tide, beginning to run down at nine and carrying us until three, we intended to keep creeping on after it turned, rowing against it until dark. We should then be well into those long reaches below Gravesend, between Kent and Essex, where the river is broad and solitary, where the riverside inhabitants are very few, and where lonely public-houses are scattered here and there, of which we could choose one for a resting-place. There we meant to lie up all night. The steamer for Hamburg and the steamer for Rotterdam would start from London at about nine on Thursday morning. We should know at what time to expect them, depending on where we were, and would hail the first; so that if by any accident we were not taken aboard, we should have another chance. We knew the distinguishing marks of each vessel.

The relief of finally being engaged in carrying out the plan was so great that I found it hard to believe in the condition I had been in a few hours before. The crisp air, the sunlight, the movement on the river, and the moving river itself — the road that ran with us, seeming to share our feelings, animate us, and urge us on — refreshed me with new hope. I felt embarrassed to be of so little use in the boat, but there were few better oarsmen than my two friends, and they rowed with a steady stroke that was to last all day.

At that time, the steam-traffic on the Thames was far below its present level, and watermen's boats were far more numerous. Of barges, sailing coal-ships, and coasting-traders there were perhaps as many as now, but of steamships, great and small, not a tenth or a twentieth as many. Early as it was, there were plenty of scullers going here and there that morning, and plenty of barges drifting down with the tide. Navigating the river between bridges in an open boat was a much easier and more common thing in those days than it is in these, and we went ahead briskly among many skiffs and wherries.

Old London Bridge was soon passed, and old Billingsgate Market with its oyster-boats and Dutchmen, and the White Tower and Traitor's Gate, and we were in among the tiers of shipping. Here were the Leith, Aberdeen, and Glasgow steamers, loading and unloading goods, looking immensely high out of the water as we passed alongside. Here were colliers by the score, with coal-haulers plunging off stages on deck as counterweights to swinging loads of coal, which were then rattled over the side into barges. Here, at her moorings, was tomorrow's steamer for Rotterdam, of which we took careful note. And here, tomorrow's for Hamburg, under whose bowsprit we crossed. And now I, sitting in the stern, could see with a faster-beating heart, Mill Pond Bank and Mill Pond stairs.
"Is he there?" said Herbert.
"Not yet."
"Right! He was not to come down till he saw us. Can you see his signal?"
"Not well from here, but I think I see it. — Now I see him! Pull both. Easy, Herbert. Oars!"

We touched the stairs lightly for a single moment, and he was on board, and we were off again. He had a boat-cloak with him and a black canvas bag, and he looked as much like a river-pilot as my heart could have wished.
"Dear boy!" he said, putting his arm on my shoulder as he took his seat. "Faithful dear boy, well done. Thank you, thank you!"

Again among the tiers of shipping, in and out, dodging rusty chain-cables and frayed hempen ropes and bobbing buoys, sinking past floating broken baskets, scattering floating chips of wood and shavings, cutting through floating scum of coal — in and out, under the figurehead of the John of Sunderland making a speech to the winds (as is done by many Johns), and the Betsy of Yarmouth with a firm formality of bosom and her knobby eyes starting two inches out of her head; in and out, hammers going in shipbuilders' yards, saws going at timber, clanking engines going at things unknown, pumps going in leaky ships, capstans going, ships going out to sea, and unintelligible sea-creatures roaring curses over the bulwarks at answering lightermen — in and out, and out at last upon the clearer river, where the ships' boys might take in their fenders, no longer dangling them over the side in troubled waters, and where the festooned sails might fly out to the wind.

At the stairs where we had taken him aboard, and ever since, I had watched carefully for any sign that we were suspected. I had seen none. We certainly had not been followed, and at that moment we certainly were not being either watched or trailed by any boat. If any boat had been hovering near us, I should have pulled in to shore and forced it either to move on or to reveal its purpose. But we held our own without any sign of interference.

He had his boat-cloak on and looked, as I have said, a natural part of the scene. It was remarkable — but perhaps the wretched life he had led accounted for it — that he was the least anxious of any of us. He was not indifferent, for he told me he hoped to live to see his gentleman become one of the best of gentlemen in a foreign country. He was not passive or resigned, as I understood it. But he had no habit of meeting danger halfway. When it came upon him, he confronted it, but it must come before he troubled himself.
"If you knew, dear boy," he said to me, "what it is to sit here alongside my dear boy and have my smoke, after being day after day between four walls, you'd envy me. But you don't know what it is."
"I think I know the delights of freedom," I answered.
"Ah," he said, shaking his head gravely. "But you don't know it as I do. You must have been under lock and key, dear boy, to know it as I do — but I ain't going to be low."

It struck me as inconsistent that, for any governing idea, he should have risked his freedom, and even his life. But I reflected that perhaps freedom without danger was too far removed from everything he had known to mean to him what it would to another man. I was not far wrong, for he said, after smoking a little:

"You see, dear boy, when I was over yonder, on the other side of the world, I was always looking toward this side. And it fell flat to be there, for all I was growing rich. Everybody knew Magwitch, and Magwitch could come and Magwitch could go, and nobody's head would be troubled about him. They ain't so easy about me here, dear boy — wouldn't be, at least, if they knew where I was."
"If all goes well," I said, "you will be perfectly free and safe again within a few hours."
"Well," he returned, drawing a long breath, "I hope so."
"And think so?"
He dipped his hand in the water over the boat's side and said, smiling with that softened air upon him which was not new to me:

"Yes, I suppose I think so, dear boy. We'd be hard put to be more quiet and easy-going than we are right now. But — it's flowing so soft and pleasant through the water, perhaps, that makes me think it — I was thinking through my smoke just then that we can no more see to the bottom of the next few hours than we can see to the bottom of this river that I'm holding. Nor can we hold their tide any more than I can hold this. And it's run through my fingers and gone, you see!" holding up his dripping hand.
"But for your face, I should think you were a little gloomy," I said.
"Not a bit of it, dear boy! It comes of flowing on so quiet, and of that rippling at the boat's bow making a sort of Sunday tune. Maybe I'm growing a little old besides."

He put his pipe back in his mouth with an untroubled expression and sat as composed and content as if we were already out of England. Yet he was as obedient to a word of advice as if he had been in constant terror. For when we pulled ashore to get some bottles of beer into the boat, and he was stepping out, I hinted that I thought he would be safest where he was, and he said, "Do you, dear boy?" and quietly sat down again.

The air felt cold on the river, but it was a bright day and the sunshine was very cheering. The tide ran strong. I took care to lose none of it, and our steady stroke carried us on thoroughly well. By imperceptible degrees, as the tide ran out, we lost more and more of the nearer woods and hills and dropped lower and lower between the muddy banks, but the tide was still with us when we were off Gravesend. As our charge was wrapped in his cloak, I purposely passed within a boat's length or two of the floating Custom House, and so out to catch the stream, alongside two emigrant ships, and under the bows of a large troop transport with soldiers on the forecastle looking down at us. And soon the tide began to slacken, and the moored craft began to swing round, and presently they had all swung, and the ships taking advantage of the new tide to get up to the Pool began to crowd upon us in a fleet, and we kept under the shore, staying out of the strength of the tide as best we could, carefully avoiding low shallows and mudbanks.

Our oarsmen were so fresh — having occasionally let the boat drift with the tide for a minute or two — that a quarter of an hour's rest proved all they needed. We got ashore among some slippery stones while we ate and drank what we had with us, and looked around. It was like my own marsh country, flat and monotonous, with a dim horizon, while the winding river turned and turned, and the great floating buoys upon it turned and turned, and everything else seemed stranded and still. For now the last of the fleet of ships had rounded the last low headland we had passed, and the last green barge, straw-laden, with a brown sail, had followed, and some ballast-lighters, shaped like a child's first crude attempt at a boat, lay low in the mud. A little squat shoal-lighthouse on open piles stood crippled in the mud on stilts and crutches, and slimy stakes stuck out of the mud, and slimy stones stuck out of the mud, and red landmarks and tidemarks stuck out of the mud, and an old landing-stage and an old roofless building had slipped into the mud, and all about us was stagnation and mud.

We pushed off again and made what progress we could. It was much harder work now, but Herbert and Startop kept at it, and rowed and rowed and rowed until the sun went down. By that time the river had lifted us enough that we could see over the bank. There was the red sun, on the low level of the shore, in a purple haze fast deepening to black. And there was the solitary flat marsh. And far away the rising grounds, between which and us there seemed to be no life, save here and there in the foreground a melancholy gull.

As night was falling fast, and as the moon, being past the full, would not rise early, we held a brief council. Clearly our course was to stop at the first lonely tavern we could find. So they bent to their oars once more, and I looked out for anything like a house. Thus we kept on, speaking little, for four or five dreary miles. It was very cold. A coal-ship coming past us, with her galley-fire smoking and flaring, looked like a comfortable home. The night was as dark by now as it would be until morning, and what light we had seemed to come more from the river than the sky, as the oars in their dipping struck at a few reflected stars.

At this dismal time we were all clearly possessed by the idea that we were being followed. As the tide made, it slapped heavily at irregular intervals against the shore, and whenever such a sound came, one or another of us was sure to start and look in that direction. Here and there, the current had worn the bank down into a little creek, and we were all suspicious of such places and eyed them nervously. Sometimes, "What was that ripple?" one of us would say in a low voice. Or another, "Is that a boat over there?" And afterwards we would fall into a dead silence, and I would sit impatiently thinking what an unusual amount of noise the oars made in the rowlocks.

At length we spotted a light and a roof, and soon afterwards pulled alongside a little causeway made of stones that had been gathered nearby. Leaving the rest in the boat, I stepped ashore and found the light to be in a window of a public-house. It was a dirty place, and I dare say not unknown to smugglers. But there was a good fire in the kitchen, and there were eggs and bacon to eat and various drinks. Also, there were two double-bedded rooms — "such as they were," the landlord said. No other company was in the house besides the landlord, his wife, and a grizzled male creature, the "Jack" of the little causeway, who was as slimy and grimy as if he had been low-water mark himself.

With this assistant I went down to the boat again, and we all came ashore and brought out the oars, rudder, boat-hook, and everything else, and hauled her up for the night. We had a very good meal by the kitchen fire and then divided up the bedrooms: Herbert and Startop were to have one, I and our charge the other. We found the air as carefully shut out of both as if it were fatal to life, and there were more dirty clothes and hatboxes under the beds than I would have thought the family possessed. But we considered ourselves well off regardless, for a more solitary place we could not have found.

While we were warming ourselves by the fire after our meal, the Jack — who was sitting in a corner and who had a bloated pair of shoes on, which he had displayed while we were eating our eggs and bacon as interesting souvenirs recently taken from the feet of a drowned seaman washed ashore — asked me if we had seen a four-oared galley going up with the tide. When I told him no, he said she must have gone down then, and yet she "went up too" when she left there.
"They must have changed their mind for some reason or other," said the Jack, "and gone down."
"A four-oared galley, did you say?" I said.
"A four," said the Jack, "and two passengers."
"Did they come ashore here?"
"They put in with a stone two-gallon jar for some beer. I'd have been glad to poison the beer myself," said the Jack, "or put some nasty medicine in it."
"Why?"
"I know why," said the Jack. He spoke in a thick voice, as if much mud had washed into his throat.
"He thinks," said the landlord, a weakly thoughtful man with a pale eye, who seemed to rely heavily on his Jack, "he thinks they were what they wasn't."
"I know what I think," the Jack observed.
"You think Customs, Jack?" said the landlord.
"I do," said the Jack.
"Then you're wrong, Jack."
"Am I!"

In the infinite meaning of his reply and his boundless confidence in his views, the Jack took one of his bloated shoes off, peered into it, knocked a few stones out of it on the kitchen floor, and put it on again. He did this with the air of a Jack who was so right that he could afford to do anything.
"Why, what do you reckon they did with their buttons then, Jack?" asked the landlord, wavering weakly.
"Done with their buttons?" returned the Jack. "Chucked them overboard. Swallowed them. Sowed them, to come up as small salad. Done with their buttons!"
"Don't be cheeky, Jack," the landlord protested, in a melancholy and pathetic way.

"A Customs officer knows what to do with his buttons," said the Jack, repeating the offensive word with the greatest contempt, "when they come between him and his own interest. A four-oar with two passengers doesn't go hanging and hovering, up with one tide and down with another, and both with and against another, without there being Customs at the bottom of it." Saying which, he went out in disdain, and the landlord, having no one to support him, found it impossible to pursue the subject.

This exchange made us all uneasy, and me very uneasy. The dreary wind was muttering round the house, the tide was slapping at the shore, and I had a feeling that we were caged and threatened. A four-oared galley hovering about in so unusual a way as to attract this notice was an alarming circumstance I could not shake. When I had persuaded Provis to go up to bed, I went outside with my two companions — Startop by this time knew the full situation — and held another council. Whether we should stay at the house until near the steamer's time, which would be about one in the afternoon, or whether we should set off early in the morning, was the question we debated. On the whole we decided it better to stay where we were until within an hour or so of the steamer's time, then get out into her track and drift easily with the tide. Having settled on this, we went back inside and to bed.

I lay down with most of my clothes on and slept well for a few hours. When I woke, the wind had risen, and the inn sign — the Ship — was creaking and banging about with noises that startled me. Rising softly, for my charge lay fast asleep, I looked out of the window. It overlooked the causeway where we had hauled up our boat, and as my eyes adjusted to the light of the clouded moon, I saw two men looking into her. They passed by under the window, examining nothing else, and they did not go down to the landing-place, which I could see was empty, but struck across the marsh in the direction of the Nore.

My first impulse was to call Herbert and show him the two men going away. But reflecting, before I reached his room at the back of the house, that he and Startop had had a harder day than I and were exhausted, I held back. Going back to my window, I could see the two men moving across the marsh. In that light, however, I soon lost them, and feeling very cold, lay down to think about it and fell asleep again.

We were up early. As we walked back and forth, all four together, before breakfast, I thought it right to describe what I had seen. Again our charge was the least anxious of the party. The men most likely belonged to the Custom House, he said calmly, and had no thought of us. I tried to convince myself that was true — as, indeed, it easily might be. However, I proposed that he and I should walk away together to a distant point we could see, and that the boat should pick us up there, or as near there as possible, at about noon. This being thought a good precaution, soon after breakfast he and I set out, without saying anything at the inn.

He smoked his pipe as we walked and sometimes stopped to clap me on the shoulder. You would have thought it was I who was in danger, not he, and that he was reassuring me. We spoke very little. As we neared the point, I asked him to wait in a sheltered spot while I went ahead to scout, for it was in that direction that the men had gone in the night. He agreed, and I went on alone. There was no boat off the point, nor any boat drawn up anywhere near it, nor were there any signs that the men had launched from there. But of course the tide was high, and footprints might have been underwater.

When he looked out from his shelter in the distance and saw me wave my hat for him to come, he joined me, and there we waited — sometimes lying on the bank wrapped in our coats, sometimes walking about to keep warm — until we saw our boat coming round. We got aboard easily and rowed out into the track of the steamer. By that time it was only ten minutes to one, and we began to watch for her smoke.

But it was half-past one before we saw her smoke, and soon after we saw behind it the smoke of another steamer. As they were coming on at full speed, we got the two bags ready and took the opportunity to say goodbye to Herbert and Startop.
