We had all shaken hands warmly, and neither Herbert's eyes nor mine were quite dry, when I saw a four-oared galley shoot out from under the bank just a little way ahead of us and row out into the same track.

A stretch of shore had been between us and the steamer's smoke, because of the bend and wind of the river, but now she was visible, coming head-on. I called to Herbert and Startop to keep ahead of the tide so she could see us waiting for her, and I urged Provis to sit perfectly still, wrapped in his cloak. He answered cheerfully, "Trust to me, dear boy," and sat like a statue. Meanwhile the galley, which was very skilfully handled, had crossed our path, let us come up with her, and fallen alongside. Leaving just room enough for the play of the oars, she kept alongside, drifting when we drifted and pulling a stroke or two when we pulled. Of the two passengers, one held the rudder-lines and watched us intently — as did all the rowers. The other passenger was wrapped up, much as Provis was, and seemed to shrink and whisper some instruction to the steersman as he looked at us. Not a word was spoken in either boat.

Startop could make out, after a few minutes, which steamer was first, and gave me the word "Hamburg" in a low voice, as we sat face to face. She was bearing down on us very fast, and the beating of her paddles grew louder and louder. I felt as if her shadow were already upon us when the galley hailed us. I answered.

"You have a returned convict there," said the man who held the lines. "That's the man, wrapped in the cloak. His name is Abel Magwitch, otherwise Provis. I apprehend that man, and call upon him to surrender, and you to assist."

At the same moment, without giving any audible order to his crew, he ran the galley across our bow. They had pulled one sudden stroke ahead, shipped their oars, run across us, and were holding on to our side before we knew what they were doing. This caused great confusion aboard the steamer, and I heard them calling to us, heard the order given to stop the paddles, heard them stop, but felt her driving down upon us unstoppably. In the same moment, I saw the steersman of the galley lay his hand on his prisoner's shoulder, and saw both boats swinging round with the force of the tide, and saw all hands on the steamer running forward in a frenzy. Still, in the same moment, I saw the prisoner start up, lean across his captor, and pull the cloak from the neck of the shrinking passenger in the galley. Still in the same moment, I saw that the face revealed was the face of the other convict of long ago. Still, in the same moment, I saw the face tilt backward with a white terror on it that I shall never forget, and heard a great cry on board the steamer and a loud splash in the water, and felt the boat sink from under me.

It was only for an instant that I seemed to struggle with a thousand mill-weirs and a thousand flashes of light. That instant past, I was taken on board the galley. Herbert was there, and Startop was there, but our boat was gone, and the two convicts were gone.

What with the cries aboard the steamer and the furious blowing off of her steam, and her driving on, and our driving on, I could not at first tell sky from water or shore from shore. But the crew of the galley righted her with great speed, and pulling certain swift strong strokes ahead, lay on their oars, every man looking silently and eagerly at the water astern. Presently a dark shape was seen in it, drifting toward us on the tide. No man spoke, but the steersman held up his hand, and all softly backed water, keeping the boat straight and true before it. As it came nearer, I saw it to be Magwitch, swimming, but not swimming freely. He was taken on board and instantly manacled at the wrists and ankles.

The galley was held steady, and the silent, eager watch of the water resumed. But the Rotterdam steamer now came up, and apparently not understanding what had happened, came on at speed. By the time she had been hailed and stopped, both steamers were drifting away from us, and we were rising and falling in a troubled wake of water. The watch was kept long after all was still again and the two steamers were gone, but everybody knew that it was hopeless now.

At length we gave it up and pulled under the shore toward the tavern we had recently left, where we were received with no little surprise. Here I was able to get some comforts for Magwitch — Provis no longer — who had received a very severe injury in the chest and a deep cut on the head.

He told me that he believed he had gone under the keel of the steamer and had been struck on the head coming up. The injury to his chest, which made his breathing extremely painful, he thought he had received against the side of the galley. He added that he did not claim to say what he might or might not have done to Compeyson, but that in the moment of laying his hand on the man's cloak to identify him, that villain had staggered up and staggered back, and they had both gone overboard together, when the sudden wrenching of him — Magwitch — out of our boat, and his captor's effort to keep him in it, had capsized us. He told me in a whisper that they had gone down fiercely locked in each other's arms, that there had been a struggle underwater, and that he had broken free, struck out, and swum away.
I never had any reason to doubt the exact truth of what he told me. The officer who steered the galley gave the same account of their going overboard.

When I asked this officer's permission to change the prisoner's wet clothes by buying any spare garments I could find at the public-house, he gave it readily, merely noting that he must take charge of everything his prisoner had about him. So the pocketbook which had once been in my hands passed into the officer's. He further gave me leave to accompany the prisoner to London but declined to extend that favour to my two friends.

The Jack at the Ship was told where the drowned man had gone down and undertook to search for the body in the likeliest places. His interest in recovering it seemed greatly increased when he heard that it had stockings on. Probably it took about a dozen drowned men to outfit him completely, and that may have been why the different articles of his clothing were in various stages of decay.

We remained at the public-house until the tide turned, and then Magwitch was carried down to the galley and put on board. Herbert and Startop were to get to London by land as soon as they could. We had a sorrowful parting, and when I took my place by Magwitch's side, I felt that that was my place from now on, as long as he lived.

For now, my revulsion toward him had entirely melted away. In the hunted, wounded, shackled creature who held my hand in his, I saw only a man who had meant to be my benefactor and who had felt affection, gratitude, and generosity toward me with great constancy through a series of years. I saw in him only a much better man than I had been to Joe.

His breathing grew more difficult and painful as the night drew on, and often he could not hold back a groan. I tried to rest him on the arm I could use, in as comfortable a position as possible. But it was dreadful to think that I could not be sorry at heart for his being badly hurt, since it was unquestionably best that he should die. That there were still living people enough who were able and willing to identify him, I could not doubt. That he would be treated leniently, I could not hope. He who had been presented in the worst light at his trial, who had since escaped from prison and been tried again, who had returned from transportation under a life sentence, and who had caused the death of the man responsible for his arrest.

As we returned toward the setting sun we had left behind us the day before, and as the stream of our hopes seemed all running back, I told him how grieved I was to think that he had come home for my sake.
"Dear boy," he answered, "I'm quite content to take my chance. I've seen my boy, and he can be a gentleman without me."

No. I had thought about that while we sat side by side. No. Quite apart from my own feelings, I understood Wemmick's hint now. I foresaw that, being convicted, his possessions would be seized by the Crown.

"Look here, dear boy," he said. "It's best that a gentleman should not be known to belong to me now. Only come to see me as if you came by chance along with Wemmick. Sit where I can see you when I'm sworn to, for the last of many times, and I don't ask for more."
"I will never leave your side," I said, "when I am allowed to be near you. Please God, I will be as true to you as you have been to me!"

I felt his hand tremble as it held mine, and he turned his face away as he lay in the bottom of the boat, and I heard that old sound in his throat — softened now, like all the rest of him. It was a good thing that he had raised this point, for it put into my mind what I might not otherwise have thought of until too late: that he need never know how his hopes of enriching me had come to nothing.

chapters.title: Chapter 55
paragraphs: He was taken to the Police Court the next day, and would have been immediately committed for trial, but it was necessary to send for an old officer of the prison-ship from which he had once escaped, to confirm his identity. Nobody doubted it, but Compeyson, who had meant to testify, was tumbling on the tides, dead, and it happened that there was not at that time any prison officer in London who could give the required evidence. I had gone directly to Mr. Jaggers at his private house on my arrival the night before, to secure his help, and Mr. Jaggers on the prisoner's behalf would admit nothing. It was the only course, for he told me the case would be over in five minutes once the witness was there, and that no power on earth could prevent it going against us.

I told Mr. Jaggers of my intention to keep him ignorant of the fate of his wealth. Mr. Jaggers was irritable and angry with me for having "let it slip through my fingers," and said we must petition by and by, and try at all events for some of it. But he did not hide from me that, although there might be many cases where the forfeiture would not be enforced, there were no circumstances in this case to make it one of them. I understood that very well. I was not related to the outlaw, or connected with him by any recognisable tie. He had put his hand to no document or settlement in my favour before his arrest, and to do so now would be useless. I had no claim, and I finally resolved — and ever afterwards kept to that resolution — that my heart should never be sickened with the hopeless task of trying to establish one.

There appeared to be reason for believing that the drowned informer had hoped for a reward from this forfeiture and had obtained some accurate knowledge of Magwitch's affairs. When his body was found, many miles from where he had drowned, and so horribly disfigured that he was only identifiable by the contents of his pockets, notes were still legible, folded in a case he carried. Among these were the name of a bank in New South Wales where a sum of money was held, and the description of certain valuable lands. Both these items of information were on a list that Magwitch, while in prison, gave to Mr. Jaggers, of the possessions he supposed I should inherit. His ignorance, poor fellow, at last served him; he never suspected that my inheritance was anything but safe, with Mr. Jaggers's help.

After three days' delay, during which the prosecution was held over awaiting the witness from the prison-ship, the witness came and completed the simple case. He was committed to stand trial at the next Sessions, which would come on in a month.
It was at this dark time of my life that Herbert came home one evening, rather downcast, and said —
"My dear Handel, I fear I shall soon have to leave you."
His partner having prepared me for that, I was less surprised than he expected.
"We shall lose a fine opportunity if I put off going to Cairo, and I'm very much afraid I must go, Handel, just when you most need me."
"Herbert, I shall always need you, because I shall always love you. But my need is no greater now than at any other time."
"You will be so lonely."

"I haven't the leisure to think of that," I said. "You know that I am always with him to the full extent of the time allowed, and that I should be with him all day long if I could. And when I come away from him, you know that my thoughts are with him."
The dreadful condition he was in was so terrible to both of us that we could not refer to it in plainer words.
"My dear fellow," said Herbert, "let the near prospect of our separation — for it is very near — be my justification for raising the subject of yourself. Have you thought of your future?"
"No, for I have been afraid to think of any future."
"But yours cannot be put aside; indeed, my dear, dear Handel, it must not be. I wish you would talk about it now, as far as a few friendly words go, with me."
"I will," I said.
"In this branch house of ours, Handel, we must have a —"
I saw that his delicacy was avoiding the right word, so I said, "A clerk."
"A clerk. And I hope it is not at all unlikely that he may grow — as a clerk of your acquaintance has grown — into a partner. Now, Handel — in short, my dear boy, will you come to me?"

There was something charmingly warm and engaging in the way that, after saying "Now, Handel" as if it were the solemn beginning of some grand business speech, he had suddenly given up that tone, stretched out his honest hand, and spoken like a schoolboy.

"Clara and I have talked about it again and again," Herbert continued, "and the dear little thing begged me only this evening, with tears in her eyes, to say to you that if you will live with us when we are together, she will do her best to make you happy, and to convince her husband's friend that he is her friend too. We should get on so well, Handel!"

I thanked her warmly and I thanked him warmly, but said I could not yet be sure of joining him as he so kindly offered. Firstly, my mind was too preoccupied to take in the subject clearly. Secondly — yes! Secondly, there was a vague something lingering in my thoughts that will come out very near the end of this brief story.
"But if you thought, Herbert, that you could, without any harm to your business, leave the question open for a little while —"
"For any length of time," cried Herbert. "Six months, a year!"
"Not so long as that," I said. "Two or three months at most."
Herbert was delighted when we shook hands on this arrangement, and said he could now find the courage to tell me that he believed he must go at the end of the week.
"And Clara?" I said.
"The dear little thing," returned Herbert, "stays dutifully by her father as long as he lasts. But he won't last long. Mrs. Whimple confides to me that he is certainly failing."
"Not to say an unkind thing," I said, "he cannot do better than go."

"I'm afraid that must be admitted," said Herbert. "And then I shall come back for the dear little thing, and the dear little thing and I will walk quietly into the nearest church. Remember! The blessed darling comes of no family, my dear Handel, and never looked into the peerage, and hasn't a notion about her grandfather. What a fortune for the son of my mother!"

On the Saturday of that same week, I said goodbye to Herbert — full of bright hope, but sad and sorry to leave me — as he climbed onto one of the seaport mail coaches. I went into a coffee-house to write a little note to Clara, telling her he had gone, sending his love to her over and over again, and then went to my lonely home — if it deserved the name, for it was now no home to me, and I had no home anywhere.

On the stairs I met Wemmick, who was coming down after an unsuccessful knocking at my door. I had not seen him alone since the disastrous outcome of the attempted escape, and he had come, in his private and personal capacity, to say a few words of explanation about that failure.

"The late Compeyson," said Wemmick, "had by little and little got to the bottom of half the regular business we transacted. And it was from the talk of some of his associates in trouble — some of his people being always in trouble — that I heard what I did. I kept my ears open, appearing to have them shut, until I heard that he was away, and I thought that would be the best time for making the attempt. I can only suppose now that it was part of his cunning, as a very clever man, to routinely deceive his own agents. You don't blame me, I hope, Mr. Pip? I am sure I tried to serve you with all my heart."
"I am as sure of that, Wemmick, as you can be, and I thank you most sincerely for all your interest and friendship."

"Thank you, thank you very much. It's a bad business," said Wemmick, scratching his head, "and I assure you I haven't been so upset for a long time. What I look at is the sacrifice of so much portable property. Dear me!"
"What I think of, Wemmick, is the poor owner of the property."

"Yes, to be sure," said Wemmick. "Of course there can be no objection to your being sorry for him, and I'd put down a five-pound note myself to get him out of it. But what I look at is this. The late Compeyson, having got ahead of him in intelligence of his return and being so determined to bring him to justice, I do not think he could have been saved. Whereas the portable property certainly could have been saved. That's the difference between the property and the owner, don't you see?"

I invited Wemmick to come upstairs and have a glass of grog before walking to Walworth. He accepted. While he was drinking his moderate share, he said, with nothing to lead up to it, and after seeming rather restless —
"What do you think of my taking a holiday on Monday, Mr. Pip?"
"Why, I suppose you haven't done such a thing these twelve months."
"These twelve years, more likely," said Wemmick. "Yes. I'm going to take a holiday. More than that, I'm going to take a walk. More than that, I'm going to ask you to take a walk with me."
I was about to beg off, being poor company just then, when Wemmick anticipated me.

"I know your commitments," he said, "and I know you're out of sorts, Mr. Pip. But if you could oblige me, I should take it as a kindness. It isn't a long walk, and it's an early one. Say it might occupy you — including breakfast on the walk — from eight to twelve. Couldn't you stretch a point and manage it?"

He had done so much for me at various times that this was very little to do for him. I said I could manage it — would manage it — and he was so very much pleased by my agreement that I was pleased too. At his particular request, I arranged to call for him at the Castle at half past eight on Monday morning, and so we parted for the time.

Punctual to my appointment, I rang at the Castle gate on Monday morning and was received by Wemmick himself, who struck me as looking smarter than usual and wearing a sleeker hat. Inside, there were two glasses of rum and milk prepared, and two biscuits. The Aged must have been stirring with the dawn, for, glancing into his bedroom, I saw that his bed was empty.

When we had fortified ourselves with the rum and milk and biscuits, and were setting out for the walk with that preparation in us, I was considerably surprised to see Wemmick pick up a fishing-rod and put it over his shoulder. "Why, we're not going fishing!" I said. "No," returned Wemmick, "but I like to walk with one."
I thought this odd, but said nothing, and we set off. We walked toward Camberwell Green, and when we were in that neighbourhood, Wemmick said suddenly —
"Hullo! Here's a church!"
There was nothing very surprising in that, but I was rather surprised again when he said, as if struck by a brilliant idea —
"Let's go in!"
We went in, Wemmick leaving his fishing-rod in the porch, and looked all around. Meanwhile, Wemmick was diving into his coat-pockets and getting something out of paper there.
"Hullo!" he said. "Here's a couple of pairs of gloves! Let's put them on!"

As the gloves were white kid gloves, and as the post-office was widened to its fullest extent, I now began to have strong suspicions. They were confirmed to certainty when I beheld the Aged enter at a side door, escorting a lady.
"Hullo!" said Wemmick. "Here's Miss Skiffins! Let's have a wedding."

That discreet lady was dressed as usual, except that she was now replacing her green kid gloves with a pair of white. The Aged was likewise occupied in preparing a similar sacrifice to the altar of marriage. The old gentleman, however, had such difficulty getting his gloves on that Wemmick found it necessary to stand him with his back against a pillar and then get behind the pillar himself and pull, while I for my part held the old gentleman round the waist so he could push back with equal and safe resistance. By means of this ingenious scheme, his gloves were got on to perfection.

The clerk and clergyman then appearing, we were arranged in order at the altar rail. True to his pretence of doing it all without preparation, I heard Wemmick say to himself as he took something out of his waistcoat pocket before the service began, "Hullo! Here's a ring!"

I acted as best man to the bridegroom, while a little limp pew-opener in a soft bonnet like a baby's pretended to be the close friend of Miss Skiffins. The responsibility of giving the lady away fell upon the Aged, which led to the clergyman being unintentionally offended, and it happened this way. When he said, "Who giveth this woman to be married to this man?" the old gentleman, not in the least knowing what stage of the ceremony we had reached, stood most amiably beaming at the Ten Commandments. The clergyman said again, "WHO giveth this woman to be married to this man?" The old gentleman being still in a state of most admirable obliviousness, the bridegroom cried out in his usual voice, "Now, Aged P., you know! Who giveth?" To which the Aged replied with great energy, before saying that he did, "All right, John, all right, my boy!" And the clergyman fell into so grim a pause that I had doubts for a moment whether we should get completely married that day.

It was completely done, however, and when we were going out of church, Wemmick took the cover off the font, put his white gloves in it, and put the cover on again. Mrs. Wemmick, more mindful of the future, put her white gloves in her pocket and put on her green ones. "Now, Mr. Pip," said Wemmick, triumphantly shouldering the fishing-rod as we came out, "let me ask you whether anybody would suppose this to be a wedding-party!"

Breakfast had been ordered at a pleasant little tavern, a mile or so away on the rising ground beyond the green. There was a bagatelle board in the room, in case we should wish to relax after the ceremony. It was pleasant to observe that Mrs. Wemmick no longer removed Wemmick's arm when it settled around her figure, but sat in a high-backed chair against the wall, like a cello in its case, and submitted to being embraced as that melodious instrument might have done.

We had an excellent breakfast, and whenever anyone declined anything on the table, Wemmick said, "Provided by contract, you know — don't be afraid of it!" I drank to the new couple, drank to the Aged, drank to the Castle, kissed the bride on parting, and made myself as agreeable as I could.
Wemmick came down to the door with me, and I shook hands with him again and wished him joy.

"Thanks!" said Wemmick, rubbing his hands. "She's such a manager of poultry, you have no idea. You shall have some eggs and judge for yourself. I say, Mr. Pip!" calling me back, and speaking low. "This is altogether a Walworth sentiment, please."
"I understand. Not to be mentioned in Little Britain," I said.
Wemmick nodded. "After what you let slip the other day, Mr. Jaggers may as well not know of it. He might think my brain was softening, or something of the kind."

chapters.title: Chapter 56
paragraphs: He lay in prison very ill during the whole interval between his committal for trial and the coming of the Sessions. He had broken two ribs, they had injured one of his lungs, and he breathed with great pain and difficulty, which worsened daily. As a result of his injuries, he spoke so quietly as to be barely audible, and therefore he spoke very little. But he was always ready to listen to me, and it became the first duty of my life to say to him, and read to him, what I knew he ought to hear.

Being far too ill to remain in the common prison, he was moved after the first day or so into the infirmary. This gave me opportunities of being with him that I could not otherwise have had. And but for his illness he would have been put in irons, for he was regarded as a determined prison-breaker, and I know not what else.

Although I saw him every day, it was only for a short time. So the regularly recurring gaps between our visits were long enough to register on his face any slight changes in his physical state. I do not recall that I ever saw any change for the better. He wasted, and became slowly weaker and worse, day by day, from the day the prison door closed upon him.

The kind of submission or resignation he showed was that of a man who was tired out. I sometimes gathered, from his manner or from a whispered word or two that escaped him, that he pondered whether he might have been a better man under better circumstances. But he never justified himself by the slightest hint in that direction, or tried to bend the past out of its eternal shape.

It happened on two or three occasions in my presence that his desperate reputation was mentioned by someone attending him. A smile crossed his face then, and he turned his eyes on me with a trusting look, as if he were confident that I had seen some small redeeming quality in him, even as long ago as when I was a little child. As for all the rest, he was humble and contrite, and I never knew him complain.

When the Sessions came round, Mr. Jaggers applied for the postponement of his trial until the following Sessions. It was clearly made with the understanding that he could not live so long, and was refused. The trial came on immediately, and when he was brought to the dock, he was seated in a chair. No objection was made to my standing close to the outside of the dock, holding the hand that he stretched out to me.

The trial was very short and very clear. Such things as could be said for him were said — how he had adopted honest habits and had prospered lawfully and respectably. But nothing could undo the fact that he had returned and was there before the Judge and Jury. It was impossible to try him for that and do anything but find him guilty.

At that time, it was the custom — as I learned from my terrible experience of that Sessions — to devote a final day to passing sentences, and to make a dramatic climax with the Sentence of Death. But for the indelible picture that my memory now holds before me, I could scarcely believe, even as I write these words, that I saw thirty-two men and women brought before the Judge to receive that sentence together. Foremost among the thirty-two was he, seated so that he might get breath enough to keep life in him.

The whole scene starts out again in the vivid colours of the moment, down to the drops of April rain on the windows of the court, glittering in the rays of April sun. Penned in the dock, as I again stood outside it at the corner with his hand in mine, were the thirty-two men and women: some defiant, some stricken with terror, some sobbing and weeping, some covering their faces, some staring gloomily about. There had been shrieks from among the women convicts, but they had been hushed, and a silence had followed. The sheriffs with their great chains and nosegays, other civic regalia and officials, criers, ushers, a great gallery full of people — a large theatrical audience — looked on as the thirty-two and the Judge were solemnly confronted. Then the Judge addressed them. Among the wretched creatures before him whom he must single out for special address was one who almost from infancy had been an offender against the laws; who, after repeated imprisonments and punishments, had at length been sentenced to transportation for a term of years; and who, under circumstances of great violence and daring, had escaped and been re-sentenced to transportation for life. That miserable man would seem for a time to have become convinced of his errors, when far removed from the scenes of his old offences, and to have lived a peaceable and honest life. But in a fatal moment, yielding to those impulses and passions, the indulgence of which had so long made him a scourge to society, he had left his haven of rest and repentance and had come back to the country that had banished him. Being presently denounced, he had for a time succeeded in evading the officers of justice, but being at length seized while in the act of flight, he had resisted them, and had — he best knew whether by deliberate design, or in the blindness of his recklessness — caused the death of his denouncer, to whom his whole career was known. The appointed punishment for his return to the land that had cast him out being Death, and his case being this aggravated case, he must prepare himself to die.

The sun was striking in at the great windows of the court through the glittering drops of rain upon the glass, and it made a broad shaft of light between the thirty-two and the Judge, linking both together and perhaps reminding some in the audience how both were passing on, with absolute equality, to the greater Judgment that knows all things and cannot err. Rising for a moment, a distinct speck of face in this way of light, the prisoner said, "My Lord, I have received my sentence of Death from the Almighty, but I bow to yours," and sat down again. There was some hushing, and the Judge went on with what he had to say to the rest. Then they were all formally condemned, and some were supported out, and some sauntered out with a strained look of bravery, and a few nodded to the gallery, and two or three shook hands, and others went out chewing fragments of herbs they had taken from the sweet herbs lying about. He went last of all, because he had to be helped from his chair and could only go very slowly. He held my hand while all the others were removed, and while the audience got up — adjusting their clothes as they might at church or anywhere else — and pointed down at this criminal or that, and most of all at him and me.

I earnestly hoped and prayed that he might die before the official report was made. But dreading that he might linger on, I began that night to write a petition to the Home Secretary, setting out my knowledge of him and how it was that he had come back for my sake. I wrote it as passionately and movingly as I could, and when I had finished and sent it in, I wrote other petitions to such men in authority as I hoped were the most merciful, and drew up one to the Crown itself. For several days and nights after he was sentenced, I took no rest except when I fell asleep in my chair, but was wholly absorbed in these appeals. And after I had sent them in, I could not keep away from the places where they were, feeling as if they were more hopeful and less desperate when I was near them. In this irrational restlessness and anguish I would roam the streets of an evening, wandering past those offices and houses where I had left the petitions. To this day, the weary western streets of London on a cold, dusty spring night, with their rows of stern, shuttered mansions and their long rows of lamps, are melancholy to me from this association.

The daily visits I could make him were shortened now, and he was more strictly guarded. Seeing — or imagining — that I was suspected of intending to bring him poison, I asked to be searched before I sat down at his bedside, and told the officer who was always there that I was willing to do anything to reassure him of my innocent intentions. Nobody was harsh with him or with me. There was duty to be done, and it was done, but not harshly. The officer always gave me the report that he was worse, and some other sick prisoners in the room, and some other prisoners who attended them as nurses — criminals, but not incapable of kindness, God be thanked — always confirmed it.

As the days went on, I noticed more and more that he would lie quietly looking at the white ceiling, with an absence of light in his face until some word of mine brightened it for an instant, and then it would fade again. Sometimes he was almost or quite unable to speak, and then he would answer me with slight pressures of my hand, and I came to understand his meaning very well.
The number of the days had risen to ten when I saw a greater change in him than I had yet seen. His eyes were turned toward the door and lit up as I entered.
"Dear boy," he said, as I sat down by his bed. "I thought you was late. But I knew you couldn't be that."
"It is just the time," I said. "I waited for it at the gate."
"You always wait at the gate, don't you, dear boy?"
"Yes. Not to lose a moment of the time."
"Thank you, dear boy, thank you. God bless you! You've never deserted me, dear boy."
I pressed his hand in silence, for I could not forget that I had once meant to desert him.
"And what's the best of all," he said, "you've been more comfortable with me since I was under a dark cloud than when the sun shone. That's best of all."
He lay on his back, breathing with great difficulty. Do what he would, and love me though he did, the light left his face again and again, and a film came over the peaceful look at the white ceiling.
"Are you in much pain today?"
"I don't complain of any, dear boy."
"You never do complain."

He had spoken his last words. He smiled, and I understood his touch to mean that he wished to lift my hand and lay it on his breast. I laid it there, and he smiled again and placed both his hands upon it.

The allotted time ran out while we were like this, but looking round, I found the governor of the prison standing near me, and he whispered, "You needn't go yet." I thanked him gratefully and asked, "Might I speak to him, if he can hear me?"

The governor stepped aside and waved the officer away. The change, though it was made without noise, drew back the film from the peaceful look at the white ceiling, and he looked at me with the greatest affection.
"Dear Magwitch, I must tell you now, at last. You understand what I say?"
A gentle pressure on my hand.
"You had a child once, whom you loved and lost."
A stronger pressure on my hand.
"She lived, and found powerful friends. She is living now. She is a lady and very beautiful. And I love her!"

With a last faint effort, which would have been powerless but for my yielding to it and helping it, he raised my hand to his lips. Then he gently let it sink upon his breast again, with his own hands lying on it. The peaceful look at the white ceiling came back, and passed away, and his head dropped quietly on his breast.

Mindful then of what we had read together, I thought of the two men who went up into the Temple to pray, and I knew there were no better words I could say beside his bed than "O Lord, be merciful to him, a sinner!"

chapters.title: Chapter 57
paragraphs: Now that I was left entirely on my own, I gave notice that I intended to leave my chambers in the Temple as soon as my lease would legally allow, and to sublet them in the meantime. I immediately put bills in the windows, because I was in debt with barely any money, and was becoming seriously alarmed by my financial situation. I should really say I would have been alarmed, if I had possessed enough energy and focus to clearly grasp any truth beyond the fact that I was falling very ill. The recent strain had allowed me to postpone my illness, but not to prevent it. I knew it was coming now, and I knew very little else, and was even indifferent about that.

For a day or two, I lay on the sofa, or on the floor—wherever I happened to collapse—with a heavy head and aching limbs, and no purpose, and no strength. Then came a night that seemed to last forever, teeming with anxiety and horror. When morning came and I tried to sit up in bed and think about it, I found I could not.

Whether I had really been down in Garden Court in the dead of night, groping about for the boat I believed was there; whether I had come to myself two or three times on the staircase in great terror, not knowing how I had gotten out of bed; whether I had found myself lighting the lamp, possessed by the idea that he was coming up the stairs and the lights had been blown out; whether I had been tormented beyond words by someone's confused talking, laughing, and groaning, and had half suspected those sounds were of my own making; whether there had been a sealed iron furnace in a dark corner of the room, and a voice had called out again and again that Miss Havisham was burning inside it—these were things I tried to sort out and put into some order as I lay in bed that morning. But the fumes of a limekiln kept drifting between me and those memories, disordering them all, and it was through that haze that I finally saw two men looking at me.
"What do you want?" I asked, startled. "I don't know you."
"Well, sir," one of them replied, bending down and touching me on the shoulder, "this is a matter you'll soon sort out, I expect, but you're under arrest."
"What is the debt?"
"A hundred and twenty-three pounds, fifteen and six. Jeweler's account, I believe."
"What is to be done?"
"You'd better come to my house," said the man. "I keep a very nice house."
I made some attempt to get up and dress myself. When I next noticed them, they were standing a little back from the bed, watching me. I still lay there.
"You can see the state I'm in," I said. "I would come with you if I could, but I truly am unable. If you take me from here, I think I'll die on the way."

Perhaps they replied, or argued the point, or tried to convince me I was better than I thought. Since they hang in my memory by only this one slender thread, I don't know what they did, except that they chose not to move me.

That I had a fever and was shunned, that I suffered terribly, that I often lost my reason, that the time seemed endless, that I confused impossible existences with my own identity—that I was a brick in the wall of a house, yet begging to be freed from the dizzying height where the builders had placed me; that I was a steel beam in some vast engine, crashing and spinning over a chasm, yet pleading to have the engine stopped and my part in it hammered off—that I passed through these stages of illness, I know from my own memory, and knew in some vague way at the time. That I sometimes struggled with real people, believing they were murderers, and would suddenly understand they meant me well, and then sink exhausted into their arms and let them lay me down—this too I knew at the time. But above all, I knew there was a constant tendency in all these people—who, when I was very ill, would take on every kind of extraordinary transformation of the human face, and would swell to enormous size—above all, I say, I knew there was an extraordinary tendency in all of them, sooner or later, to settle down into the likeness of Joe.

After I had passed the worst point of my illness, I began to notice that while all its other features changed, this one constant feature did not. Whoever came near me still settled down into Joe. I opened my eyes in the night, and there in the great chair at the bedside sat Joe. I opened my eyes in the day, and sitting on the window seat, smoking his pipe by the shaded open window, there was Joe. I asked for a cool drink, and the dear hand that brought it was Joe's. I sank back on my pillow after drinking, and the face that looked so hopefully and tenderly at me was Joe's.
At last, one day, I gathered my courage and said, "Is it Joe?"
And the dear old familiar voice answered, "Which it air, old chap."
"Oh Joe, you break my heart! Look angry at me, Joe. Strike me, Joe. Tell me how ungrateful I've been. Don't be so good to me!"
For Joe had actually laid his head down on the pillow beside mine, and put his arm around my neck, in his joy that I knew him.
"Which dear old Pip, old chap," said Joe, "you and me was ever friends. And when you're well enough to go out for a ride—what larks!"

After which, Joe went to the window and stood with his back to me, wiping his eyes. And as my extreme weakness prevented me from getting up and going to him, I lay there, penitently whispering, "Oh God bless him! Oh God bless this gentle Christian man!"
Joe's eyes were red when I next found him beside me, but I was holding his hand, and we both felt happy.
"How long, dear Joe?"
"Which you meantersay, Pip, how long have your illness lasted, dear old chap?"
"Yes, Joe."
"It's the end of May, Pip. Tomorrow is the first of June."
"And have you been here all that time, dear Joe?"

"Pretty nigh, old chap. For, as I says to Biddy when the news of your being ill were brought by letter, which it were brought by the post, and being formerly single he is now married though underpaid for a deal of walking and shoe-leather, but wealth were not a object on his part, and marriage were the great wish of his hart—"
"It's so wonderful to hear you, Joe! But I interrupted what you were saying to Biddy."

"Which it were," said Joe, "that how you might be amongst strangers, and that how you and me having been ever friends, a wisit at such a moment might not prove unacceptabobble. And Biddy, her word were, 'Go to him, without loss of time.' That," said Joe, summing up with his judicial air, "were the word of Biddy. 'Go to him,' Biddy say, 'without loss of time.' In short, I shouldn't greatly deceive you," Joe added, after a little grave reflection, "if I represented to you that the word of that young woman were, 'without a minute's loss of time.'"

There Joe cut himself short and told me that I was to be spoken to only in great moderation, and that I was to take a little nourishment at regular intervals, whether I felt like it or not, and that I was to submit to all his orders. So I kissed his hand and lay quiet, while he set about writing a note to Biddy, with my love in it.

Evidently Biddy had taught Joe to write. As I lay in bed watching him, it made me, in my weak state, cry again with pleasure to see the pride with which he tackled his letter. My bed, stripped of its curtains, had been moved with me on it into the sitting room, as the airiest and largest room, and the carpet had been taken up, and the room kept always fresh and clean night and day. At my own writing table, pushed into a corner and cluttered with little bottles, Joe now sat down to his great work. First he selected a pen from the pen tray as if it were a chest of large tools, and rolled up his sleeves as if he were about to wield a crowbar or sledgehammer. It was necessary for Joe to press down heavily on the table with his left elbow and to get his right leg well out behind him before he could begin. When he did begin, he made every downstroke so slowly that it might have been six feet long, while at every upstroke I could hear his pen sputtering wildly. He had a curious idea that the inkstand was on the opposite side from where it actually was, and constantly dipped his pen into empty air, seeming quite satisfied with the result. Occasionally he was tripped up by some spelling obstacle, but on the whole he got on very well indeed. When he had signed his name and transferred a finishing blot from the paper to the crown of his head with two fingers, he got up and hovered about the table, studying his work from various angles with unbounded satisfaction.
Not wanting to tire Joe by talking too much, even if I had been able to, I put off asking him about Miss Havisham until the next day. He shook his head when I asked.
"Is she dead, Joe?"
"Why you see, old chap," said Joe, in a tone of gentle protest, easing into the subject by degrees, "I wouldn't go so far as to say that, for that's a deal to say; but she ain't—"
"Living, Joe?"
"That's nigher where it is," said Joe. "She ain't living."
"Did she linger long, Joe?"
"Arter you was took ill, pretty much about what you might call (if you was put to it) a week," said Joe, still determined, for my sake, to approach everything by degrees.
"Dear Joe, have you heard what became of her property?"

"Well, old chap," said Joe, "it do appear that she had settled the most of it, which I meantersay tied it up, on Miss Estella. But she had wrote out a little coddleshell in her own hand a day or two afore the accident, leaving a cool four thousand to Mr. Matthew Pocket. And why, do you suppose, above all things, Pip, she left that cool four thousand unto him? 'Because of Pip's account of him, the said Matthew.' I am told by Biddy, that air the writing," said Joe, repeating the legal turn as if it gave him infinite pleasure, "'account of him the said Matthew.' And a cool four thousand, Pip!"

I never discovered where Joe got the idea that the four thousand pounds should be described as "cool," but it appeared to make the sum more impressive to him, and he took obvious relish in insisting on it.
This news gave me great joy, as it completed the only good thing I had done. I asked Joe whether he had heard if any of the other relatives had received any legacies.

"Miss Sarah," said Joe, "she have twenty-five pound per annum fur to buy pills, on account of being bilious. Miss Georgiana, she have twenty pound down. Mrs.—what's the name of them wild beasts with humps, old chap?"
"Camels?" I said, wondering why he could possibly want to know.
Joe nodded. "Mrs. Camels," by which I soon understood he meant Camilla, "she have five pound fur to buy rushlights to put her in spirits when she wake up in the night."

The accuracy of these accounts was obvious enough to give me great confidence in Joe's information. "And now," said Joe, "you ain't that strong yet, old chap, that you can take in more nor one additional shovelful today. Old Orlick he's been a bustin' open a dwelling-house."
"Whose?" I said.

"Not, I grant you, but what his manners is given to blusterous," said Joe, apologetically. "Still, a Englishman's ouse is his Castle, and castles must not be busted 'cept when done in war time. And wotsume'er the failings on his part, he were a corn and seedsman in his hart."
"Is it Pumblechook's house that was broken into, then?"

"That's it, Pip," said Joe. "And they took his till, and they took his cash-box, and they drinked his wine, and they partook of his wittles, and they slapped his face, and they pulled his nose, and they tied him up to his bedpust, and they giv' him a dozen, and they stuffed his mouth full of flowering annuals to prewent his crying out. But he knowed Orlick, and Orlick's in the county jail."

Through these gradual conversations we arrived at unrestricted talk. I was slow to gain strength, but I did slowly and surely become less weak, and Joe stayed with me, and I felt as though I were little Pip again.

For the tenderness of Joe was so perfectly matched to my need that I was like a child in his hands. He would sit and talk to me with the old trust, and the old simplicity, and the old quiet, protective way, so that I could half believe that all my life since the days of the old kitchen had been one of the feverish delusions now gone. He did everything for me except the household work, for which he had hired a respectable woman, after dismissing the laundress on his first arrival. "Which I do assure you, Pip," he would often say by way of explanation, "I found her a-tapping the spare bed, like a cask of beer, and drawing off the feathers in a bucket, for sale. Which she would have tapped yourn next, and drawn it off with you a-laying on it, and was then a-carrying away the coals gradiwally in the soup tureen and vegetable dishes, and the wine and spirits in your Wellington boots."

We looked forward to the day when I would be well enough to go out for a ride, just as we had once looked forward to the day of my apprenticeship. And when the day came and an open carriage was brought into the lane, Joe wrapped me up, took me in his arms, carried me down to it, and settled me in, as if I were still the small helpless creature to whom he had so generously given the wealth of his great nature.

And Joe got in beside me, and we drove away together into the country, where the rich summer growth was already on the trees and the grass, and sweet summer scents filled the air. The day happened to be Sunday, and when I looked at the loveliness around me and thought how it had been growing and changing—how the little wildflowers had been forming, and the voices of the birds had been strengthening, by day and by night, under the sun and under the stars, while poor I lay burning and tossing in my bed—the mere memory of having burned and tossed there came as a check upon my peace. But when I heard the Sunday bells and looked around a little more upon that spread of beauty, I felt that I was not nearly thankful enough—that I was too weak even for that—and I laid my head on Joe's shoulder, as I had done long ago when he took me to the Fair, and it was too much for my young senses.

Greater composure came to me after a while, and we talked as we used to talk, lying on the grass at the old Battery. There was no change in Joe. Exactly what he had been in my eyes then, he was in my eyes now—just as simply faithful, and as simply right.

When we got back and he lifted me out and carried me—so easily!—across the court and up the stairs, I thought of that eventful Christmas Day when he had carried me over the marshes. We had not yet made any mention of my change of fortune, nor did I know how much of my recent history he was aware of. I was so doubtful of myself now, and placed so much trust in him, that I could not decide whether I ought to raise the subject when he did not.
"Have you heard, Joe," I asked him that evening, upon further reflection, as he smoked his pipe by the window, "who my patron was?"
"I heerd," Joe replied, "as it were not Miss Havisham, old chap."
"Did you hear who it was, Joe?"
"Well! I heerd as it were a person what sent the person what giv' you the bank-notes at the Jolly Bargemen, Pip."
"So it was."
"Astonishing!" said Joe, in the most placid way.
"Did you hear that he was dead, Joe?" I asked presently, with growing hesitation.
"Which? Him as sent the bank-notes, Pip?"
"Yes."
"I think," said Joe, after meditating for a long time and looking rather evasively at the window seat, "as I did hear tell that how he were something or another in a general way in that direction."
"Did you hear anything about his circumstances, Joe?"
"Not partickler, Pip."
"If you would like to hear, Joe—" I was beginning, when Joe got up and came to my sofa.
"Lookee here, old chap," said Joe, bending over me. "Ever the best of friends; ain't us, Pip?"
I was ashamed to answer him.

"Wery good, then," said Joe, as if I had answered. "That's all right; that's agreed upon. Then why go into subjects, old chap, which as betwixt two sech must be for ever onnecessary? There's subjects enough as betwixt two sech, without onnecessary ones. Lord! To think of your poor sister and her Rampages! And don't you remember Tickler?"
"I do indeed, Joe."

"Lookee here, old chap," said Joe. "I done what I could to keep you and Tickler in sunders, but my power were not always fully equal to my inclinations. For when your poor sister had a mind to drop into you, it were not so much," said Joe, in his favorite way of reasoning, "that she dropped into me too, if I put myself in opposition to her, but that she dropped into you always heavier for it. I noticed that. It ain't a grab at a man's whisker, not yet a shake or two of a man (to which your sister were quite welcome), that 'ud put a man off from getting a little child out of punishment. But when that little child is dropped into heavier for that grab of whisker or shaking, then that man naterally up and says to himself, 'Where is the good as I am a-doing? I grant you I see the 'arm,' says the man, 'but I don't see the good. I call upon you, sir, theerfore, to pint out the good.'"
"The man says?" I observed, as Joe waited for me to speak.
"The man says," Joe agreed. "Is he right, that man?"
"Dear Joe, he is always right."

"Well, old chap," said Joe, "then abide by your words. If he's always right (which in general he's more likely wrong), he's right when he says this: Supposing ever you kep any little matter to yourself, when you was a little child, you kep it mostly because you know'd as J. Gargery's power to part you and Tickler in sunders were not fully equal to his inclinations. Theerfore, think no more of it as betwixt two sech, and do not let us pass remarks upon onnecessary subjects. Biddy giv' herself a deal o' trouble with me afore I left (for I am almost awful dull), as I should view it in this light, and, viewing it in this light, as I should so put it. Both of which," said Joe, quite charmed with his own judicial acuteness, "being done, now this to you a true friend, say. Namely. You mustn't go a overdoing on it, but you must have your supper and your rest. Old chap!"

The delicacy with which Joe dismissed this subject, and the sweet tact and kindness with which Biddy—who with her woman's insight had understood me so soon—had prepared him for it, made a deep impression on me. But whether Joe knew how poor I was, and how my great expectations had all dissolved, like our own marsh mists before the sun, I could not tell.

Another thing about Joe that I could not understand when it first began, but which I soon came to comprehend with sorrow, was this: as I became stronger and better, Joe became a little less easy with me. In my weakness and total dependence on him, the dear fellow had fallen into the old tone and called me by the old names—the dear "old Pip, old chap" that now were music to my ears. I too had fallen into the old ways, only happy and thankful that he allowed it. But gradually, though I held fast to them, Joe's hold on them began to loosen. And whereas I wondered at this at first, I soon began to understand that the cause was in me, and that the fault was all mine.
Had I given Joe no reason to doubt my loyalty, and to think that as I grew stronger his hold on me would weaken, and that he had better loosen it in time and let me go, before I pulled myself away?

It was on the third or fourth occasion of my going out walking in the Temple Gardens, leaning on Joe's arm, that I noticed this change in him very clearly. We had been sitting in the bright warm sunlight, looking at the river, and I happened to say as we stood up:
"See, Joe! I can walk quite strongly. Now you shall see me walk back by myself."
"Which do not overdo it, Pip," said Joe, "but I shall be happy fur to see you able, sir."
That last word stung me, but how could I protest? I walked no further than the garden gate, then pretended to be weaker than I was and asked Joe for his arm. Joe gave it, but was thoughtful.

I, for my part, was thoughtful too. How best to stop this growing change in Joe was a great puzzle to my remorseful mind. I was ashamed to tell him exactly how things stood with me and what I had come down to—I don't try to hide that—but I hope my reluctance was not entirely unworthy. He would want to help me out of his small savings, I knew, and I knew he ought not to, and that I must not let him.

It was a thoughtful evening for both of us. But before we went to bed, I had resolved to wait through tomorrow—tomorrow being Sunday—and to begin my new course with the new week. On Monday morning I would speak to Joe about this change. I would cast aside this last trace of reserve. I would tell him what I had been thinking (that "Secondly," not yet fully formed), and why I had not yet decided to go out to Herbert. Then the change would be conquered forever. As I brightened, Joe brightened too, and it seemed as though he had arrived at a resolution of his own.
We had a quiet day on Sunday, and we rode out into the country, and then walked in the fields.
"I feel thankful that I've been ill, Joe," I said.
"Dear old Pip, old chap, you're a'most come round, sir."
"It has been a memorable time for me, Joe."
"Likeways for myself, sir," Joe returned.
"We have had a time together, Joe, that I can never forget. There were days once, I know, when I did forget for a while; but I never shall forget these."
"Pip," said Joe, looking a little hurried and troubled, "there has been larks. And, dear sir, what have been betwixt us—have been."
At night, when I had gone to bed, Joe came into my room, as he had done all through my recovery. He asked if I was sure I felt as well as I had in the morning.
"Yes, dear Joe, quite."
"And are always a getting stronger, old chap?"
"Yes, dear Joe, steadily."
Joe patted the covers on my shoulder with his great good hand and said, in what I thought was a husky voice, "Good night!"

When I got up in the morning, refreshed and stronger still, I was full of my resolution to tell Joe everything, without delay. I would tell him before breakfast. I would dress at once and go to his room and surprise him, for it was the first day I had been up early. I went to his room, and he was not there. Not only was he not there, but his bag was gone.
I hurried to the breakfast table, and on it found a letter. These were its brief contents:
"Not wishful to intrude I have departured fur you are well again dear Pip and will do better without
JO.
"P.S. Ever the best of friends."

Enclosed in the letter was a receipt for the debt and costs on which I had been arrested. Until that moment, I had assumed my creditor had withdrawn or suspended proceedings until I recovered. I had never dreamed that Joe had paid the money, but Joe had paid it, and the receipt was in his name.

What remained for me now but to follow him to the dear old forge, and there to make my full confession to him, and my penitent appeal, and there to unburden my mind and heart of that lingering "Secondly"—which had begun as a vague something in my thoughts and had hardened into a settled purpose?

The purpose was this: I would go to Biddy. I would show her how humbled and repentant I had come back. I would tell her how I had lost everything I once hoped for. I would remind her of our old confidences in my first unhappy time. Then I would say to her, "Biddy, I think you once liked me very well, when my restless heart, even while it strayed from you, was quieter and better with you than it has ever been since. If you can like me only half as well once more, if you can take me with all my faults and disappointments, if you can receive me like a forgiven child (and indeed I am as sorry, Biddy, and have as much need of a soothing voice and a gentle hand), I hope I am a little worthier of you than I was—not much, but a little. And, Biddy, it shall rest with you to say whether I shall work at the forge with Joe, or whether I shall try for some different occupation in this part of the country, or whether we shall go away to a distant place where an opportunity awaits me that I set aside when it was offered, until I knew your answer. And now, dear Biddy, if you can tell me that you will go through the world with me, you will surely make it a better world for me, and me a better man for it, and I will try hard to make it a better world for you."
Such was my purpose. After three more days of recovery, I went down to the old place to carry it out. And how I fared is all I have left to tell.

chapters.title: Chapter 58
paragraphs: The news of my high fortunes having taken a heavy fall had reached my native place and its neighborhood before I did. I found the Blue Boar already in possession of the story, and I found that it made a great change in the Boar's manner. Where the Boar had cultivated my good opinion with eager devotion when I was coming into property, the Boar was exceedingly cool on the subject now that I was going out of it.

It was evening when I arrived, thoroughly worn out by the journey I had so often made so easily. The Boar could not put me in my usual bedroom, which was taken (probably by someone who had expectations), and could only give me a very poor room among the pigeons and carriages up in the yard. But I slept as soundly in that lodging as in the best room the Boar could have offered, and the quality of my dreams was about the same.

Early in the morning, while my breakfast was being prepared, I strolled over to Satis House. There were printed notices on the gate and on bits of carpet hanging from the windows, announcing an auction sale of the Household Furniture and Effects the following week. The house itself was to be sold as old building materials and pulled down. LOT 1 was marked in whitewashed, knock-kneed letters on the brewhouse; LOT 2 on the part of the main building that had been shut up so long. Other lots were marked on other parts of the structure, and the ivy had been torn down to make room for the inscriptions, much of it trailing low in the dust, already withered. Stepping in for a moment at the open gate and looking around with the uncomfortable air of a stranger who had no business there, I saw the auctioneer's clerk walking on the casks and counting them off for a man with a pen and catalogue, who had made a temporary desk of the wheeled chair I had so often pushed along to the tune of Old Clem.

When I got back to my breakfast in the Boar's coffee room, I found Mr. Pumblechook talking with the landlord. Mr. Pumblechook (not improved in appearance by his recent nighttime adventure) was waiting for me, and addressed me in the following terms:
"Young man, I am sorry to see you brought low. But what else could be expected! What else could be expected!"
As he extended his hand with a magnificently forgiving air, and as I was broken by illness and in no state to quarrel, I took it.
"William," said Mr. Pumblechook to the waiter, "put a muffin on the table. And has it come to this! Has it come to this!"
I sat down to my breakfast with a frown. Mr. Pumblechook stood over me and poured out my tea—before I could touch the teapot—with the air of a benefactor determined to be true to the last.

"William," said Mr. Pumblechook mournfully, "put the salt on. In happier times," he said, turning to me, "I think you took sugar? And did you take milk? You did. Sugar and milk. William, bring a watercress."
"Thank you," I said shortly, "but I don't eat watercress."

"You don't eat 'em," returned Mr. Pumblechook, sighing and nodding his head several times, as if he might have expected that, and as if not eating watercress were entirely consistent with my downfall. "True. The simple fruits of the earth. No. You needn't bring any, William."
I went on with my breakfast, and Mr. Pumblechook continued to stand over me, staring fishily and breathing noisily, as he always did.

"Little more than skin and bone!" mused Mr. Pumblechook aloud. "And yet when he went from here (I may say with my blessing), and I spread before him my humble store, like the Bee, he was as plump as a Peach!"

This reminded me of the striking difference between the servile way he had offered his hand in the days of my new prosperity, saying, "May I?" and the showy generosity with which he had just now extended those same fat five fingers.
"Hah!" he went on, handing me the bread and butter. "And are you going to Joseph?"
"In heaven's name," I said, flaring up in spite of myself, "what does it matter to you where I'm going? Leave that teapot alone."
It was the worst thing I could have done, because it gave Pumblechook exactly the opportunity he wanted.

"Yes, young man," he said, releasing the teapot handle, stepping back from my table, and speaking for the benefit of the landlord and waiter at the door. "I will leave that teapot alone. You are right, young man. For once you are right. I forget myself when I take such an interest in your breakfast as to wish your frame, exhausted by the debilitating effects of prodigality, to be stimulated by the wholesome nourishment of your forefathers. And yet," said Pumblechook, turning to the landlord and waiter and pointing me out at arm's length, "this is him as I ever sported with in his days of happy infancy! Tell me not it cannot be; I tell you this is him!"
A low murmur from the two replied. The waiter appeared to be particularly affected.

"This is him," said Pumblechook, "as I have rode in my shay-cart. This is him as I have seen brought up by hand. This is him untoe the sister of which I was uncle by marriage, as her name was Georgiana M'ria from her own mother, let him deny it if he can!"
The waiter seemed convinced that I could not deny it, and that it gave the case a black look.

"Young man," said Pumblechook, screwing his head at me in the old way, "you are going to Joseph. What does it matter to me, you ask me, where you are going? I say to you, Sir, you are going to Joseph."
The waiter coughed, as if he modestly invited me to get past that point.

"Now," said Pumblechook, with the most infuriating air of stating what was perfectly convincing and conclusive in the cause of virtue, "I will tell you what to say to Joseph. Here is Squires of the Boar present, known and respected in this town, and here is William, whose father's name was Potkins if I do not deceive myself."
"You do not, sir," said William.

"In their presence," Pumblechook continued, "I will tell you, young man, what to say to Joseph. Says you, 'Joseph, I have this day seen my earliest benefactor and the founder of my fortunes. I will name no names, Joseph, but so they are pleased to call him up town, and I have seen that man.'"
"I swear I don't see him here," I said.
"Say that likewise," retorted Pumblechook. "Say you said that, and even Joseph will probably betray surprise."
"There you quite mistake him," I said. "I know better."

"Says you," Pumblechook went on, "'Joseph, I have seen that man, and that man bears you no malice and bears me no malice. He knows your character, Joseph, and is well acquainted with your pig-headedness and ignorance; and he knows my character, Joseph, and he knows my want of gratitude. Yes, Joseph,' says you"—here Pumblechook shook his head and finger at me—"'he knows my total deficiency of common human gratitude. He knows it, Joseph, as none can. You do not know it, Joseph, having no call to know it, but that man do.'"
Windy donkey that he was, it truly amazed me that he could have the nerve to talk this way to my face.

"Says you, 'Joseph, he gave me a little message, which I will now repeat. It was that, in my being brought low, he saw the finger of Providence. He knowed that finger when he saw it, Joseph, and he saw it plain. It pointed out this writing, Joseph. Reward of ingratitude to his earliest benefactor, and founder of fortunes. But that man said he did not repent of what he had done, Joseph. Not at all. It was right to do it, it was kind to do it, it was benevolent to do it, and he would do it again.'"
"It's a pity," I said scornfully, as I finished my interrupted breakfast, "that the man didn't say what he had done and would do again."

"Squires of the Boar!" Pumblechook was now addressing the landlord. "And William! I have no objections to your mentioning, either up town or down town, if such should be your wishes, that it was right to do it, kind to do it, benevolent to do it, and that I would do it again."

With those words the Impostor shook them both by the hand, with an air, and left the house—leaving me far more astonished than impressed by the virtues of that same indefinite "it." I was not long after him in leaving too, and when I went down the High Street I saw him holding forth (no doubt to the same effect) at his shop door to a select group, who honored me with very unfavorable glances as I passed on the opposite side of the street.

But it was only the more pleasant to turn to Biddy and to Joe, whose great forbearance shone even more brightly than before, if that were possible, contrasted with this brazen pretender. I walked toward them slowly, for my legs were weak, but with a growing sense of relief as I drew nearer, and a sense of leaving arrogance and dishonesty further and further behind.

The June weather was glorious. The sky was blue, the larks were soaring high over the green corn, and I thought the countryside more beautiful and peaceful by far than I had ever known it. Many pleasant pictures of the life I would lead there, and of the change for the better that would come over my character when I had a guiding spirit at my side whose simple faith and clear home wisdom I had proven, brightened my way. They stirred a tender emotion in me, for my heart was softened by my return, and such a change had taken place that I felt like someone toiling home barefoot from distant travels, whose wanderings had lasted many years.

The schoolhouse where Biddy was mistress I had never seen, but the little roundabout lane by which I entered the village for quietness' sake took me past it. I was disappointed to find that the day was a holiday. No children were there, and Biddy's house was closed. I had cherished some hopeful notion of seeing her busily at her daily work before she saw me, and that was defeated.

But the forge was only a short distance off, and I went toward it under the sweet green limes, listening for the clink of Joe's hammer. Long after I should have heard it, and long after I fancied I heard it and found it was only my imagination, all was still. The lime trees were there, and the white thorns were there, and the chestnut trees were there, and their leaves rustled harmoniously when I stopped to listen—but the clink of Joe's hammer was not in the midsummer wind.

Almost afraid, without knowing why, to come in view of the forge, I saw it at last and saw that it was closed. No glow of fire, no glittering shower of sparks, no roar of bellows. All shut up, and still.

But the house was not deserted, and the best parlor seemed to be in use, for there were white curtains fluttering in its window, and the window was open and bright with flowers. I walked softly toward it, meaning to peep over the flowers, when Joe and Biddy stood before me, arm in arm.

At first Biddy gave a cry, as if she thought I was a ghost, but the next moment she was in my arms. I wept to see her, and she wept to see me—I, because she looked so fresh and lovely; she, because I looked so worn and pale.
"But dear Biddy, how beautiful you look!"
"Yes, dear Pip."
"And Joe, how fine you look!"
"Yes, dear old Pip, old chap."
I looked at both of them, from one to the other, and then—
"It's my wedding day!" cried Biddy, in a burst of happiness. "And I am married to Joe!"

They had taken me into the kitchen, and I had laid my head down on the old deal table. Biddy held one of my hands to her lips, and Joe's comforting touch was on my shoulder. "Which he warn't strong enough, my dear, fur to be surprised," said Joe. And Biddy said, "I ought to have thought of it, dear Joe, but I was too happy." They were both so overjoyed to see me, so proud to see me, so touched by my coming, so delighted that I should have arrived by chance to make their day complete!

My first thought was one of deep thankfulness that I had never breathed this last defeated hope to Joe. How often, while he was with me in my illness, had it risen to my lips! How irrevocable his knowledge of it would have been, if he had stayed with me only one more hour!
"Dear Biddy," I said, "you have the best husband in the whole world, and if you could have seen him by my bed you would have—But no, you couldn't love him better than you do."
"No, I couldn't indeed," said Biddy.
"And, dear Joe, you have the best wife in the whole world, and she will make you as happy as even you deserve to be, you dear, good, noble Joe!"
Joe looked at me with a quivering lip, and put his sleeve before his eyes.

"And Joe and Biddy both, as you have been to church today and are in charity and love with all mankind, accept my humble thanks for all you have done for me, and all I have so poorly repaid! And when I say that I am going away within the hour, for I am soon going abroad, and that I shall never rest until I have worked for the money with which you kept me out of prison, and have sent it to you, don't think, dear Joe and Biddy, that if I could repay it a thousand times over, I imagine I could cancel a farthing of the debt I owe you, or that I would do so if I could!"
They were both moved to tears by these words, and both begged me to say no more.

"But I must say more. Dear Joe, I hope you will have children to love, and that some little fellow will sit in this chimney corner on a winter night who may remind you of another little fellow gone out of it forever. Don't tell him, Joe, that I was thankless; don't tell him, Biddy, that I was selfish and unjust; only tell him that I honored you both, because you were both so good and true, and that, as your child, I said it would be natural for him to grow up a much better man than I did."
"I ain't a-going," said Joe, from behind his sleeve, "to tell him nothink o' that natur, Pip. Nor Biddy ain't. Nor yet no one ain't."

"And now, though I know you have already done it in your own kind hearts, please tell me, both of you, that you forgive me! Please let me hear you say the words, so that I may carry the sound of them away with me, and then I shall be able to believe that you can trust me and think better of me in the time to come!"
"O dear old Pip, old chap," said Joe. "God knows as I forgive you, if I have anythink to forgive!"
"Amen! And God knows I do!" echoed Biddy.

"Now let me go up and look at my old little room, and rest there a few minutes by myself. And then, when I have eaten and drunk with you, walk with me as far as the finger-post, dear Joe and Biddy, before we say goodbye!"

I sold everything I had and set aside as much as I could to settle with my creditors—who gave me ample time to pay in full—and I went out and joined Herbert. Within a month I had left England, and within two months I was a clerk at Clarriker and Co., and within four months I had taken on my first independent responsibility. For the beam across the parlor ceiling at Mill Pond Bank had ceased to tremble under old Bill Barley's growls and was at peace, and Herbert had gone away to marry Clara, and I was left in sole charge of the Eastern Branch until he brought her back.

Many a year passed before I became a partner in the firm, but I lived happily with Herbert and his wife, and lived frugally, and paid my debts, and kept up a constant correspondence with Biddy and Joe. It was not until I became third in the firm that Clarriker revealed my secret to Herbert; but he then declared that the secret of Herbert's partnership had been on his conscience long enough, and he must tell it. So he told it, and Herbert was as much moved as amazed, and the dear fellow and I were no worse friends for the long concealment. I should not leave it to be supposed that we were ever a great house, or that we made fortunes. We were not in a grand way of business, but we had a good name, and worked for our profits, and did very well. We owed so much to Herbert's ever-cheerful industry and readiness that I often wondered how I had ever conceived that old idea of his ineptitude, until I was enlightened one day by the reflection that perhaps the ineptitude had never been in him at all, but had been in me.

chapters.title: Chapter 59
paragraphs: For eleven years I had not seen Joe or Biddy with my own eyes—though they had both appeared often in my imagination in the East—when, on an evening in December, an hour or two after dark, I softly laid my hand on the latch of the old kitchen door. I touched it so gently that I was not heard, and looked in unseen. There, smoking his pipe in the old place by the kitchen firelight, as hale and strong as ever though a little grey, sat Joe. And there, fenced into the corner by Joe's leg, and sitting on my own little stool looking at the fire, was—I again!

"We giv' him the name of Pip for your sake, dear old chap," said Joe, delighted, when I took another stool by the child's side (but I did not rumple his hair), "and we hoped he might grow a little bit like you, and we think he do."

I thought so too, and I took him out for a walk the next morning, and we talked endlessly, understanding each other perfectly. And I took him down to the churchyard and set him on a certain tombstone, and he showed me from that height which stone was sacred to the memory of Philip Pirrip, late of this Parish, and Also Georgiana, Wife of the Above.
"Biddy," I said, when I spoke with her after dinner, as her little girl lay sleeping in her lap, "you must give Pip to me one of these days; or lend him, at the very least."
"No, no," said Biddy, gently. "You must marry."
"So Herbert and Clara say, but I don't think I shall, Biddy. I have so settled into their home that it's really not likely. I am already quite an old bachelor."

Biddy looked down at her child, and put its little hand to her lips, and then placed the good motherly hand with which she had touched it into mine. There was something in the gesture, and in the light pressure of Biddy's wedding ring, that had a very eloquent meaning.
"Dear Pip," said Biddy, "you are sure you don't grieve for her?"
"Oh no—I think not, Biddy."
"Tell me as an old, old friend. Have you quite forgotten her?"

"My dear Biddy, I have forgotten nothing in my life that ever held a foremost place there, and little that ever held any place there. But that poor dream, as I once used to call it, has all gone by, Biddy—all gone by!"
Nevertheless, I knew, while I said those words, that I secretly intended to revisit the site of the old house that evening, alone, for her sake. Yes, even so. For Estella's sake.

I had heard of her as leading a most unhappy life, and as being separated from her husband, who had used her with great cruelty and who had become quite notorious as a combination of pride, greed, brutality, and meanness. And I had heard of the death of her husband, from an accident caused by his mistreatment of a horse. This release had come to her some two years before; for all I knew, she was married again.

The early dinner hour at Joe's left me plenty of time, without cutting short my conversation with Biddy, to walk over to the old spot before dark. But what with lingering on the way to look at old landmarks and to think of old times, the day had quite faded when I reached the place.

There was no house now, no brewery, no building of any kind, but the wall of the old garden. The cleared space had been enclosed with a rough fence, and looking over it, I saw that some of the old ivy had taken root again and was growing green on low, quiet mounds of ruin. A gate in the fence stood ajar, and I pushed it open and went in.

A cold silvery mist had veiled the afternoon, and the moon was not yet up to scatter it. But the stars were shining beyond the mist, and the moon was coming, and the evening was not dark. I could trace where every part of the old house had stood, and where the brewery had been, and where the gates, and where the casks. I had done so, and was looking along the desolate garden path, when I saw a solitary figure.

The figure became aware of me as I approached. It had been moving toward me, but it stopped. As I drew nearer, I saw it was a woman. As I drew nearer still, she was about to turn away, when she paused and let me come up to her. Then she faltered, as if much surprised, and spoke my name, and I cried out—
"Estella!"
"I am greatly changed. I wonder you know me."

The freshness of her beauty was indeed gone, but its indescribable majesty and its indescribable charm remained. Those qualities I had seen before. What I had never seen before was the saddened, softened light in the once proud eyes. What I had never felt before was the friendly touch of the once unfeeling hand.
We sat down on a bench nearby, and I said, "After so many years, it is strange that we should meet again here, Estella, where we first met! Do you often come back?"
"I have never been here since."
"Nor I."

The moon began to rise, and I thought of the peaceful look on the white ceiling, which had passed away. The moon began to rise, and I thought of the pressure on my hand when I had spoken the last words he ever heard on earth.
Estella was the next to break the silence that fell between us.
"I have very often hoped and intended to come back, but have been prevented by many things. Poor, poor old place!"

The silvery mist was touched with the first rays of moonlight, and the same rays touched the tears that fell from her eyes. Not knowing that I saw them, and steadying herself to overcome them, she said quietly—
"Were you wondering, as you walked along, how it came to be left in this state?"
"Yes, Estella."

"The ground belongs to me. It is the only possession I have not given up. Everything else has gone from me, little by little, but I have kept this. It was the subject of the only determined resistance I made in all the wretched years."
"Is it to be built on?"
"At last, it is. I came here to say goodbye to it before it changes. And you," she said, in a voice of touching interest to a wanderer, "you live abroad still?"
"Still."
"And do well, I am sure?"
"I work fairly hard for a decent living, and therefore—yes, I do well."
"I have often thought of you," said Estella.
"Have you?"

"Of late, very often. There was a long, hard time when I kept far from me the memory of what I had thrown away when I was entirely ignorant of its worth. But since my duty has not been incompatible with admitting that memory, I have given it a place in my heart."
"You have always held your place in my heart," I answered.
And we were silent again until she spoke.
"I little thought," said Estella, "that I should take leave of you in taking leave of this place. I am very glad to do so."
"Glad to part again, Estella? To me, parting is a painful thing. To me, the memory of our last parting has been forever mournful and painful."

"But you said to me," returned Estella, very earnestly, "'God bless you, God forgive you!' And if you could say that to me then, you will not hesitate to say it to me now—now, when suffering has been stronger than all other teaching, and has taught me to understand what your heart used to be. I have been bent and broken, but—I hope—into a better shape. Be as considerate and good to me as you were, and tell me we are friends."
"We are friends," I said, rising and bending over her as she rose from the bench.
"And will continue friends apart," said Estella.

I took her hand in mine, and we went out of the ruined place; and, as the morning mists had risen long ago when I first left the forge, so the evening mists were rising now, and in all the broad expanse of tranquil light they showed to me, I saw no shadow of another parting from her.
